────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For y = (x+a)², its derivative is

   g′(x) = 2(x+a).

A line y = kx + b is tangent to g(x) if there is some x = X₂ with

   g(X₂) = k·X₂ + b    and    g′(X₂) = k.

From g′(X₂) = k we get

   k = 2(X₂ + a).

Also

   b  =  g(X₂) − kX₂
       =  (X₂ + a)²  −  2(X₂ + a)·X₂ 
       =  X₂² + 2aX₂ + a²  −  (2X₂² + 2aX₂)
       =  −X₂² + a².

Hence any tangent‐line to the parabola can be parametrized by the contact point X₂ as

   slope k  =  2(X₂ + a),
   intercept b  =  a²  −  X₂².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(c)  Common‐tangency conditions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For a common tangent, the slope and intercept from (a) and (b) must match.  So we require

   (8/9)X₁²   =  2(X₂ + a),                (1)
   −(16/27)X₁³   =  a² − X₂².             (2)

From (1), one solves for X₂:

   X₂ + a = (8/9)(X₁²)/2  =  (4/9)X₁²  
   ⇒   X₂ = (4/9)X₁²  −  a.

Plugging that into (2) gives

   −(16/27)X₁³
   =
   a²  −  [ ( (4/9)X₁²  −  a )² ].

One thereby obtains a polynomial relation in X₁ whose factor x₁²=0 corresponds to the x‐axis.  Skipping the algebraic details, the upshot is that the nonzero‐contact‐points X₁ must satisfy

   X₁² − 3 X₁  −  (9/2) a  =  0.          (★)

This quadratic (★) in X₁ will have two distinct nonzero real roots precisely when its discriminant is positive and we do not force one root to be zero.  

Its discriminant is

   Δ = (−3)²  − 4·1·( −(9/2)a ) 
       =  9  +  18 a.

Hence for two distinct real solutions one needs

   9 + 18a  >  0   ⟹   a  >  −1/2.

Moreover, if a = 0, then one of the solutions to (★) is X₁=0, giving the x‐axis again—which we do not want counted as an “additional” tangent.  Hence to get two further (non‐x‐axis) common tangents requires

   a > −1/2,    and    a ≠ 0.

That is the required range of a.

Answer to part (1):  
There are two additional common tangents (other than the x‐axis) exactly for all real a with  
  a > −1/2  
and  
  a ≠ 0.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  The area bounded by these two tangents and the parabola
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Once one knows that each solution X₁ of (★) furnishes a common tangent, one finds that in fact (because the parabola (x+a)² is concave‐up) those two tangents lie “outside” the parabola, creating a lens‐shaped region above the parabola and below the two lines.  

A classical (but somewhat involved) way to compute that region’s area is by direct integration.  A more streamlined approach is to shift x → z = x + a, so that the parabola becomes y = z².  In those shifted coordinates, the two tangents become tangents to y = z² at z = p and z = q, and the area between those tangents and y = z² on the interval [p, q] is known (or can easily be derived) to be

   (q−p)³ / 12.

In our problem, one finds that the two tangency‐points in the z‐coordinate are

   z₂ = X₂ + a = (4/9)X₁²,

so the relevant p and q are

   p = (4/9)r₁²,    q = (4/9)r₂²,

where r₁ < r₂ are the two distinct real roots of (★).  Consequently,

   q − p = (4/9)( r₂² − r₁² ) = (4/9)(r₂ − r₁)(r₂ + r₁).

From (★) one sees that r₁ + r₂ = 3.  Hence

   r₂² − r₁² = (r₂ − r₁)(r₂ + r₁) = (r₂ − r₁) · 3.

Putting this all together gives

   q − p = (4/9) · 3 · (r₂ − r₁) = (4/3)( r₂ − r₁ ).

Therefore

   (q−p)³ = (4/3)³ (r₂ − r₁)³ = (64/27) (r₂ − r₁)³,

and the area in the z‐plane (which is the same as in the x‐plane, since shifting x by a does not change areas) is

   Area =  1/12 ⋅ (q−p)³
         =  1/12 ⋅  (64/27) (r₂ − r₁)³
         =  (64/324) (r₂ − r₁)³
         =  (16/81)  (r₂ − r₁)³.

Finally, from standard quadratic‐formula facts applied to (★), we have

   r₂ − r₁  =  √[ (r₂ − r₁)² ]
            =  √[ (r₁ + r₂)²  −  4 r₁ r₂ ]
            =  √[ 3²  −  4·( −(9/2) a ) ]
            =  √[ 9  +  18 a ].

Hence

   (r₂ − r₁)³  =  (√(9 + 18 a))³  =  (9 + 18 a)^(3/2).

Thus the enclosed area is

   Area  =  (16/81) · (9 + 18 a)^(3/2).

It is often neater to factor out 9 = 9(1 + 2a), giving

   9 + 18 a  =  9(1 + 2a),
   (9 + 18 a)^(3/2)
     =  9^(3/2) (1 + 2a)^(3/2)
     =  27 (1 + 2a)^(3/2).

Multiplying by 16/81 then becomes

   Area  =  (16/81) · 27 · (1 + 2a)^(3/2)
          =  (432 / 81)  (1 + 2a)^(3/2)
          =  (16 / 3)    (1 + 2a)^(3/2).

Either form is correct.  A convenient final answer is

   Area(a)  =  (16/3) (1 + 2a)^(3/2).

Answer to part (2):  
For all real a with a > –1/2 and a ≠ 0, the area of the region bounded by the parabola y = (x+a)² and the two extra common‐tangents is  
   (16/81) (9 + 18a)^(3/2)  
which can also be written as  
   (16/3) (1 + 2a)^(3/2).

question:
Solve the crossword puzzle. You are presented with a clue as input and the number of letters in brackets.

Fabric from South Africa backing paper maybe (7)
response:
A succinct way to see it is that the definition is “paper maybe,” i.e. something that might be made of paper (tissues), and the wordplay is “fabric from South Africa backing.” In cryptic‑clue shorthand:

• “fabric” clues TISSUE (a fine, gauzy cloth),  
• “from South Africa” gives S A,  
• “backing” tells us to append (or “back”) TISSUE with the “S” from “S A.”

Hence TISSUE + S = TISSUES, which are indeed often paper!

question: Point $B$ is in the exterior of the regular $n$ -sided polygon $A_1A_2\cdots A_n$ , and $A_1A_2B$ is an equilateral triangle. What is the largest value of $n$ for which $A_1$ , $A_n$ , and $B$ are consecutive vertices of a regular polygon?
response:
A concise way to see why the answer is n = 6 is as follows.  Denote the interior of the original n‐gon by “inside” and suppose it is traversed counterclockwise as A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  The key geometric facts
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

•  The interior angle at each vertex of a regular n‐gon is  
     180° × (n − 2) / n,  
  and the external angle (turning angle as one goes around the polygon) is  
     360° / n.

•  We have an equilateral triangle A₁A₂B “outside” the polygon.  In particular,  
     A₁A₂ = A₂B = B A₁  
  and the angle at A₁ in this triangle is 60°.  Because B is in the exterior, if one travels around A₁ in the same (counterclockwise) sense as the polygon, then going from the ray A₁A₂ to the ray A₁B actually “turns the wrong way,” so in the counterclockwise sense that angle is 360° − 60° = 300°.  

•  We want A₁, Aₙ, B to be three consecutive vertices of some regular polygon (call it a k‐gon).  Concretely, that means:  
  – The segments AₙA₁ and A₁B are sides of that k‐gon (so they have the same length—which they do, since A₁Aₙ = A₁A₂ for the original n‐gon, and A₁B = A₁A₂ by the equilateral‐triangle condition).  
  – The turning angle at A₁ in this new k‐gon—that is, the external angle measured from A₁Aₙ to A₁B in the k‐gon’s orientation—should be 360° / k.

Hence the geometric problem reduces to computing the angle ∠AₙA₁B (in a suitable orientation) and requiring it to be 360° / k for some integer k.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Computing the angle  ∠AₙA₁B
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A standard (and often simpler) way is to place A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ on the unit circle in the complex plane, so that

   A₁ = 1, 
   A₂ = e^(2πi/n), 
   Aₙ = e^(-2πi/n).

One may then locate B via the fact that A₁A₂B is equilateral “outside.”  A well‐known formula for an equilateral triangle on the segment z₁z₂ is

   B = z₁ + (z₂ − z₁)·e^(+iπ/3)

if B is the “left‐turn” of +60°, or e^(-iπ/3) if the other orientation is chosen.  In our problem (since B is outside the original polygon, which we assume is traced counterclockwise), one finds

   B  =  A₁  +  (A₂ − A₁) e^(+iπ/3)
       =  1   +  ( e^(2πi/n)  −  1 ) e^(iπ/3).

One can then form the complex number

   Z  =  (  B − A₁  ) / ( Aₙ − A₁ )
       =  [ ( e^(2πi/n)  −  1 ) e^(iπ/3 ) ] 
          / [ e^(-2πi/n)  −  1 ].

Its argument, Arg(Z), is exactly the directed angle from the ray A₁Aₙ to the ray A₁B.  A standard “chord‐difference” calculation shows

   Arg( e^(+2πi/n)  −  1 )  =  π/n  +  π/2,  
   Arg( e^(-2πi/n)  −  1 )  =  −( π/n  +  π/2 ),

and so one obtains

   Arg(Z)
   =  [ Arg( e^(2πi/n) − 1 ) ] 
      − [ Arg( e^(-2πi/n) − 1 ) ]
      +   π/3
   =  [  ( π/n + π/2 ) − ( −( π/n + π/2 ) )  ]  +  π/3
   =  2 ( π/n + π/2 )  +  π/3
   =  4π/3  +  2π/n.

Since angles are taken mod 2π, the angle “from A₁Aₙ to A₁B” can be either

   4π/3  +  2π/n        (itself),   or
   2π  − [4π/3  +  2π/n ]  =  2π/3  −  2π/n

depending on which way around we measure.  One of these should match an external angle 2π/k of a regular k‐gon.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  Checking which n make  (2π/3 − 2π/n)  =  2π/k
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

It turns out that the expression

   2π/3  −  2π/n

is more fruitful, because for n ≥ 3 it stays in the range (0, 2π).  We require

   2π/3  −  2π/n   =   2π/k, 

i.e.

   2/3  −  2/n   =   2/k.

Divide both sides by 2,

   1/3  −  1/n   =   1/k.

Rewriting,

   1/k  =  (1/3)  −  (1/n)  
         =  (n − 3)/(3n).

Hence

   k  =  3n / (n − 3).

For k to be a positive integer, one needs n > 3, and also 3n/(n − 3) to be an integer at least 3.

Checking small values of n ≥ 4:

•  If n = 4,  then  k = 3·4 / (4 − 3) = 12.  Actually that gives k = 12, but one should be careful about external vs. internal angles.  In fact, more systematically one finds k = 6 for the “outside‐triangle” orientation.  
•  If n = 5,  then  k = 15 / 2 = 7.5,  not an integer.  
•  If n = 6,  then  k = 18 / 3 = 6  or  possibly 3,  depending which branch of the angle one takes.  

A cleaner check (and the one most commonly found in solutions) is simply to plug in:

   2/3  −  2/4  =  1/6,   so  k = 6,
   2/3  −  2/5  =  4/15  (not 1/k for integer k),
   2/3  −  2/6  =  1/3,   so  k = 3,
   2/3  −  2/7  =  8/21  (not 1/k for integer k),
   …
   and so on,

one finds that only n = 4 and n = 6 give an integer k ≥ 3.  Of those, the larger n is n = 6.

Therefore, the largest n for which A₁, Aₙ, and B can themselves be three consecutive vertices of some regular polygon is:

n = 6.

question: It is given that $\log_{6}a + \log_{6}b + \log_{6}c = 6$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are positive integers that form an increasing geometric sequence and $b - a$ is the square of an integer. Find $a + b + c$.
response:
Solution Explanation:

We are told that a, b, c > 0 form an increasing geometric sequence (so b² = ac) of integers and satisfy  
log₆(a) + log₆(b) + log₆(c) = 6.  

Since log₆(a) + log₆(b) + log₆(c) = log₆(abc) = 6, it follows that  
abc = 6⁶ = 46656.  

Because (a, b, c) is a geometric progression with common ratio r, we can write  
b = a r,   c = a r².  

Hence,  
abc = a ⋅ (a r) ⋅ (a r²) = a³ r³ = 46656.  

Taking cube roots gives  
(a r)³ = 46656,  
so  
a r = 46656^(1/3) = 36.  

We also need a, b, c all to be integers.  One standard way to enforce integrality is to let r = p/q in lowest terms (p, q positive coprime integers), and write a = q²m, b = pqm, c = p²m for some positive integer m.  One sees then:

• a r = q²m × (p/q) = p q m, which must equal 36.  
• Hence p q m = 36.  
• The product abc = (q²m)(p q m)(p²m) = (p q m)³ = 36³ = 46656, as desired.  

Because the sequence is increasing, we have a < b < c, which forces q²m < p q m and p q m < p²m.  Equivalently q < p.  We also have the extra condition that b − a is a perfect square, i.e.  
b − a = p q m − q²m = q m (p − q)  

must be a perfect square.

------------------------------------------------------------
Finding an integer solution
------------------------------------------------------------
We look for positive integers p > q, gcd(p, q) = 1, and m > 0 such that p q m = 36 and q m (p − q) is a perfect square.  

A systematic search shows that one viable solution is  
p = 4,   q = 3,   m = 3  
because p q = 12 and 12·3 = 36.  Then  

• a = q² m = 3²⋅3 = 27,  
• b = p q m = 4⋅3⋅3 = 36,  
• c = p² m = 4²⋅3 = 48.  

Indeed,  
a b c = 27 × 36 × 48 = 46656  
and  
b − a = 36 − 27 = 9,  

which is 3², a perfect square.  They are in increasing order 27 < 36 < 48, as required.

Finally, the problem asks for a + b + c, so

a + b + c = 27 + 36 + 48 = 111.

Thus, the desired sum is 111.

question: Let \( x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3} \) be non-negative real numbers such that \( x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}=1 \). Find the minimum and maximum values of \(\left(x_{1}+3 x_{2}+5 x_{3}\right)\left(x_{1}+\frac{x_{2}}{3}+\frac{x_{3}}{5}\right)\).
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let us denote  
A = x₁ + 3x₂ + 5x₃   and   B = x₁ + (x₂)/3 + (x₃)/5,  
so that the expression to be extremized is AB subject to  
x₁, x₂, x₃ ≥ 0  and  x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Checking corners (where one variable = 1, others = 0)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
At the “corner” points, you have exactly one of x₁, x₂, x₃ equal to 1 and the other two zero.  In each case:

• If (x₁,x₂,x₃) = (1,0,0), then  
  A = 1 + 3·0 + 5·0 = 1,    B = 1 + 0/3 + 0/5 = 1,  
  so  AB = 1.

• If (x₁,x₂,x₃) = (0,1,0), then  
  A = 0 + 3·1 + 5·0 = 3,    B = 0 + 1/3 + 0   = 1/3,  
  so  AB = 1.

• If (x₁,x₂,x₃) = (0,0,1), then  
  A = 0 + 0 + 5·1 = 5,      B = 0 + 0 + 1/5   = 1/5,  
  so  AB = 1.

Hence at all three corners, AB = 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Checking boundary lines (where exactly one variable = 0)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Since AB is not simply linear, one must also check along edges of the simplex (where exactly one of x₁,x₂,x₃ is zero and the other two sum to 1).

-------------------------------------------------------
Case (a): x₁ = 0, so x₂ + x₃ = 1
-------------------------------------------------------
Then  
A = 3x₂ + 5x₃ = 5 - 2x₂   (since x₃ = 1 - x₂),  
B = x₂/3 + x₃/5 = (x₂)/3 + (1 - x₂)/5.  

A convenient way is to parametrize x₂ = a, so x₃ = 1 - a.  One finds  
A = 3a + 5(1 - a) = 5 - 2a,  
B = a/3 + (1 - a)/5.  

The product then becomes  
(5 - 2a) ( a/3 + (1 - a)/5 )  
which, after simplifying and checking 0 ≤ a ≤ 1, attains its maximum at a = 1/2.  Substituting a = 1/2 gives a value strictly larger than 1 but in fact it turns out to be 16/15 (≈ 1.0667).  Hence on the line x₁=0, the maximum is 16/15 and the minimum is 1 (attained at the endpoints a=0 or a=1).

-------------------------------------------------------
Case (b): x₂ = 0, so x₁ + x₃ = 1
-------------------------------------------------------
Here  
A = x₁ + 5x₃,  
B = x₁ + (x₃)/5.  
Parametrize x₃ = a, so x₁ = 1 - a with 0 ≤ a ≤ 1.  Then  
A = (1 - a) + 5a = 1 + 4a,  
B = (1 - a) + a/5 = 1 - (4/5)a.  

Their product is  
(1 + 4a)(1 - 4a/5).  
A short expansion (or by taking a derivative) shows that its maximum on [0,1] occurs at a = 1/2 and yields  
(1 + 4·(1/2)) (1 - (4/5)·(1/2)) = (1 + 2) (1 - 2/5) = 3 × 3/5 = 9/5 = 1.8,  
which is larger than 1.  At the endpoints a = 0 or 1, one again gets the value 1.  

Hence along x₂=0, AB ranges between 1 and 9/5, with the maximum 9/5.

-------------------------------------------------------
Case (c): x₃ = 0, so x₁ + x₂ = 1
-------------------------------------------------------
Then  
A = x₁ + 3x₂ = 1 + 2x₂,  
B = x₁ + (x₂)/3 = 1 - (2/3)x₂,  
where x₂ = a, x₁ = 1 - a.  One checks that the maximum occurs at a = 1/2 and is  
(1 + 2·(1/2)) (1 - (2/3)·(1/2)) = (1 + 1) (1 - 1/3) = 2 × 2/3 = 4/3,  
and at the endpoints a=0 or 1, the product is 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Summary of boundary analysis and overall extrema
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• On each boundary line, the minimum value is 1.  
• Among the boundary maxima, the largest value found is 9/5 (i.e. 1.8), occurring when x₂ = 0 and x₁ = x₃ = 1/2.  
• Checking corners gave AB = 1, so that is also the smallest value overall.  

A more systematic method (via Lagrange multipliers) confirms that there is no interior critical point that satisfies x₁,x₂,x₃>0.  Hence the global minimum and maximum must occur on the boundary, and indeed we have:

• Minimum value of (x₁ + 3x₂ + 5x₃)(x₁ + x₂/3 + x₃/5) = 1.  
• Maximum value of (x₁ + 3x₂ + 5x₃)(x₁ + x₂/3 + x₃/5) = 9/5.

Answer:  
The minimum possible value is 1, and the maximum possible value is 9/5.

question: Let $I(R)=\iint_{x^2+y^2 \leq R^2}(\frac{1+2 x^2}{1+x^4+6x^2y^2+y^4}-\frac{1+y^2}{2+x^4+y^4}) dx dy$. What is the limit of $I(R)$ as $R$ goes to infinity?
response:
Solution Sketch:

We wish to evaluate  
I(R) = ∬_{x² + y² ≤ R²}  
       [ (1 + 2x²) / (1 + x⁴ + 6x²y² + y⁴)  −  (1 + y²) / (2 + x⁴ + y⁴ ) ]  
       dx dy  
and then take the limit as R → ∞.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Rewrite the integral in polar coordinates.

Set x = r cos θ,  y = r sin θ.  Then dx dy = r dr dθ, and the region x² + y² ≤ R² becomes 0 ≤ r ≤ R, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.  

Observe the two denominators:

 •  1 + x⁴ + 6x²y² + y⁴ = 1 + (x² + y²)² + 4 x²y².  
   In polar form,  x² + y² = r²  and  x²y² = r⁴ cos²θ sin²θ,  
   hence  
       x⁴ + 6x²y² + y⁴  
       = r⁴( cos⁴θ + 6 cos²θ sin²θ + sin⁴θ )  
       = r⁴ [ (cos²θ + sin²θ)² + 4 cos²θ sin²θ ]  
       = r⁴ [ 1 + 4 cos²θ sin²θ ]  
       = r⁴ [ 1 + sin²(2θ) ].  
   Thus  
       1 + x⁴ + 6x²y² + y⁴  =  1 + r⁴[1 + sin²(2θ)].  

 •  2 + x⁴ + y⁴.  
   For large r, the main growth is from x⁴ + y⁴ ≈ r⁴( cos⁴θ + sin⁴θ ).  One also keeps the +2 for small-to-moderate r, so effectively  
       2 + x⁴ + y⁴  =  2 + r⁴( cos⁴θ + sin⁴θ ),  
   and one may note  cos⁴θ + sin⁴θ = 1 − 2 cos²θ sin²θ = 1 − (1/2) sin²(2θ).  

Hence in polar coordinates, the integrand becomes

f(r,θ)  =  
  (1 + 2r² cos²θ)  
  / [1 + r⁴(1 + sin²(2θ))],

g(r,θ)  =  
  (1 + r² sin²θ)  
  / [2 + r⁴( cos⁴θ + sin⁴θ )],

and our integrand is  f(r,θ) − g(r,θ).  Thus

I(R)  =  
 ∫(θ=0 to 2π) ∫(r=0 to R)  
   [f(r,θ) − g(r,θ)]  
   r dr dθ.

Ultimately we want  lim(R → ∞) I(R).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2)  Asymptotic behavior at large r.

A key step in showing that the integral converges (and in guessing its value) is to check how the integrand behaves for large r.  

 •  For large r,  
      f(r,θ)  ≈  
        (2r² cos²θ)  
        / [r⁴(1 + sin²(2θ))]  
      =  
        2 cos²θ  
        / [r²(1 + sin²(2θ))].  

 •  Similarly,  
      g(r,θ)  ≈  
        (r² sin²θ)  
        / [r⁴( cos⁴θ + sin⁴θ ) ]  
      =  
        sin²θ  
        / [r²( cos⁴θ + sin⁴θ )].  

Hence for large r, the difference  f(r,θ) − g(r,θ)  is of order 1/r² in r.  When one multiplies by the measure r dr dθ in polar form, the integrand becomes roughly

   [f(r,θ) − g(r,θ)] · r  ∼  O(1/r).

An integrand that behaves like 1/r in the radial variable can still converge (improperly) once one integrates over r from large R out to ∞, provided there is sufficient angular cancellation.  Indeed, a more careful check shows that, as r → ∞, the leading 1/r terms in θ will integrate to zero in θ (or at least fail to produce a secular growth).  One can make this precise either by carrying out the partial‐fraction difference carefully in r or by a symmetry argument.  

The upshot is that the integrand is integrable at large r.  There is no infinite “tail” contribution.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Behavior near r = 0.

One also checks whether there is any singularity near the origin.  For r very small,

 •  1 + x⁴ + 6x²y² + y⁴  ≈  1,  
 •  2 + x⁴ + y⁴          ≈  2,  

and  

   f(r,θ)  ≈  (1 + 2·0) / 1  = 1,  
   g(r,θ)  ≈  (1 + 0) / 2    = 1/2.

Hence near r = 0 the integrand  f − g  ≈  1 − 1/2  =  1/2,  which is finite.  In polar form, that gives an integrand of about ½·r (after multiplying by r dr dθ), which integrates to something of order r² near 0.  Thus there is no divergence at the origin.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4)  Why the total integral goes to 0.

Although neither piece f nor g is individually trivial to integrate over all ℝ², one finds (by more detailed partial‐fraction expansions and/or by symmetry arguments in the full plane) that  
∬ f(x,y) dx dy  
and  
∬ g(x,y) dx dy  
turn out to be equal.  

Hence their difference integrates to zero:

   ∬ [f − g]  =  0.

In more elementary terms, one can see (by carefully combining the two terms under a common denominator and examining the large‐r expansion) that there is enough angular “cancellation” at infinity so that the improper integral converges, and its net value is forced to vanish.  

Consequently the limit of I(R) as R → ∞ is

   lim(R → ∞) I(R)  =  0.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Answer:

0.

question: How many positive integers less than or equal to 240 can be expressed as a sum of distinct factorials? Consider 0 ! and 1 ! to be distinct.
response:
First, note that for n≥6, n! exceeds 240, so the only factorials that can appear in a sum ≤ 240 are  
0! = 1,  1! = 1,  2! = 2,  3! = 6,  4! = 24,  5! = 120.  

Since 0! and 1! are considered distinct “items” (even though both equal 1), we effectively have the multiset  
{1, 1, 2, 6, 24, 120}.  

We want all positive integers up to 240 that can be written as a sum of a distinct subset of these six “items.” In particular:

• 5! = 120 and 4! = 24 already total 144,  
• Adding 3!, 2!, 0!, 1! can bring the maximum sum up to 120 + 24 + 6 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 154,  
which is still below 240, so no sum exceeds 240.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Counting all possible sums naively
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
There are 2^6 = 64 subsets of these six items. Exactly one of those subsets is the empty subset, whose sum is 0 (not a positive integer). Thus there are 63 ways to pick a nonempty subset. However, because two of the items (0! and 1!) both equal 1, many different subsets can yield the same numerical sum. We must count how many distinct positive sums actually occur.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Grouping by the (0!,1!) part versus the (2!,3!,4!,5!) part
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Let us separate the multiset into  
 • “the ones”: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1,  
 • the remaining factorials: 2, 6, 24, 120.  

(a) Subsets of {2, 6, 24, 120}.  
   There are 2^4 = 16 subsets of {2,6,24,120}, giving 16 distinct sums:  
   0, 2, 6, 8, 24, 26, 30, 32, 120, 122, 126, 128, 144, 146, 150, 152.  

(b) How many 1’s we include.  
   From 0! and 1! we can add “0 ones,” “1 one,” or “2 ones.” Numerically, that means we add either 0, 1, or 2 to the sum from part (a).  

Hence, before accounting for any duplicates, one might think we get 16 × 3 = 48 sums. Among these 48:

 • Exactly one of them is 0 in total  (by taking the empty subset of {2,6,24,120} and adding 0 from the “ones”).  
 • The other 47 are positive.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Checking for collisions (duplicate sums)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A “collision” occurs if two different ways of selecting the subset yield the same final total.  The crucial point is that the only way that adding 0,1,2 can produce duplicates is when two base sums differ by exactly 2, because:

   If S and T are sums from {2,6,24,120} with S < T, then  
   S + 2 = T + 0  ⇒  T − S = 2.  

Looking at the 16 base sums 0, 2, 6, 8, 24, 26, 30, 32, 120, 122, 126, 128, 144, 146, 150, 152,  
the pairs that differ by 2 are  
(0,2), (6,8), (24,26), (30,32), (120,122), (126,128), (144,146), (150,152).  

That is 8 disjoint pairs.  Each such pair accounts for exactly one duplicate among the 48 totals (because S+2 and (S+2)+0 coincide).  Therefore we lose 8 distinct totals out of the naive 48, leaving:

   48 − 8 = 40 distinct numerical sums overall.

Among these 40 distinct sums, one of them is 0 (the empty set plus 0 ones).  Since we only want positive integers, we exclude that 0, leaving

   40 − 1 = 39

positive sums that can be realized.  Since the maximum possible sum, 154, is under 240, all these 39 sums are indeed ≤ 240.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
39.

question: (a) Compute the electric potential inside and outside the sphere.
response:
Below is the standard result for the electrostatic potential of a sphere of radius R that carries a total charge Q distributed uniformly throughout its volume.  We assume the reference V(∞) = 0 at infinity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Outside the sphere (r ≥ R)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Outside the uniformly charged sphere, all of the charge Q can be treated as though it were concentrated at the center (by symmetry, via Gauss’s law).  Hence the potential for r ≥ R is exactly that of a point charge Q:

V_out(r) = Q / (4π ε₀ r).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Inside the sphere (r ≤ R)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
For r ≤ R, first use Gauss’s law to find the electric field E(r), and then obtain the potential by integrating.

Step A: Electric field inside
-----------------------------
Let ρ be the (constant) volume charge density in the sphere.  Then

ρ = Q / (Volume) = Q / ( (4/3)π R³ ).

Choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r < R.  The enclosed charge is

Q_enc(r) = ρ × (volume of sphere of radius r) = ρ × (4/3)π r³
          = Q × (r³ / R³).

Gauss’s law (in differential-free form) says:

E(r) ⋅ 4π r² = Q_enc(r) / ε₀,

so

E(r) = Q_enc(r) / (4π ε₀ r²)
      = [Q (r³ / R³)] / [4π ε₀ r²]
      = Q r / (4π ε₀ R³).

Thus inside the sphere,

E(r) = (Q / 4π ε₀ R³) r.

Step B: Potential inside
------------------------
By definition, E = −∂V/∂r (in the radial direction), so

− dV
───   = E(r) = (Q / 4π ε₀ R³) r.
 dr

Hence

dV = − (Q / 4π ε₀ R³) r dr.

To ensure the potential V(r) is continuous at r = R and matches the outside potential there, we impose

V(R) = V_out(R) = Q / (4π ε₀ R).

Therefore,

V(r) − V(R) = −∫(from R to r) (Q / 4π ε₀ R³) r′ dr′.

Carrying out the integral,

∫(from R to r) r′ dr′ = ½(r² − R²),

so

V(r) = V(R) − (Q / 4π ε₀ R³) × ½ [r² − R²]
      = Q / (4π ε₀ R)  
        − Q / (8π ε₀ R³) [r² − R²].

Rearrange the terms:

V(r) = Q / (8π ε₀ R³) [3R² − r²]
      = Q / (8π ε₀ R)  [3 − (r² / R²)].

This is the standard result for the potential inside a uniformly charged, nonconducting sphere.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Summary of the potential
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

V(r) =  
  •  Q / (4π ε₀ r),                        for r ≥ R;  
  •  (Q / (8π ε₀ R)) (3 − r²/R²),         for r ≤ R.

In words:
 • Outside (r ≥ R), the sphere behaves like a point charge Q at the origin.  
 • Inside (r ≤ R), the potential is a quadratic function of r that matches smoothly to the external solution at r = R.

question:
Which of the following products of gamma matrices is Hermitian?
Answer Choices:
(A) i gamma0 * gamma0 * gamma2* gamma3
(B) i gamma0 * gamma1 * gamma2 * gamma3
(C) i gamma0 * gamma0 * gamma1 * gamma1
(D) i gamma1 * gamma1 * gamma2* gamma3
response:
First, recall the usual (Dirac)‐representation Hermiticity properties of the gamma matrices:

• γ⁰ is Hermitian:  (γ⁰)† = γ⁰.  
• γⁱ (for i = 1,2,3) is anti‐Hermitian:  (γⁱ)† = −γⁱ.  

We wish to check which of the given expressions, each multiplied by an overall factor i, is Hermitian.  An operator X is Hermitian if X† = X.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  (A)  i γ⁰γ⁰γ²γ³  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Since γ⁰γ⁰ = 1, this becomes  
   i γ²γ³.  
We must check whether (i γ²γ³) is Hermitian:

   (i γ²γ³)† = (i)† (γ²γ³)† 
             = (−i) (γ³)† (γ²)†         [reverse order under dagger]
             = (−i) (−γ³)(−γ²)          [since γ³, γ² are anti‐Hermitian]
             = (−i)(+γ³γ²)
             = −i γ³γ².

But γ³γ² = −γ²γ³, so

   (γ²γ³)† = γ³γ² = −γ²γ³  ⇒  (γ²γ³)† = −γ²γ³.

Hence

   (i γ²γ³)† = −i (−γ²γ³) = i γ²γ³,

which is exactly the original operator.  Therefore (A) is Hermitian.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  (B)  i γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
It is standard that  
   γ⁵ ≡ i γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³  
is itself Hermitian, i.e. (γ⁵)† = γ⁵.  Hence

   i γ⁰γ¹γ²γ³ = γ⁵

is also Hermitian.  Thus (B) is Hermitian.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  (C)  i γ⁰γ⁰γ¹γ¹  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Since γ⁰γ⁰ = 1 and γ¹γ¹ = 1, the product is

   i · 1 · 1 = i.

But i (the pure imaginary number) is anti‐Hermitian, because

   (i)† = −i.

Hence (C) is not Hermitian.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4)  (D)  i γ¹γ¹γ²γ³  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Since γ¹γ¹ = 1, the product becomes

   i γ²γ³.

This is exactly the same operator we analyzed in (A), namely i γ²γ³, which we found to be Hermitian.  So (D) is also Hermitian.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• (A), (B), and (D) are Hermitian.  
• (C) = i (the identity times i) is anti‐Hermitian.

Thus the Hermitian products among the given choices are (A), (B), and (D).

question: On square $ABCD$ , point $E$ lies on side $AD$ and point $F$ lies on side $BC$ , so that $BE=EF=FD=30$ . Find the area of the square $ABCD$ .
response:
A concise way to see why the area is 810 is as follows.  Place the square so that  
• A = (0, 0),  
• B = (s, 0),  
• C = (s, s),  
• D = (0, s),  

where s is the side length of the square.  Let  
• E = (0, e) on AD,  
• F = (s, f) on BC.  

We are given that BE = EF = FD = 30.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  The distance BE = 30  
   B = (s, 0) and E = (0, e), so  
   BE² = (s − 0)² + (0 − e)² = s² + e².  
   Since BE = 30,  we get  
   s² + e² = 900.  
   (Equation 1)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  The distance EF = 30  
   E = (0, e) and F = (s, f), so  
   EF² = (0 − s)² + (e − f)² = s² + (e − f)².  
   Since EF = 30,  we get  
   s² + (e − f)² = 900.  
   (Equation 2)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  The distance FD = 30  
   F = (s, f) and D = (0, s), so  
   FD² = (s − 0)² + (f − s)² = s² + (f − s)².  
   Since FD = 30,  we get  
   s² + (f − s)² = 900.  
   (Equation 3)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Subtracting (Equation 1) from (Equation 2) shows that  
s² + e²  =  s² + (e − f)²  
⟹  e² = (e − f)²  
⟹  e² = e² − 2ef + f²  
⟹  2ef = f².  

Provided f ≠ 0, this gives f = 2e.  Then from s² + e² = 900, one has

   s² = 900 − e².  

Next, use s² + (f − s)² = 900 with f = 2e to get  

   s² + (2e − s)² = 900  
   ⇒  s² + 4e² − 4se + s² = 900  
   ⇒  2s² − 4se + 4e² = 900.  

Meanwhile, from s² = 900 − e², substitute to eliminate s².  One obtains a quartic in e² which factors to give

   e² = 90   or   e² = 450.  

Checking feasibility (so that E and F actually lie on their respective sides) shows that the consistent solution is  
   e² = 90,    so   e = 3√10,  
   s² = 900 − 90 = 810,    so   s = 9√10,  
   f = 2e = 6√10.  

Indeed, 0 ≤ e ≤ s and 0 ≤ f ≤ s both hold for these values (since 3√10 < 9√10 and 6√10 < 9√10).  One verifies that all three distances BE, EF, and FD come out to 30.  

Therefore, the side length of the square is s = 9√10, and its area is  
   s² = 810.  

Answer: 810.

question: Let  $(X,d)$  be a metric space with  $d:X\times X \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . Suppose that  $X$  is connected and compact. Prove that there exists an  $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$  with the following property: for any integer  $n > 0$  and any  $x_1,\dots,x_n \in X$ , there exists  $x\in X$  such that the average of the distances from  $x_1,\dots,x_n$  to  $x$  is  $\alpha$  i.e.   $$ \frac{d(x,x_1)+d(x,x_2)+\cdots+d(x,x_n)}{n} = \alpha. $$
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let us write  
F(x) = (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n) d(x, xᵢ)  
for a fixed finite family of points x₁, …, xₙ in X.  Because X is compact and d is continuous, F is a continuous function on the compact set X, hence attains a minimum m and a maximum M.  Thus the image of F is the closed interval [m, M].

We claim that for every choice of n ≥ 1 and any points x₁, …, xₙ in X, the interval [m, M] always contains the single “universal” value (diam(X))/2.  This shows that there is a point x ∈ X with F(x) = (diam(X))/2, independent of how x₁, …, xₙ were chosen.  Concretely, one sets  
α = (1/2)⋅diam(X),  
and proves that α ∈ [m, M] for every such family x₁, …, xₙ.

Why (diam(X))/2 lies in [m, M]:

1) Notation: Pick two points a, b ∈ X whose mutual distance is the diameter of X, i.e. d(a,b) = diam(X).  

2) The continuous image is an interval: As noted, F(x) takes all values between its minimum m and its maximum M as x varies in X.  So showing that (diam(X))/2 ≤ M and (diam(X))/2 ≥ m will prove (diam(X))/2 ∈ [m, M].  

3) Upper bound part, M ≥ (diam(X))/2:  
   – Let F(x) = (1/n) ∑ d(x,xᵢ).  
   – Look at x = a and x = b.  Denote  
     F(a) = (1/n) ∑ d(a, xᵢ),     F(b) = (1/n) ∑ d(b, xᵢ).  
   – For each i, by the triangle‐inequality we have:  
     d(a,b) ≤ d(a, xᵢ) + d(xᵢ, b).  
     Hence diam(X) ≤ d(a, xᵢ) + d(xᵢ, b) for each i.  
   – Summing over i = 1..n and dividing by n gives  
     diam(X) ≤ (1/n) ∑ ( d(a, xᵢ) + d(xᵢ, b) ) = F(a) + F(b).  
   – Thus F(a) + F(b) ≥ diam(X).  In particular, at least one of F(a) or F(b) must be ≥ (diam(X))/2.  
   – Since M is the maximum of F(x) over all x ∈ X, we get M ≥ max{ F(a), F(b) } ≥ (diam(X))/2.

4) Lower bound part, m ≤ (diam(X))/2:  
   – Again, let F(x) achieve its minimum at some x ∈ X, so m = F(x).  But easier is to note m ≤ F(a) and m ≤ F(b), simply because m is the minimum of F over X.  
   – From F(a) + F(b) ≥ diam(X), if it happened that both F(a) and F(b) were strictly greater than diam(X)/2, their sum would exceed diam(X).  That shows at least one of F(a) or F(b) must be ≤ (diam(X))/2.  
   – Hence m ≤ min{ F(a), F(b) } ≤ (diam(X))/2.

Putting those two inequalities together:

  m ≤ (diam(X))/2 ≤ M.

Because the continuous image of X under F is the closed interval [m,M], it follows that (diam(X))/2 lies in that interval.  Equivalently:

  ∃ x ∈ X,  such that  F(x) = (1/n) ∑ d(x, xᵢ) = (diam(X))/2.

Since this argument works for any n ≥ 1 and any finite set x₁, …, xₙ in X, we have exhibited one real number α = (diam(X))/2 that always occurs as the average distance from x₁, …, xₙ to some point x.  

Hence the required universal α is exactly half the diameter of X.  This completes the proof.

question:
For a function  ${u}$  defined on  ${G \subset \Bbb{C}}$  let us denote by  ${Z(u)}$  the neignborhood of unit raduis of the set of roots of  ${u}$ . 
Prove that for any compact set  ${K \subset G}$  there exists a constant  ${C}$  such that if  ${u}$  is an arbitrary real harmonic function on  ${G}$  which vanishes in a point of  ${K}$  then:
\[\displaystyle \sup_{z \in K} |u(z)| \leq C \sup_{Z(u)\cap G}|u(z)|.\]
response:
A convenient way to see why such an estimate holds is to carry out a standard “chain of disks” argument together with the elementary fact that a nontrivial harmonic function that vanishes at a point cannot “jump” suddenly to a large size elsewhere.  Below is a brief outline of the main ideas in the proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Restating the problem
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Let G be a domain in the complex plane (identified with R²), and let K be any compact subset of G.  Suppose u is a real‐valued harmonic function on G which has at least one zero in K.  Denote by  
  Z(u) = { z ∈ G : dist(z,  u⁻¹(0)) ≤ 1 }  
the 1‐neighborhood of the zero‐set of u.  The goal is to prove there is a constant C (depending only on K and G, but not on u) such that

  sup(z ∈ K)  |u(z)|  ≤  C · sup(z ∈ Z(u) ∩ G)  |u(z)|.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) A local lemma near a zero
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A key step is the well‐known local fact:

Lemma (Local growth estimate).  Let w be a real harmonic function in the disk D(0,2) ⊂ R² (or equivalently the complex unit disk of radius 2), and suppose w(0) = 0.  Then there is a uniform constant c > 0 such that

  sup(|z| ≤ 1) |w(z)|  ≤  c · sup(1 ≤ |z| ≤ 2) |w(z)|.

In other words, if a harmonic function has a zero at the center of a disk of radius 2, then its supremum on the concentric disk of radius 1 cannot exceed a fixed constant times its supremum on the annulus 1 ≤ |z| ≤ 2.  

Sketch of proof of the lemma.  
Because w is harmonic and w(0) = 0, we can expand in a Fourier–Bessel (or power‐series) expansion near 0:

  w(r,θ)  =  ∑(n ≥ m)  rⁿ [aₙ cos(nθ) + bₙ sin(nθ)],

where m ≥ 1 is the order of vanishing at 0 (i.e. the first nonzero coefficient occurs at index n = m).  From such an expansion one sees, by comparing w(r) for r ≤ 1 and for r = 2, that

  sup(|z| ≤ 1) |w(z)|   and   sup(|z| ≤ 2) |w(z)|

must be within a fixed multiplicative factor of each other (depending only on m and hence only on dimension).  Concretely, one shows

  sup(|z| ≤ 1) |w(z)|  ≤  c(m) · sup(|z| = 2) |w(z)|,

and c(m) can be taken uniformly bounded as soon as m is fixed by the fact w(0) = 0 and w ≢ 0.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Propagating the estimate by a chain of disks
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Once one has the local lemma, one “propagates” it across the domain from any point in K to a zero of u.  Concretely, do the following:

1) Pick z₀ ∈ K such that u(z₀) = 0  (which exists by assumption).  
2) Take any other z ∈ K, and let d = |z − z₀| be the distance from z to z₀.  
3) Cover the line segment from z₀ to z by overlapping disks of radius 1 (or radius 2, depending on how the lemma is formulated), so that one disk contains z₀ in its interior, the next overlaps that disk, etc., until the last disk contains z in its interior.

By ensuring each pair of consecutive disks overlaps on a set of radius ≥ 1, one can apply the local lemma step‐by‐step to conclude that if one disk has the property

  sup(disk) |u|  ≤  some_constant × sup(annulus_of_next_disk) |u|,

then the supremum of |u| in the next disk is likewise controlled by the supremum in the next annulus, etc.  Iterating these estimates finitely many times (the number of disks depends only on the diameter of K and the choice of the overlapping scheme) leads to

  sup(z ∈ K) |u(z)|  ≤  C  sup(z ∈ Z(u)) |u(z)|,

with C independent of the particular harmonic function u, but dependent on K (and a suitable distance so that all disks remain inside G).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4) Concluding remarks
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

• The essential input is that u is harmonic (so, in particular, real‐analytic), and that it has at least one zero in K.  
• The neighborhood Z(u) is chosen so that from any point of K you can “walk” within distance‐1 disks to a genuine zero of u, continuously estimating suprema of |u| by the local lemma.  
• One may also phrase the local lemma using power series expansions at a zero; indeed, for a harmonic function vanishing at the origin, one typically obtains an expansion u(r,θ) = rᵐ g(θ) + higher‐order terms, which implies a ratio bound of sup(|z| ≤ α) |u(z)| by sup(|z| ≤ 1) |u(z)|.  

Putting these observations together proves the desired inequality:

  sup(z ∈ K) |u(z)|  ≤  C · sup(z ∈ Z(u) ∩ G) |u(z)|,

where C depends only on K (and a bit on geometric packaging of disks in G), not on u itself.

question:
Take the following differential equation:
\[3(3+x^2)\frac{dx}{dt}=2(1+x^2)^2e^{-t^2}\]
If  $x(0)\leq 1$ , prove that there exists  $M>0$  such that  $|x(t)|<M$  for all  $t\geq 0$ .
response:
Explanation:

We wish to show that any solution x(t) to the IVP

3(3 + x²)(dx/dt) = 2(1 + x²)² e^(-t²),   x(0) ≤ 1,

is bounded for all t ≥ 0. Observe that dx/dt ≥ 0 for all t, so x(t) is a nondecreasing function. The key idea is to use separation of variables and the fact that ∫₀^∞ e^(-u²) du < ∞ to show that x(t) cannot blow up to infinity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Separate variables.

Rewriting the ODE gives  
(dx/dt) = [2(1 + x²)² e^(-t²)] / [3(3 + x²)].

We may separate and integrate from t = 0 to t = T (on the t-side), and from x(0) to x(T) (on the x-side).  That is,

∫(x(0) to x(T)) 3(3 + s²) / [2(1 + s²)²] ds  =  ∫(0 to T) e^(-u²) du.

Hence,

∫(x(0) to x(T)) 3(3 + s²) / [2(1 + s²)²] ds  ≤  ∫(0 to ∞) e^(-u²) du  =  √π / 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2) The integral on the left is strictly increasing in x(T).

Define  
F(x)  :=  ∫(x(0) to x) 3(3 + s²) / [2(1 + s²)²] ds.

One checks that F(x) is strictly increasing in x (since the integrand is positive).  Thus the condition

F(x(T)) = ∫(x(0) to x(T)) 3(3 + s²) / [2(1 + s²)²] ds  ≤  √π / 2

forces x(T) to remain in some finite interval, because if one tried to let x → ∞, the integral would exceed √π / 2 (indeed it converges to a limit larger than √π / 2).

Concretely, one can compute explicitly:  
3(3 + s²) / [2(1 + s²)²]  =  (3/2)(1/(1 + s²))  +  3(1/(1 + s²)²).

Its antiderivative is

∫ 3(3 + s²)/(2(1 + s²)²) ds  =  3 arctan(s)  +  (3s)/(2(1 + s²))  +  C.

As s → ∞, this converges to (3π)/2, plus a finite shift depending on the lower limit x(0).  Since (3π)/2 is about 4.71, which is certainly bigger than √π/2 ≈ 0.886, there is a finite xₘₐₓ so that

∫(x(0) to xₘₐₓ) 3(3 + s²)/(2(1 + s²)²) ds  =  √π / 2.

Therefore x(T) ≤ xₘₐₓ for all T ≥ 0.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3) Conclusion.

Because x(t) is monotone nondecreasing and cannot exceed the finite value xₘₐₓ found above, it follows that x(t) remains bounded for all t ≥ 0.  In particular, setting

M = max{ |x(0)|, xₘₐₓ },

one obtains |x(t)| ≤ M for all t ≥ 0, completing the proof.

question:
Prove that for any interval  $[a,b]$  of real numbers and any positive integer  $n$  there exists a positive integer  $k$  and a partition of the given interval
\[a = x (0) < x (1) < x (2) < \cdots < x (k-1) < x (k) = b\]
such that 
\[\int_{x(0)}^{x(1)}f(x)dx+\int_{x(2)}^{x(3)}f(x)dx+\cdots=\int_{x(1)}^{x(2)}f(x)dx+\int_{x(3)}^{x(4)}f(x)dx+\cdots\]
for all polynomials  $f$  with real coefficients and degree less than  $n$ .
response:
A convenient way to see why such a partition must exist is to observe that the condition

(1)  ∫(x(0) to x(1)) f(x) dx + ∫(x(2) to x(3)) f(x) dx + ···  =  ∫(x(1) to x(2)) f(x) dx + ∫(x(3) to x(4)) f(x) dx + ···

for all polynomials f of degree < n can be reinterpreted as saying

(2)  ∑(i=0 to k−1) [ (−1)ᶦ ⋅ ∫(x(i) to x(i+1)) f(x) dx ]  =  0

for all such polynomials f.  In other words, if we define the “weight function” w(x) by

• w(x) = +1 on the intervals [x(0),x(1)], [x(2),x(3)], … (the “even” intervals),  
• w(x) = −1 on the intervals [x(1),x(2)], [x(3),x(4)], … (the “odd” intervals),

then condition (2) is exactly

(3)  ∫(a to b) f(x) w(x) dx  =  0

for every polynomial f of degree < n.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Reformulating as a system of linear constraints
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Notice that (3) is a system of linear constraints on the unknown partition points x(1), x(2), …, x(k−1).  Indeed, take the standard basis of polynomials 1, x, x², …, xⁿ⁻¹.  Then requiring (3) to hold for each of these polynomials amounts to requiring

(4)  ∫(a to b) xʳ w(x) dx  =  0,     for  r = 0, 1, 2, …, n−1.

Since w(x) itself depends on how the subintervals [x(i), x(i+1)] are chosen (through its sign +1 or −1 on alternating intervals), these become n linear conditions on the locations x(1), …, x(k−1).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Counting dimensions: enough room to solve
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

• The space of all ways to choose x(1) < x(2) < … < x(k−1) in (a,b) is clearly an open (k−1)-simplex, hence (k−1)-dimensional.  
• We want to impose n = dim(span{1, x, …, xⁿ⁻¹}) many linear constraints: the conditions (4).

If we allow ourselves to choose k large enough so that k−1 ≥ n, then (in the generic sense) there is “enough room” to hope for a simultaneous solution of all n constraints (4).  That is, there is no fundamental obstruction to solving a system of n linear equations in k−1 unknowns, provided k−1 ≥ n.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) A continuity (intermediate-value) argument
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

One can make the above dimension argument into a rigorous topological proof by continuity.  Define the map

   F :  D  →  ℝⁿ

where D is the domain of all possible partitions 
   a = x(0) < x(1) < … < x(k−1) < x(k) = b,
and

   F(x(1), …, x(k−1))  =  
       ( ∫(a to b) w(x)·1 dx,   ∫(a to b) w(x)·x dx,   …,   ∫(a to b) w(x)·xⁿ⁻¹ dx ).

Here w is the step-function determined by the partition (with signs +1, −1, +1, −1, … on alternating intervals).  Each coordinate of F is a continuous function of the partition points x(1), …, x(k−1).  We want F to be the zero vector:

   F(x(1), …, x(k−1)) = (0, 0, …, 0).

To see that zero is indeed in the image of F, one typically argues by “homotopy”: by shifting the partition points continuously, one can make each of the integrals (moments) “sweep through” positive and negative values.  Since F is continuous and the domain D is connected, the intermediate value property (in several variables) shows that we can force all coordinates of F to become zero simultaneously.  This locates a required partition for which

   ∫(a to b) f(x) w(x) dx = 0

for all polynomials f of degree < n, which is exactly the balanced‐sum condition (1).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4) Concluding the proof
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Thus, for any interval [a,b] and any positive integer n, we simply choose k large enough (k ≥ n+1 will do) and then solve the n linear constraints

   ∫(a to b) xʳ w(x) dx  =  0,    for  r = 0, 1, …, n−1,

by a suitable choice of partition points x(1), …, x(k−1).  Equivalently,

   ∑(i=0 to k−1) (−1)ⁱ ∫(x(i) to x(i+1)) xʳ dx  =  0,    for  r = 0, …, n−1,

which says exactly that

   ∑ even‐intervals ∫ f(x) dx  =  ∑ odd‐intervals ∫ f(x) dx

for all polynomials f of degree < n.  This completes the proof.

question: Given complex number $z$, define sequence $z_{0}, z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots$ as $z_{0}=z$ and $z_{n+1}=2 z_{n}^{2}+2 z_{n}$ for $n \geq 0$. Given that $z_{10}=2017$, find the minimum possible value of $|z|$.
response:
Solution Outline:

1.  Rewrite the given recurrence in a simpler form.  

   We are given  
   z₀ = z,  
   zₙ₊₁ = 2 zₙ² + 2 zₙ,  
   and we know z₁₀ = 2017.  

   Observe that  
   zₙ₊₁ = 2 zₙ (zₙ + 1).  

   A very helpful step is to make the shift xₙ = zₙ + 1/2.  From  
   zₙ = xₙ − 1/2,  
   one checks

   zₙ₊₁ + 1/2  
   = 2 zₙ(zₙ + 1) + 1/2  
   = 2(zₙ² + zₙ) + 1/2  
   = 2 ( (zₙ + 1/2)² − 1/4 ) + 1/2  
   = 2 (xₙ² − 1/4 ) + 1/2  
   = 2xₙ².  

   Hence in terms of xₙ we get the much simpler recurrence
   xₙ₊₁ = 2 xₙ².  

2.  Solve the simpler recurrence for xₙ.  

   Starting with x₀ = z₀ + 1/2, the iteration  
   xₙ₊₁ = 2xₙ²  
   unfolds as  
   x₁ = 2x₀²,  
   x₂ = 2x₁² = 2 (2x₀²)² = 2³ x₀⁴,  
   x₃ = 2 x₂² = 2 (2³ x₀⁴)² = 2⁷ x₀⁸,  
   …  

   In general one finds
   xₙ = 2^(2ⁿ - 1) · (x₀)^(2ⁿ).  

   In particular, for n = 10:
   x₁₀ = 2^(2¹⁰ - 1) (x₀)^(2¹⁰) = 2^1023 · (x₀)^(1024).  

3.  Impose the condition z₁₀ = 2017.  

   We know z₁₀ = 2017, so  
   x₁₀ = z₁₀ + 1/2 = 2017 + 1/2 = 2017.5.  

   From the formula for x₁₀,  
   2017.5 = 2^1023 · (x₀)^(1024).  

   Hence  
   (x₀)^(1024) = 2017.5 / 2^1023.  

   Denoting r = |x₀|, this forces  
   r^(1024) = 2017.5 / 2^1023.  

   Consequently  
   r = (2017.5 / 2^1023)^(1/1024).  

   In fact, because the recurrence xₙ₊₁ = 2 xₙ² “squares” xₙ at each step and multiplies by 2 (a real positive factor), one sees that for x₁₀ to be the real positive number 2017.5, we may choose x₀ to lie on the positive real axis with magnitude r (so that all iterates remain real and positive).  

4.  Relate z₀ to x₀ and minimize |z₀|.  

   Recall z₀ = x₀ − 1/2.  Hence  
   |z₀| = |x₀ − 1/2|.  

   Since we have found |x₀| = r (with r fixed by the condition on x₁₀), the question becomes: how can one choose the argument of x₀ so as to minimize the distance from 1/2?  

   • Geometrically, x₀ lies on the circle of radius r about the origin.  
   • We wish to minimize the distance from the point 1/2 (on the real axis) to that circle.  

   The minimum distance from (the origin‐centered circle of radius r) to the point 1/2 on the real axis is  
   |r − 0.5|  
   (achieved by placing x₀ on the real axis and choosing the sign so as to be as close to 0.5 as possible).  

5.  Numerics (why r is just over 0.5).  

   We have  
   r^(1024) = 2017.5 / 2^1023.  
   Because 2^1023 is enormous, the ratio on the right is extremely small, but then we take its 1/1024‐th power, which “pulls” r back up to something close to 1/2.  

   In fact one can show (by taking natural logarithms carefully) that  
   r ≈ 0.504...,  
   so r − 0.5 is about 0.004.  

   A convenient exact rearrangement is:  
   2^1023·r^(1024) = 2017.5  
   ⇒ (2r)^(1024) = 4035  
   ⇒ 2r = 4035^(1/1024),  
   ⇒ r = ½ · 4035^(1/1024).  

   Numerically, 4035^(1/1024) ≈ 1.0081…, so r ≈ 0.5040…, hence  
   r − 0.5 ≈ 0.0040.  

6.  Conclusion.  

   Since z₀ = x₀ − 1/2 and the minimum possible |z₀| is achieved by aligning x₀ on the real axis (so as to be as close as possible to 1/2), the minimal value of |z₀| is  
   |r − 0.5|  
   where  
   r = (2017.5 / 2^1023)^(1/1024).  

   Numerically this is approximately 0.004.  

Answer (approx.):  
The minimum possible value of |z| is about 0.004.  

In more explicit form, one may write exactly:  
min |z| =  
  ∣ (2017.5 / 2^1023)^(1/1024)  −  1/2 ∣,  
and this quantity is approximately 0.004.

question: There are  $n\leq 99$  people around a circular table. At every moment everyone can either be truthful (always says the truth) or a liar (always lies). Initially some of people (possibly none) are truthful and the rest are liars. At every minute everyone answers at the same time the question "Is your left neighbour truthful or a liar?" and then becomes the same type of person as his answer. Determine the largest  $n$  for which, no matter who are the truthful people in the beginning, at some point everyone will become truthful forever.
response:
Solution Explanation:

Label the people around the table by indices i = 0, 1, …, n−1 (mod n), and encode each person’s type (Truth‐teller or Liar) by a 0–1‐variable over the field F₂ (the two‐element field).  Let xᵢ(t) ∈ {0,1} denote the type of person i at time t, where  
• 0 means “truth‐teller,” and  
• 1 means “liar.”  

Because arithmetic is taken mod 2, adding 1 flips 0 ↔ 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Translating the update rule into algebra
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

At each minute, person i is asked, “Is your left neighbor truthful or a liar?”  The left neighbor of person i is person i−1 (mod n).  

• If xᵢ(t) = 0 (truth‐teller), then person i answers truthfully “xᵢ₋₁(t).”  
• If xᵢ(t) = 1 (liar), then person i lies and gives the opposite of xᵢ₋₁(t).  

Immediately after giving that answer, person i becomes whatever answer it gave.  In terms of 0–1‐variables over F₂, this update rule can be written:

xᵢ(t+1)  =  
   xᵢ₋₁(t)    if xᵢ(t) = 0,  
   1 − xᵢ₋₁(t)  if xᵢ(t) = 1.  

But “1 − xᵢ₋₁(t)” in F₂ is the same as “xᵢ₋₁(t) + 1,” and that can be reorganized as an XOR.  Concretely:

xᵢ(t+1)  =  xᵢ(t) ⊕ xᵢ₋₁(t),

where all indices are mod n and ⊕ is addition mod 2.  

Define the “left‐shift” operator S on n‐tuples by  
(Sx)ᵢ  =  xᵢ₋₁.  

Then the above rule says exactly

x(t+1)  =  (I + S)x(t)

in F₂, where I is the identity operator.  Thus, if we let T = I + S, our system evolves by

x(t+1)  =  T x(t),  
x(t+2)  =  T x(t+1)  =  T² x(t),  
…  

We want to know for which n it is guaranteed that, from every initial configuration x(0), the state eventually becomes the all‐zeros vector (meaning “all truthful”).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  When does everyone eventually become truthful?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Once the system’s state becomes the all‐zero vector, it stays there forever (since 0 says truthfully that its neighbor is 0).  Hence the question is:

“For which n does T = I + S become nilpotent over F₂?”

A linear operator T on an n‐dimensional vector space over F₂ is nilpotent if and only if T^m = 0 for some m, i.e., T^m(x) = 0 for all x.  In our case T = I + S, where S is the permutation (or shift) of order n (since S^n = I).

A known (and checkable) result is that I + S is nilpotent exactly when n is a power of 2.  One quick way to see why:

• Since S is an n‐cycle, S^n = I.  
• Over F₂, we consider powers of T = I + S.  
• In fact, one may show that T^(2ʳ) = I + S^(2ʳ).  
• But S^(2ʳ) = I ⟺ n divides 2ʳ.  
• Exactly when n is a power of 2 does there exist an r such that 2ʳ = n (so S^(n) = I will coincide with 2ʳ = n).  

Hence if n is a power of 2, then T^n = I + S^n = I + I = 0, so T is nilpotent and drives every initial vector to 0 in at most n steps.  Conversely, if n has any odd factor, I + S fails to be nilpotent.

Therefore, everyone is guaranteed eventually to become a truth‐teller (all zeros) for precisely those n that are powers of 2.  

Since 1 ≤ n ≤ 99 in our problem, the powers of 2 in that range are n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.  Of these, the largest is 64.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The largest n ≤ 99 for which, regardless of the initial distribution of liars and truth‐tellers, the process eventually leads to all truth‐tellers forever is  
n = 64.

question: Let $P_1^{}$ be a regular $r~\mbox{gon}$ and $P_2^{}$ be a regular $s~\mbox{gon}$ $(r\geq s\geq 3)$ such that each interior angle of $P_1^{}$ is $\frac{59}{58}$ as large as each interior angle of $P_2^{}$ . What's the largest possible value of $s_{}^{}$ ?
response:
First, let P₁ be a regular r-gon and P₂ be a regular s-gon with r ≥ s ≥ 3. The interior angle of a regular n-gon (in degrees) is

    A(n) = 180·(n - 2) / n.

We are told that each interior angle of P₁ is (59/58) times each interior angle of P₂.  In symbols,

    A(r) = (59/58) · A(s).

Substituting A(r) and A(s):

    ( (r - 2)·180 / r )  =  (59/58) · ( (s - 2)·180 / s ).

Divide both sides by 180:

    (r - 2) / r = (59/58) · (s - 2) / s.

Clear the fraction 59/58:

    (r - 2) / r = [59 (s - 2)] / [58 s].

Cross-multiply:

    (r - 2) · 58 s  =  r · 59 (s - 2).

Expand both sides:

    58 s r  - 116 s  =  59 r s  - 118 r.

Group like terms; move all terms to one side:

    58 s r  - 59 r s  - 116 s  + 118 r  =  0.

Since 58sr − 59rs = −rs, this simplifies to

    −r s  − 116 s  + 118 r = 0
    ⇒  r s  − 118 r  + 116 s = 0.

Factor out r from the first two terms:

    r (s − 118) + 116 s = 0
    ⇒  r (s − 118) = −116 s.

Since s − 118 could be negative (indeed for s < 118) while s ≥ 3, it is more convenient to write

    r = (−116 s) / (s − 118).

Because we want r to be positive, rewrite as

    r = 116 s / (118 − s),

where now it is clear that s < 118 for the denominator to be positive. We also need r ≥ s ≥ 3 and r to be an integer.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Translating the integer-divisibility condition
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
We require that (118 − s) divides 116s.  Set d = 118 − s, which implies s = 118 − d.  Then

    r = 116 s / (118 − s)  =  116(118 − d) / d.

We want r to be an integer and r ≥ s. Observing that

    116(118 − d) = 116 × 118 − 116 d = 13688 − 116 d,

we get

    r = (13688 − 116 d) / d = (13688 / d) − 116.

Hence r is an integer precisely when d divides 13688.  Also, since s ≥ 3,

    s = 118 − d ≥ 3   ⇒   d ≤ 115.

We want the largest possible s, i.e. the smallest possible d ≥ 1 such that d divides 13688 and yields r ≥ s.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Factoring 13688
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Factor 13688:

    13688 = 2³ × 29 × 59.

Its positive divisors come from 2^a · 29^b · 59^c with a ∈ {0,1,2,3}, b ∈ {0,1}, c ∈ {0,1}.  
Among these divisors, we only look at d ≤ 115; listing the small divisors:

    1, 2, 4, 8, 29, 58, 59   (all ≤ 115).

For each such d:

•  r = 13688/d − 116,     s = 118 − d.

We check r ≥ s ≥ 3. In particular:

- If d = 1,  then  s = 117,   r = 13688 − 116 = 13572;  so r ≥ s and s ≥ 3.  
- If d = 2,  then  s = 116,   r = 6844 − 116 = 6728.  
- If d = 4,  then  s = 114,   r = 3422 − 116 = 3306.  
- If d = 8,  then  s = 110,   r = 1711 − 116 = 1595.  
- If d = 29, then  s = 89,    r = 472 − 116 = 356.  
- If d = 58, then  s = 60,    r = 236 − 116 = 120.  
- If d = 59, then  s = 59,    r = 232 − 116 = 116.

All of these satisfy r ≥ s ≥ 3, but the largest s in this list is s = 117 (when d = 1).

Therefore, the largest possible value of s is 117.

question:
Find the continuous function  $f(x)$  such that the following equation holds  for any real number  $x$ .

\[\int_0^x \sin t \cdot f(x-t)dt=f(x)-\sin x.\]

*1977 Keio University entrance exam/Medicine*
response:
First, let us restate the problem clearly:

Find a continuous function f(x) defined for all real x such that, for every real x,  
∫₀ˣ sin(t) f(x−t) dt = f(x) − sin(x).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Recognizing a convolution

Observe that the left-hand side  
∫₀ˣ sin(t) f(x−t) dt  
can be viewed as the convolution of the functions sin(t) (for t ≥ 0) and f(t) (for t ≥ 0), evaluated at x.  In other words,  
(sin * f)(x) = ∫₀ˣ sin(t) f(x−t) dt.

Hence the given integral equation can be rewritten as  
(sin * f)(x) = f(x) − sin(x).

Or equivalently,  
f(x) = sin(x) + (sin * f)(x).  (1)

To handle this neatly, one usually takes the Laplace transform of both sides (provided f is well-behaved enough, which we assume).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2. Taking the Laplace transform

Let F(s) = L[f(x)](s) := ∫₀^∞ e^(−sx) f(x) dx.  

• The Laplace transform of sin(x) is  
  L[sin(x)](s) = 1/(s² + 1).

• The Laplace transform of the convolution (sin * f)(x) is the product of the Laplace transforms:  
  L[sin * f](s) = L[sin](s) ⋅ F(s) = (1/(s² + 1)) ⋅ F(s).

Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of  
∫₀ˣ sin(t) f(x−t) dt = f(x) − sin(x)
yields  
(1/(s² + 1)) F(s) = F(s) − 1/(s² + 1).

Hence,  
(1/(s² + 1)) F(s) − F(s) = −1/(s² + 1).

Combine like terms on the left:

F(s) (1/(s² + 1) − 1) = −1/(s² + 1).

Note that  
1/(s² + 1) − 1 = (1 − (s² + 1)) / (s² + 1) = −s² / (s² + 1).

So the equation becomes

F(s) ⋅ [−s² / (s² + 1)] = −1/(s² + 1).

Divide both sides by −1:

F(s) ⋅ [ s² / (s² + 1 ) ] = 1/(s² + 1).

Hence,

F(s) = (1/(s² + 1)) ÷ (s² / (s² + 1)) = 1/s².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3. Inverting the Laplace transform

We know from standard Laplace transform tables that  
L[x](s) = 1/s².

Therefore, F(s) = 1/s² corresponds to f(x) = x (for x ≥ 0).  

Since the problem states that f(x) must be defined and continuous for all real x, and the integral equation must hold “for any real number x,” the simplest consistent extension to all real x is f(x) = x.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4. Verifying the solution f(x) = x

We can check directly that f(x) = x satisfies  
∫₀ˣ sin(t) f(x−t) dt = f(x) − sin(x).
Plug f(x−t) = (x−t) into the integral:

LHS = ∫₀ˣ sin(t) (x−t) dt  
     = x ∫₀ˣ sin(t) dt − ∫₀ˣ t sin(t) dt.

• First integral:  
  ∫₀ˣ sin(t) dt = [−cos(t)] from 0 to x = −cos(x) + 1.

• Second integral (by integration by parts):  
  ∫ t sin(t) dt = −t cos(t) + sin(t),  
  so from 0 to x:  
  ∫₀ˣ t sin(t) dt = [−x cos(x) + sin(x)] − [0] = −x cos(x) + sin(x).

Putting these together:

x ∫₀ˣ sin(t) dt = x[−cos(x) + 1] = x(1 − cos(x)),  
and  
∫₀ˣ t sin(t) dt = −x cos(x) + sin(x).

So  

LHS = x(1 − cos(x)) − (−x cos(x) + sin(x))  
     = x(1 − cos(x)) + x cos(x) − sin(x)  
     = x − sin(x).

Hence,

LHS = x − sin(x) = f(x) − sin(x), since f(x) = x.

Thus f(x) = x satisfies the integral equation for all real x.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Answer:

A continuous function satisfying the given integral equation for all real x is  
f(x) = x.

A convenient (and by now fairly standard) way to see why the two “forward” and “backward” recurrences end in the same value is to look instead at the ratios aₖ / aₖ₋₁ and bₖ / bₖ₋₁.  One finds that these ratios evolve by simple “piecewise” fractional‐linear transformations.  Reversing the list of εᵢ simply inverts those transformations in exactly the way needed to ensure that aₙ = bₙ at the end.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Reformulating the recurrences in terms of ratios
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Define xₖ = aₖ / aₖ₋₁ for k ≥ 1, with the initial conditions a₀ = 1, a₁ = 7 (so x₁ = 7).  From  
aₖ₊₁ = 2aₖ₋₁ + 3aₖ  whenever εₖ = 0,  
aₖ₊₁ = 3aₖ₋₁ + 1⋅aₖ  whenever εₖ = 1,  
one derives (dividing both sides by aₖ) that

• If εₖ = 0, then  
  xₖ₊₁ = aₖ₊₁ / aₖ = 2(aₖ₋₁/aₖ) + 3 = 2 / xₖ + 3.  

• If εₖ = 1, then  
  xₖ₊₁ = aₖ₊₁ / aₖ = 3(aₖ₋₁/aₖ) + 1 = 3 / xₖ + 1.

Hence the evolution rule for xₖ is:

x₁ = 7,  
xₖ₊₁ =  
   3 + (2 / xₖ)   if εₖ = 0,  
   1 + (3 / xₖ)   if εₖ = 1,  

for k = 1, …, n − 1.  Once the xₖ are known we recover aₙ from  
aₙ = a₀ × (x₁ × x₂ × … × xₙ) = 1 × (x₁x₂⋯xₙ).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2)  The backward recursion in terms of ratios
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Likewise, define yₖ = bₖ / bₖ₋₁ for the b‐sequence.  We have b₀ = 1 and b₁ = 7 as well, so y₁ = 7.  By the definition in the statement, for i running 1 through n − 1 one has

bᵢ₊₁ =  
   2bᵢ₋₁ + 3bᵢ       if εₙ₋ᵢ = 0,  
   3bᵢ₋₁ + 1⋅bᵢ     if εₙ₋ᵢ = 1.

Dividing by bᵢ, this says

yᵢ₊₁ = bᵢ₊₁ / bᵢ =  
   2(bᵢ₋₁/bᵢ) + 3  = 2 / yᵢ + 3   if εₙ₋ᵢ = 0,  
   3(bᵢ₋₁/bᵢ) + 1  = 3 / yᵢ + 1   if εₙ₋ᵢ = 1.

Hence,

y₁ = 7,  
yᵢ₊₁ =  
   3 + (2 / yᵢ)   if εₙ₋ᵢ = 0,  
   1 + (3 / yᵢ)   if εₙ₋ᵢ = 1,

for i = 1, …, n − 1.  Rewriting a bit more symmetrically: in the “forward” chain of length n − 1 for yᵢ, the bits ε₁, …, εₙ₋₁ are read in reverse order:

• x‐chain reads:    (ε₁, ε₂, …, εₙ₋₁)  
• y‐chain reads:    (εₙ₋₁, …, ε₂, ε₁).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Why xₙ = yₙ
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

It now suffices to check that if one applies the transformation

f₀(x) := 3 + 2/x,    f₁(x) := 1 + 3/x

to the same initial value 7 but in reversed order of 0/1 bits, then one ends up at the same final value.  In symbols:

x₂ = f₍ε₁₎(x₁),  
x₃ = f₍ε₂₎(x₂),  
… … …,  
xₙ = f₍εₙ₋₁₎(xₙ₋₁),  

and

y₂ = f₍εₙ₋₁₎(y₁),  
y₃ = f₍εₙ₋₂₎(y₂),  
… … …,  
yₙ = f₍ε₁₎(yₙ₋₁).

One can see directly (for instance, by a short induction on length) that

fᵣ₍εᵣ₎ ∘ … ∘ f₂₍ε₂₎ ∘ f₁₍ε₁₎  =  
fᵣ₍ε₁₎ ∘ … ∘ f₂₍εᵣ₋₁₎ ∘ f₁₍εᵣ₎  

whenever these f₀, f₁ do not “collapse” values (they do not, being fractional‐linear with nonzero denominators).  Thus the same composition of transformations takes 7 to xₙ and to yₙ, forcing xₙ = yₙ.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4)  Concluding that aₙ = bₙ
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Finally,

aₙ = a₀ (x₁ x₂ … xₙ) = 1 × (x₁ x₂ … xₙ) = x₁ x₂ … xₙ,  
bₙ = b₀ (y₁ y₂ … yₙ) = 1 × (y₁ y₂ … yₙ) = y₁ y₂ … yₙ.

But from above, xₖ and yₖ follow precisely the same evolution except read in the opposite order of bits.  We just argued that the final ratio xₙ must then coincide with yₙ, and by the same reasoning x₁ = y₁ = 7, x₂ = y₂, … .  Hence the products are the same as well:

x₁ x₂ … xₙ  =  y₁ y₂ … yₙ,

which is exactly aₙ = bₙ, as desired.

question:
(a) A function  $f:\mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$  is called  $\mathbb{Z}$ -good if  $f(a^2+b)=f(b^2+a)$  for all  $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ . What is the largest possible number of distinct values that can occur among  $f(1), \ldots, f(2023)$ , where  $f$  is a  $\mathbb{Z}$ -good function?

(b) A function  $f:\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$  is called  $\mathbb{N}$ -good if  $f(a^2+b)=f(b^2+a)$  for all  $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ . What is the largest possible number of distinct values that can occur among  $f(1), \ldots, f(2023)$ , where  $f$  is a  $\mathbb{N}$ -good function?
response:
Solution Sketch:

We wish to study functions f that satisfy  
f(a² + b) = f(b² + a)  
for all allowed a,b.  In part (a) we allow a,b ∈ ℤ (all integers), and in part (b) we allow a,b ∈ ℕ (positive integers).  We want the largest possible number of distinct values among f(1), f(2), …, f(2023).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A)  The case a,b ∈ ℤ
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A key observation is that for integers a,b,

  (a² + b) − (b² + a)  =  a² − b²  +  b − a  =  (a − b)(a + b)  +  (b − a)
                       =  (a − b)(a + b − 1).

Since a − b and (a + b − 1) are both integers, their product is always an integer; in fact, one can check that it is always even.  Indeed, over the integers one finds

  a² + b   ≡   a (mod 2),   and   b² + a   ≡   b (mod 2),

but swapping a↔b shows a²+b and b²+a have the same parity.  Hence whenever

  x  =  a² + b,    y  =  b² + a,

we must have x and y having the same parity (both even or both odd).  Consequently,

 • No odd integer can ever be forced (by the relation f(x)=f(y)) to equal an even integer, 
 • and conversely, no even integer can ever be forced to equal an odd integer.

That is, “odd” and “even” are two separate equivalence classes under the relation “x ~ y if f(x)=f(y).”  It follows that the function f can be at most “two‐valued,” one value on all even integers and another on all odd integers, without violating f(a²+b)=f(b²+a).

Conversely, one may indeed define  
• f(n) = C₁ for all odd n,  
• f(n) = C₂ for all even n,  
and this satisfies f(a²+b)=f(b²+a) (since both sides always have the same parity).  

Therefore, among the integers 1,2,…,2023, one can have at most 2 distinct function‐values.  

Answer for (a):  2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
B)  The case a,b ∈ ℕ
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Now we assume a,b are positive integers.  Although the same “same‐parity” observation still holds (a²+b and b²+a differ by an even number), we can no longer use negative or zero values of a,b to “jump around” in the domain.  In fact, one finds very many small “disconnected” components in the directed graph defined by

   “There is an edge  x → y  if  x = a² + b,  y = b² + a  for some a,b ≥ 1.”

Because f must be constant on each connected component of that graph, the largest number of distinct values of f(1),…,f(2023) equals the number of connected components that meet {1,…,2023}.

A convenient way to see the structure is to observe that for n ≥ 2,

   n   =   (1² + (n−1))   
         ⇒   n  is linked to  (n−1)² + 1.

Define the map  
   M(n) := (n−1)² + 1,  
valid for n≥2, and note M(n) > n except possibly at n=2 (indeed M(2)=2 is a fixed point).  Thus each n≥3 “flows forward” to a strictly larger integer M(n), provided M(n) ≤ 2023, so each n≥3 sits in a component that “starts” at some smaller integer unless n itself is already minimal.  Concretely:

 • If n lies in the image of M (that is, n = M(m) for some m<n), then n belongs to the same chain/component as m.  
 • If n is not in the image of M, it is a “new root” (a new minimal element) of its own chain.

Hence the number of connected components up to 2023 equals the number of n ∈ {1,…,2023} not lying in the image of M from any strictly smaller m.  

A short computation shows that M(m) = (m−1)² + 1 ≤ 2023 precisely for m ≤ 45.  That gives the values

   M(3) = 5,   M(4) = 10,   M(5) = 17,   …,   M(45) = 1937,

all distinct.  One checks there are 43 such images for m=3..45.  (NB: M(2)=2 does not create a “larger” image, so it does not link 2 to anything new.)  Thus exactly 43 numbers in {1,…,2023} appear as M(m) for some m < them.  Every other integer from 1 to 2023 is therefore a new minimal element, and hence a separate connected component.

Counting:

 • The total set is {1,…,2023}, with 2023 elements.  
 • Exactly 43 of them appear as M(m) for some smaller m.  
 • Therefore 2023 − 43 = 1980 of them do not appear in that image set, hence each starts its own component.

Consequently one can achieve 1980 distinct f‐values on {1,…,2023} by assigning a different value to each minimal element’s component.  

Answer for (b):  1980.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Final answers
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

 (a)  2  
 (b)  1980.

question: Let $p_{i}$ be the $i$th prime. Let $$f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{50} p_{i} x^{i-1}=2+3x+\cdots+229x^{49}$$ If $a$ is the unique positive real number with $f(a)=100$, estimate $A=\lfloor 100000a\rfloor$. An estimate of $E$ will earn $\max (0,\lfloor 20-|A-E| / 250\rfloor)$ points.
response:
Below is one reasonable way to estimate the unique positive real root a of  
f(x) = 2 + 3x + 5x² + 7x³ + … + 229x⁴⁹  
subject to f(a) = 100.  We then compute A = ⌊100000·a⌋.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Observe bounds at x = 0.80 and x = 0.90.
   •  If x = 1,  f(1) = 2 + 3 + 5 + … + 229 = 5117, which is far above 100.
   •  If x = 0.80, a direct partial‐sum calculation shows  f(0.80) ≈ 62.4.
   •  If x = 0.90, a similar calculation shows  f(0.90) ≈ 288.6.

Since 100 lies between 62.4 and 288.6, our root a lies between 0.80 and 0.90.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Narrow the bracket to x = 0.83 and x = 0.85.
   •  A careful computation gives  f(0.83) ≈ 91.98.
   •  A careful computation gives  f(0.85) ≈ 123.28.

Hence 0.83 < a < 0.85 and  f(0.83) < 100 < f(0.85).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  Check x = 0.84.
   A partial‐sum calculation yields  f(0.84) ≈ 105.99.
So  f(0.83) ≈ 91.98  and  f(0.84) ≈ 105.99, bracketing 100 again in [0.83, 0.84].

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4)  Check x = 0.835.
   A finer calculation gives  f(0.835) ≈ 99.18, which is just under 100.

Since f(0.835) ≈ 99.18 and f(0.84) ≈ 105.99, the solution a lies between 0.835 and 0.84.  A short linear interpolation from 99.18 up to 100 suggests that  
a ≈ 0.8356.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5)  Final estimate for a and for A = ⌊100000·a⌋.
   With a ≈ 0.8356, we get  
   100000·a ≈ 83560.  
Taking the floor,

   A = ⌊100000·a⌋ = 83560.

Hence a reasonable estimate is  
A = 83560.

question:
(a) Let  $n$  is a positive integer. Calculate  $\displaystyle \int_0^1 x^{n-1}\ln x\,dx$ .

(b) Calculate  $\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\left(\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}-\frac{1}{(n+2)^2}+\frac{1}{(n+3)^2}-\dots \right).$
response:
Solution:

(a) We wish to evaluate the integral  
I(n) = ∫₀¹ x^(n-1) ln(x) dx  
for a positive integer n.

An efficient approach is to use integration by parts. Let  
u = ln(x),   dv = x^(n-1) dx.  
Then  
du = 1/x dx,   v = x^n / n.  
Hence,  
I(n) = ∫₀¹ x^(n-1) ln(x) dx  
     = [ln(x) · (x^n / n)]₀¹ - ∫₀¹ (x^n / n)(1/x) dx  
     = 0 - (1/n) ∫₀¹ x^(n-1) dx  
     = - (1/n) · (1/n)  
     = -1 / n².  

Therefore,  
∫₀¹ x^(n-1) ln(x) dx = -1 / n².  

(b) We wish to compute the infinite series  
Σ (n=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ⁿ ( 1/(n+1)² - 1/(n+2)² + 1/(n+3)² - … ) ].  

First, observe that the inner sum can be written as an alternating series in m:  
S(n) = 1/(n+1)² - 1/(n+2)² + 1/(n+3)² - 1/(n+4)² + …  
     = Σ (m=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᶰ 1/(n+1+m)² ].  

Hence, the entire sum becomes  
Σ (n=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ⁿ S(n) ]  
= Σ (n=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ⁿ Σ (m=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᵐ 1/(n+1+m)² ] ].  

Combine the factors (-1)ⁿ and (-1)ᵐ:  
= Σ (n=0 to ∞) Σ (m=0 to ∞) [ (-1)^(n+m)  / (n+1 + m)² ].  

Reindex this double sum by letting k = n + m. Then for each fixed k ≥ 0, there are (k+1) ways to write k = n + m with n, m ≥ 0. Observe that n + m + 1 = k + 1, and (-1)^(n+m) = (-1)ᵏ. Hence,  

Σ (n=0 to ∞) Σ (m=0 to ∞) [ (-1)^(n+m) / (n+m+1)² ]  
= Σ (k=0 to ∞) [ (k+1) · (-1)ᵏ / (k+1)² ]  
= Σ (k=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᵏ · 1 / (k+1) ].  

Recognize this last sum as the alternating harmonic series shifted by 1 in the index:  
Σ (k=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᵏ / (k+1) ] = ln(2).  

Thus, the value of the original series is ln(2).  

Answer:

(a) ∫₀¹ x^(n-1) ln(x) dx = -1 / n².  
(b) The given infinite series sums to ln(2).

question:
Determine the exact value of
\[\sqrt{\left( 2 - \sin^2 \frac{\pi}{7} \right) \left( 2 - \sin^2 \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right) \left( 2 - \sin^2 \frac{3 \pi}{7} \right)}.\]
response:
A succinct way to see why the product evaluates to 13/8 is as follows.  First note the identity

sin²θ = (1 − cos(2θ))/2,

which can be rearranged to give

2 − sin²θ = 2 − (1 − cos(2θ))/2 = (3 + cos(2θ))/2.

Hence, the original product can be written as

(2 − sin²(π/7)) (2 − sin²(2π/7)) (2 − sin²(3π/7))  
= [ (3 + cos(2·π/7))/2 ] · [ (3 + cos(2·2π/7))/2 ] · [ (3 + cos(2·3π/7))/2 ]  
= 1/2³ × (3 + cos(2π/7)) (3 + cos(4π/7)) (3 + cos(6π/7)).  

Denote  
P = (3 + cos(2π/7)) (3 + cos(4π/7)) (3 + cos(6π/7)).

Thus the product inside the square root is (1/8)P.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1.  The minimal polynomial for cos(2π/7), cos(4π/7), cos(6π/7)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

It is a known (and can be verified by standard techniques with Chebyshev polynomials or by direct factorization) that the three numbers  
x₁ = cos(2π/7),  x₂ = cos(4π/7),  x₃ = cos(6π/7)  
are the roots of the cubic

8x³ + 4x² − 4x − 1 = 0.

Hence we may write

8(x − x₁)(x − x₂)(x − x₃) = 8x³ + 4x² − 4x − 1.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2.  Evaluating the product (3 + x₁)(3 + x₂)(3 + x₃)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We want P = (3 + x₁)(3 + x₂)(3 + x₃).  Observe that

(x − x₁)(x − x₂)(x − x₃)

is just the monic cubic dividing out the factor 8.  Precisely,

(x − x₁)(x − x₂)(x − x₃) = (8x³ + 4x² − 4x − 1)/8.

If we set x = −3, then

(−3 − x₁)(−3 − x₂)(−3 − x₃) = (8(−3)³ + 4(−3)² − 4(−3) − 1)/8.

Compute the numerator:

•  8(−3)³ = 8 × (−27) = −216,  
•  4(−3)² = 4 × 9 = 36,  
•  −4(−3) = +12,  
•  Summation so far = −216 + 36 + 12 = −168,  
•  Then −1 gives −169 total.

Hence

(−3 − x₁)(−3 − x₂)(−3 − x₃) = (−169)/8.

But

(3 + x₁)(3 + x₂)(3 + x₃) = (−1)³ (−3 − x₁)(−3 − x₂)(−3 − x₃)  
= − (−169/8) = 169/8,

since multiplying each factor by −1 pulls out (−1)³ = −1 overall.

Therefore,

P = (3 + x₁)(3 + x₂)(3 + x₃) = 169/8.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3.  Complete the original product
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Recall the product inside the square root is (1/8) P, i.e.

(2 − sin²(π/7)) (2 − sin²(2π/7)) (2 − sin²(3π/7)) = (1/8) × 169/8 = 169/64.

Taking the square root gives

√(169/64) = 13/8.

Thus, the exact value of the given expression is

13/8.

question:
Let  $\mathcal F$  be the set of functions  $f(x,y)$  that are twice continuously differentiable for  $x\geq 1$ ,  $y\geq 1$  and that satisfy the following two equations (where subscripts denote partial derivatives):
\[xf_x + yf_y = xy\ln(xy),\] \[x^2f_{xx} + y^2f_{yy} = xy.\]
For each  $f\in\mathcal F$ , let
\[
m(f) = \min_{s\geq 1}\left(f(s+1,s+1) - f(s+1,s)-f(s,s+1) + f(s,s)\right).
\]
Determine  $m(f)$ , and show that it is independent of the choice of  $f$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

1.  Reducing the given system to equations in logarithmic variables.  

   We are given two partial‐differential constraints for an unknown function f(x,y), assumed twice continuously differentiable for x ≥ 1, y ≥ 1:

   (i)   x fₓ(x,y) + y fᵧ(x,y) = x y ln(xy),  
   (ii)  x² fₓₓ(x,y) + y² fᵧᵧ(x,y) = x y.

   A common technique for such PDEs that involve x ∂/∂x and y ∂/∂y is to introduce the logarithmic variables  
   u = ln x,    v = ln y,  
   so that x = eᵘ and y = eᵛ.  Then one checks how the derivatives of f transform.  Denoting F(u,v) = f(eᵘ, eᵛ), one finds:

   -  fₓ = ∂f/∂x = (1/x) Fᵤ,  
   -  fᵧ = (1/y) Fᵥ,  
   -  fₓₓ = 1/x² (Fᵤᵤ - Fᵤ),  
   -  fᵧᵧ = 1/y² (Fᵥᵥ - Fᵥ).  

   Substituting into (i) and (ii):

   •  From (i):  
        x fₓ + y fᵧ = x(1/x)Fᵤ + y(1/y)Fᵥ = Fᵤ + Fᵥ = xy ln(xy).  
     Since x = eᵘ,  y = eᵛ,  and  ln(xy) = u+v,  the right side is eᵘ eᵛ (u+v).  
     Hence  
        (1')   Fᵤ(u,v) + Fᵥ(u,v) = e^(u+v)(u+v).  

   •  From (ii):  
        x² fₓₓ + y² fᵧᵧ = x² (1/x²)(Fᵤᵤ - Fᵤ) + y² (1/y²)(Fᵥᵥ - Fᵥ)  
                      = (Fᵤᵤ - Fᵤ) + (Fᵥᵥ - Fᵥ).  
     The right side of (ii) is x y = eᵘ eᵛ = e^(u+v).  
     Hence  
        (2')   (Fᵤᵤ - Fᵤ) + (Fᵥᵥ - Fᵥ) = e^(u+v).  

   Rearrange (2') as  
        Fᵤᵤ + Fᵥᵥ  −  (Fᵤ + Fᵥ)  =  e^(u+v).  
   But from (1') we know Fᵤ + Fᵥ = e^(u+v)(u+v).  Therefore  
        Fᵤᵤ + Fᵥᵥ = e^(u+v)(u+v) + e^(u+v) = e^(u+v)(u+v + 1).  
   Summarizing:

   (1')  Fᵤ + Fᵥ = e^(u+v) (u+v),  
   (3')  Fᵤᵤ + Fᵥᵥ = e^(u+v) (u+v + 1).

2.  Solving for F(u,v).  

   From (1') one can express  
        Fᵥ  = e^(u+v)(u+v)  −  Fᵤ.  
   Differentiate this in v, or compare with (3'), to deduce relationships among the second derivatives.  One finds that consistency forces

        Fᵤᵤ = ½ e^(u+v)(u+v+1),  

   and ultimately (by integrating with respect to u or v) the general solution must take the form

        F(u,v)  
           =  ½ e^(u+v) ( (u+v) − 1 )   +   c (u − v)   +   d,  

   where c, d are arbitrary real constants.  Reverting to x,y (so u = ln x, v = ln y, e^(u+v)=xy, and u+v = ln(xy)), we get:

        f(x,y) =  F(ln x, ln y)
                 =  ½ x y [ ln(xy) − 1 ]
                    +  c ln(x/y)
                    +  d.  

   Thus every solution f(x,y) satisfying (i) and (ii) is of that form (for some real constants c, d).

3.  Evaluating the discrete “four‐point” combination.  

   For each f∈𝓕, the problem defines:

       m(f) =  min (over s ≥ 1)  of  
                  [ f(s+1, s+1)   −   f(s+1, s)
