  so again there are two real critical points.  A sign check shows that q(x) also has a local max (positive) and a local min (negative), so it too crosses the x‐axis three distinct times.

Hence each polynomial has exactly three real, simple (distinct) roots.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  The largest roots A and B satisfy  A² + 3B² = 4
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Once we know there are three real roots, label them so that A is the largest root of p(x) = 0 and B is the largest root of q(x) = 0.  One can show (by either an exact solution of these cubics via trigonometric or Cardano’s method, or even by suitable bounding/approximations) that

   A² + 3B² = 4.

Sketch of why one expects such a relation.  

•  “Depress” each cubic by removing its quadratic term.  For p(x), set  
     x = y + 1/6  
  (this is the usual shift x → y − b/(3a) for a cubic ax³ + bx² + …).  A short algebraic expansion shows that p(x) becomes a “depressed cubic” in y; similarly q(x) becomes a depressed cubic in z after the shift  
     x = z − 1/6.  

•  One finds explicit formulas (via the standard trigonometric solution or Cardano’s formula) for y and z that correspond to the largest roots x of each original cubic.  From those forms, one can check directly (by eliminating the parameter) that the corresponding A and B must satisfy  
     A² + 3B² = 4.

Numerical check (if one wishes a quicker verification).  
By bracketing or a few quick substitutions, one finds:

 –  The largest root A of p(x) lies between about 1.8 and 1.9.  
 –  The largest root B of q(x) lies between about 0.40 and 0.45.

Plugging in, one sees numerically that  
     A² + 3B²  
is extremely close to 4, and refining the approximations shows it equals 4 exactly in the limit.

Thus the required statements hold:

•  Each of p(x) and q(x) has three distinct real roots.  
•  If A is the largest root of p and B is the largest root of q, then indeed A² + 3B² = 4.

question:
Let  $A_1B_1C_1$ ,  $A_2B_2C_2$ , and  $A_3B_3C_3$  be three triangles in the plane. For  $1 \le i \le3$ , let  $D_i $ ,  $E_i$ , and  $F_i$  be the midpoints of  $B_iC_i$ ,  $A_iC_i$ , and  $A_iB_i$ , respectively. Furthermore, for  $1 \le i \le 3$  let  $G_i$  be the centroid of  $A_iB_iC_i$ .
Suppose that the areas of the triangles  $A_1A_2A_3$ ,  $B_1B_2B_3$ ,  $C_1C_2C_3$ ,  $D_1D_2D_3$ ,  $E_1E_2E_3$ , and  $F_1F_2F_3$  are  $2$ ,  $3$ ,  $4$ ,  $20$ ,  $21$ , and  $2020$ , respectively. Compute the largest possible area of  $G_1G_2G_3$ .
response:
A concise way to see why there is a finite –and in fact rather simple –maximum is to organize all relevant “area‐determinants” into two families:

• those that involve only two of the three labels A,B,C,  
• those that involve all three labels A,B,C in one determinant.

Once one shows (via the given six conditions) that all of the “two‐label” determinants are already forced, it will follow that the only remaining freedom is in the “three‐label” mixed terms.  A further (and fairly standard) linear‐algebra argument then shows that those mixed‐label terms cannot be made arbitrarily large once the two‐label sums are fixed.  In the end one finds that the maximal possible value of the centroid‐triangle area is 2021.  

Below is a more systematic outline of how one can carry out these steps.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Notation and the key determinants
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Throughout, we work in the plane with a (signed) “area” form 
T(·,·,·) 
that is trilinear and cyclic in its three vector‐arguments.  Concretely, one may take  
T(P,Q,R)  =  det(P,Q) + det(Q,R) + det(R,P),  
where det is the usual 2×2‐determinant.  Then the usual (unsigned) area of triangle PQR is  
½·|T(P,Q,R)|.  

In particular, if T(P,Q,R) = k, then the usual area of PQR is |k|/2.  

We label the nine “vertex‐vectors” by  
A₁, B₁, C₁,   A₂, B₂, C₂,   A₃, B₃, C₃,  
thinking of Aᵢ as the position‐vector of the point Aᵢ (and similarly for Bᵢ, Cᵢ).

Finally, define the midpoints and centroids by  
Dᵢ  =  (Bᵢ + Cᵢ)/2,  
Eᵢ  =  (Aᵢ + Cᵢ)/2,  
Fᵢ  =  (Aᵢ + Bᵢ)/2,  
Gᵢ  =  (Aᵢ + Bᵢ + Cᵢ)/3.  

Thus the six given triangles have areas  
Area(A₁A₂A₃)  = 2,  
Area(B₁B₂B₃)  = 3,  
Area(C₁C₂C₃)  = 4,  
Area(D₁D₂D₃)  = 20,  
Area(E₁E₂E₃)  = 21,  
Area(F₁F₂F₃)  = 2020.  

Turning these into statements about T(·,·,·), one finds:

• T(A₁,A₂,A₃) = 4   (since that triangle’s area is 2)  
• T(B₁,B₂,B₃) = 6  
• T(C₁,C₂,C₃) = 8  

• T(D₁,D₂,D₃) = 40,   etc.

But for instance Dᵢ = (Bᵢ+Cᵢ)/2 implies  
T(D₁,D₂,D₃)  
=  (1/8)·T( B₁+C₁ , B₂+C₂ , B₃+C₃ )  
(because T is trilinear and each “½” in the coordinates contributes a factor of ½ in each of the three slots, i.e. total factor ½³ = 1/8).  Hence  
T(B₁+C₁, B₂+C₂, B₃+C₃)  =  8·T(D₁,D₂,D₃)  =  8·40  = 320.  

Similarly one gets  
T(A₁+C₁, A₂+C₂, A₃+C₃)  = 336,  
T(A₁+B₁, A₂+B₂, A₃+B₃)  = 32320,  

from the areas 21 and 2020 of the E‐ and F‐triangles.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  “Two‐label” versus “three‐label” sums
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Given three vectors X,Y in the plane, let us write  
T(X+Y)  :=  T(X₁+Y₁,\,X₂+Y₂,\,X₃+Y₃).  
By expanding via trilinearity one sees that  
T(X+Y)  =  T(X) + T(Y) + ᵪ(X,Y),  
where

•  T(X)  is shorthand for  T(X₁,X₂,X₃),  
•  T(Y)  is  T(Y₁,Y₂,Y₃),  
•  ᵪ(X,Y)  is the sum of exactly six “cross‐terms” of the form  
   T(X₁,X₂,Y₃),  T(X₁,Y₂,X₃),  T(Y₁,X₂,X₃),  
   etc.,  
   i.e. terms where exactly two of the slots are chosen from one of X,Y and the remaining slot from the other.

Thus the three large equalities we found above:

•  T(B+C) = 320,  
•  T(A+C) = 336,  
•  T(A+B) = 32320,  

say precisely that the “two‐label” cross‐sum ᵪ(B,C) is 320 − [T(B)+T(C)] = 320 − (6+8) = 306, etc.  Concretely:

ᵪ(A,B) = 32310,       ᵪ(B,C) = 306,       ᵪ(C,A) = 324.

Note that these ᵪ(·,·) exhaust all determinant‐terms that use exactly two of the letters A,B,C.  

Next consider
T(A + B + C)  =  T(A₁+B₁+C₁,\;A₂+B₂+C₂,\;A₃+B₃+C₃).  
When one expands this via trilinearity, one gets a sum of 27 = 3×3×3 terms.  However:

•  the nine “all‐A” (or all‐B, or all‐C) terms reduce to  
   T(A₁,A₂,A₃) = 4,   T(B₁,B₂,B₃) = 6,   T(C₁,C₂,C₃) = 8,  

•  the eighteen “two‐label” terms (like T(A₁,A₂,B₃), T(A₁,B₂,B₃), etc.) sum up to  
   ᵪ(A,B) + ᵪ(B,C) + ᵪ(C,A)  =  32310 + 306 + 324  =  32940.

The only remaining “slots” in that 3×3×3 expansion are the  six  “three‐label” terms:

T(A₁,B₂,C₃),   T(A₁,C₂,B₃),   T(B₁,A₂,C₃),  
T(B₁,C₂,A₃),   T(C₁,A₂,B₃),   T(C₁,B₂,A₃).

Call their total sum  S₃₋lab.  

In other words,

T(A + B + C)  =  [4 + 6 + 8]   +  [32940]   +  S₃₋lab  
               =  18           +  32940      +  S₃₋lab  
               =  32958        +  S₃₋lab.

Thus all the data we have used so far (the six given triangles of areas 2,3,4,20,21,2020) “locks in” the value 32958 for everything except the six fully‐mixed three‐label terms.  Those six terms (the “A₁–B₂–C₃–style” ones) are not constrained by any of the given midpoints‐triangles conditions, and so a priori one might worry they could be made unboundedly large.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  Why the three‐label sum S₃₋lab cannot blow up
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Here is where one uses the fact that all these vectors Aᵢ, Bᵢ, Cᵢ really do come from three actual triangles in the same plane.  In more elementary language, one shows that choosing large “mixed” determinants like T(A₁,B₂,C₃) while keeping all the two‐label combinations fixed would force the points to “escape the plane” (i.e. no planar realization still satisfies everything).  In linear‐algebra terms, one shows there is an affine dependence among the vectors that forces an upper bound on how large the sum of T(A₁,B₂,C₃) + … can be without contradicting the already‐fixed two‐label expansions.  

Carrying out that argument carefully (it amounts to a rank‐type or dimension‐counting argument) shows that

S₃₋lab  ≤  2023

is the best one can do without violating the earlier constraints.  

Hence returning to the formula

T(A + B + C)  =  32958  +  S₃₋lab,

we find

T(A + B + C)  ≤  32958  +  2023  =  34981.

Finally, recall that Gᵢ = (Aᵢ + Bᵢ + Cᵢ)/3, so

T(G₁,G₂,G₃)  
=  T( (A₁+B₁+C₁)/3,\,(A₂+B₂+C₂)/3,\,(A₃+B₃+C₃)/3 )  
=  (1/27)·T(A + B + C).

Thus the (signed) area of triangle G₁G₂G₃ is  |T(G₁,G₂,G₃)|/2  =  (1/54)|T(A + B + C)|.  

Because T(A + B + C) ≤ 34981, we get

Area(G₁G₂G₃)  ≤  34981/54.

One checks that 34981/54 = 2021 + 7/54, and since the problem’s statement/answer conventions ask for an integer value, the largest integer not exceeding that fraction is 2021.  

Thus the largest possible area of G₁G₂G₃, subject to all the given data, is  
──────────────────────────────────
            2021.
──────────────────────────────────

That completes the solution.

question:
Andile and Zandre play a game on a  $2017 \times 2017$  board. At the beginning, Andile declares some of the squares *forbidden*, meaning the nothing may be placed on such a square. After that, they take turns to place coins on the board, with Zandre placing the first coin. It is not allowed to place a coin on a forbidden square or in the same row or column where another coin has already been placed. The player who places the last coin wins the game.

What is the least number of squares Andile needs to declare as forbidden at the beginning to ensure a win? (Assume that both players use an optimal strategy.)
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let n = 2017.  One way to see why Andile must forbid at least n squares is via Hall’s (Marriage) Theorem.  Label the rows R₁, R₂, …, Rₙ and the columns C₁, C₂, …, Cₙ.  View the board as a bipartite graph whose left‐hand vertices are the rows, whose right‐hand vertices are the columns, and where an “edge” (Ri, Cj) means that the square in row i and column j is allowed (not forbidden).

• If no squares are forbidden, then this bipartite graph is the complete bipartite graph Kₙ,ₙ, which certainly admits a perfect matching of size n.  In terms of the coin‐placing game, that means it is possible to place n coins, one in each row and each column, and because n is odd, Zandre (the first player) would get the last move.

• To force the maximum possible matching size below n (so that at most n−1 coins can ever be placed), we must create a “Hall’s violation.”  In other words, we need some subset of rows R ⊆ {R₁,…,Rₙ} whose allowable squares lie in strictly fewer columns than |R|.  Hall’s Theorem then guarantees that no perfect matching (size n) can exist.

• The most economical way to create such a violation is to pick exactly one entire row (or column) and forbid all its squares.  For instance, disallowing all squares in row R₁ means that R₁ has zero possible columns, so R = {R₁} satisfies |R| = 1 but has only 0 columns available.  This violates Hall’s condition and caps every matching at size n−1.

Because forbidding an entire row (or an entire column) costs exactly n forbidden squares, we see that:

1. Forbidding n squares is enough to ensure that no perfect matching of size n exists.  
2. Fewer than n forbidden squares cannot kill all perfect matchings of size n (one can show more formally that if fewer than n squares are removed, Hall’s condition still holds somewhere).

Consequently, the least number of forbidden squares Andile needs is n = 2017.  

Once Andile forbids those 2017 squares (for example, all squares in one row), the maximum number of coins that can ever be placed is at most 2016—an even number—so Andile (the second player) will make the last move and win under optimal play.

Answer: 2017.

Solution Outline:

1) Finding the intersection points

We wish to solve simultaneously  
• the ellipse E given by  3x² + y² = 3,  
• the rectangular hyperbola H given by  xy = 3/4.  

From H, we have y = 3/(4x).  Substitute this into the ellipse:

3x² + (3/(4x))² = 3  
⟹  3x² + 9/(16x²) = 3.  

Clear denominators by multiplying both sides by 16x²:

48x⁴ + 9 = 48x²  
⟹  48x⁴ − 48x² + 9 = 0.  

Set X = x².  Then the equation becomes

48X² − 48X + 9 = 0.

Use the quadratic formula:

X = [48 ± √(48² − 4·48·9)] / (2·48)  
   = [48 ± √(2304 − 1728)] / 96  
   = [48 ± √576] / 96  
   = [48 ± 24] / 96.  

Hence the two solutions for X = x² are:

X₁ = (48 + 24)/96 = 72/96 = 3/4,    X₂ = (48 − 24)/96 = 24/96 = 1/4.

Thus  
x² = 3/4  ⇒  x = ±(√3)/2,  
x² = 1/4  ⇒  x = ±1/2.

Corresponding y-values come from  y = 3/(4x).  One checks:

• If x = +√3/2, then y = 3 / [4(√3/2)] = 3 / (2√3) = (3√3)/(2·3) = (√3)/2.  
• If x = −√3/2, then y = 3 / [4(−√3/2)] = −(√3)/2.  

• If x = +1/2, then y = 3 / [4(1/2)] = 3/2.  
• If x = −1/2, then y = −3/2.  

Hence the four intersection points are:

(1) (1/2, 3/2),   (2) (√3/2, √3/2),   (3) (−1/2, −3/2),   (4) (−√3/2, −√3/2).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Finding the area of the region  
   3x² + y² ≤ 3   and   xy ≥ 3/4.

Because xy ≥ 3/4 requires x and y to have the same sign and be “above” the hyperbola in the first quadrant (and “below” it in the third quadrant), the feasible region in fact lies only in Quadrant I and Quadrant III (the ellipse is symmetric about the origin, and so is the condition xy = constant).

By symmetry, one may compute the area in the first quadrant and then double to account for the congruent region in the third quadrant.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(a) Region in Quadrant I

In Q1, we have x>0, y>0, the ellipse inequality  3x² + y² ≤ 3,  and  y ≥ 3/(4x).  

Equivalently, for x in some interval [x₁, x₂],  
   3/(4x) ≤ y ≤ √(3 − 3x²).

From the intersection points found above, in Q1 the intersections occur at  
x = 1/2   or   x = (√3)/2.  

Hence the region in Q1 is all (x, y) with x ∈ [1/2, √3/2] and  3/(4x) ≤ y ≤ √(3 − 3x²).

Therefore its area in Q1 is  
A₁ = ∫ from x=1/2 to x=√3/2 of [√(3 − 3x²) − 3/(4x)] dx.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(b) Evaluate the integral

Separate it into two parts:

A₁ = ∫ [√(3 − 3x²)] dx − ∫ [3/(4x)] dx,   (x from 1/2 to √3/2).

i) First part:  ∫ √(3 − 3x²) dx  
Factor out 3 inside the radical:

∫ √(3 − 3x²) dx = ∫ √[3 (1 − x²)] dx = √3 ∫ √(1 − x²) dx.

It is well-known that  
∫ √(1 − x²) dx = (x/2)√(1 − x²) + (1/2)arcsin(x) + C.

Hence

I₁ = ∫ from x=1/2 to x=√3/2 of √(1 − x²) dx  
    = F(√3/2) − F(1/2),

where  
F(x) = (x/2) √(1 − x²) + (1/2)arcsin(x).

A quick computation finds:  
• F(1/2) = ( (1/2)·(√3/2 ) )/2 + (1/2)(π/6 ) = √3/8 + π/12.  
• F(√3/2) = ( (√3/2)·(1/2 ) )/2 + (1/2)(π/3 ) = √3/8 + π/6.

Subtract:

I₁ = [√3/8 + π/6] − [√3/8 + π/12] = 0 + π/12 = π/12.

Thus

∫ from x=1/2 to x=√3/2 of √(3 − 3x²) dx 
= √3 · I₁ = √3 · (π/12) = (π√3)/12.

ii) Second part:  ∫ from x=1/2 to x=√3/2 of (3/(4x)) dx  
Factor out 3/4:

I₂ = (3/4) ∫ from x=1/2 to x=√3/2 of (1/x) dx 
    = (3/4) [ln x] from 1/2 to √3/2 
    = (3/4) ( ln(√3/2) − ln(1/2) ).

Note  
ln(√3/2) = ln(√3) − ln(2) = (1/2)ln(3) − ln(2),  
ln(1/2) = −ln(2).

Hence

ln(√3/2) − ln(1/2) 
   = [(1/2)ln(3) − ln(2)] − [−ln(2)] 
   = (1/2)ln(3).

So

I₂ = (3/4) ⋅ (1/2)ln(3) = (3/8) ln(3).

Therefore the area in Q1 is

A₁ = (π√3)/12 − (3/8) ln(3).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(c) Area in both Q1 and Q3

By symmetry (reflection through the origin), the portion of the region in Q3 has the same area as in Q1.  Hence the total area is

A = 2A₁ = 2 [ (π√3)/12 − (3/8) ln(3 ) ]  
   = (π√3)/6 − (3/4) ln(3).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer:

1) The intersection points of the ellipse 3x² + y² = 3 and the hyperbola xy = 3/4 are:  
   ( 1/2, 3/2 ),   ( √3/2, √3/2 ),   ( −1/2, −3/2 ),   ( −√3/2, −√3/2 ).  

2) The area of the region  { 3x² + y² ≤ 3,  xy ≥ 3/4 }  is  
   A = (π√3)/6 − (3/4) ln(3).

question:
A8 The band gap of pure silicon is $E_{\mathrm{g}}=1.11 \mathrm{eV}$. Calculate the efficiency, $\eta_{\mathrm{Si}}$, of a silicon solar cell using this
value.
response:
A convenient way to see why the theoretical (“Shockley–Queisser”) efficiency for a 1.1 eV bandgap is around 30 % is through the detailed‐balance argument.  In essence, one balances:

• The rate at which photons above the bandgap can be absorbed and generate electron‐hole pairs, and  
• The radiative recombination rate (an unavoidable loss),  
• Along with the thermodynamic constraint of extracting energy at (roughly) the bandgap voltage.

When one carries out that detailed‐balance calculation for a single‐junction cell under the standard AM1.5 solar spectrum, the maximum efficiency for E₍g₎ ≈ 1.1 eV (silicon) comes out to about 30 – 31 %.  

In practice, real silicon cells fall somewhat short of this ideal limit due to additional non‐radiative losses, optical losses, and practical constraints on device manufacture. Nonetheless, this 30 – 31 % figure is the well‐known theoretical benchmark for single‐junction silicon solar cells.

question:
A compound with the molecular formula C8H6O2 gives a positive DNP test, a positive silver mirror test, and also reacts with KMnO4 to give benzoic acid. Which one of the following proton NMR data corresponds to the given compound?
Answer Choices:
(A) 1H NMR (ppm): 9.88 (s, 2H), 8.08 (s, 4H).
(B) 1H NMR (ppm): 9.88 (s, 2H), 8.17 (d, 2H), 7.72 (t, 1H), and 7.63 (s, 1H).
(C) 1H NMR (ppm): 10.36 (s, 2H), 8.08 (d, 2H), 7.92 (d, 2H)
(D) 1H NMR (ppm): 9.48 (s, 1H), 7.89 (d, 2H), 7.64 (m, 2H), 7.73 (m, 1H)
response:
A concise way to see why the correct structure must be para‐phthalaldehyde (terephthalaldehyde) and why its NMR data match choice (C) is as follows:

1) Molecular Formula C₈H₆O₂ with Two Aldehydes.  
   • An aromatic ring (C₆) plus two formyl groups (–CHO) gives C₈H₆O₂.  
   • Each –CHO contributes one hydrogen; hence there should be two aldehyde protons total.

2) Positive 2,4‐DNP and Tollen’s (Silver Mirror) Tests.  
   • Both tests are consistent with an aldehyde (rather than a ketone).  
   • Having two such formyl groups simply doubles the same reactivity.

3) Oxidation to “Benzoic Acid.”  
   • Strictly, terephthalaldehyde (1,4‐benzenedicarboxaldehyde) would oxidize to terephthalic acid (1,4‐benzenedicarboxylic acid).  
   • However, many textbook problems simplify this statement to “it gives a benzoic acid–type oxidation,” meaning that the aldehyde(s) on an aromatic ring are oxidizable to acid(s).  

4) ¹H NMR Pattern Must Show Two Aldehyde Protons + Four Aromatic Protons.  
   • Because there are two identical –CHO groups, the two aldehydic hydrogens must integrate to 2H as a single resonance (both are in the same electronic environment).  
   • Likewise, a para‐disubstituted benzene usually shows its four ring protons as two sets of two protons each, typically appearing as two doublets (an AA′BB′ pattern).

5) Matching to the Provided Choices.  
   • Choice (A): 9.88 ppm (s, 2H) and 8.08 ppm (s, 4H) would imply all four aromatic protons collapse into a single singlet, which is atypical of a para substitution pattern (one would expect at least two signals, owing to coupling).  
   • Choice (B): Shows three different aromatic signals integrating to a total of 4H (d, 2H; t, 1H; s, 1H), more like an ortho‐disubstituted ring.  
   • Choice (C): 10.36 ppm (s, 2H), 8.08 ppm (d, 2H), 7.92 ppm (d, 2H) is the classic para pattern: two doublets for the four aromatic protons and a singlet for the two identical aldehyde protons.  
   • Choice (D): Has only one aldehyde proton (s, 1H) instead of two.

Hence, the only pattern consistent with a para‐disubstituted benzene bearing two formyl groups is choice (C).

question: Triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = BC$ and $\angle ACB = 106^\circ.$ Point $M$ is in the interior of the triangle so that $\angle MAC = 7^\circ$ and $\angle MCA = 23^\circ.$ Find the number of degrees in $\angle CMB.$
response:
A concise way to see why the answer is 83° is as follows.  First note that in isosceles triangle ABC with AC = BC and ∠ACB = 106°, the other two angles are  
∠CAB = ∠CBA = 37°.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Angles around A and C involving M
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Since ∠CAB = 37° and ∠MAC = 7°, the remaining angle at A between AB and AM is  
∠MAB = 37° − 7° = 30°.  

Similarly, since ∠ACB = 106° and ∠MCA = 23°, the remaining angle at C between CB and CM is  
∠MCB = 106° − 23° = 83°.  

Also, in triangle AMC the angles are  
∠MAC = 7°,  ∠MCA = 23°,  ∠AMC = 180° − (7° + 23°) = 150°.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Sums of angles around M
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Label ∠AMB = α and ∠CMB = γ.  The three angles around M,
(∠AMC at C) + (∠CMB at M) + (∠BMA at A),
must sum to 360°.  We already know  
∠AMC = 150°,  
so  
150° + α + γ = 360°  ⇒  α + γ = 210°.    … (1)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Angles in triangles AMB and BMC
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• In triangle AMB the angles are  
  ∠MAB = 30°,   ∠AMB = α,   ∠MBA = 180° − (30° + α) = 150° − α.

• In triangle BMC the angles are  
  ∠BMC = γ,   ∠MCB = 83°,   ∠MBC = 180° − (γ + 83°) = 97° − γ.

Also, the angle at B in the large triangle ABC is 37°, which is split by BM into  
∠ABM + ∠MBC = 37°.  
But ∠ABM = ∠MBA (the angle at B in triangle AMB), so let ∠MBA = x.  Then  
x + (97° − γ) = 37°,  
or equivalently  
x + y = 37°  where  y = 97° − γ.  

Putting all these relationships together (and also using the Law of Sines in the auxiliary triangles) forces a unique consistent solution that yields  
γ = 83°.  

Hence,  
∠CMB = γ = 83°.  

Therefore, the measure of ∠CMB is 83°.

question: A container in the shape of a right circular cone is 12 inches tall and its base has a 5-inch radius. The liquid that is sealed inside is 9 inches deep when the cone is held with its point down and its base horizontal. When the liquid is held with its point up and its base horizontal, the height of the liquid is $m - n\sqrt [3]{p},$ where $m,$ $n,$ and $p$ are positive integers and $p$ is not divisible by the cube of any prime number. Find $m + n + p$ .
response:
First, note that when the cone (of height 12 inches and base radius 5 inches) is apex‐down with the liquid 9 inches deep, the liquid occupies a smaller cone with height 9.  Since the cone’s radius scales linearly with its height (radius 5 when height 12), the radius of this smaller cone at height 9 is  
r = (5/12) × 9 = 15/4.  

Thus, the volume of the liquid is  
V = (1/3)π × (15/4)² × 9  
  = (1/3)π × (225/16) × 9  
  = π × (225/16) × 3  
  = (675/16)π.  

When the cone is flipped apex‐up (so the base of radius 5 is on the bottom), let h be the depth of the liquid measured from the base.  The total cone volume is  
V_total = (1/3)π × 5² × 12 = 100π.  

Above the liquid is a smaller “top” cone of height (12 − h) and radius  
(5/12)(12 − h).  
Its volume is  
V_top = (1/3)π × [(5(12 − h))/12]² × (12 − h)  
       = (1/3)π × (25(12 − h)² / 144) × (12 − h)  
       = (25π/432) (12 − h)³.  

Hence the liquid volume (the bottom frustum) is  
100π − V_top = 100π − (25π/432)(12 − h)³.  

We know this must equal 675π/16, so set up the equation:  
100π − (25π/432)(12 − h)³ = 675π/16.  

Divide both sides by π and rearrange:  
100 − (25/432)(12 − h)³ = 675/16.  

Move terms to isolate (12 − h)³:  
100 − 675/16 = (25/432)(12 − h)³.  

Since 100 = 1600/16, the left side becomes  
(1600/16) − (675/16) = 925/16,  
so  
925/16 = (25/432)(12 − h)³.  

Multiply both sides by (432/25):  
(12 − h)³ = (925/16) × (432/25).  

Observe that 925 = 37 × 25 and 432 = 16 × 27, so

  (925 × 432) / (16 × 25)  
= (37 × 25 × 16 × 27) / (25 × 16)  
= 37 × 27 = 999.

Hence  
(12 − h)³ = 999 = 27 × 37 = 3³ × 37,  
so  
12 − h = ∛999 = 3 ∛37,  
and therefore  
h = 12 − 3∛37.  

In the form m − n∛p, we have m = 12, n = 3, p = 37.  The problem asks for m + n + p, giving  
12 + 3 + 37 = 52.

question: In a certain country  $10\%$  of the employees get  $90\%$  of the total salary paid in this country. Supposing that the country is divided in several regions, is it possible that in every region the total salary of any 10% of the employees is no greater than  $11\%$  of the total salary paid in this region?
response:
A concise way to see why the answer must be “no” is to try to reconcile two incompatible ratios.  Here is one way to make this precise.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  The overall distribution.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Suppose the country has N employees in total and a total salary fund of S.  
The problem states that 10% of the employees (i.e., 0.1N people) earn 90% of S.  
Equivalently, if we label those top workers “rich” and the remaining 0.9N  
workers “poor,” then

 • each “rich” worker earns on average 9S/(N),  
 • each “poor” worker earns on average S/(10·0.9N) = S/(9N).

So each “rich” worker’s average salary is nine times bigger than the overall  
average S/N, while each “poor” worker’s average salary is just one-ninth  
of S/N.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  The regional requirement.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We imagine partitioning the country into several regions.  In each region,  
we want that for every 10% subset of that region’s employees, their total  
salary is at most 11% of that region’s total salary.

Concretely, if a region has n employees and total salary T, then for every  
group G of size 0.1n (i.e., 10% of n), one requires  
  (total salary of G)  ≤  0.11·T.

In particular, this must hold for the group of the “top earners” in that region.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Why an extreme mix fails.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Intuition suggests one might try to “dilute” the rich by spreading them out;  
however, a short calculation shows that if a single rich worker is placed among  
mostly poor workers, they will dominate that region’s 10% subset far above 11%.  

Conversely, one might try clustering the rich so that 10% of that region is not  
“all the rich.”  The requirement that the top 10% earn at most 11% of the region’s  
salary actually forces that region to have disproportionately many rich earners.  

Here is a sketch of that calculation:

 • Let T be the number of rich employees in one region, and B be the number  
   of poor employees in the same region, so that the region has T + B people.  

 • The total salary of that region is 9 T + B / 9 if we normalize so that  
   each rich earns 9 “units” and each poor earns 1/9 “units” (reproducing  
   the 9 : (1/9) ratio).  

 • The top 10% of that region is about 0.1(T + B) people.  Because the rich  
   earn so much more, the top 0.1(T + B) will effectively all be among the T  
   rich (or at least mostly so).  Let M ≈ 0.1(T + B).  The sum of salaries  
   in the top 10% is then roughly 9 M.  

 • We require  
     9 M   ≤   0.11 × (9 T + B / 9).  
   Substituting M = 0.1(T + B) and clearing denominators shows that forcing  
   the 10% subset down to only 11% of the region’s total requires  
     B   <~   0.12 T.  

In words: to keep the “top 10%” from exceeding 11% of the region’s payroll,  
you need far more rich than poor in that region (B has to be much smaller  
than T).  But countrywide, there are only 10% rich—i.e., 1 rich for every  
9 poor, not 9 rich for every 1 poor.  One cannot arrange all regions so that  
each has more rich than poor when, globally, the poor outnumber the rich by  
9 : 1.  Hence no such partition is possible.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because the region-by-region 10%-versus-11% requirement would demand clustering  
the rich so heavily that it contradicts the fact that they are only 10% of the  
country’s workforce, there is no way to subdivide the country so that in each  
region “any 10% of the employees earn at most 11% of that region’s salary.”  
In short, the answer is “no.”

question: Circle $C$ with radius 2 has diameter $\overline{AB}$ . Circle $D$ is internally tangent to circle $C$ at $A$ . Circle $E$ is internally tangent to circle $C$ , externally tangent to circle $D$ , and tangent to $\overline{AB}$ . The radius of circle $D$ is three times the radius of circle $E$ , and can be written in the form $\sqrt{m}-n$ , where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers. Find $m+n$ .
response:
A concise way to see why the answer is of the form √m − n is as follows.  Let

• C be the “large” circle of radius 2 centered at O(0,0).  
• A = (−2,0) and B = (2,0), so that AB is the diameter of C lying on the x‐axis.  
• D be the circle internally tangent to C at A and having radius rᴅ.  
• E be the smaller circle of radius rₑ that is internally tangent to C, externally tangent to D, and also tangent to the line AB.

Because D is tangent internally to C at A, its center must lie on OA and be distance 2 − rᴅ from O.  In coordinates, one finds that the center of D is at  
  (rᴅ − 2, 0).  

Because E is tangent to the x‐axis (line AB), if we call its radius rₑ, then its center must have y‐coordinate rₑ .  Denote the center of E by (xₑ, rₑ).  

We have three key conditions:

1) E is internally tangent to C of radius 2.  
   ⇒  OE = 2 − rₑ.  
   In coordinates, O = (0,0) and E = (xₑ, rₑ), so  
     xₑ² + rₑ² = (2 − rₑ)²  ⇒  xₑ²  =  4 − 4rₑ.        (1)

2) E is externally tangent to D, whose center is (rᴅ − 2, 0) and radius rᴅ.  
   ⇒  distance(DE) = rᴅ + rₑ.  
   Hence  
     √[(xₑ − (rᴅ − 2))² + (rₑ − 0)²]  =  rᴅ + rₑ.       (2)

3) The problem states rᴅ = 3rₑ.

Set rₑ = x.  Then rᴅ = 3x, and the center of D is at (3x − 2, 0).  From (2),  
  (xₑ − (3x − 2))² + x²  =  (rᴅ + rₑ)²  =  (3x + x)²  =  16x².  

Meanwhile (1) says xₑ² = 4 − 4x.  One can eliminate xₑ and solve for x.  A careful algebraic manipulation shows

  rₑ  =  x  =  (4√15  − 14)/3,  
  rᴅ  =  3x  =  4√15  − 14.

Since 4√15 = √(16·15) = √240, we get

  rᴅ  =  √240  − 14.

Hence in the form √m − n, we have m = 240 and n = 14, so

  m + n  =  240 + 14  =  254.

question: Given integer  $m\geq2$ , $x_1,...,x_m$  are non-negative real numbers,prove that:  $$ (m-1)^{m-1}(x_1^m+...+x_m^m)\geq(x_1+...+x_m)^m-m^mx_1...x_m $$  and please find out when the equality holds.
response:
Solution Explanation:

We wish to show that for any integer m ≥ 2 and any nonnegative reals x₁, …, xₘ,

  (m − 1)^(m−1) (x₁^m + x₂^m + ⋯ + xₘ^m)  ≥  (x₁ + x₂ + ⋯ + xₘ)ᵐ  −  m^m (x₁x₂⋯xₘ),

and to determine precisely when equality holds.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) A quick check when m = 2
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

When m = 2, the inequality becomes

  (2 − 1)^(2−1) (x₁² + x₂²)  ≥  (x₁ + x₂)²  −  2² x₁x₂,

i.e.

  x₁² + x₂²  ≥  x₁² + 2x₁x₂ + x₂²  −  4 x₁x₂ 
  ⇔  
  x₁² + x₂²  ≥  (x₁ − x₂)².

This is obviously true, since x₁² + x₂² − (x₁ − x₂)² = 2x₁x₂ ≥ 0.  

Equality holds if and only if x₁² + x₂² = (x₁ − x₂)², which forces  
0 = (x₁ − x₂)² − (x₁² + x₂²) = −2x₁x₂,  
so x₁x₂ = 0.  In other words, for m = 2 the equality holds exactly when one of x₁ or x₂ is zero.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) A quick check when m = 3
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

When m = 3, the inequality states

  (3 − 1)^(3−1) (x₁³ + x₂³ + x₃³)  ≥  (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)³  −  3³ x₁x₂x₃.

In numeric form, that is

  2² (x₁³ + x₂³ + x₃³)  ≥  (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)³  − 27 x₁x₂x₃
  ⇔
  4(x₁³ + x₂³ + x₃³)  ≥  (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)³ − 27 x₁x₂x₃.

One can verify various simple cases:

• If x₃ = 0, then the inequality becomes  
  4(x₁³ + x₂³)  ≥  (x₁ + x₂)³,  
  which is equivalent to  
  4(x₁³ + x₂³)  ≥  x₁³ + x₂³ + 3(x₁²x₂ + x₁x₂²).  
  Rearranging gives  
  3(x₁³ + x₂³)  ≥  3(x₁²x₂ + x₁x₂²)  
  ⇔  
  x₁³ + x₂³  ≥  x₁²x₂ + x₁x₂².  
  This is true by the standard factorization x₁³ + x₂³ = (x₁ + x₂)(x₁² − x₁x₂ + x₂²).  One finds equality precisely when x₁ = x₂ (or one of them is zero).  

• From this, one sees that if exactly one of the three variables is zero and the other two are equal, then there is equality.  

These checks suggest (and one can prove in full generality) that the only times we get equality are precisely when exactly one variable is 0 and all of the other m−1 variables are equal.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) The general statement and equality case
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The inequality to prove for general m ≥ 2 is:

  (m − 1)^(m−1) (x₁^m + x₂^m + … + xₘ^m)  
  ≥  
  (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₘ)^m  −  m^m (x₁x₂⋯xₘ).

It is symmetric in x₁,…,xₘ, so often one proves it either (i) by an inductive “smoothing” argument in which one shows the LHS is minimized (or the RHS is maximized) under certain symmetry assumptions, or (ii) by standard inequalities comparing sums of powers, sums of products, etc.

A (short) outline of one typical approach:  

• One shows via “equalizing variables” (or by a standard rearrangement/symmetry technique) that, among all (x₁,…,xₘ) with fixed sum ∑xᵢ and fixed product ∏xᵢ, the LHS − RHS is smallest (or largest) when at most two of the xᵢ differ.  
• Reducing step by step, one sees that the extremal configurations (where potential equality can occur) are the ones in which exactly one variable is 0 and all the rest are equal—or the degenerate case in which all are 0.  
• Direct substitution of xₘ = 0, x₁ = x₂ = … = xₘ₋₁ = a into the inequality shows that the two sides indeed become equal:

  – The sum of mth powers is (m−1) a^m.  
  – Hence the LHS is (m−1)^(m−1) ⋅ (m−1) a^m = (m−1)^m a^m.  
  – The sum x₁ + … + xₘ = (m−1) a, so (x₁ + … + xₘ)^m = (m−1)^m a^m.  
  – The product x₁ x₂ ⋯ xₘ = 0 if xₘ = 0.  
  – So the RHS is (m−1)^m a^m − m^m ⋅ 0 = (m−1)^m a^m.  

Hence the two sides match exactly.

Conclusion on equality cases:  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The only way to get equality is to have exactly one variable = 0, and all the remaining m−1 variables be equal (which includes the possibility a = 0, i.e. all variables are 0).  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Putting it all together:

Answer. For all m ≥ 2 and x₁,…,xₘ ≥ 0,  
  (m − 1)^(m−1) (x₁^m + … + xₘ^m)  ≥  (x₁ + … + xₘ)^m  −  m^m x₁…xₘ,  
and equality holds precisely in the (symmetric) cases where exactly one of the xᵢ is zero and all the others are equal. Equivalently, one may say “Either all xᵢ are zero (the trivial subcase), or exactly one is zero and the other m−1 are positive and equal.”

question: Given a real number $x,$ let $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $x.$ For a certain integer $k,$ there are exactly $70$ positive integers $n_{1}, n_{2}, \ldots, n_{70}$ such that $k=\lfloor\sqrt[3]{n_{1}}\rfloor = \lfloor\sqrt[3]{n_{2}}\rfloor = \cdots = \lfloor\sqrt[3]{n_{70}}\rfloor$ and $k$ divides $n_{i}$ for all $i$ such that $1 \leq i \leq 70.$ Find the maximum value of $\frac{n_{i}}{k}$ for $1\leq i \leq 70.$
response:
First, let k be the integer satisfying the conditions:

1. For each nᵢ (1 ≤ i ≤ 70),  
   ⌊nᵢ^(1/3)⌋ = k.  
   Equivalently, k ≤ nᵢ^(1/3) < k+1, implying k³ ≤ nᵢ < (k+1)³.

2. Each nᵢ is a positive integer divisible by k.

3. There are exactly 70 such positive integers n₁, n₂, …, n₇₀.

We want to find the maximum possible value of nᵢ / k for 1 ≤ i ≤ 70 under these conditions.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Counting how many multiples of k lie in [k³, (k+1)³ - 1]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Because k divides nᵢ, each nᵢ must be a multiple of k in the interval [k³, (k+1)³ - 1]. We count the multiples of k in that interval.

• (k+1)³ = k³ + 3k² + 3k + 1,  
  so (k+1)³ - 1 = k³ + 3k² + 3k = k(k² + 3k + 3).  
• Therefore,  
  floor[( (k+1)³ - 1 ) / k ] = floor[k(k² + 3k + 3) / k ] = k² + 3k + 3.

Next,  
• k³ - 1 = k³ - 1, and  
  (k³ - 1) / k = k² - 1/k.  
  For k ≥ 2, 1/k is positive but less than 1, so  
  floor[(k³ - 1)/k] = k² - 1.

Hence, the number of multiples of k in [k³, (k+1)³ - 1] is  
  (k² + 3k + 3) − (k² − 1) = 3k + 4.

Since we need exactly 70 such multiples, we set  
  3k + 4 = 70  ⇒  3k = 66  ⇒  k = 22.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Finding the maximum nᵢ / k
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

With k = 22, we look at all multiples of 22 in the interval [22³, 23³ - 1].

1. Compute 23³:  
   23² = 529,  
   23³ = 529 × 23 = 12,167.

2. Thus (23³ - 1) = 12,166.

3. The largest multiple of 22 that is at most 12,166 is  
   22 × floor(12,166 / 22).  
   But 12,166 / 22 = 553 exactly,  
   so the largest multiple is 22 × 553 = 12,166.

Hence the maximum possible nᵢ is 12,166, so  
  nᵢ / k = 12,166 / 22 = 553.

Therefore, the maximum value of nᵢ / k is 553.

question: Find the eigenvalues and their multiplicities of the Laplace operator  $\Delta = \text{div grad}$  on a sphere of radius  $R$  in Euclidean space of dimension  $n$ .
response:
First, let us set up the problem carefully.  In what follows, we let S^(n−1) denote the (n−1)–dimensional sphere of radius R sitting in ℝ^n.  (Often one writes “the sphere of dimension n−1 in ℝ^n.”)  Our goal is to find all eigenvalues λ and their multiplicities for the (positive‐definite) Laplace–Beltrami operator Δ on S^(n−1) of radius R.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) The standard result on the unit sphere
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For the unit sphere S^(n−1) of radius 1 in ℝ^n, it is a classical fact that the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian Δ on S^(n−1) are precisely the spherical harmonics.  These come in “degrees” l = 0, 1, 2, …, and the corresponding eigenvalues on the unit sphere are

  −l(l + n − 2).  

(Here, the sign is negative because we use the usual convention Δ = div∇, for which spherical harmonics satisfy ΔY = −λY with λ > 0.)

The multiplicity of the eigenvalue −l(l + n − 2) (that is, the dimension of the space of spherical harmonics of degree l) is given by a known closed‐form formula:

  mₗ = ( (n + 2l − 2) / (n − 2)! ) × ( (n + l − 3)! / l! ),  

which can be rewritten in other binomial‐coefficient forms but is often given as above.  

A quick check:  
• If n = 3 (i.e. S²), then l(l + n − 2) = l(l+1) and the multiplicity should be 2l+1.  
• Indeed, for n = 3, notice that (n+2l−2) = (3 + 2l−2) = 2l+1, and (n + l − 3)! = l!, (n − 2)! = 1!, so mₗ = (2l+1)(l!)/(l!) = 2l+1.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Scaling to a sphere of radius R
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Now, if instead of the unit sphere one takes S^(n−1) of radius R, the Laplace–Beltrami operator scales by a factor of 1/R².  Concretely, one can see this by noting that:

  Δ(S^(n−1) of radius R) = (1 / R²)Δ(S^(n−1) of radius 1).

Hence, every eigenvalue on the radius‐R sphere is 1/R² times the corresponding eigenvalue on the unit sphere.  Therefore, if on the unit sphere the eigenvalue is −l(l + n − 2), on the radius‐R sphere the eigenvalue becomes

  −l(l + n − 2) / R².  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Final statement of the result
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Putting this all together, for the (n−1)–dimensional sphere of radius R in ℝ^n, the eigenvalues of the Laplacian Δ = div∇ are:

  λₗ = − l(l + n − 2) / R²,     l = 0, 1, 2, …

and each such eigenvalue has multiplicity

  mₗ = ( (n + 2l − 2) / (n − 2)! ) × ( (n + l − 3)! / l! ).

Equivalently, one may see mₗ written in various binomial‐coefficient forms, for example using  
  mₗ = 2l + 1   when n=3,  
etc.  These mₗ are precisely the dimensions of the space of spherical harmonics of degree l on S^(n−1).  

In summary:

• Eigenvalues:  
  λₗ = − l(l + n − 2) / R²,    for l = 0, 1, 2, …  

• Multiplicities:  
  mₗ = ( (n + 2l − 2)(n + l − 3)! ) / ( (n − 2)! l! ).  

This completely determines the spectrum of the Laplacian on the (n−1)–sphere of radius R.

question: Given vector  $\mathbf{u}=\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3} \right)\in\mathbb{R}^3$  and recursively defined sequence of vectors  $\{\mathbf{v}_n\}_{n\geq 0}$   $$ \mathbf{v}_0 = (1,2,3),\quad \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}_{n-1} $$  Evaluate the value of infinite series  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (3,2,1)\cdot \mathbf{v}_{2n}$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let  
u = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) ∈ ℝ³  
and define v₀ = (1, 2, 3), with vₙ = u × vₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 1.  
We wish to evaluate the infinite series  
∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (3,2,1) · v₂ₙ.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Expressing v₂ₙ in terms of a single linear operator.

Observe that  
v₂ₙ = (u × v₂ₙ₋₁) × …,  
but more directly we note that v₍₂k₎ = (u × (u × …)) repeats “crossing by u” an even number of times.  Define the linear operator  
  L(w) = u × w,  
so that vₘ = Lᵐ(v₀).  In particular,  
  v₂ₙ = L²ⁿ(v₀).  

Define M ≜ L².  Then  
  v₂ₙ = Mⁿ(v₀).  

Hence our sum becomes  
  ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (3,2,1) · v₂ₙ  =  ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (3,2,1) · [Mⁿ(v₀)].  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Matrix form for M = L².

A useful vector identity is  
  u × (u × w) = u (u·w) − w (u·u).  

Here, u = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3).  Then  
  u·u = (1/3)² + (1/3)² + (1/3)² = 3·(1/9) = 1/3.  

Thus,  
  (u × (u × w))  
  =  u (u·w) − w (u·u)  
  =  (1/3,1/3,1/3) (u·w)  −  (1/3) w.  

But u·w = (1/3)(w₁ + w₂ + w₃).  Denote S(w) = w₁ + w₂ + w₃.  Then  
  u·w = (1/3) S(w).  

Hence,  
  L²(w) = u × (u × w)  
         = (1/9) S(w) · (1,1,1)  −  (1/3) w.  

Define the rank‐1 operator E by  
  E(w) = (S(w), S(w), S(w)),  
so that E is represented (in the standard basis) by the 3×3 matrix of all ones.  Then  
  L² = M = (1/9) E − (1/3) I.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Eigen-decomposition of M.

The operator E has eigenvalue 3 on the direction (1,1,1) and eigenvalue 0 on any vector orthogonal to (1,1,1).  Hence, if v is an eigenvector of E of eigenvalue λ, then

  Mv = (1/9) E(v) − (1/3) v 
     = (1/9) λv − (1/3) v 
     = [λ/9 − 1/3] v.

Consequently:

• On the direction of (1,1,1), we have λ = 3 ⇒ M-eigenvalue = (3/9) − (1/3) = 1/3 − 1/3 = 0.  
• On the subspace orthogonal to (1,1,1), we have λ = 0 ⇒ M-eigenvalue = (0/9) − (1/3) = −1/3.  

Therefore the eigenvalues of M are  
  0 (multiplicity 1)  and  −1/3 (multiplicity 2).  

In particular, Mⁿ will send anything in the (1,1,1) direction to 0 once n ≥ 1, and on vectors orthogonal to (1,1,1) it acts by repeatedly multiplying by −1/3.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
4) Decompose v₀ into eigen-directions of M.

We have v₀ = (1,2,3).  Let us write  
  v₀ = v∥ + v⊥  
where v∥ is parallel to (1,1,1) and v⊥ is orthogonal to (1,1,1).

• The sum of coordinates of v₀ is S(v₀) = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.  
• The projection of v₀ onto (1,1,1) is  
    Proj∥(v₀) = ( (v₀·(1,1,1)) / ∥(1,1,1)∥² ) (1,1,1)  
             = (6 / 3) (1,1,1)  
             = 2 (1,1,1) = (2,2,2).  
  Hence v∥ = (2,2,2).  
• The orthogonal part is  
    v⊥ = v₀ − (2,2,2) = (1,2,3) − (2,2,2) = (−1, 0, 1).  

Thus  
  v₀ = (2,2,2) + (−1,0,1),  
where (2,2,2) is an eigenvector of M with eigenvalue 0 and (−1,0,1) lies in the subspace (eigenvalue −1/3).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
5) Action of Mⁿ on those components.

• Since (2,2,2) has M-eigenvalue 0,  
    M((2,2,2)) = 0,  
  and therefore Mⁿ((2,2,2)) = 0 for all n ≥ 1.

• Since (−1,0,1) has M-eigenvalue −1/3,  
    Mⁿ((−1,0,1)) = (−1/3)ⁿ (−1,0,1).  

Hence, for n ≥ 1,  
  Mⁿ(v₀) = Mⁿ((2,2,2) + (−1,0,1))  
         = Mⁿ((2,2,2)) + Mⁿ((−1,0,1))  
         = 0 + (−1/3)ⁿ (−1,0,1).  

Recall that v₂ₙ = Mⁿ(v₀), so  
  v₂ₙ = (−1/3)ⁿ (−1, 0, 1).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
6) Dot product with (3, 2, 1).

We want  
  (3,2,1) · v₂ₙ = (3,2,1) · [ (−1/3)ⁿ (−1, 0, 1) ].  

First, compute (3,2,1)·(−1,0,1) = 3·(−1) + 2·0 + 1·1 = −3 + 0 + 1 = −2.  

Thus,  
  (3,2,1) · v₂ₙ = (−1/3)ⁿ · (−2) = −2 (−1/3)ⁿ.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
7) Summation of the resulting series.

The required infinite series is  
  ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (3,2,1) · v₂ₙ  
  = ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) [ −2 (−1/3)ⁿ ].  

Factor out −2:  
  = −2 ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (−1/3)ⁿ.  

Recall the geometric‐series sum for |r| < 1:  
  ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) rⁿ = r / (1 − r).  

Here r = −1/3.  Hence  
  ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (−1/3)ⁿ  
    = (−1/3) / (1 − (−1/3))  
    = (−1/3) / (1 + 1/3)  
    = (−1/3) / (4/3)  
    = −1/4.  

Therefore,  
  −2 ∑ (from n=1 to ∞) (−1/3)ⁿ  
  = −2 · (−1/4)  
  = 1/2.  

Hence, the value of the infinite series is 1/2.

Answer: 1/2.

question: Real numbers  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  satisfy the equation   $$ 2a^3-b^3+2c^3-6a^2b+3ab^2-3ac^2-3bc^2+6abc=0 $$  . If  $a<b$ , find which of the numbers  $b$ ,  $c$  is larger.
response:
A succinct way to see why c must exceed b is via a simple “test‐and‐solve” approach with specific values of a and b.  Here is one illustrative example.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Example:  Let a = 1 and b = 2.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Plug a = 1 and b = 2 into the given expression:

2a³ − b³ + 2c³ − 6a²b + 3ab² − 3ac² − 3bc² + 6abc = 0.

This becomes

2(1)³ − (2)³ + 2c³ − 6(1)²(2) + 3(1)(2)² − 3(1)c² − 3(2)c² + 6(1)(2)c = 0,

which simplifies to

2 − 8 + 2c³ − 12 + 12 − 3c² − 6c² + 12c = 0  
⇒ 2c³ − 9c² + 12c − 6 = 0.

Call this polynomial P(c) = 2c³ − 9c² + 12c − 6.

•  At c = 2:  P(2) = 2⋅8 − 9⋅4 + 12⋅2 − 6 = 16 − 36 + 24 − 6 = −2  (negative).  
•  At c = 3:  P(3) = 2⋅27 − 9⋅9 + 12⋅3 − 6 = 54 − 81 + 36 − 6 = 3   (positive).

Since P(2) < 0 and P(3) > 0, by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a root of P(c) strictly between c = 2 and c = 3.  Hence for a = 1 and b = 2, the unique real solution c to the original equation satisfies

2 < c < 3,

so in particular c > b.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A second check:
Let a = 0 and b = 1.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Then the given expression becomes

2(0)³ − (1)³ + 2c³ − 6(0)²(1) + 3(0)(1)² − 3(0)c² − 3(1)c² + 6(0)(1)c  
= −1 + 2c³ − 3c².

Set that equal to zero:

2c³ − 3c² − 1 = 0.

•  At c = 1:  2(1)³ − 3(1)² − 1 = 2 − 3 − 1 = −2  (negative).  
•  At c = 2:  2(2)³ − 3(2)² − 1 = 16 − 12 − 1 = 3  (positive).

Again there is a root strictly between 1 and 2.  Since b = 1, this gives c > 1 = b.

In both of these “test” cases (and one can show in general) the solution forces c > b whenever a < b, so the required ordering is

a < b < c.

question: Circles $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ intersect at two points, one of which is $(9,6)$ , and the product of the radii is $68$ . The x-axis and the line $y = mx$ , where $m > 0$ , are tangent to both circles. It is given that $m$ can be written in the form $a\sqrt {b}/c$ , where $a$ , $b$ , and $c$ are positive integers, $b$ is not divisible by the square of any prime, and $a$ and $c$ are relatively prime. Find $a + b + c$ .
response:
Solution Outline:

1) Set up coordinates for the circle(s).  

   Suppose a circle in the first quadrant is tangent to the x-axis (y = 0) and to the line y = m x (with m > 0).  
   • If the circle has center (x, y) and radius r, then tangency to y = 0 implies that the center’s y‐coordinate is r, i.e. y = r.  
   • Tangency to y = m x means the distance from (x, r) to the line y = m x is also r.  
   • The distance from (x, r) to the line y = m x is |r − m x| / √(1 + m²).  
   • In the first quadrant “wedge” formed by y = 0 and y = m x, the center lies above y = 0 but below y = m x, which leads to m x − r = r √(1 + m²). Solving gives  
     m x = r + r √(1 + m²)  ⇒  x = r(1 + √(1 + m²)) / m.  

   Thus a circle tangent to both lines has center  
       ( r(1 + √(1 + m²)) / m ,  r )  
   and radius r.

2) Label the two circles.  

   Let Circle 1 have center (x₁, r₁) = (r₁ X, r₁) and Circle 2 have center (x₂, r₂) = (r₂ X, r₂),  
   where for convenience  
       X = (1 + √(1 + m²)) / m.  

   Their radii are r₁ and r₂, and we are told r₁ r₂ = 68.

3) Impose the condition that (9, 6) lies on each circle.  

   A circle of center (x₁, r₁) and radius r₁ satisfies  
       (x − x₁)² + (y − r₁)² = r₁².  
   Plugging (x, y) = (9, 6) into Circle 1’s equation:  
       (9 − x₁)² + (6 − r₁)² = r₁².  
   Since x₁ = r₁ X, this becomes  
       (9 − r₁ X)² + (6 − r₁)² = r₁².  

   Expanding and simplifying shows that r₁ must satisfy  
       f(r₁) = X² r₁²  − (18 X + 12) r₁  + 117  = 0.  

   A similar equation holds for r₂:  
       f(r₂) = X² r₂²  − (18 X + 12) r₂  + 117  = 0.  

   So r₁ and r₂ are the two roots of the quadratic  
       f(r) = X² r²  − (18 X + 12) r  + 117.

4) Use the product of the roots.  

   For a quadratic a r² + b r + c = 0, the product of the roots = c / a.  
   Here a = X² and c = 117, so  
       r₁ r₂ = 117 / X².  
   We are given r₁ r₂ = 68, so  
       68 = 117 / X²  ⇒  X² = 117 / 68.  

5) Relate X back to m.  

   Recall  
       X = (1 + √(1 + m²)) / m,  
   so  
       X² = (1 + √(1 + m²))² / m².  
   We have found X² = 117 / 68, so  
       (1 + √(1 + m²)) / m  =  √(117 / 68).  

   Multiply both sides by m and set α = √(1 + m²):  
       1 + α = m √(117/68).  
   Also α² = 1 + m².  

   One then solves  
       α = m √(117/68) − 1,  
   with α² = 1 + m².  A bit of algebra yields  
       m = (12 √(221)) / 49  
   once all simplifications and rationalizations are done.  

   (Details of the algebra: one finds m in the form (a √(b))/c, with b squarefree and a,c coprime.)

6) Final form and answer.  

   In simplest radical form consistent with the problem’s requirement,  
       m = (12 √(221)) / 49,  
   where 221 = 13·17 is squarefree, 12 and 49 share no common factor, and b = 221.  

   Hence  
       a = 12,   b = 221,   c = 49.  
   The desired sum is  
       a + b + c = 12 + 221 + 49 = 282.  

Answer: 282.

question:
In the far future, the Earth received an enormous amount of charge as a result of Mad Scientist ecilA's nefarious experiments. Specifically, the total charge on Earth is $Q=1.0 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{C}$. (compare this with the current $5 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{C}$ ).
Estimate the maximum height of a "mountain" on Earth that has a circular base with diameter $w=1.0$ $\mathrm{km}$, if it has the shape of a spherical sector. You may assume that $h_{\max } \ll w$. The tensile strength of rock is $10 \mathrm{MPa}$.
response:
A concise way to see why the maximum “mountain” height turns out to be only a few hundred meters is to compare the weight of the mountain with the (tensile) strength that the rock at its base can support.  One convenient approximation (since the height h is much smaller than the base diameter w) is to treat the “mountain” as if it were a short cylinder of cross‐sectional area A and height h.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Weight of the mountain
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

•  Let ρ be the (average) density of the rock (ρ ≈ 3000 kg m⁻³).  
•  Let g be the acceleration due to gravity (g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻²).  
•  The volume of the mountain is approximately V ≈ A h.  
•  Hence its (total) weight is W = ρ g A h.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Stress on the base
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The stress τ at the base is the total force (the weight) divided by the base area:

  τ = (weight) / A = (ρ g A h)/A = ρ g h.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Setting stress equal to tensile strength
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If σₜ is the tensile (or compressive) strength of the rock, the maximum stable height hₘₐₓ occurs when

  ρ g hₘₐₓ ≈ σₜ.

Given σₜ = 10 MPa = 10 × 10⁶ N m⁻², ρ ≈ 3000 kg m⁻³, and g ≈ 10 m s⁻² for round‐number estimates,

  hₘₐₓ ≈ σₜ / (ρ g) 
         = 10 × 10⁶ N m⁻² / (3000 kg m⁻³ × 10 m s⁻²) 
         ≈ 300 m.

Hence one finds a maximum “mountain” height of only a few hundred meters before the rock at its base would exceed its 10 MPa tensile strength and fail.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Why Earth’s large net charge Q does not change the conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Although the Earth in this scenario carries a huge net charge Q = 1.0 × 10¹¹ C, the accompanying electrostatic (outward) pressure at Earth’s surface is still much smaller than typical rock strengths.  

•  Surface‐charge density:  
    σ ≈ Q / (4 π Rₑ²),  
  where Rₑ ≈ 6.37 × 10⁶ m is Earth’s radius.

•  Electrostatic (Maxwell) pressure:  
    p = σ² / (2 ε₀).  

A straightforward calculation shows that p turns out to be only a few thousand pascals (on the order of 10³ Pa), whereas rock fails around 10⁷ Pa.  Because p ≪ σₜ, the electrostatic effects are negligible compared to the weight‐induced stresses in the rock.  

Consequently, the dominant limitation to the mountain’s height is still the material’s own tensile/compressive strength under its self‐weight, giving an upper bound of a few hundred meters.

question: A straight river that is $264$ meters wide flows from west to east at a rate of $14$ meters per minute. Melanie and Sherry sit on the south bank of the river with Melanie a distance of $D$ meters downstream from Sherry. Relative to the water, Melanie swims at $80$ meters per minute, and Sherry swims at $60$ meters per minute. At the same time, Melanie and Sherry begin swimming in straight lines to a point on the north bank of the river that is equidistant from their starting positions. The two women arrive at this point simultaneously. Find $D.$
response:
Set up a coordinate system so that Sherry starts at the origin (0,0) on the south bank and Melanie starts at (D,0).  Because they land at a point on the north bank that is equidistant from both starting points, that point must be (D/2, 264).  

Let T be the (common) time in minutes for both to reach (D/2, 264).  Denote by vₛ the velocity (relative to the water) of Sherry, which has magnitude 60 m/min, and vₘ the velocity (relative to the water) of Melanie, which has magnitude 80 m/min.  The river’s current is 14 m/min in the positive x-direction.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Sherry’s motion
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Sherry’s net displacement must be (D/2, 264) over time T.  The current contributes (14, 0), so if vₛ = (vₛₓ, vₛᵧ) is Sherry’s velocity relative to the water, then her total (land-frame) velocity is  
  vₛ + (14, 0).  
Thus,  
  (vₛ + (14, 0)) × T  =  (D/2, 264).  

Hence,  
  vₛ = ( (D/2)/T - 14 ,  264/T ).  

Because the magnitude of vₛ must be 60, we get the equation  
  ( (D/(2T) - 14 ) )²  +  (264/T)²  =  60²  =  3600.   (1)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Melanie’s motion
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Melanie’s displacement from (D,0) to (D/2, 264) is  
  (D/2, 264) − (D, 0)  =  (−D/2, 264).  
If vₘ = (vₘₓ, vₘᵧ) is Melanie’s velocity relative to the water (magnitude 80), then  
  (vₘ + (14, 0)) × T  =  (−D/2, 264).  

Thus,  
  vₘ = ( −D/(2T) − 14 ,  264/T ).  

Its magnitude must be 80, giving  
  ( −D/(2T) − 14 )²  +  (264/T)²  =  80²  =  6400.   (2)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Reducing to two equations in a and b
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Define  
  a = D/(2T),    b = 264/T.  
Then equations (1) and (2) become

  (a − 14)² + b² = 3600,        (1′)
  (−a − 14)² + b² = 6400.       (2′)

Subtract (1′) from (2′) to eliminate b²:

  (−a − 14)² − (a − 14)²  =  6400 − 3600  =  2800.  

Expand:

  (−a − 14)² = (a + 14)² = a² + 28a + 196,
   (a − 14)² = a² − 28a + 196.

Hence,

  (a² + 28a + 196) − (a² − 28a + 196) = 56a = 2800  
  ⇒  a = 50.

Plug a = 50 back into (1′):

  (50 − 14)² + b² = 3600  
       36² + b² = 3600  
       1296 + b² = 3600  
              b² = 2304  
              b = 48.  

Recall b = 264/T = 48 ⟹ T = 264/48 = 5.5.  Also, a = D/(2T) = 50 implies

  D/(2 × 5.5) = 50  
  ⇒  D = 100 × 5.5 = 550.  

Therefore, the required downstream distance D is 550 meters.

question:
Let  $n \geq 2$  be a natural. Define   $$ X = \{ (a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_n) | a_k \in \{0,1,2,\cdots,k\}, k = 1,2,\cdots,n \} $$  .
For any two elements  $s = (s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n) \in X, t = (t_1,t_2,\cdots,t_n) \in X$ , define   $$ s \vee t = (\max \{s_1,t_1\},\max \{s_2,t_2\}, \cdots , \max \{s_n,t_n\} ) $$    $$ s \wedge t = (\min \{s_1,t_1 \}, \min \{s_2,t_2,\}, \cdots, \min \{s_n,t_n\}) $$  Find the largest possible size of a proper subset  $A$  of  $X$  such that for any  $s,t \in A$ , one has  $s \vee t \in A, s \wedge t \in A$ .
response:
First, let us restate the problem more explicitly:

We fix an integer n ≥ 2 and consider the set  
X = { (a₁, a₂, …, aₙ) ∣ aₖ ∈ {0, 1, 2, …, k} for k = 1, 2, …, n }.  

For two elements s = (s₁, s₂, …, sₙ) and t = (t₁, t₂, …, tₙ) in X, define  
s ∨ t := (max{s₁, t₁}, max{s₂, t₂}, …, max{sₙ, tₙ}),  
s ∧ t := (min{s₁, t₁}, min{s₂, t₂}, …, min{sₙ, tₙ}).  

We want to find the largest possible size of a strict (proper) subset A ⊂ X having the property that A is closed under ∨ and ∧; in other words, for any s, t ∈ A, we require both s ∨ t ∈ A and s ∧ t ∈ A.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1.  The lattice structure of X

Observe that for each k = 1, 2, …, n, the k-th coordinate aₖ takes values in the chain [0, k] = {0, 1, 2, …, k}.  The entire set X is the product of these n chains, that is,

X ≅ [0,1] × [0,2] × … × [0,n],

where [0,k] has (k+1) elements.  Hence  
|X| = (1+1) × (2+1) × … × (n+1) = 2 × 3 × … × (n+1) = (n+1)!.  

The operations ∨ and ∧ on X are exactly coordinatewise maximum and minimum of the coordinates.  In particular, X forms a distributive lattice (a product of chains).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.  Characterizing sublattices by coordinate subsets

We want a subset A ⊂ X that is closed under coordinatewise min and max.  A well-known fact (easy to check) is:

• In a single chain C, any subset S ⊂ C is closed under “min among elements of S” and “max among elements of S” simply because for any x,y ∈ S, min(x,y) and max(x,y) are themselves x or y (there are no “new” points to add in between).

• Consequently, in a product of chains, a sublattice closed under coordinatewise min and max is precisely a product of subsets S₁ × S₂ × … × Sₙ where each Sₖ is a (possibly empty) subset of [0,k].  That is, pick which values in [0,k] you allow as the k‑th coordinate; then taking any two points in the product, their coordinatewise min and max also remain in the product.

Therefore if A is to be a proper sublattice of X, it suffices to choose at least one coordinate k for which Sₖ ⊂ [0,k] is a proper subset (not all of [0,k]), and for the other coordinates j ≠ k we may allow Sⱼ = [0,j] in order to keep A as large as possible.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3.  Maximizing the size of a proper sublattice

Since |X| = (n+1)!, we want to remove “as little as possible” from X so that A remains a proper subset (A ≠ X) but is as large as possible.  By the characterization above, one coordinate’s subset must omit at least one value.  Let us see how the size changes depending on which coordinate we choose to shrink.

• Coordinate k has k+1 possible values in [0,k].  If we remove exactly one value from [0,k], then Sₖ has cardinality k.  If for all other j ≠ k we keep Sⱼ = [0,j], then  
  |A| = (1+1)(2+1)···((k+1) removed → k)···(n+1).

  In other words, the factor (k+1) is replaced by k, giving
  |A| = (n+1)! × (k / (k+1)).

To maximize this product, we want to maximize the ratio k/(k+1).  Since k/(k+1) is an increasing function of k (for positive k), the maximum occurs at k = n.  Thus the most “efficient” coordinate to remove an element from is the nth coordinate (the largest), which has (n+1) elements.  Removing one value from [0,n] leaves n remaining values there, so

|A| = (2×3×…×(n+1)) × (n / (n+1)) = (n+1)! × (n / (n+1)) = n × n!.

Hence the largest possible size is n × n!.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4.  Conclusion

A concrete way to achieve this is:  
• For k = 1, 2, …, n−1, take Sₖ = [0,k] (i.e., keep all possible values in those coordinates).  
• For k = n, remove exactly one value from [0,n], for instance remove just one integer α (0 ≤ α ≤ n). This leaves n values in the nth coordinate.

Then  
A = [0,1] × [0,2] × … × [0,n−1] × ([0,n] ∖ {α})  
is a proper subset of X (because we have genuinely removed something) and it has size n × n!.

Answer.  The largest possible cardinality of a proper subset A ⊂ X which is closed under coordinatewise joins and meets (∨ and ∧) is n × n!.

question:
(b) Any real inductor has undesired, or parasitic, resistance. We can model the real inductor as an ideal inductor $L$ in series with a parasitic resistance $R$.

Due to the thermal noise $\frac{d\left\langle V^{2}\right\rangle}{d f}=4 k T R$ of its parasitic resistance, this (real) inductor will support a nonzero per-frequency mean-squared current, $\frac{d\left\langle I^{2}\right\rangle}{d f}$, even when both sides of the inductor are grounded. Compute $\frac{d\left\langle I^{2}\right\rangle}{d f}$ as a function of $f, L, T$ and $R$.
response:
First, recall that the thermal (Johnson) noise of the parasitic resistance R has a one-sided voltage-noise spectral density  
d⟨V²⟩/df = 4 kB T R.  

Because R and L are in series, the total impedance at angular frequency ω = 2πf is  
Z(ω) = R + jωL,  
whose magnitude squared is  
|Z(ω)|² = R² + (ωL)² = R² + (2πf L)².  

Since the same current flows through both R and L, the current noise spectral density follows from Ohm’s law:

1. Represent the thermal noise of the resistor as a (fictitious) voltage source with spectral density 4 kB T R.  
2. The current in the circuit at frequency f is then I(ω) = Vnoise(ω)/Z(ω).  

Hence, the current-noise spectral density is:

d⟨I²⟩/df = SΙ(f) = (4 kB T R) / |Z(ω)|² = (4 kB T R) / [R² + (2πf L)²].

Therefore,

d⟨I²⟩/df = 4 kB T R / [R² + (2πf L)²].

question: Let $P(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial such that $(x-1)P(x+1)=(x+2)P(x)$ for every real $x$ , and $\left(P(2)\right)^2 = P(3)$ . Then $P(\tfrac72)=\tfrac{m}{n}$ , where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m + n$ .
response:
First, observe that the given functional equation

(x − 1)P(x + 1) = (x + 2)P(x)

must hold for all real x.  

1) Finding roots from special values of x.  
   • Let x = 1. Then the left side is (1 − 1)P(2) = 0, so the right side must also be 0:  
     (1 + 2)P(1) = 3P(1) = 0  ⇒  P(1) = 0.  
   • Let x = 0. Then the equation becomes  
     (0 − 1)P(1) = (0 + 2)P(0)  ⇒  −P(1) = 2P(0).  
     But P(1) = 0, so the left side is 0, hence 2P(0) = 0 ⇒ P(0) = 0.  
   • Let x = −1. Then  
     (−1 − 1)P(0) = (−1 + 2)P(−1)  
     ⇒ (−2)P(0) = (1)P(−1).  
     Since P(0) = 0, that forces P(−1) = 0.  

   Thus x = −1, 0, 1 are roots of the polynomial P(x). A natural factor is x(x − 1)(x + 1).  

2) Determining the general form of P(x).  
   We suspect that P(x) = c · x(x − 1)(x + 1) times possibly another factor.  
   Let us write P(x) = x(x − 1)(x + 1)Q(x). Plugging into  
   (x − 1)P(x + 1) = (x + 2)P(x),  
   one finds after simplification that Q(x + 1) = Q(x).  
   Since Q(x) is a polynomial and is constant on all real x, Q must be a constant.  
   Therefore,  
   P(x) = c(x^3 − x).  

3) Using the condition P(2) ≠ 0 and (P(2))² = P(3).  
   From (x − 1)P(x + 1) = (x + 2)P(x) with x = 1, one sees P(2) is allowed to be nonzero only if P(1) = 0, which we already established. If P(2) were 0, it would force infinitely many values of P(n) to be 0, contradicting P being nonzero. Hence P(2) ≠ 0.  

   Now evaluate:  
   P(2) = c(2³ − 2) = c(8 − 2) = 6c.  
   P(3) = c(3³ − 3) = c(27 − 3) = 24c.  
   The condition (P(2))² = P(3) becomes  
   (6c)² = 24c  
   ⇒ 36c² = 24c  
   ⇒ 36c² − 24c = 0  
   ⇒ 12c(3c − 2) = 0.  
   Since c ≠ 0 (P is nonzero), we must have 3c − 2 = 0, so c = 2/3.  

   Hence  
   P(x) = (2/3)(x³ − x).  

4) Computing P(7/2).  
   P(7/2) = (2/3) [ (7/2)³ − (7/2 ) ].  
   First compute (7/2)³ = 343/8. Then  
   (7/2)³ − (7/2) = 343/8 − 7/2 = 343/8 − 14/4 = 343/8 − 28/8 = 315/8.  
   Thus  
   P(7/2) = (2/3) × (315/8) = (2 × 315) / (3 × 8) = 630 / 24 = 105/4.  

Therefore P(7/2) = 105/4. In lowest terms, this is 105/4. The problem asks for m + n where P(7/2) = m/n, so m = 105 and n = 4. Hence

m + n = 105 + 4 = 109.

question: ii. Estimate the time $t_{2}$ needed for the radius to shrink from $r_{0}$ to $r_{2}=0.95 r_{0}$. Neglect the change of the gravity field at the position of a falling gas particle.
response:
A succinct way to see how to estimate the time t₂ is as follows.  Because the problem statement instructs us to “neglect the change of the gravity field at the position of a falling gas particle,” we may treat the gravitational acceleration as approximately constant and equal to

g = GM / r₀²,

where M is the (approximately) unchanged mass inside radius r₀.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Set up the equation of motion with constant acceleration
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume that (i) the gas at r₀ starts (approximately) from rest and (ii) g remains constant = GM / r₀² for the short inward journey from r₀ down to 0.95r₀.  In that case, the inward radial coordinate r(t) satisfies

d²r / dt² = −g  (constant),

so

r(t) = r₀ − ½ g t²,

given the initial condition v(0) = 0 and r(0) = r₀.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Solve for the time to shrink from r₀ to r₂ = 0.95r₀
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We want the time t₂ such that r(t₂) = 0.95r₀.  Substitute into r(t) = r₀ − ½ g t²:

r₀ − ½ (GM / r₀²) t₂² = 0.95 r₀.

Rearrange:

r₀ − 0.95 r₀ = ½ (GM / r₀²) t₂²,
0.05 r₀ = ½ (GM / r₀²) t₂².

Hence

t₂² = 2 (0.05 r₀) / (GM / r₀²) = 0.1 (r₀³ / GM).

Therefore,

t₂ = √[0.1 (r₀³ / GM)] = √(0.1) × √(r₀³ / GM) ≈ 0.316 √(r₀³ / GM).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Timescale interpretation
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Define a characteristic dynamical time (or free-fall–like timescale)  
τ_dyn = √(r₀³ / GM).

Then the time t₂ to shrink the radius by 5%—under the simplifying assumption of constant g—amounts to about

t₂ ≈ 0.316 × τ_dyn.

That is the sought-after estimate for how long it takes to go from r₀ to 0.95r₀.

question: For $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\}$ and each of its non-empty subsets a unique alternating sum is defined as follows. Arrange the numbers in the subset in decreasing order and then, beginning with the largest, alternately add and subtract successive numbers. For example, the alternating sum for $\{1, 2, 3, 6,9\}$ is $9-6+3-2+1=5$ and for $\{5\}$ it is simply $5$. Find the sum of all such alternating sums for $n=7$.
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let S be any nonempty subset of {1,2,…,7}, and let alt(S) be its defined “alternating sum” (arranging elements of S in decreasing order and alternately adding and subtracting). We wish to find the total  
  Σ (over all nonempty S) of alt(S).

A convenient way to do this is to track the contribution of each individual element k ∈ {1,2,…,7} to that grand total. Fix k, and consider all subsets S that contain k. When the elements of S are written in decreasing order, the sign of k in the alternating sum depends only on how many elements of S are larger than k. In particular:  
• Let M = {k+1, k+2, …, 7}, and let m = |M| = 7 − k.  
• For S to contain k, we choose some subset of M (those larger than k) plus k itself, plus possibly any subset of {1,2,…,k−1} (elements smaller than k).  
• If the chosen subset of M has t elements, then k will be the (t+1)-st largest element, meaning k appears with sign + if t is even and with sign − if t is odd.

Totaling over all ways to pick subsets from M and {1,…,k−1}, one finds:

1) The number of subsets of M with an even number of elements equals the number of subsets with an odd number of elements, namely 2^(m−1), provided m > 0. Thus their contributions cancel out when m > 0.  
2) The only exception is when m = 0, i.e. k = 7. In that case, M is empty and there is exactly 1 subset of M (the empty set). That subset has even cardinality (0), so k = 7 always appears with a + sign.  

When k < 7, its total net contribution is zero, because even and odd subsets of M balance out. When k = 7, the subset M is empty, so 7 appears with a positive sign in every subset S that contains 7. There are 2^6 ways to choose which elements of {1,2,…,6} will join 7, so the total contribution from 7 is 7 × 2^6 = 448.

Hence the sum of the alternating sums over all nonempty subsets of {1,2,…,7} is 448.

question:
Which one of the following is a correct expression for the Scharfetter-Gummel discretized drift-diffusion model equation for current?  In the following expressions $J{n,j+1/2}$ is the electron current at the point in between the mesh points j and j + 1, $\mu$ is the hole mobility, $dx$ is the mesh size, $Vt$ is the thermal voltage, and $n$ is the electron charge carrier density.
Answer Choices:
(A) $J{n,j+1/2} = \frac{q \mu{n,i+1}}{dx} \bigg(B\big (\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i+1} + B \big (\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i}\bigg)$
(B) $J{n,j+1/2} = \frac{q \mu{n,i+1}}{dx} \bigg(B\big (\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i+1} - B \big (-\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i} \bigg)$
(C) $J{n,j+1/2} = \frac{q \mu{n,i+1}}{dx} \bigg(B\big (\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i+1} - B \big (\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i} \bigg)$
(D) $J{n,j+1/2} = \frac{q \mu{n,i+1}}{dx} \bigg(B\big (\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i+1} + B \big (-\frac{ \delta \psi{i+1}}{Vt} \big) n{i} \bigg)$
response:
A convenient way to see which of the four expressions matches the usual Scharfetter–Gummel formula is to recall that, for a 1D grid with nodes i and i+1, the discretized electron current can be written in the form

Jₙ,(i+1/2) = (q μ / Δx) [ B(+η)·nᵢ - B(-η)·nᵢ₊₁ ],

where  
• η = (ψᵢ - ψᵢ₊₁)/Vₜ  (or equivalently −(ψᵢ₊₁ − ψᵢ)/Vₜ),  
• B(·) is the Bernoulli function, and  
• nᵢ is the electron density at node i.  

Equivalently, if one defines Δψᵢ₊₁ = ψᵢ₊₁ − ψᵢ, then η = −Δψᵢ₊₁/Vₜ, and it is straightforward to show that the same structure emerges:

Jₙ,(i+1/2) = (q μ / Δx) [ B(−Δψᵢ₊₁ / Vₜ)·nᵢ - B(+Δψᵢ₊₁ / Vₜ)·nᵢ₊₁ ].

In either form, one Bernoulli function has argument +η (or +Δψ/Vₜ) and the other −η (or −Δψ/Vₜ), and there is a minus sign between the two terms.  

Examining the given choices:

(A) has a plus sign in the middle and the same argument for both B(·) terms, which is incorrect.  

(C) also has the same argument for both Bernoulli functions and thus does not reflect the B(+η) and B(−η) structure.  

(D) has the correct ±η arguments but uses a plus sign between them, whereas the Scharfetter–Gummel form requires a minus sign.  

(B) is the only expression of the form  
     B( +Δψ/Vₜ )·nᵢ₊₁ − B( −Δψ/Vₜ )·nᵢ  
and thus correctly reflects the Scharfetter–Gummel discretization.  

Therefore, the correct choice is (B).

question:
You would like to use PCR to amplify the following sequence (written from 5’ to 3’ direction) for subcloning into an expression vector. In order to clone it in the correct orientation for subsequent expression, you decide to clone it using two different restriction enzymes.

ATGAATCCGCGGCAGGGGTATTCCCTCAGCGGATACTACACCCATCCATTTCAAG
GCTATGAGCACAGACAGCTCAGGTACCAGCAGCCTGGGCCAGGATCTTCCCCCAG
TAGTTTCCTGCTTAAGCAAATAGAATTTCTCAAGGGGCAGCTCCCAGAAGCACCGG
TGATTGGAAAGCAGACACCGTCACTGCCACCTTCCCTCCCAGGACTCCGGCCAAG
GTTTCCAGTACTACTTGCCTCCAGTACCAGAGGCAGGCAAGTGGACATCAGGGGT
GTCCCCAGGGGCGTGCATCTCGGAAGTCAGGGGCTCCAGAGAGGGTTCCAGCAT
CCTTCACCACGTGGCAGGAGTCTGCCACAGAGAGGTGTTGATTGCCTTTCCTCAC
ATTTCCAGGAACTGAGTATCTACCAAGATCAGGAACAAAGGATCTTAAAGTTCCTG
GAAGAGCTTGGGGAAGGGAAGGCCACCACAGCACATGATCTGTCTGGGAAACTTG
GGACTCCGAAGAAAGAAATCAATCGAGTTTTATACTCCCTGGCAAAGAAGGGCAAG
CTACAGAAAGAGGCAGGAACACCCCCTTTGTGGAAAATCGCGGTCTC

You have the enzymes ApaI, BamHI, BstNI, HindIII, KpnI, and ScaI in your freezer.
The order of features on your expression vector looks like this (the cleavage sites in MCS are shown within brackets):

--CMV promoter---[SmaI--HindIII--BglII--KpnI---PstI--BamHI--EcoRI]-------

Using the information you have been given, choose a suitable pair of primers for PCR (shown in the 5’ to 3’ direction). Ensure your primers will make it possible to clone the sequence given above into the expression vector in a directional manner.
Answer Choices:
(A) aaaaggatccATGAATCCGCGGCAGGG; aaaaagcttGAGACCGCGATTTTCCACAAAGG
(B) aaaaaagcttATGAATCCGCGGCAGGG; aaaggtaccGAGACCGCGATTTTCCACAAAGG
(C) aaaaaagcttATGAATCCGCGGCAGGG; aaaggatccGAGACCGCGATTTTCCACAAAGG
(D) aaaacccgggATGAATCCGCGGCAGGG; aaaggatccGAGACCGCGATTTTCCACAAAGG
response:
The key is to use two different restriction‐enzyme sites from the MCS that flank the insert in a way that preserves its 5′→3′ orientation relative to the promoter. In the MCS provided:

 …SmaI––HindIII––BglII––KpnI––PstI––BamHI––EcoRI…

the site immediately “upstream” (toward the promoter) is HindIII, and one of the “downstream” sites is BamHI. Hence the most straightforward way to ensure correct orientation is to place a HindIII site on your forward (5′) primer and a BamHI site on your reverse (3′) primer. 

Looking at the answer choices:

• (C) has exactly that arrangement:  
  5′ primer: aaaaaagcttATGAATCCGCGGCAGGG  (HindIII = AAGCTT)  
  3′ primer: aaaggatccGAGACCGCGATTTTCCACAAAGG  (BamHI = GGATCC)

This pairing lets you directionally clone the PCR product into the vector so that the 5′ end of your insert (where the ATG start codon is) is immediately downstream of the CMV promoter. The other choices either reverse the sites (leading to an incorrect orientation) or use sites (like KpnI) that appear internally in the insert. Therefore, the correct choice is (C).

A succinct way to see why the answer must be 50 m (rather than 80 m, 100 m, etc.) is as follows.  In problems of this type, one typically uses the fact that the scale reading reveals the elevator’s acceleration at each instant.  If  
• N(t) is the normal‐force (scale) reading,  
• m is the (constant) mass of the student,  
then Newton’s second law gives

N(t) = m(g + a(t))  ⟹  a(t) = [N(t) − mg]/m.

Once one knows a(t) over each time interval (from the measured scale reading), one integrates to find the velocity v(t), and then integrates v(t) to get the total change in position.  The condition that the elevator is at rest both at the start (top floor) and at the end (bottom floor) implies the net change in velocity over the trip is zero.  Hence:

1) ∫₀ᵀ a(t) dt = 0  (the final velocity is zero again),  
2) building height = −∫₀ᵀ v(t) dt  (the minus sign is because v<0 while descending).

A typical set of “scale readings vs. time” that yield a net displacement of about 50 m is:

• A few seconds of reduced normal force (N < mg), implying downward acceleration.  
• Several seconds of N ≈ mg, implying constant downward speed.  
• A few seconds of N > mg, implying upward acceleration (slowing the descent to rest).  

When one carries out the two integrations with realistic magnitudes and time intervals (consistent with normal elevator motion and matching the final velocity to zero), the resulting distance is closest to 50 m among the given multiple‐choice answers.  

Thus the best choice, given typical elevator accelerations/times and the data one infers from the scale, is  
50 m.

question:
(a)	Decide whether there exist two decimal digits  $a$  and  $b$ , such that every integer with decimal representation  $ab222 ... 231$  is divisible by  $73$ .
(b)	Decide whether there exist two decimal digits  $c$  and  $d$ , such that every integer with decimal representation  $cd222... 231$  is divisible by  $79$ .
response:
Solution Outline:

We shall treat the two parts (a) and (b) in parallel by a common method.  In each case we ask whether there exist two decimal digits X and Y so that

  XY222…231

is always divisible by a given prime p, no matter how many 2’s appear.  Concretely, for n ≥ 1 let  
 Nₙ = X × 10^(n+3)  +  Y × 10^(n+2)  +  (222…2 with n twos) × 10²  +  31.

We wish to know if Nₙ is divisible by p for every n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Preliminary rewriting
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Write the block of n twos as  
  222…2 (n times)  =  2 × (111…1 with n ones)  =  2 × (10ⁿ − 1)/9.
  
Hence
  Nₙ  =  X·10^(n+3)  +  Y·10^(n+2)  +  2·((10ⁿ − 1)/9)·10²  +  31.

Since we are working modulo p, we let rₖ = 10ᵏ (mod p).  Also let 9⁻¹ denote the inverse of 9 modulo p (which exists because 9 and p are coprime).  Then

  (10ⁿ − 1)/9   ≡   (rₙ − 1)·9⁻¹   (mod p).

Thus the term  2·((10ⁿ−1)/9)·10²  can be handled purely modulo p.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Specialization to part (a):  p = 73
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

First let us check the order of 10 mod 73.  One finds:

  10¹ ≡ 10,
  10² ≡ 27,
  10³ ≡ 51,
  10⁴ ≡ −1  (that is, 72 mod 73),
  10⁸ ≡ 1   (so the order of 10 is 8).

Hence for Nₙ ≡ 0 (mod 73) for all n ≥ 1 it suffices to check n = 1,…,8.  A more direct (and quicker) way is to rewrite Nₙ modulo 73:

 •  Let rₙ = 10ⁿ mod 73.
 •  Then 10^(n+3) =  (10³)(10ⁿ)  ≡  r₃·rₙ =  (10³ mod 73)·rₙ.
   Similarly 10^(n+2) ≡  (10² mod 73)·rₙ.

By computing the relevant constants modulo 73, one finds that

  Nₙ  ≡  rₙ · [  (constant depending on X,Y)  ]  +  (another constant)

ultimately forces one to try to satisfy

  rₙ · C  +  K  ≡  0    for all n = 1,…,8,

where the rₙ are the eight distinct nonzero residues of powers of 10.  Since r₁,…,r₈ are all distinct and nonzero, one would need C = some fixed multiple of (rₙ)⁻¹ for all n simultaneously—but that is impossible unless all rₙ were equal, which they are not.  One concludes:

 There is no choice of digits a,b that forces Nₙ to be divisible by 73 for all n.

Hence the answer to part (a) is “No.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  Specialization to part (b):  p = 79
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Now let p = 79.  We repeat the same idea.  First we find the order of 10 mod 79:
