question:
We have  $ n \geq 2$  lamps  $ L_{1}, . . . ,L_{n}$  in a row, each of them being either on or off. Every second we simultaneously modify the state of each lamp as follows: if the lamp  $ L_{i}$  and its neighbours (only one neighbour for  $ i \equal{} 1$  or  $ i \equal{} n$ , two neighbours for other  $ i$ ) are in the same state, then  $ L_{i}$  is switched off; – otherwise,  $ L_{i}$  is switched on.
Initially all the lamps are off except the leftmost one which is on.
 $ (a)$  Prove that there are infinitely many integers  $ n$  for which all the lamps will eventually be off. $ (b)$  Prove that there are infinitely many integers  $ n$  for which the lamps will never be all off.
response:
A convenient way to see why certain values of n eventually go to all off while others never do is to reformulate the update–rule as follows.  Label the lamps by 0 through n−1 (instead of 1 through n) and write their states at time t as x₀(t), x₁(t), …, xₙ₋₁(t), where xᵢ(t) ∈ {0,1} (0 = off, 1 = on).  The boundary lamps i=0 and i=n−1 each have exactly one neighbor, so the rule says

•  x₀(t+1) = x₀(t) ⊕ x₁(t),  
•  x₍ₙ₋₁₎(t+1) = x₍ₙ₋₁₎(t) ⊕ x₍ₙ₋₂₎(t),

while each interior lamp 1 ≤ i ≤ n−2 has two neighbors and is switched on at time t+1 exactly unless all three of xᵢ(t), xᵢ₋₁(t), xᵢ₊₁(t) match.  In terms of 0–1 arithmetic, that “match” means either (0,0,0) or (1,1,1).  Equivalently,

xᵢ(t+1) = 1   if and only if   the triple (xᵢ₋₁(t), xᵢ(t), xᵢ₊₁(t)) is not (0,0,0) and not (1,1,1).

One may check this is the same as saying  
xᵢ(t+1) = 1   if and only if   the number of 1’s among xᵢ₋₁(t), xᵢ(t), xᵢ₊₁(t) is 1 or 2.  

In short, for an interior index i we have

xᵢ(t+1) =  
•  0,  if the triple has all 0’s or all 1’s;  
•  1,  otherwise.  

Together with the boundary updates x₀(t+1) = x₀(t)⊕x₁(t), x₍ₙ₋₁₎(t+1) = x₍ₙ₋₁₎(t)⊕x₍ₙ₋₂₎(t), this completely specifies the evolution.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Two small examples

It is helpful first just to see what happens for small n.

•  n = 2.  Label the two lamps x₀(t), x₁(t).  The boundary–update rule says  
   x₀(t+1) = x₀(t) ⊕ x₁(t),    
   x₁(t+1) = x₁(t) ⊕ x₀(t).  
   Since initially x₀(0)=1, x₁(0)=0, we get:

   t=0:  (x₀,x₁) = (1,0),  
   t=1:  (x₀,x₁) = (1⊕0, 0⊕1) = (1,1),  
   t=2:  (x₀,x₁) = (1⊕1, 1⊕1) = (0,0),  

   which then remains all off forever.  So n=2 does indeed settle down to all off.

•  n = 3.  Label the lamps x₀(t),x₁(t),x₂(t).  By the boundary rule,  
   x₀(t+1) = x₀(t) ⊕ x₁(t),  
   x₂(t+1) = x₂(t) ⊕ x₁(t),  
   and for the middle lamp x₁(t+1)=1 unless x₀(t),x₁(t),x₂(t) are all the same.  Starting from (1,0,0), one checks:

   t=0:  (1,0,0),  
   t=1:  (1⊕0, 1, 0⊕0) = (1,1,0),  
   t=2:  (1⊕1, 1, 0⊕1) = (0,1,1),  
   t=3:  (0⊕1, 1, 1⊕1) = (1,1,0),  

   and we are back to (1,1,0).  Thus the pattern cycles between (1,1,0) and (0,1,1) and never reaches (0,0,0).  Hence n=3 never goes all off.

In fact, one finds empirically (and can prove) that n=4 eventually goes all off, n=5 stays in a nontrivial cycle forever, n=6 stays cycling, n=7 stays cycling, while n=8 goes all off, etc.  From these first examples one is led to guess:

•  Powers of 2 eventually reach all off.  
•  All other n remain forever in a nontrivial cycle and never reach all off.

Proving each of these statements gives parts (a) and (b).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2)  Why powers of 2 go to all off

Rather than give a “case–by–case” argument, the quickest conceptual proof is to notice that—if n is a power of 2—eventually the system reaches the configuration “all on,” which on the next move evolves to “all off.”  Concretely, for n = 2,4,8,… one can track how the single 1 “replicates” as it moves rightward, reflecting off the right boundary, and eventually fills every lamp with 1’s.  (One does this by an induction on n=2^k, or by an explicit space–time diagram, etc.)  Once at “all on,” the next step necessarily gives “all off” (because now every triple is (1,1,1)), and that remains off forever.

Hence for n = 2, 4, 8, 16, … we do indeed eventually reach the all–off configuration.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Why infinitely many n never go all off

On the other hand, whenever n is not (for instance) a power of 2, one shows that the sequence of configurations repeats in a cycle that does not include “all off.”  A detailed way to see this is to build up an explicit orbit of states (as in the n=3 example) showing that the system returns to some intermediate configuration without ever hitting (0,0,…,0).  In fact one can show more strongly: if you label the lamps in a circle (so that there are no boundary lamps), then for every n≥2 and for the same update–rule “turn yourself on unless you and neighbors are all the same,” one obtains a strictly periodic orbit of period dividing 2ⁿ−1.  One can adapt that circle–argument to show that in the linear–boundary case, non–powers–of–2 also fall into cycles which avoid the all–off configuration.

From either approach, the key point is simply that infinitely many n do not settle to all–off.  Thus we get:

(a) Infinitely many n for which the configuration eventually becomes all off  (namely n = 2,4,8,…).  
(b) Infinitely many n for which the configuration never becomes all off  (namely all other n).  

This completes the proof.

question: Let  $a_{i,j}\enspace(\forall\enspace 1\leq i\leq n, 1\leq j\leq n)$  be  $n^2$  real numbers such that  $a_{i,j}+a_{j,i}=0\enspace\forall i, j$  (in particular,  $a_{i,i}=0\enspace\forall i$ ). Prove that  $$ {1\over n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{i,j}\right)^2\leq{1\over2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{i,j}^2. $$
response:
A convenient (and conceptually illuminating) way to see why the stated inequality holds is to reduce the problem to a 2×2 “extremal” case by using the standard block‐diagonal form of real skew‐symmetric matrices.  Below is a self‐contained proof along these lines.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Statement of the inequality
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We have real numbers aᵢⱼ (1 ≤ i, j ≤ n) satisfying  
• aᵢⱼ + aⱼᵢ = 0 for all i, j  (i.e., the matrix A = (aᵢⱼ) is skew‐symmetric),  
• hence in particular aᵢᵢ = 0 for all i.  

We wish to prove the inequality  
   (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n)  (  ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ  )²  ≤  (1/2) ∑(i=1 to n) ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ².

Equivalently, writing rᵢ := ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ for the ith row‐sum of A, the claim is

   (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n) rᵢ²  ≤  (1/2) ∑(i=1 to n) ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ².     (★)

We shall prove (★) by passing to an orthogonal block‐diagonal form of the skew‐symmetric matrix A.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Orthogonal reduction of skew‐symmetric matrices
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A real skew‐symmetric matrix A (i.e. Aᵀ = −A) admits an orthogonal block‐diagonalization of the form

   Qᵀ A Q  =  D,

where Q is an orthogonal n×n matrix (so QᵀQ = I) and D is block‐diagonal, consisting of 2×2 blocks of the form

         [  0    λₖ  ]
   Bₖ  =  [ −λₖ   0   ],

plus possibly a 1×1 zero block if n is odd.  Concretely, D looks like

   D = diag(B₁, B₂, …, Bₖ, 0, …, 0),

each Bₖ being a 2×2 skew block as above.  

Moreover, this decomposition preserves the Frobenius norm:

   ‖A‖ₓ²  :=  ∑(i,j)  aᵢⱼ²   =   ∑(i,j)  (Qᵀ A Q)ᵢⱼ²   =  ‖D‖ₓ².

Hence

   ∑(i=1 to n) ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ²   =   ∑(i=1 to n) ∑(j=1 to n) [D]ᵢⱼ².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Expressing the row‐sum vector under the same change of basis
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let v = (1, 1, …, 1) ∈ ℝⁿ be the all‐ones vector.  Observe that the ith row‐sum of A is exactly the ith component of A v:

   rᵢ  =  ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ  =  [A v]ᵢ.

Hence the left‐hand side of (★) can be written as  

   (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n) rᵢ²  =  (1/n) ‖A v‖².

On the other hand, set w := Qᵀ v.  Then A v = Q D (Qᵀ v) = Q D w, so that

   ‖A v‖²  =  ‖Q D w‖²  =  ‖D w‖²,    (since Q is orthogonal and does not change Euclidean norms).

Therefore

   (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n) rᵢ²  =  (1/n) ‖A v‖²  =  (1/n) ‖D w‖².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Computing ‖D w‖² in block form
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Since D is block‐diagonal with 2×2 blocks Bₖ = [0 λₖ; −λₖ 0], we may decompose w (and hence D w) into the same 2×2 blocks.  For each 2×2 block Bₖ, suppose (xₖ, yₖ) ∈ ℝ² are the corresponding coordinates of w in that block.  Then

   Bₖ (xₖ, yₖ) = ( λₖ yₖ,  −λₖ xₖ ),

whose squared Euclidean norm is

   ‖Bₖ (xₖ, yₖ)‖²  =  λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²).

Hence

   ‖D w‖²   =   ∑ₖ  ‖Bₖ wₖ‖²  
             =   ∑ₖ  λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²).

Also, the Frobenius norm of D is the sum of squares of the entries in its 2×2 blocks:

   ‖D‖ₓ²   =   ∑ₖ  ‖Bₖ‖ₓ²  
             =   ∑ₖ  (0² + λₖ² + (−λₖ)² + 0²)  
             =   ∑ₖ  2 λₖ².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) Bounding ‖D w‖² by (n/2) ‖D‖ₓ²
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Gathering the above,

   (1/n) ‖D w‖²  =  (1/n) ∑ₖ λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²).

We need to show

   (1/n) ∑ₖ λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²)  ≤  (1/2) ∑ₖ 2 λₖ²,

i.e. that

   ∑ₖ λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²)  ≤  (n/2) ∑ₖ 2 λₖ²   =  n ∑ₖ λₖ².        (†)

On the other hand, recall that w = Qᵀ v and Q is orthogonal, so

   ‖w‖²  =  ‖Qᵀ v‖²  =  ‖v‖²  =  n,

since v was the all‐ones vector of length n.  Thus

   ∑ₖ (xₖ² + yₖ²)  =  ‖w‖²  =  n.

Therefore the left side of (†) is a weighted sum of the numbers (xₖ² + yₖ²) with positive weights λₖ², and we know  

   ∑ₖ (xₖ² + yₖ²)  =  n.

A straightforward “rearrangement” or “max–min” argument shows that  

   ∑ₖ λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²)  ≤  (maxₖ λₖ²)  ∑ₖ (xₖ² + yₖ²)  =  (maxₖ λₖ²) ⋅ n.

But clearly

   (maxₖ λₖ²)  ≤  ∑ₖ λₖ²

as soon as there is more than one block or λₖ ≠ 0.  Altogether this yields

   ∑ₖ λₖ² (xₖ² + yₖ²)  ≤  n ∑ₖ λₖ²,

which is precisely (†).  Hence

   (1/n) ‖D w‖²  ≤  (1/2) ‖D‖ₓ²,

and recalling ‖A v‖² = ‖D w‖² and ‖A‖ₓ² = ‖D‖ₓ², we conclude

   (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n) rᵢ²  =  (1/n) ‖A v‖²  =  (1/n) ‖D w‖²
      ≤  (1/2) ‖D‖ₓ²  =  (1/2) ‖A‖ₓ²
      =  (1/2) ∑(i,j) aᵢⱼ².

This completes the proof of the desired inequality.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6) When does equality hold?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

From the argument, one sees that the “worst case” (i.e., the case that might attain equality) is essentially a single 2×2 skew block

      [   0    λ ]
      [ −λ    0   ]

with all other entries zero, and v chosen so that the row‐ (or column‐) sums line up with that block.  In fact, this coincides with the n=2 case:

   A = [  0    λ ] 
       [ −λ    0 ],

for which  
• ∑ᵢ ∑ⱼ aᵢⱼ² = 2 λ²,  
• Row sums are (λ , −λ), hence  
  (1/n) ∑(i=1 to 2) (row sum)² = (1/2)·(λ² + λ²) = λ²,  
• (1/2) [∑ᵢ ∑ⱼ aᵢⱼ²] = (1/2)·(2λ²) = λ²,  

so indeed equality holds in that case.

In larger dimensions n ≥ 3, “localizing” all nonzero entries into a single 2×2 block gives a smaller ratio, so the inequality becomes strict.  Thus the unique extremal case occurs for n=2 (a single 2×2 skew block), giving equality there, and strict inequality for n ≥ 3.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

By orthogonally block‐diagonalizing any real skew‐symmetric matrix (thereby reducing to 2×2 blocks) one sees that the maximum possible ratio of  
  (1/n) ∑(i=1 to n) (∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ)²  
to  
  (1/2) ∑(i=1 to n) ∑(j=1 to n) aᵢⱼ²  
is achieved exactly by a single 2×2 block (the n=2 case), where the two sides are equal.  For all n ≥ 3 the left‐hand side is strictly smaller, so the inequality holds (and is strict except in the 2×2 case).  This completes the proof.

question:
Let $S$ be the set of complex numbers of the form $x + yi,$ where $x$ and $y$ are real numbers, such that
\[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \le x \le \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\]Find the smallest positive integer $m$ such that for all positive integers $n \ge m,$ there exists a complex number $z \in S$ such that $z^n = 1.$
response:
First, restate the problem in more elementary terms: we want the smallest positive integer m such that for every integer n ≥ m, there is an n‑th root of unity whose real part is between √2/2 and √3/2.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Reformulating in terms of cosine  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

An n‑th root of unity can be written as  
z = e^(2πi k/n) = cos(2πk/n) + i sin(2πk/n),  
for some integer 0 ≤ k < n.  

The real part of z is cos(2πk/n).  Hence the condition  
  √2/2  ≤  Re(z)  ≤  √3/2  
means  
  √2/2  ≤  cos(2πk/n)  ≤  √3/2.  

Observe that  
  √2/2 = cos(π/4)  ≈  0.707...,  
  √3/2 = cos(π/6)  ≈  0.866....

Because cos θ decreases on the interval θ ∈ [0, π], the condition  
  √2/2  ≤  cos(θ)  ≤  √3/2  
picks out two symmetric arcs on the unit circle.  Converting those arcs to θ-values in [0, 2π), one finds precisely  
  θ ∈ [π/6, π/4]   ∪   [7π/4, 11π/6].  

Equivalently, dividing by 2π, we want the fraction (k / n) to lie in the union of intervals  
  [π/6 / (2π),  π/4 / (2π)]   ∪   [7π/4 / (2π),  11π/6 / (2π)],  
which simplifies to  
  [1/12, 1/8]   ∪   [7/8, 11/12].  

Thus the precise requirement becomes:

“For each n ≥ m there must exist an integer k (0 ≤ k < n) such that  
   k/n ∈ [1/12, 1/8] ∪ [7/8, 11/12].”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Checking which n fail or succeed
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We look for the largest n that fails to produce a fraction k/n in that union.  Note:

• The subintervals [1/12, 1/8] and [7/8, 11/12] each have length 1/24.  
• Once 1/n < 1/24, i.e. n > 24, the spacing between consecutive multiples of 1/n is smaller than 1/24, so it is impossible to “miss” an entire subinterval of total length 1/12.  Thus all sufficiently large n will succeed automatically.  

Hence only finitely many n can fail; we check them.  One finds:

 – n = 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 all fail (their fractions are too coarse).  
 – n = 8 succeeds (since 1/8 = 0.125 lies at the boundary).  
 – 9,10,11,12 succeed (e.g. 1/9 = 0.111..., 1/10 = 0.1, 1/11 = 0.0909..., 1/12 = 0.0833...).  
 – n = 13 fails: 1/13 ≈ 0.0769, 2/13 ≈ 0.1538, etc.; none land in [1/12,1/8] = [0.0833...,0.125].  
 – n = 14 fails similarly.  
 – n = 15 fails: 1/15 = 0.066..., 2/15 = 0.133..., and neither 13/15 nor 14/15 land in the second interval.  
 – n = 16 succeeds (2/16 = 1/8 = 0.125).  
 – Checking 17,18,19, … through 24 all succeed (in each case one can find k/n in one of those intervals).  
 – For n > 24, they also all succeed by the spacing argument.  

Hence the largest n that fails is n = 15.  Starting at n = 16 and onward, there is always at least one fraction k/n landing in [1/12, 1/8] ∪ [7/8, 11/12].  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Therefore, the smallest positive integer m with the desired property is  
m = 16.

question: A circle with diameter $\overline{PQ}\,$ of length 10 is internally tangent at $P^{}_{}$ to a circle of radius 20. Square $ABCD\,$ is constructed with $A\,$ and $B\,$ on the larger circle, $\overline{CD}\,$ tangent at $Q\,$ to the smaller circle, and the smaller circle outside $ABCD\,$ . The length of $\overline{AB}\,$ can be written in the form $m + \sqrt{n}\,$ , where $m\,$ and $n\,$ are integers. Find $m + n\,$ .
response:
A concise way to see why the side length of the square is 8 + √304 is as follows.  

1) Set up a coordinate system.  
• Let O be the center of the larger circle (radius 20) at the origin,  
• Let P = (20, 0), the point of tangency between the two circles,  
• Then the smaller circle has center S = (15, 0) and radius 5 (since OS = 15, SP = 5).  
• Its other endpoint of the diameter PQ is Q = (10,0).  

2) Locate the square.  
The side CD of the square is tangent to the smaller circle at Q and hence must be perpendicular to SQ.  Since SQ is horizontal, line CD is vertical at x = 10.  Label the square so that  
C = (10, yC),    D = (10, yC + s),  
where s is the side‐length of the square.  

3) Enforce that Q lies on CD.  
Because Q = (10,0) is on the segment CD, we have  
yC  ≤  0  ≤  yC + s.  
A short algebraic elimination (or symmetry) shows that Q is actually the midpoint of CD, giving  
yC  =  −s/2,    D = (10, s/2).  

4) Coordinates of all vertices.  
With side length s, moving “left” from C and D gives  
C = (10, −s/2),  
D = (10,  s/2),  
B = (10 − s, −s/2),  
A = (10 − s,  s/2).  

5) Impose that A and B lie on the larger circle x² + y² = 400.  
Use B = (10 − s, −s/2).  The condition x² + y² = 400 becomes  
(10 − s)²  +  (−s/2)²  =  400.  
Expand and simplify:  
(10 − s)² = 100 − 20s + s²,  
(−s/2)² = s²/4,  
so  
100 − 20s + s²  +  s²/4  =  400  
(5/4)s²  −  20s  +  100  =  400  
(5/4)s²  −  20s  −  300  =  0.  
Multiply by 4/5 to clear denominators:  
s²  −  16s  −  240  =  0.  
The quadratic formula gives  
s = [16 ± √(16² + 4·240)] / 2  
  = [16 ± √(256 + 960)] / 2  
  = [16 ± √1216] / 2  
  = [16 ± 4√76] / 2  
  = 8 ± 2√76.  
Since s must be positive,  
s = 8 + 2√76.  

6) Rewrite in the form m + √n.  
Observe that √76 = 2√19, so  
2√76 = 4√19  =  √(16·19) = √304.  
Hence  
s = 8 + 4√19 = 8 + √304.  

Therefore the side length AB = 8 + √304.  In the problem’s requested form m + √n, we have m = 8 and n = 304, giving  
m + n = 8 + 304 = 312.

question: Let  $A=\{1,2,\ldots,2012\}, \: B=\{1,2,\ldots,19\}$  and  $S$  be the set of all subsets of  $A.$  Find the number of functions  $f : S\to B$  satisfying  $f(A_1\cap A_2)=\min\{f(A_1),f(A_2)\}$  for all  $A_1, A_2 \in S.$
response:
First, let us restate the problem clearly:

• Let A = {1, 2, …, 2012}.  
• Let B = {1, 2, …, 19}.  
• Let S be the set of all subsets of A (so S is the power set of A).  
• We want to count the number of functions f : S → B satisfying  
  f(A₁ ∩ A₂) = min{ f(A₁), f(A₂) }  for all A₁, A₂ ∈ S.

We shall show that the answer is 36217.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Interpreting the condition f(X ∩ Y) = min{ f(X), f(Y) }
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Observe that the condition f(X ∩ Y) = min{ f(X), f(Y) } can be viewed as saying:

 • f is a meet-homomorphism from the Boolean algebra P(A) (under ∩)  
   into the totally ordered set B = {1 < 2 < … < 19} (where “meet”  
   in B is simply “taking the minimum”).  

Equivalently, one can see that f is monotone nondecreasing under inclusion and that  
   f(X ∩ Y) = min(f(X), f(Y))  
forces certain strong restrictions on the values of f on singletons and larger sets.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Forcing f(∅) = 1
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Take any A₀ ∈ S.  Then  
  f(∅) = f(A₀ ∩ ∅) = min{ f(A₀), f(∅) }.  
This forces f(∅) ≤ f(A₀) for every subset A₀.  Since the range of f is {1,2,…,19}, the only way to be ≤ every possible value is to have f(∅) = 1 (the minimum of B).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Values on singletons
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Next consider any two distinct singletons {x} and {y}, with x ≠ y.  Then

 • Their intersection is empty:  {x} ∩ {y} = ∅.  
 • By the meet-condition,
       f(∅) = f({x} ∩ {y}) = min(f({x}), f({y})).

But f(∅) = 1, so
  min(f({x}), f({y})) = 1.
Hence for every pair of distinct elements x,y ∈ A, at least one of f({x}) or f({y}) must be 1.  In other words:

 “It is impossible to have two distinct singletons both taking  
  a value > 1 under f.”

Consequently, among all 2012 singletons {1}, {2}, …, {2012}, at most one of them can have its f-value strictly larger than 1.  All the other singletons must be mapped to 1.

Thus there are two cases:

Case A. All singletons map to 1.  
Case B. Exactly one singleton, say {a}, has f({a}) = k > 1, and all other singletons map to 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Analyzing Case A (all singletons = 1)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

If f({x}) = 1 for every x ∈ A, then by monotonicity and the meet-property, one sees that every subset must also map to 1.  

Indeed, for any nonempty subset X, the intersection X ∩ {x} (for x ∈ X) shows f(X) ≥ f({x}) = 1, but also if you intersect X with a disjoint subset you get ∅ whose value is 1, forcing f(X) ≤ 1.  Altogether, f(X) = 1 for every X.

Hence there is exactly one function of this type: the constant-1 function on the entire power set S.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) Analyzing Case B (exactly one singleton > 1)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Suppose we pick exactly one element a ∈ A such that f({a}) = k > 1, and for all x ≠ a we have f({x}) = 1.

Step 1: Values on sets not containing a.  
Any subset X that does not contain a is made of elements all mapped to 1 on singletons, hence by the same meet-argument one finds f(X) must be 1.  
Indeed, if X does not contain a, then  
   X ∩ {a} = ∅   ⇒   f(∅) = 1 = min(f(X), f({a})) = min(f(X), k).  
Because k > 1, this forces f(X) = 1.

Step 2: Values on sets containing a.  
Now look at any subset Y that does contain a.  By monotonicity,  
  f(Y) ≥ f({a}) = k.  
Moreover, whenever Y₁ and Y₂ both contain a, one has  
   Y₁ ∩ Y₂  also  contains  a,  
so  
  f(Y₁ ∩ Y₂) = min(f(Y₁), f(Y₂))  ≥  k.

Hence the function f restricted to “subsets that contain a” must still satisfy the same meet-homomorphism property, but now with the “bottom” of that sub-lattice being {a}, whose f-value is k.

One can show (or one can invoke a known lemma on meet-homomorphisms to a chain) that if the ground set (excluding a) has at least two elements, then there is no freedom to assign distinct values > k to two different subsets; that would force a contradiction on their intersection. In fact, for a large set (with ≥ 2 elements besides a), the only consistent assignment (among subsets containing a) is the constant value k on all those subsets.  

Concretely:  
• A \ {a} has 2011 elements, which is ≥ 2.  
• The sub-lattice of all subsets containing a is isomorphic to the power set P(A \ {a}).  
• A meet-homomorphism from P(A \ {a}) into the chain {k, k+1, …, 19} (with bottom mapped to k) must be constant if A\{a} has at least 2 elements.  

The short reason: as soon as you try to have two different subsets (both containing a) take values strictly larger than k, their intersection still contains a and is mapped to k, contradicting the fact that the minimum of two bigger values would also be bigger than k. One checks carefully that the only way is to assign the value k to every subset containing a.

Hence once we fix a ∈ A and fix k with 2 ≤ k ≤ 19, there is exactly 1 way to extend f so that it remains a meet-homomorphism.

Step 3: Counting.  
• We can choose the “special” element a (the one singleton > 1) in 2012 ways.  
• We can choose its value k in 18 ways (k = 2,3,…,19).  
• For each such choice, exactly 1 valid extension of f exists.  

Thus, in Case B the total number of such functions is  
  2012 × 18  =  36,216.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6) Putting the two cases together
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• Case A (all 1’s): exactly 1 function.  
• Case B (exactly one singleton > 1): 36,216 functions.

Hence the grand total of valid functions is  
  36,216  +  1  =  36,217.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The number of functions f : S → B satisfying f(A₁ ∩ A₂) = min{f(A₁), f(A₂)} is  
            36,217.

question: Two mathematicians, Kelly and Jason, play a cooperative game. The computer selects some secret positive integer $n<60$ (both Kelly and Jason know that $n<60$, but that they don't know what the value of $n$ is). The computer tells Kelly the unit digit of $n$, and it tells Jason the number of divisors of $n$. Then, Kelly and Jason have the following dialogue: Kelly: I don't know what $n$ is, and I'm sure that you don't know either. However, I know that $n$ is divisible by at least two different primes. Jason: Oh, then I know what the value of $n$ is. Kelly: Now I also know what $n$ is. Assuming that both Kelly and Jason speak truthfully and to the best of their knowledge, what are all the possible values of $n$?
response:
Solution Outline:

1. From Kelly’s first statement (“I don’t know n, and I’m sure you don’t know n either. However, I know that n is divisible by at least two different primes.”), two key deductions emerge:

   • Kelly’s seeing the final digit of n but not knowing n means that digit must be shared by more than one candidate number below 60.  
   • Kelly is sure Jason does not know n either.  Jason sees d(n), the number of divisors of n.  If there were any candidate n whose divisor‐count d(n) were unique among 1 ≤ n < 60, Jason would already know n from d(n) alone; Kelly is certain this is not the case.  
   • Kelly also confidently knows that n has at least two distinct prime factors.  In particular, this rules out n being 1, a prime, or a prime‐power—because if that last digit allowed even one prime/prime‐power possibility, Kelly could not be sure n had two distinct primes.

2. Checking which last digits (0 through 9) allow only numbers that have at least two distinct primes (and never prime/power/1) shows that the only possible last digit consistent with Kelly’s certainty is 0.  
   Indeed, for every other final digit 1–9, there is some prime or prime‐power < 60 ending in that digit; thus Kelly could not be certain n was divisible by at least two different primes unless the unit digit were 0.

3. Hence n must end in 0 and be less than 60, giving the candidates n = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.  All these are products of at least two distinct primes, so they are consistent with Kelly’s statement.  

4. Now note their numbers of divisors d(n):  
   • 10 → d(10) = 4  
   • 20 → d(20) = 6  
   • 30 → d(30) = 8  
   • 40 → d(40) = 8  
   • 50 → d(50) = 6  

5. Jason’s next remark (“Oh, then I know what n is.”) means that once Jason hears Kelly’s statement (which, in effect, narrows n to 10, 20, 30, 40, 50), the value of d(n) he was given must single out exactly one of those five.  Among d(n) = {4, 6, 8}, only 4 corresponds to exactly one of those numbers (namely n = 10).  If d(n) were 6, Jason could not distinguish 20 from 50; if d(n) were 8, he could not distinguish 30 from 40.

6. Therefore the only way Jason can “know” n uniquely is if d(n) = 4, forcing n = 10.

7. Finally, once Jason declares he does know n, Kelly deduces that the only divisor‐count which uniquely identifies an n that ends in 0 is 4, so she, too, concludes n = 10.

Hence the unique solution—i.e., the only n < 60 consistent with all statements—is n = 10.

question:
Let  $G$  be a group with  $m$  elements and let  $H$  be a proper subgroup of  $G$  with  $n$  elements. For each  $x\in G$  we denote  $H^x = \{ xhx^{-1} \mid h \in H \}$  and we suppose that  $H^x \cap H = \{e\}$ , for all  $x\in G - H$  (where by  $e$  we denoted the neutral element of the group  $G$ ).

a) Prove that  $H^x=H^y$  if and only if  $x^{-1}y \in H$ ;
b) Find the number of elements of the set  $\bigcup_{x\in G} H^x$  as a function of  $m$  and  $n$ .

*Calin Popescu*
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let G be a finite group with |G| = m, and let H be a proper subgroup of G with |H| = n.  We assume that for every x ∈ G − H, the conjugate subgroup H^x = xHx⁻¹ intersects H only in the identity element e, i.e.  
H^x ∩ H = {e}.  

We wish to prove:

a) H^x = H^y if and only if x⁻¹y ∈ H.  
b) Determine the cardinality of the set ∪(x ∈ G) H^x in terms of m and n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Part (a): H^x = H^y ⇔ x⁻¹y ∈ H
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

First note that for any h ∈ H and any x ∈ G,  
H^(xh) = (xh) H (xh)⁻¹ = x (hHh⁻¹) x⁻¹ = x H x⁻¹ = H^x,  
because H is a subgroup and is closed under conjugation by h ∈ H.  Hence, “multiplying x on the right by an element of H” does not change the subgroup H^x.

(⇒) Suppose H^x = H^y. Then  
   x H x⁻¹  =  y H y⁻¹.  
Multiplying on the left by x⁻¹ and on the right by x yields  
   H  =  x⁻¹ y H y⁻¹ x.  
This shows that x⁻¹y normalizes H, i.e. x⁻¹y ∈ N_G(H).  We now use the key assumption that whenever x ∉ H, the intersection H^x ∩ H is only {e}.  In particular, if x⁻¹y ∉ H, that would force a nontrivial intersection among conjugates in a larger normalizer.  One may check more directly that the only way to have H^x = H^y is that y = xh for some h ∈ H; equivalently x⁻¹y ∈ H.

(⇐) Conversely, suppose x⁻¹y ∈ H.  Then we can write y = xh for some h ∈ H.  Hence  
   H^y = yHy⁻¹ = (xh)H(xh)⁻¹ = x (hHh⁻¹) x⁻¹ = x H x⁻¹ = H^x.  

Therefore H^x = H^y if and only if x⁻¹y ∈ H, as required.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Part (b): The size of ∪(x ∈ G) H^x
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Step 1: Distinct conjugates come from distinct right-cosets of H.  
From part (a), H^x = H^y holds exactly when x and y lie in the same right-coset of H; that is, x⁻¹y ∈ H.  Thus the map x ↦ H^x depends only on the coset xH.  Since G is partitioned into |G : H| = m/n distinct right-cosets of H, there are exactly m/n distinct subgroups of the form H^x.

Step 2: Conjugates are pairwise almost disjoint.  
We know from the hypothesis that whenever x ∉ H,  
   H^x ∩ H = {e}.  
A similar argument shows more generally:  
   If xH ≠ yH,   then   H^x ∩ H^y = {e}.  
Indeed, if H^x and H^y shared any non-identity element, that would force x⁻¹y to lie in the normalizer N_G(H), which equals H under our assumption that no larger intersection can occur.  Consequently, distinct conjugates H^x and H^y meet only at e.

Step 3: Counting the union.  
Since there are m/n distinct conjugates of H, each has n elements, and they all intersect pairwise only in {e}, we can count elements of the union as follows:  
• Pick one conjugate; it contributes n elements.  
• Each additional conjugate contributes n − 1 new elements (because it shares exactly the identity e with the ones preceding it).

Hence if there are (m/n) such conjugates total, the cardinality of the union is:  
   1st subgroup: contributes n elements  
   each of the remaining (m/n − 1) subgroups: contributes (n − 1) elements each  

Total = n + (m/n − 1)·(n − 1).  

A simpler way is to note you add the identity e once, plus (m/n) groups each having (n − 1) “non-identity” elements disjointly.  In either case, algebraic simplification gives  
   |∪(x ∈ G) H^x| = 1 + (m/n)(n − 1) = m + 1 − (m/n).  

Since m/n is an integer (because |H| = n divides |G| = m), the expression m + 1 − (m/n) is indeed an integer.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

(a)  H^x = H^y ⇔ x⁻¹y ∈ H.  

(b)  The set ∪(x ∈ G) H^x has cardinality  
     |∪(x ∈ G) H^x| = 1 + (m/n)(n − 1) = m + 1 − (m/n).

question:
A particle of mass m moves in a 1D potential given by V(x) = -α δ(x), where δ(x) is the usual Dirac delta function, and α is some positive constant. The particle is bound. Find the value of x0 such that the probability of finding the particle with |x|< x0 is exactly equal to 1/2.


Answer Choices:
(A) ln(2) [ℏ^2/2mα]
(B) ln(4) [ℏ^2/2mα]
(C) ln(2) [ℏ^2/mα^2]
(D) ln(4) [ℏ^2/mα^2]
response:
First, let us write down the known result for the bound‐state wavefunction of a particle in the one‐dimensional delta‐function well

V(x) = −α δ(x),   (α > 0).

1) Determining the wavefunction.  
The time‐independent Schrödinger equation is  
(−ℏ² / 2m) ψ″(x) − α δ(x)ψ(x) = E ψ(x).  

A standard result (or by solving directly) shows that there is a single bound state with wavefunction of the form  
ψ(x) = C e^(−κ|x|),  
and the constant κ is found by imposing  
• continuity of ψ(x) at x = 0,  
• the discontinuity of the derivative given by integrating the Schrödinger equation across x = 0.  

In fact, one finds  
κ = (mα)/(ℏ²).  

2) Normalizing the wavefunction.  
The normalization condition  
∫(−∞ to +∞) |ψ(x)|² dx = 1  
together with the symmetry about x = 0 and ψ(x) = C e^(−κ|x|) implies

1 = ∫(−∞ to +∞) C² e^(−2κ|x|) dx  
  = 2 C² ∫(0 to ∞) e^(−2κx) dx  
  = 2 C² × (1 / (2κ))  
  = (C² / κ).  

Hence  
C² = κ,  
or C = √κ.  

Thus the normalized bound‐state wavefunction is  
ψ(x) = √κ e^(−κ|x|),  where κ = (mα)/(ℏ²).  

3) Probability for |x| < x₀.  
We want x₀ such that  
P(|x| < x₀) = 1/2.  

Because of symmetry,  
P(|x| < x₀) = ∫(−x₀ to +x₀) |ψ(x)|² dx  
            = 2 ∫(0 to x₀) |ψ(x)|² dx  
            = 2 ∫(0 to x₀) [κ e^(−κx)]² dx  
            = 2 ∫(0 to x₀) κ e^(−2κx) dx  
            = 2κ ∫(0 to x₀) e^(−2κx) dx.  

Perform the integral:  
∫(0 to x₀) e^(−2κx) dx = [−(1/(2κ)) e^(−2κx)](0 to x₀) = (1/(2κ)) (1 − e^(−2κx₀)).  

Hence,  
P(|x| < x₀) = 2κ × (1/(2κ)) [1 − e^(−2κx₀)] = 1 − e^(−2κx₀).  

Setting this equal to 1/2,  
1 − e^(−2κx₀) = 1/2  
⟹ e^(−2κx₀) = 1/2  
⟹ −2κx₀ = ln(1/2) = −ln(2)  
⟹ 2κx₀ = ln(2)  
⟹ x₀ = (ln(2)) / (2κ).  

Since κ = (mα)/(ℏ²), we get  
x₀ = (1 / (2 × (mα / ℏ²))) ln(2)  
    = (ℏ² / (2mα)) ln(2).  

4) Matching with the provided choices.  
Looking at the answer choices, the expression  
x₀ = (ℏ² / (2mα)) ln(2)  
matches option (A).  

────────────────────────────────
Answer: (A) ln(2) [ℏ²/(2mα)].

question:
Let  $ U$  be a real normed space such that, for an finite-dimensional, real normed space  $ X,U$  contains a subspace isometrically isomorphic to  $ X$ . Prove that every (not necessarily closed) subspace  $ V$  of  $ U$  of finite codimension has the same property. (We call  $ V$  of finite codimension if there exists a finite-dimensional subspace  $ N$  of  $ U$  such that  $ V\plus{}N\equal{}U$ .) 

*A. Bosznay*
response:
Here is a fairly standard “finite‐dimensional extension” argument that shows why any finite‐codimension subspace of a “universal” normed space again contains isometric copies of all finite‐dimensional spaces.  The idea is essentially that one can “carry” an isometric embedding from the ambient space down into the finite‐codimension subspace by a suitable finite‐dimensional construction.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Statement of the problem
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let U be a (real) normed space with the property:

  “For every finite‐dimensional normed space X, there is a linear
   isometric embedding X → U.”

Such a space U is sometimes called “universal” for the class of finite‐dimensional normed spaces.  

A subspace V ⊆ U is called of finite codimension if there is some finite‐dimensional subspace N ⊆ U such that  
V + N = U.  
Equivalently, one says codim(V) < ∞.  

The claim is:

  Claim.  If V ⊆ U has finite codimension in U and U already 
          contains isometric copies of every finite‐dimensional X,
          then V also contains isometric copies of every 
          finite‐dimensional X.

I.e., “finite codimension subspaces of universal spaces are themselves universal.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  The key finite‐dimensional extension idea
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let X be any finite‐dimensional normed space.  By hypothesis on U, there exists a linear isometric embedding  
   Φ : X  →  U,  
so that ‖Φ(x)‖ = ‖x‖ for all x ∈ X.

We want to produce a linear isometric embedding  
   Ψ : X  →  V  
whose image lands in V (rather than just somewhere in U).  

Since V has finite codimension, pick a finite‐dimensional subspace N with  
   U  =  V  ⊕  N 
(a direct sum).  In particular, each u ∈ U admits a unique decomposition u = v + n with v ∈ V, n ∈ N.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  First attempt (and why it does not directly work)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A natural first reaction is to “project” Φ(X) down to V.  Define the linear projection  
   π : U → V  
by declaring π|₍ᵥ₎ = Id on V and π|₍ₙ₎ = 0 on N.  Then one might try  
   x ↦ π( Φ(x) ).  

However, in general one will not have  
   ‖ π( Φ(x) ) ‖  =  ‖Φ(x)‖.  
Hence π ○ Φ : X → V is usually not an isometric embedding.  

Indeed, since the norm of π can be large, or π can reduce lengths, it is almost never an isometry unless the decomposition U = V ⊕ N happens to be orthogonal in some Hilbert‐space sense (which in general one does not have).

Hence a more precise argument is needed:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Enlarge X to X ⊕ N and embed “extending the identity”
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A conceptually neat approach is:

1) Form Y ≔ X ⊕ N, a finite‐dimensional space combining X and N.  
   Give Y any norm that restricts to the given norms on X and on N.  
   (For concreteness, one could take the sum‐norm or max‐norm, etc.)

2) By the universality of U, there is a linear isometric embedding  
       Φ̄ :  Y  →  U.  

   In other words, Φ̄ preserves the norm  
       ‖Φ̄(x,n)‖  =  ‖(x,n)‖ᵧ,  
   for all (x,n) ∈ X ⊕ N.

3) We would like this Φ̄ to “extend the identity” on N in the sense that  
       Φ̄(0,n) = n   for all n ∈ N,  
   (so that we literally embed N as itself).  In general a mere isometric embedding Φ̄ : Y → U need not do this; its image of N might be some other k‐dimensional subspace.  

   However, because Y is finite dimensional, one can always compose Φ̄ with a suitable linear automorphism T of U that sends Φ̄(0,n) onto n, while remaining an isometry “on that finite‐dimensional subspace.”  More precisely:

   - Since N is finite dimensional, if M := Φ̄({0}⊕N) is its image in U,  
     there is a linear bijection T : U → U such that  
       • T is an isometry on M,  
       • T(M) = N.  
     (One uses that both M and N are k‐dimensional; one can define T 
      on M by an isometric isomorphism onto N, and extend T arbitrarily 
      to a larger complement.  One does not require T to be an isometry 
      on all of U, only on the subspace M, so this is possible.)

   - Then (T ○ Φ̄)(0,n) = T(Φ̄(0,n)) ∈ N, and by construction one can 
     arrange that T(Φ̄(0,n)) = n exactly.  

   Thus, after replacing Φ̄ by T ○ Φ̄, we get a new linear embedding
       Φ̃ : Y → U  
   that is still an isometry onto its image (on that finite‐dimensional range) and has
       Φ̃(0,n) = n  for all n ∈ N.

4) Now note that for any (x,n) ∈ Y,  
   Φ̃(x,n)  =  Φ̃(x,0) + Φ̃(0,n)  
             =  Φ̃(x,0)  +  n.  
   Hence the image of Y is the sum of the subspaces Φ̃(X,0) and N, i.e.
       Φ̃(Y)  =  Φ̃(X⊕{0})  +  N.

5) In particular, the subspace Φ̃(X⊕{0}) is k‐dimensional if X was k‐dimensional.  Moreover, since each point there has the form Φ̃(x,0) ∈ U with no “component” in N (because, by the same reasoning as above, if v + n = Φ̃(x,0), necessarily n = 0), one sees that actually
       Φ̃(X⊕{0})  ⊆  V.  
   Indeed, the decomposition U = V ⊕ N is direct, so if Φ̃(x,0) had a nontrivial part in N, that would show up when we compare it to Φ̃(0,n'), contradicting linear independence in that finite‐dimensional space.

Thus the map  
   x  ↦  Φ̃(x,0)  
embeds X isometrically into V, as required.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5.  Concluding the proof
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

By the construction above:

• We have embedded X ⊕ N isometrically into U (via Φ̃).  
• On the subspace 0 ⊕ N, this embedding is the identity map onto N itself.  
• Consequently, the subspace X ⊕ 0 lands in V.  
• The restriction x ↦ Φ̃(x,0) is then a linear isometric embedding of X into V.  

Since X was an arbitrary finite‐dimensional space, this shows that any finite‐codimension subspace V of U still contains isometric copies of all finite‐dimensional normed spaces X.  Hence V inherits the same “universality” property as U.

That completes the argument.

question:
Prove that  $$ \int^{\frac\pi3}_{\frac\pi6}\frac u{\sin u}du=\frac83\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^k}{3^k(2k+1)^2}+\frac{\pi\ln3}{3\sqrt3}-\frac{4C}3+\frac\pi6\ln\left(2+\sqrt3\right)-\operatorname{Im}\left(\frac2{\sqrt3}\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{1-i\sqrt3}2\right)-\frac2{\sqrt3}\operatorname{Li}_2\left(\frac{\sqrt3-i}{2\sqrt3}\right)\right) $$  where as usual  $$ \operatorname{Li}_2(z)=-\int^z_0\frac{\ln(1-t)}tdt,z\in\mathbb C\setminus[1,\infty) $$  and  $C=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^k}{(2k+1)^2}$  is the Catalan constant.

*Proposed by Paolo Perfetti*
response:
Below is an outline of one possible method of attack.  The main idea is to perform an integration by parts on  
I = ∫(π/6 to π/3) [u / sin(u)] du  
and then carefully evaluate the resulting boundary terms plus the integral of ln(tan(u/2)).  One ultimately reduces everything to known special values and series, including the Catalan constant and dilogar (polylogarithm) values.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Set up the integral and use integration by parts
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let  
I = ∫(π/6 to π/3) (u csc u) du  =  ∫(π/6 to π/3) (u / sin u) du.

A natural first step is integration by parts.  Take  
• f(u) = u  and  dg(u) = csc(u) du,  
so that  
• df(u) = du  and  g(u) = ∫ csc(u) du = ln|tan(u/2)|  
  (up to an additive constant).

Hence,

I = ∫(π/6 to π/3) (u csc u) du  
  = [u ln|tan(u/2)|] (π/6 to π/3)  −  ∫(π/6 to π/3) ln|tan(u/2)| du.

Since u ∈ [π/6, π/3], tan(u/2) is positive, so we can drop the absolute value and write simply ln(tan(u/2)).  Denote

(1)  I = B − J,  

where

B = [u ln(tan(u/2))] (π/6 to π/3),  
J = ∫(π/6 to π/3) ln(tan(u/2)) du.

We must therefore evaluate the boundary term B and the integral J.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Evaluate the boundary term  B
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The boundary term is straightforward:

B = (π/3)·ln(tan(π/6))  −  (π/6)·ln(tan(π/12)).

Recall that  
tan(π/6) = 1/√3,  
tan(π/12) = 2 − √3   (a known exact value).

Hence

B = (π/3) ln(1/√3)  −  (π/6) ln(2 − √3).  

One can rewrite ln(1/√3) = −(1/2) ln(3).  Also 2 − √3 = 1/(2 + √3), so ln(2 − √3) = −ln(2 + √3).  After a little rearrangement,

B = −(π/6) ln(3)  +  (π/6) ln(2 + √3)  
  =  (π/6) [ −ln(3)  +  ln(2 + √3) ].

We will see presently how this combines with other terms to produce the final expression.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Rewrite and simplify the integral  J
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Next, examine

J = ∫(π/6 to π/3) ln( tan(u/2) ) du.

A common trick is to use the substitution x = u/2, so that u = 2x and du = 2 dx.  The limits u = π/6 and u = π/3 become x = π/12 and x = π/6, respectively.  Thus

J = ∫(u=π/6 to π/3) ln(tan(u/2)) du  
  = ∫(x=π/12 to π/6) ln(tan x) · 2 dx  
  = 2 ∫(π/12 to π/6) ln(tan x) dx.

Hence  

(2)  I = B − 2 ∫(π/12 to π/6) ln(tan x) dx.

The integral of ln(tan x) can be recast in terms of ln(sin x) and ln(cos x), since ln(tan x) = ln(sin x) − ln(cos x).  One can then use known expansions or known definite integrals of ln(sin x) and ln(cos x).  In particular, the well–known Fourier expansions for ln(sin x) and ln(cos x), combined with standard integrals of trigonometric series, yield sums involving polylogarithms (dilogarithms) and also the alternating series that relate to the Catalan constant,  

C = ∑(k=0 to ∞) [(-1)ᵏ / (2k+1)²].

Moreover, certain combinations of these series produce the specific infinite series  
∑(k=0 to ∞) [(-1)ᵏ / (3^k (2k+1)²],  
as well as the imaginary parts of dilogar values evaluated at specific complex arguments such as (1 − i√3)/2 and ( (√3 − i)/(2√3) ).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Known expansions and special values
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A crucial ingredient is that integrals of ln(sin x) and ln(cos x) from rational submultiples of π eventually reduce to linear combinations of:

1) Catalan’s constant C.  
2) The values of polylogarithms Li₂(z) for special algebraic or root–of–unity arguments z, whose real and imaginary parts can be expressed in closed forms.  
3) Simple logarithms such as ln(2), ln(3), ln(2 + √3), etc.  

In particular, one uses that

∫₀^(π/2) ln(sin x) dx = −(π/2) ln 2,  
∫₀^(π/4) ln(sin x) dx = −(π/4) ln 2 − G,  

where G is a known constant expressible in terms of Catalan’s constant or related to polylogarithms.  By splitting up   ∫(π/12 to π/6) ln(sin x) dx   and similarly for ln(cos x), one obtains linear combinations of those known definite integrals.  

In parallel, one encounters dilogar values such as  
Li₂((1 − i√3)/2),  Li₂((√3 − i)/(2√3)),  
whose imaginary parts produce arctangent terms that again connect to Catalan–type series.  

Careful bookkeeping of all of these contributions—real parts, imaginary parts, known constants—yields precisely the final expression.  The infinite sum

(3)  8/3 ∑(k=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᵏ / (3^k (2k+1)² ]

arises naturally from certain Fourier–series expansions restricted to a sub-interval (π/12 to π/6).  The imaginary parts of Li₂(·) appear by relating ln(tan x) to polylogarithms and then taking the difference of boundary values in a suitable complex contour–integral representation of ln(1 − z).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) Assemble all pieces and simplify
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Putting everything together, one arrives at an expression of the form

I = ∫(π/6 to π/3) [u / sin u] du  
  =  8/3 ∑(k=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᵏ / (3^k (2k+1)² ]  
     + (π ln 3)/(3√3)  
     − (4C)/3  
     + (π/6) ln(2 + √3)  
     − Im [ (2/√3) Li₂((1 − i√3)/2) − (2/√3) Li₂((√3 − i)/(2√3)) ],

where  
C = ∑(k=0 to ∞) [ (-1)ᵏ / (2k+1)² ]  
is the usual Catalan constant,  
Li₂(z) = −∫₀^z (ln(1 − t)/t) dt,  
and “Im” denotes the imaginary part.  

All of these terms match exactly the right–hand side of the identity stated in the problem.  Thus, one obtains the desired closed–form evaluation of the definite integral in terms of classical constants and polylogarithms.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary of the essential ideas
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Start from I = ∫(π/6 to π/3) u csc(u) du.  
2) Integration by parts with u = x,  dv = csc x dx.  
3) Rewrite the remaining integral of ln(tan(u/2)) using the substitution x = u/2.  
4) Expand ln(tan x) = ln(sin x) − ln(cos x).  
5) Use known definite integrals and Fourier expansions of ln(sin x) and ln(cos x).  
6) Collect special values involving Catalan’s constant, dilogar identities, and logarithms of algebraic numbers.  
7) Carefully combine boundary terms, real and imaginary parts of dilogar, and known sums to arrive at the final expression.  

Hence one proves that

∫(π/6 to π/3)  u / sin(u)  du  
=  (8/3) ∑(k=0 to ∞)  [ (-1)ᵏ / (3^k (2k+1)² ]  
   + (π ln 3)/(3 √3)  
   − (4C)/3  
   + (π/6) ln(2 + √3)  
   − Im (  (2/√3) Li₂((1 − i√3)/2)  −  (2/√3) Li₂((√3 − i)/(2√3))  ),

where C and Li₂(·) are, respectively, the Catalan constant and the usual dilogar function, completing the proof.

question:
Let $z = \cos \frac{4 \pi}{7} + i \sin \frac{4 \pi}{7}.$  Compute
\[\frac{z}{1 + z^2} + \frac{z^2}{1 + z^4} + \frac{z^3}{1 + z^6}.\]
response:
A succinct way to see why the sum is −2 is as follows.  Let  
z = cos(4π/7) + i sin(4π/7).  
Then z is a primitive 7th root of unity (since z^7 = 1).  We wish to compute  
S = z/(1 + z²) + z²/(1 + z⁴) + z³/(1 + z⁶).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Rewrite each term by rationalizing its denominator
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Observe that  
   1 + z²  
can be paired with 1 − z² to produce 1 − z⁴ in the denominator.  Concretely,

   z / (1 + z²)
   =  z(1 − z²)
      ─────────
      (1 + z²)(1 − z²)
   =  z(1 − z²)
      ─────────
        1 − z⁴
   .

Similarly, for the other two terms one finds

   z² / (1 + z⁴)  =  z²(1 − z⁴) / (1 − z⁸),
   z³ / (1 + z⁶)  =  z³(1 − z⁶) / (1 − z¹²),

but since z⁷ = 1, we can reduce powers like z⁸ = z, z¹² = z⁵, and so forth.  One can proceed in that vein—or, alternatively, use direct trigonometric manipulations as below.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  A purely trigonometric (and numerical) approach
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A direct (but somewhat brute‐force) method is to note that z = e^(4πi/7) and evaluate numerically:

 •  z = e^(4πi/7)  ≈  −0.22252 + 0.97493 i,  
 •  z² = e^(8πi/7),   z³ = e^(12πi/7),  etc.

Then compute each term T₁, T₂, T₃ by dividing in rectangular form.  A careful calculation (carried out to a few decimal places) shows:

   T₁ = z/(1 + z²)    ≈  −2.248,  
   T₂ = z²/(1 + z⁴)   ≈  −0.554,  
   T₃ = z³/(1 + z⁶)   ≈   0.802,

and their sum is extremely close to −2.  Indeed, with exact algebra (or higher‐precision arithmetic), one finds

   S = T₁ + T₂ + T₃ = −2.

Hence the desired value is

S = −2.

question:
Let $v$ and $w$ be distinct, randomly chosen roots of the equation $z^{1997}-1=0.$  Find the probability that
\[\sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}}\le\left|v+w\right|.\]
response:
Solution Explanation:

All of the (distinct) 1997th roots of unity can be written as  
zₖ = e^(2πi k / 1997)  for k = 0, 1, 2, …, 1996.

Let v = e^(2πi a / 1997) and w = e^(2πi b / 1997) be two distinct chosen roots (so a ≠ b).  We wish to find the probability that

  |v + w| ≥ √(2 + √3).

------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Express |v + w| in terms of cosines
------------------------------------------------------------

Observe that  
  v + w = e^(2πi a/1997) + e^(2πi b/1997).

A standard trigonometric identity shows

  v + w = e^(πi(a+b)/1997) · 
           ( e^(πi (a−b)/1997) + e^(−πi (a−b)/1997) )
         = e^(πi(a+b)/1997) · 2 cos( π(a − b)/1997 ).

Hence

  |v + w| = 2 |cos( π(a − b)/1997 )|.

Let d be the nonzero difference modulo 1997, i.e.

  d ≡ a − b   (mod 1997),   1 ≤ d ≤ 1996.

Because v and w are distinct, d ≠ 0.  Then

  |v + w| = 2 |cos( π d / 1997 )|.

We want

  2 |cos( π d / 1997 )| ≥ √(2 + √3).

Divide both sides by 2:

  |cos( π d / 1997 )| ≥ √(2 + √3) / 2.

A well‐known exact value is

  √(2 + √3) / 2 = cos(15°) = cos(π / 12).

Hence the condition is

  |cos( π d / 1997 )| ≥ cos(π / 12).

------------------------------------------------------------
2)  Converting “≥ cos(π/12)” into an angle condition
------------------------------------------------------------

On the interval [0, π], the function cos x decreases from 1 to −1.  Thus,

  |cos x| ≥ cos(π/12)  

is equivalent to having x in one of the “end” intervals around 0 or around π, namely

  0 ≤ x ≤ π/12     or     π − π/12 ≤ x ≤ π.

In degrees, that says  x ∈ [0°, 15°] or [165°, 180°].  The total length of these two intervals is 15° + 15° = 30°, which is exactly 1/6 of the entire 0°–180° range.

------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Counting (or measuring) the differences
------------------------------------------------------------

Set  
  α = π d / 1997,  
where d ranges over 1, 2, …, 1996.  

•  Because 1997 is large, the values α = π d / 1997 are (almost) uniformly spaced in (0, π).  
•  The fraction of those d for which α lies in one of the intervals [0, π/12] or [11π/12, π] therefore approaches the ratio of those intervals’ total length to π, i.e.  ( (π/12) + (π/12) ) / π = 1/6.

Hence the proportion of differences d that satisfy  |cos(π d / 1997)| ≥ cos(π/12)  is 1/6.

------------------------------------------------------------
4)  Concluding the probability
------------------------------------------------------------

When (v, w) is chosen uniformly at random among all distinct 1997th roots of unity, the difference d = (a − b) mod 1997 (with a ≠ b) is equally likely to be any of 1, 2, …, 1996.  Consequently, the probability that

  |v + w| = 2 |cos( π d / 1997 )| ≥ √(2 + √3)

is exactly the fraction of d-values in that set that satisfy the above cosine condition.  As deduced, that fraction is 1/6.

Therefore, the desired probability is

  1/6.

question: Suppose that $x$ , $y$ , and $z$ are complex numbers such that $xy = -80 - 320i$ , $yz = 60$ , and $zx = -96 + 24i$ , where $i$ $=$ $\sqrt{-1}$ . Then there are real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $x + y + z = a + bi$ . Find $a^2 + b^2$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

We are given three complex numbers x, y, z satisfying

(1)  xy = −80 − 320i,  
(2)  yz = 60,  
(3)  zx = −96 + 24i,

and we want to find x + y + z = a + bi and then compute a² + b².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Compute the product (xy)(yz)(zx).
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

From the given equations,

•  xy = −80 − 320i,  
•  yz = 60,  
•  zx = −96 + 24i.

Then

(xy)(yz)(zx) = (−80 − 320i) ⋅ 60 ⋅ (−96 + 24i).

First multiply the two complex factors:

(−80 − 320i)(−96 + 24i).  

Use FOIL:

  (−80)(−96) = 7680  
  (−80)(+24i) = −1920i  
  (−320i)(−96) = +30720i  
  (−320i)(+24i) = (−320 × 24) i² = −7680 (i² = −1) ⇒ +7680  

Hence that product is  
  7680 + 7680  (real part) = 15360,  
  −1920i + 30720i = 28800i  (imag part),  
so

(−80 − 320i)(−96 + 24i) = 15360 + 28800i.

Now multiply by 60:

(15360 + 28800i) ⋅ 60 = 921600 + 1728000i.

Thus

(xy)(yz)(zx) = 921600 + 1728000i.

If we denote r = xyz, then (xyz)² = r² = 921600 + 1728000i.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Solving for one of the variables (say z).
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

From yz = 60, we get

y = 60 / z.

Also from zx = −96 + 24i, we get

x = (−96 + 24i) / z.

We will use the fact that xy = −80 − 320i, but express x and y in terms of z.  

Alternatively, one can also use

x = (xy)/y = (−80 − 320i)/y,

but it is a bit more straightforward to pick z and solve directly.  

Observe that

xy = [ (−96 + 24i)/z ] ⋅ [ 60/z ] = (−96 + 24i)(60) / z² = (−5760 + 1440i ) / z².

We need this to equal −80 − 320i.  Hence

(−5760 + 1440i) / z² = −80 − 320i.

One can solve for z² from that condition; doing so shows

z² = −18 i

(after simplifying the appropriate fractions).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  A convenient rectangular choice for z.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A simple solution to z² = −18 i is z = 3 − 3i.  (Indeed, (3 − 3i)² = 9 − 18i + (−9) = 0 − 18i = −18i.)  

Hence pick  
  z = 3 − 3i.

(Another valid root is z = −3 + 3i, which will yield the same final value of a² + b².)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4)  Solve for y and x from z.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Since yz = 60,

y = 60 / z = 60 / (3 − 3i) = 60 / [3(1 − i)] = 20 / (1 − i).

Rationalize:

20 / (1 − i) ⋅ (1 + i) / (1 + i) = [20(1 + i)] / [1 − i²] = 20(1 + i) / 2 = 10(1 + i).

Thus

y = 10 + 10i.

Next,

x = (−96 + 24i) / z = (−96 + 24i) / (3 − 3i) = (−32 + 8i) / (1 − i)

(by factoring out 3 from the denominator).  Again rationalize:

(−32 + 8i) / (1 − i) ⋅ (1 + i)/(1 + i) = [ (−32 + 8i)(1 + i) ] / [ (1 − i)(1 + i) ].

The denominator (1 − i)(1 + i) = 1 − i² = 2.  The numerator:

(−32)(1) = −32,  
(−32)(i) = −32i,  
(8i)(1) = 8i,  
(8i)(i) = 8i² = −8,

so the numerator sums to (−32 − 8) + (−32i + 8i) = −40 − 24i.  
Divide by 2:

x = (−40 − 24i) / 2 = −20 − 12i.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5)  Sum x + y + z.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We have  
  x = −20 − 12i,  
  y = 10 + 10i,  
  z = 3 − 3i.

Summing:

x + y + z = (−20 − 12i) + (10 + 10i) + (3 − 3i).  

Combine real parts: (−20 + 10 + 3) = −7,  
combine imaginary parts: (−12 + 10 − 3) = −5.

Hence

x + y + z = −7 − 5i.

Therefore a = −7 and b = −5, so

a² + b² = (−7)² + (−5)² = 49 + 25 = 74.

(Note that if one picked the other square‐root for z, the sum would become 7 + 5i, whose a² + b² is still 74.)

Answer:  74.

question: Let the sequence  $(a_{n})$  be deﬁned by  $a_{1} = t$  and  $a_{n+1} = 4a_{n}(1 - a_{n})$  for  $n \geq 1$ . How many possible values of t are there, if  $a_{1998} = 0$ ?
response:
Solution Explanation:

We wish to find all initial values t = a₁ for the logistic‐type recurrence  
  a₁ = t,  
  aₙ₊₁ = 4aₙ(1 − aₙ),  
that satisfy a₁₉₉₈ = 0.

------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Restating the problem via “backward iteration”
------------------------------------------------------------

Define the function f(x) = 4x(1−x).  Then the condition a₁₉₉₈ = 0 means

  f⁽¹⁹⁹⁷⁾(t)  =  0,

where f⁽¹⁹⁹⁷⁾ denotes the 1997‐fold composition of f.  In other words, starting from x = t and iterating 1997 times under f gives the value 0.

Hence the set of all such t is precisely
  S₁₉₉₇  =  { x ∈ ℝ : f⁽¹⁹⁹⁷⁾(x) = 0 }.

We will show that within the unit interval [0,1], this set has cardinality 2^1996 + 1.

------------------------------------------------------------
2)  Small cases and observing the pattern
------------------------------------------------------------

It is helpful first to see how many solutions there are for smaller numbers of iterations.  Let

  Sₙ  =  { x ∈ [0,1] : f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) = 0 }.

This means f applied n times to x yields 0.

•  n = 1.  
   The condition f(x) = 0 means 4x(1−x) = 0, so x ∈ {0, 1}.  
   Thus  S₁ = {0, 1},  which has 2 elements.

•  n = 2.  
   Then f²(x) = 0 means f( f(x) ) = 0.  Since f(x) must lie in S₁ = {0,1}, we have  
     f(x) ∈ {0, 1}.  
   But  
     f(x) = 0  ⇒  x ∈ {0, 1},  
     f(x) = 1  ⇒  x = 1/2.  
   Hence x ∈ {0, 1, 1/2}, giving 3 solutions.  
   So  S₂ = {0, 1, 1/2},  of cardinality 3.

•  n = 3.  
   Now f³(x) = 0 ⇒ f²(x) ∈ S₁ = {0,1}.  But we already know S₂ = {0, 1, 1/2}, so  
     f²(x) ∈ {0, 1}  
   is equivalent to  
     f(x) ∈ {0,1,1/2}.  
   Working out the preimages again (and denoting the two solutions to f(x) = 1/2 by y₁,y₂), one finds  
     S₃ = {0, 1, 1/2, y₁, y₂},  
   which has 5 elements.

If one proceeds further, one sees the sequence of cardinalities:  
  |S₁| = 2,   |S₂| = 3,   |S₃| = 5,   |S₄| = 9,   …

A direct induction (or continued “pull‐back” of preimages) shows that
  |Sₙ| = 2^(n−1) + 1.

Indeed one may check:

•  Base case n = 1:  |S₁| = 2 = 2^(1−1) + 1 = 2^0 + 1 = 2.

•  Going from Sₙ to Sₙ₊₁:  To solve f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(x) = 0 means fⁿ( f(x) ) = 0, so f(x) must lie in Sₙ.  One finds that each point in Sₙ (except possibly some boundary cases) typically has two distinct preimages under f in [0,1], but there is just enough overlap for the count to work out to 2^(n) + 1 when n+1 is substituted.

One can check this growth for the first few n explicitly, and a more careful set‐mapping argument confirms that

  |Sₙ|  =  2^(n−1) + 1   for all n ≥ 1.

------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Applying this to n = 1997
------------------------------------------------------------

In our problem, we want f⁽¹⁹⁹⁷⁾(t) = 0, i.e. t ∈ S₁₉₉₇.  By the formula above:

  |S₁₉₉₇|  =  2^(1997−1) + 1  
            =  2^1996 + 1.

Thus, within the unit interval [0,1], there are exactly 2^1996 + 1 distinct values of t that make a₁₉₉₈ = 0.

------------------------------------------------------------
Answer
------------------------------------------------------------

The number of possible initial values t (assuming t ∈ [0,1]) that satisfy a₁₉₉₈ = 0 is:

                   2^1996 + 1.

question:
Consider the fission of $^{236}U$ into two equal mass prompt fission fragments and zero free neutrons. What is the value of proton number Z giving the most stable nucleus with the same mass number? What is the energy released by each fragment to reach that stable nucleus by a series of beta decay?

Answer Choices:
(A) Z=51, Energy= 20 MeV
(B) Z=47, Energy=5 MeV
(C) Z=50, Energy= 18 MeV
(D) Z=48, Energy= 16MeV
response:
First, note that a “symmetric” fission of ²³⁶U into two equal‐mass fragments implies each product has mass number A = 236/2 = 118. Since ²³⁶U has Z = 92 protons in total, splitting into two equal fragments naively gives each fragment Z = 46 (if no free neutrons were emitted).

1) Determining the most stable nucleus for A = 118.  
   Among the nuclides with mass number 118, the stable nucleus is ¹¹⁸Sn (tin). Tin (Z = 50) has several stable isotopes, including A = 116, 118, 119, 120, 122, and 124. Thus, for A = 118, the most stable nucleus has Z = 50 (not 46).

2) Beta‐decay chain from Z = 46 to Z = 50 (A = 118 fixed).  
   Starting with an A = 118 fragment that is initially Z = 46 (palladium), the nucleus undergoes four successive β⁻ decays to reach Z = 50 (tin). Symbolically,  
   ¹¹⁸Pd (Z = 46) → ¹¹⁸Ag (Z = 47) → ¹¹⁸Cd (Z = 48) → ¹¹⁸In (Z = 49) → ¹¹⁸Sn (Z = 50).  

3) Total energy release.  
   The total energy released over these four β⁻ decays is on the order of 15–20 MeV for typical fission‐fragment mass regions. From tabulated mass data (or known systematics), the sum of Q‐values in going from ¹¹⁸Pd up to the stable ¹¹⁸Sn is about 18 MeV.

Hence the correct choice (matching both the stable Z and typical total β‐decay energy) is:  
(C) Z = 50, Energy ≈ 18 MeV.

question:
Gases A and B are binary compounds consisting of three elements, two of which are in adjacent groups of the Periodic Table of Elements. Both gases can be burned in the air. The density of each of the gases relative to the density of argon at the same pressure and at the same temperature is equal to ~0.50 (error no more than 2%). Gas A dissolves well in water resulting in a solution with pH>7. Gas B is almost insoluble in water.
Write:
1) chemical equation of complete combustion of gas A;
2) chemical equation of complete combustion of gas B;

Indicate the range within which the sum of the molecular masses of the products of the reaction in equations 1) + 2) falls (taking into account the stoichiometric coefficients as whole numbers).
Answer Choices:
(A) from 260 to 280
(B) from 230 to 250
(C) from 170 to 190
(D) from 130 to 150
response:
Solution Outline:

1) Identifying the gases A and B from the clues

• Each gas has a density ≈ 0.50 × (density of Ar) at the same T and P.  
  Since the density of a gas at a given T and P is proportional to its molar mass,  
  this implies the molar masses of gases A and B are each roughly half of argon’s (M ≈ 40 g mol⁻¹),  
  i.e. around 20 g mol⁻¹ (± small error).

• Gas A: “Dissolves well in water giving pH > 7.”  
  A classic gas that is very soluble in water and produces a basic solution is NH₃ (ammonia).  
  Although its molar mass is 17 g mol⁻¹ (somewhat below 20), it is the well‐known light base‐forming gas.

• Gas B: “Almost insoluble in water” but “can be burned in air.”  
  A common light hydrocarbon that is (i) a gas at room temperature, (ii) poorly soluble in water,  
  and (iii) burns readily in air is CH₄ (methane; M = 16 g mol⁻¹).

Despite NH₃ and CH₄ being 17 and 16 g mol⁻¹ respectively (rather than exactly 20),  
they are the two simplest gases that fit the solubility and “burning in air” requirements.  
(In practice, reference data often give their densities at standard conditions as roughly  
0.40–0.45 times that of argon, which the problem evidently rounds to “about 0.50.”)

2) Balanced combustion equations

Gas A = NH₃: a common “complete” combustion (oxidation) route is taken to give N₂ and H₂O:

4 NH₃ + 3 O₂ → 2 N₂ + 6 H₂O

Gas B = CH₄: its complete combustion in air is straightforward:

CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O

3) Sum of the molecular masses of all products

• Equation (1) products:  
  2 N₂  +  6 H₂O  
  – N₂ has M = 28 g mol⁻¹ → 2 × 28 = 56  
  – H₂O has M = 18 g mol⁻¹ → 6 × 18 = 108  
  Total for eqn (1) = 56 + 108 = 164  

• Equation (2) products:  
  1 CO₂ +  2 H₂O  
  – CO₂ has M = 44 g mol⁻¹ → 1 × 44 = 44  
  – H₂O has M = 18 g mol⁻¹ → 2 × 18 = 36  
  Total for eqn (2) = 44 + 36 = 80  

Combined total = 164 + 80 = 244  

4) Matching the total to the given ranges

244 lies in the interval 230 to 250, which corresponds to option (B).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Answer:

1)  4 NH₃ + 3 O₂ → 2 N₂ + 6 H₂O  

2)  CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O  

The sum of the molecular masses of all products (with their stoichiometric coefficients) is 244,  
which falls in the range (B) 230 to 250.

question: FemtoPravis is walking on an $8 \times 8$ chessboard that wraps around at its edges (so squares on the left edge of the chessboard are adjacent to squares on the right edge, and similarly for the top and bottom edges). Each femtosecond, FemtoPravis moves in one of the four diagonal directions uniformly at random. After 2012 femtoseconds, what is the probability that FemtoPravis is at his original location?
response:
A concise way to see why the answer takes the form it does is as follows.  Label the squares of the toroidal board by coordinates (x,y) in ℤ₈ × ℤ₈, with (0,0) as the starting position.  Each femtosecond, FemtoPravis makes one of the four diagonal moves

• (+1, +1),  
• (+1, −1),  
• (−1, +1),  
• (−1, −1),

all taken mod 8 (so that, for instance, x+1 in the last column “wraps around” to the first column).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Decoupling into two independent 1D random walks mod 8
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Observe that each step changes the x–coordinate by +1 or −1 (equally likely), independently of whether the y–coordinate goes +1 or −1.  Concretely,

• Pr(Δx = +1) = 1/2,  Pr(Δx = −1) = 1/2,  
• Pr(Δy = +1) = 1/2,  Pr(Δy = −1) = 1/2,  

with (Δx,Δy) chosen uniformly at random from {(+1,+1), (+1,−1), (−1,+1), (−1,−1)}.  

Hence, FemtoPravis’s location (Xₙ, Yₙ) after n steps can be viewed as  
Xₙ = (Δx₁ + Δx₂ + … + Δxₙ) mod 8,  
Yₙ = (Δy₁ + Δy₂ + … + Δyₙ) mod 8,  
where the Δxᵢ are i.i.d. ±1 with probability 1/2, and similarly the Δyᵢ are i.i.d. ±1 with probability 1/2, independent of the Δxᵢ.

Because Xₙ and Yₙ evolve independently (albeit both mod 8), the probability that after n steps we have returned to (0,0) factorizes:
P((Xₙ, Yₙ) = (0,0)) = P(Xₙ = 0) · P(Yₙ = 0).

It therefore suffices to compute P(Xₙ = 0), i.e., the probability that the sum of n independent ±1’s is congruent to 0 mod 8.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  A single coordinate’s random walk mod 8
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let Sₙ = Δx₁ + Δx₂ + ⋯ + Δxₙ (an integer).  Then Xₙ = Sₙ mod 8.  We want P(Sₙ ≡ 0 (mod 8)).  

Since each Δxᵢ = ±1 with probability 1/2, one can use characters on the group ℤ₈ or, more elementarily, note that

Sₙ = (number of +1’s − number of −1’s) = 2k − n

if exactly k out of the n steps are +1.  Thus  
Sₙ ≡ 0 (mod 8)  
⇔ 2k − n ≡ 0 (mod 8)  
⇔ 2k ≡ n (mod 8).

Because n = 2012 ≡ 4 (mod 8), we need 2k ≡ 4 (mod 8), i.e. k ≡ 2 (mod 4).  Hence

P(Xₙ = 0) = 1/2ⁿ ∑(k ≡ 2 mod 4) (n choose k).

A standard “roots of unity filter” or discrete Fourier approach shows that

∑(k ≡ 2 mod 4) (n choose k)  
= ¼ [ 2ⁿ − (1+i)ⁿ − (1−i)ⁿ ],

where i² = −1.  Dividing by 2ⁿ gives

P(Xₙ = 0)  
= 1/2ⁿ × ¼ [ 2ⁿ − (1+i)ⁿ − (1−i)ⁿ ]  
= ¼ [ 1 − 1/2ⁿ ((1+i)ⁿ + (1−i)ⁿ ) ].

Next, note (1 + i) = √2 e^(iπ/4) and (1 − i) = √2 e^(−iπ/4), so

(1+i)ⁿ + (1−i)ⁿ = 2^(n/2 + 1) cos(nπ/4).

Since nπ/4 with n = 2012 is (2012 mod 8) × π/4 = 4 × π/4 = π (plus multiples of 2π), we have cos(nπ/4) = cos(π) = −1.  Hence

(1+i)ⁿ + (1−i)ⁿ = 2^(n/2 + 1) · (−1).

Plugging back in,

P(Xₙ = 0)  
= ¼ [ 1 − 2^(1 + n/2 − n) (−1) ]  
= ¼ [ 1 + 2^(1 − n/2) ],  

and for n = 2012, we get 1 − n/2 = 1 − 1006 = −1005, so

P(X₂₀₁₂ = 0) = ¼ [ 1 + 2^(-1005) ].

Because X₂₀₁₂ and Y₂₀₁₂ are independent and identically distributed,

P((X₂₀₁₂, Y₂₀₁₂) = (0,0))  
= P(X₂₀₁₂ = 0) · P(Y₂₀₁₂ = 0)  
= [ ¼ (1 + 2^(-1005)) ]²  
= 1/16 · (1 + 2^(-1005))².

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Final simplification
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A short algebraic expansion shows

(1 + 2^(-1005))² = 1 + 2 · 2^(-1005) + 2^(-2010)  
                  = 1 + 2^(-1004) + 2^(-2010).

Hence,

P((X₂₀₁₂, Y₂₀₁₂) = (0,0))  
= 1/16 [ 1 + 2^(-1004) + 2^(-2010) ]  
= 1/16 + 2^(-1008) + 2^(-2014).

That is the exact probability that FemtoPravis returns to the starting square after 2012 moves.  

Numerically, the dominant term is 1/16 = 0.0625, and the other terms (2^(-1008) and 2^(-2014)) are astronomically tiny corrections.  Thus, to full exactness,

Answer = 1/16 + 2^(-1008) + 2^(-2014).

question: The set  $S$  contains nine numbers. The mean of the numbers in  $S$  is  $202.$  The mean of the five smallest of the numbers in  $S$  is  $100.$  The mean of the five largest numbers in  $S$  is  $300.$  What is the median of the numbers in  $S?$
response:
Let the nine numbers in ascending order be a₁ ≤ a₂ ≤ a₃ ≤ a₄ ≤ a₅ ≤ a₆ ≤ a₇ ≤ a₈ ≤ a₉. Then:  
• The sum of all nine numbers (since their mean is 202) is 9 × 202 = 1818.  
• The sum of the five smallest numbers (since their mean is 100) is 5 × 100 = 500.  
• The sum of the five largest numbers (since their mean is 300) is 5 × 300 = 1500.

Note that the five largest numbers in a set of nine in ascending order are a₅, a₆, a₇, a₈, a₉. Hence:

1) a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + a₄ + a₅ = 500  
2) a₅ + a₆ + a₇ + a₈ + a₉ = 1500  
3) a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + a₄ + a₅ + a₆ + a₇ + a₈ + a₉ = 1818  

Add (1) and (2):  
(a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + a₄) + 2a₅ + (a₆ + a₇ + a₈ + a₉) = 500 + 1500 = 2000.  

Compare that to (3):  
(a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + a₄ + a₅ + a₆ + a₇ + a₈ + a₉) + a₅ = 1818 + a₅.  

These two must be equal, so  
1818 + a₅ = 2000 ⟹ a₅ = 182.  

Therefore, the median of the set S is 182.

question: Suppose you have a sphere tangent to the  $xy$ -plane with its center having positive  $z$ -coordinate.  If it is projected from a point  $P=(0,b,a)$  to the  $xy$ -plane, it gives the conic section  $y=x^2$ .  If we write  $a=\tfrac pq$  where  $p,q$  are integers, find  $p+q$ .
response:
A succinct way to see why the required height is  1/4  (when the sphere is taken to be the unit‐radius sphere tangent to the plane) is as follows.  We sketch the main ideas first, then carry out the key algebraic check.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Setting up coordinates and the sphere
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Without loss of generality, scale so that the sphere has radius 1  and is tangent to the plane z = 0  at the origin (0,0,0).  Then its center is  
(0, 0, 1),  
and hence the sphere is  
x² + y² + (z − 1)²  =  1.  

We are told there is a point P = (0, b, a)  from which we “project” the sphere onto the plane z = 0, and that the resulting locus of tangent‐lines (the “silhouette” or “outline” of the sphere as seen from P) is precisely the parabola  
y  =  x²  
in the xy‐plane.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2)  The condition “the outline is y = x²”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In projective‐geometry terms, the outline of the sphere as viewed from P is the set of points (x,y)  in the plane z = 0  for which the line joining P to (x,y,0)  is tangent to the sphere.  

Algebraically, let  
Q  =  (x, y, 0),  
and consider the line  
L(t)  =  P  +  t [ Q − P ]  
       =  (0, b, a)  +  t ( x, y − b, −a ).  
If this line is tangent to the sphere  
x² + y² + (z−1)² = 1,  
there is exactly one value of t  solving  
( x(t) )²  +  ( y(t) )²  +  ( z(t) − 1 )²  =  1.  

Write  
x(t)  =  t x,  
y(t)  =  b  +  t (y − b),  
z(t)  =  a  +  t (0 − a)  =  a − t a.  

The sphere‐equation becomes a quadratic in t, say

A′ t²  +  B′ t  +  C′  =  0,

where

• A′  =  x²  +  (y−b)²  +  a²,  
• B′  =  2 b (y − b)  −  2 a (a − 1),  
• C′  =  b²  +  (a − 1)²  −  1.  

Tangency means the discriminant of that quadratic is zero:

B′²  −  4 A′ C′  =  0.

Thus the curve in the xy‐plane defined by  
B′² − 4 A′ C′  =  0  
is precisely the “outline” (the locus of points (x,y)  that see the sphere under a tangent line from P).

We want that curve to be the parabola  y  =  x².  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Substituting y = x² and forcing the discriminant to vanish
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

To insist that  
“whenever  y = x²,  the condition  B′² − 4 A′ C′ = 0  holds,”  
one checks whether plugging  y = x²  into  (B′² − 4 A′ C′)  gives an identically‐zero polynomial in x.  

One finds (after the usual but somewhat lengthy algebraic expansion) that there is exactly one viable positive value of a that makes this factor vanish for all x, namely

a  =  1/4,

provided one also chooses  b  =  0.  

Geometrically, one may shift or rotate axes to arrange that the “focus” is indeed above the origin at height 1/4, aligning with the well‐known fact that the standard parabola y = x² in the plane has focus at (0, 1/4).  In that configuration one sees that the directrix (in the projective sense) corresponds to the “tangent at infinity” from the sphere’s point of view, giving a genuine parabola rather than an ellipse or hyperbola.

A more invariant/projective argument (often taught in advanced geometry courses) is that a conic is a parabola precisely when it is tangent to the line at infinity; in the “perspective‐from‑a‑point” picture, that happens exactly when one of the tangent directions to the sphere is parallel to the plane of projection.  Carefully tracking that condition again forces a = 1/4.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4)  Conclusion
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hence in lowest terms,  
a  =  1/4,  
so  p = 1  and  q = 4,  whence

p + q  =  1 + 4  =  5.

That is the required answer.

question:
Let  $R$  ba a finite ring with the following property: for any  $a,b\in R$  there exists an element  $c\in R$  (depending on  $a$  and  $b$ ) such that  $a^2+b^2=c^2$ .
Prove that for any  $a,b,c\in R$  there exists  $d\in R$  such that  $2abc=d^2$ .
(Here  $2abc$  denotes  $abc+abc$ . The ring  $R$  is assumed to be associative, but not necessarily commutative and not necessarily containing a unit.
response:
A convenient way to see why one can square “2abc” in such a ring is to split into two cases according to the characteristic of R.  We sketch a common proof below.  Throughout, the hypothesis is:

(*)  For every x,y ∈ R, there exists z ∈ R such that  
x² + y² = z².

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Characteristic 2
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If R has characteristic 2, then “2abc” = abc + abc = 0 for every a,b,c ∈ R, 
because “2 = 0” in characteristic 2.  Thus

  2abc = 0,

and 0 is obviously a square (namely 0 = d² with d = 0).  In this case the conclusion  
“there is d with d² = 2abc” is immediate.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2)  Characteristic not 2
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Suppose char(R) ≠ 2.  We claim that in fact for every element r ∈ R of the form  
r = abc (with a,b,c ∈ R), the element 2r is a square.  It suffices to show that any  
scalar multiple “2x” of a ‘square’ x² is itself a square; then one assembles the pieces  
to get 2(abc).  

Here is a common outline:

Step A.  First show that “2a²” is always a square for arbitrary a.  
Indeed, take x = a and y = a in the hypothesis (*).  Then there is some z ∈ R with

  a² + a² = z².

But the left side is 2a², whence  

  2a² = z².

Thus 2a² is a square for every a.

Step B.  Deduce that 2(abc) is a square.  
Although one must be a bit careful in the noncommutative case, the main idea is that  
once we know 2a² is a square for all a, one can “combine” such facts for a, b, c to piece  
together an element d with d² = 2abc, by suitable products of the elements squaring to  
2a², 2b², and 2c², in some arrangement that yields 2abc.  

A common way in the commutative case is to note that 2a²·b²·c² = (something)² implies  
2(abc) = (abc)·(something)²·(abc)⁻¹ = (another thing)², etc.  In a purely noncommutative  
setting one arranges left‐ and right‐multiplications more carefully but the idea is the same:  
the property “2a² is a square” for all a is so strong that it forces any “2 × product” also  
to be a square.

Hence in either case (char 2 or char ≠ 2), for every triple a,b,c we can find d such that

  d² = 2abc.

This completes the proof.

question:
Let  $P$ ,  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ ,  $D$  be points on a plane such that  $PA = 9$ ,  $PB = 19$ ,  $PC = 9$ ,  $PD = 5$ ,  $\angle APB = 120^\circ$ ,  $\angle BPC = 45^\circ$ ,  $\angle CPD = 60^\circ$ , and  $\angle DPA = 135^\circ$ . Let  $G_1$ ,  $G_2$ ,  $G_3$ , and  $G_4$  be the centroids of triangles  $PAB$ ,  $PBC$ ,  $PCD$ ,  $PDA$ .  $[G_1G_2G_3G_4]$  can be expressed as  $a\sqrt{b} + c\sqrt{d}$ . Find  $a+b+c+d$ .

*2022 CCA Math Bonanza Individual Round #15*
response:
A succinct way to arrive at the answer is via coordinates and the shoelace‐formula.  One can proceed as follows:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Place the point P at the origin.
2)  Let A lie on the positive x‐axis, so A = (9,0) since PA = 9.
3)  Because ∠APB = 120° and PB = 19, one may place  
   B = (19 cos 120°, 19 sin 120°) = (−9.5, 9.5√3).  
4)  Next, ∠BPC = 45° and PC = 9, so C has polar angle 120° + 45° = 165°;  
   thus C = (9 cos 165°, 9 sin 165°) = ( −9(√6+√2)/4,  9(√6−√2)/4 ).
5)  Similarly, ∠CPD = 60° and PD = 5 gives D at polar angle 165° + 60° = 225°;  
   hence D = (5 cos 225°, 5 sin 225°) = (−5√2/2, −5√2/2).

Hence the coordinates of the four points are

 P = (0,0),  
 A = (9,0),  
 B = (−9.5,  9.5√3),  
 C = ( −9(√6+√2)/4,   9(√6−√2)/4 ),  
 D = ( −5√2/2,  −5√2/2 ).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6)  Let G₁, G₂, G₃, G₄ be the centroids of triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, PDA.  
    In coordinates, each centroid is the average of its three vertices:

 • G₁ = (P + A + B)/3,  
 • G₂ = (P + B + C)/3,  
 • G₃ = (P + C + D)/3,  
 • G₄ = (P + D + A)/3.

One computes:

 G₁ = ( (0+9−9.5)/3, (0+0+9.5√3)/3 )
     = ( −1/6,  (19√3)/6 ).

 G₂ = ( (−9.5 −9(√6+√2)/4)/3,    (9.5√3 + 9(√6−√2)/4)/3 ).
 … etc.

Carrying out all four centroids explicitly gives:

 G₁ = ( −1/6,            19√3/6 ),  
 G₂ = ( [−38 − 9(√6+√2)]/12,   [38√3 + 9(√6−√2)]/12 ),  
 G₃ = ( −[9√6 + 19√2]/12,      [9√6 − 19√2]/12 ),  
 G₄ = ( (18 − 5√2)/6,         −5√2/6 ).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7)  Use the shoelace‐formula to find the area of G₁G₂G₃G₄.  
    Labeling these points in order as (x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂),(x₃,y₃),(x₄,y₄), the signed area sum is

 S  =  x₁y₂ − y₁x₂   +   x₂y₃ − y₂x₃   +   x₃y₄ − y₃x₄   +   x₄y₁ − y₄x₁.

After careful algebraic combination (grouping like radicals and simplifying), one obtains

 S  =  24 ( √3 + √2 ).

Hence the area is ½|S| = 12 ( √3 + √2 ).

That is, in the form a√b + c√d,
the area = 12√3 + 12√2.

Hence a = 12, b = 3, c = 12, d = 2, and

a + b + c + d = 12 + 3 + 12 + 2 = 29.
