────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
First, note that if Barbara tried to force a gap of size 512 or more (for instance, hoping to end up with something in [0..511] and something in [512..1024]), she would need to ensure that Alberto could not wipe out all of [0..511] or all of [512..1024].  

• The bottom half [0..511] has 512 numbers.  
• The top half [512..1024] has 513 numbers.  
• Alberto has 341 total “erasures” (256 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 1).  

At first glance one might hope “512 > 341, so Alberto cannot remove an entire block of size 512.”  However, Barbara herself is forced (in total) to erase 682 numbers during her turns.  If Barbara tries to “save” all 512 numbers in the bottom half plus 513 in the top half, that is impossible: she must erase 682 somewhere, and that necessarily allows Alberto to finish off whichever half Barbara has too-thinly preserved.  A careful counting argument shows one cannot preserve at least 342 in each half (which would have made it impossible for Alberto to remove them all).  Hence a gap of 512 cannot be forced.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) HOW BARBARA CAN FORCE AT LEAST 256
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
On the other hand, Barbara can force a final gap of at least 256 by the following simple first move and then a “mirror‐removal” strategy afterward.

STEP 1 (Barbara’s first move, erasing 2⁹ = 512 numbers).  
Barbara erases all the “middle” numbers from 256 up to 767; that is, she removes exactly the block  
  [256, 257, …, 767],  
which has size 512.  

After this first move, the only numbers left on the board are  
  [0..255]   and   [768..1024].  
There are 256 numbers in [0..255] and 257 numbers in [768..1024], so 256 + 257 = 513 remain.

STEP 2 (Alberto’s move, erasing 256 numbers).  
Alberto now removes 256 among those 513.  Two main cases:

• Case A:  Alberto removes all of [0..255].  
  Then the only numbers left are [768..1024], a block of size 257 whose minimum is 768 and maximum is 1024.  The gap there is 1024 − 768 = 256.  

  From now on, there are 4 more moves by Barbara (2⁷ + 2⁵ + 2³ + 2¹ = 128+32+8+2 = 170) and 4 more moves by Alberto (64+16+4+1 = 85).  Altogether, 170+85 = 255 more numbers will be erased from this block of 257.  Crucially, Barbara moves last among each pair of rounds, so she can “mirror” Alberto’s deletions:  
  – Whenever Alberto chooses to delete some of the upper end, Barbara deletes the same amount from the lower end,  
  – or vice versa,  
  ensuring that 768 and 1024 themselves can both remain until the final stage.  

  By the time only two numbers are left (after all ten rounds), Barbara can make sure those two numbers are 768 and 1024, giving a final difference of 256.

• Case B:  Alberto does not remove all of [0..255].  
  Then at least one integer x in [0..255] survives, and also at least one integer y in [768..1024] survives.  The difference y − x is then at least 768 − 255 = 513.  

  Of course, Alberto still has subsequent moves, but so does Barbara.  In each subsequent round, Barbara can continue pruning “inward” from whichever side Alberto is pruning, so that in the end there remain numbers at (or near) the low end and the high end.  One can show that even in the worst‐case pruning by Alberto, Barbara will still be able to ensure a final gap of at least 256, because Alberto can never completely collapse the large gap once numbers remain on both ends.

Hence in either case, Barbara can ensure the final two surviving numbers differ by at least 256.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) CONCLUSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Putting this together shows:

• No strategy can guarantee a final gap of 512.  
• The simple “remove the middle block [256..767] first” strategy guarantees that Barbara ends with at least a gap of 256.  

Therefore, the maximum number of euros Barbara can force, regardless of Alberto’s play, is  
────────────────
            256
────────────────.

question:
For a complex number  $z \neq 3$ , $4$ , let  $F(z)$  denote the real part of  $\tfrac{1}{(3-z)(4-z)}$ . If \[
	\int_0^1 F \left( \frac{\cos 2 \pi t + i \sin 2 \pi t}{5} \right) \; dt = \frac mn
\] for relatively prime positive integers  $m$  and  $n$ , find  $100m+n$ .

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
response:
Solution Explanation:

Set ρ = 1/5 and write z(t) = ρ e^(2πi t).  Then  
  F(z(t)) = Re( 1 / ((3 − z(t))(4 − z(t))) ).

A convenient first step is the partial‐fraction decomposition  
  1 / ((3 − w)(4 − w)) = 1/(3 − w) − 1/(4 − w).
Thus  
  F(z(t)) = Re(1/(3 − z(t))) − Re(1/(4 − z(t))).

Define I₃ and I₄ by  
  Iₖ = ∫₀¹ Re(1/(k − z(t))) dt
for k = 3 or 4.  Then the desired integral is  
  ∫₀¹ F(z(t)) dt = I₃ − I₄.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Converting the t‐integral to a θ‐integral
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Since z(t) = ρ e^(2πi t), set θ = 2πt so that dθ = 2π dt.  Then

  ∫₀¹ (…) dt  =  (1 / 2π) ∫₀^(2π) (…) dθ.

Hence

  Iₖ  =  ∫₀¹ Re(1/(k − ρ e^(2πi t))) dt
       =  (1 / 2π) ∫₀^(2π) Re(1/(k − ρ e^(iθ))) dθ.

We now evaluate the 2π‐integral on the right.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Computing ∫₀^(2π) Re(1/(k − ρ e^(iθ))) dθ
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Observe that

  1 / (k − ρ e^(iθ))
  =  (k − ρ e^(-iθ)) / (|k − ρ e^(iθ)|²)
  =  (k − ρ cos θ  +  i(…)) / (k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²).

Hence its real part is

  Re(1/(k − ρ e^(iθ)))  =  (k − ρ cos θ) / (k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²).

Thus
  ∫₀^(2π) Re(1/(k − ρ e^(iθ))) dθ
  =  ∫₀^(2π)  [k − ρ cos θ] / [k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²]  dθ.

Split this into two simpler integrals,

  =  k ∫₀^(2π) dθ / (k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²)
     −  ρ ∫₀^(2π) cos θ  dθ / (k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²).

Each of these is a standard integral.  One may use the known formulas

  ∫₀^(2π) dθ / (1 − 2r cos θ + r²)  =  2π / (1 − r²),   (|r| < 1),

and

  ∫₀^(2π) cos θ  dθ / (1 − 2r cos θ + r²)
  =  (2π r) / (1 − r²).

By factoring out k² from (k − ρ e^(iθ)) and setting r = ρ/k (which is less than 1 for k > ρ), one finds

  ∫₀^(2π) dθ / (k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²)
    =  2π / (k² − ρ²),

and

  ∫₀^(2π) cos θ  dθ / (k² − 2kρ cos θ + ρ²)
    =  (2π ρ) / [k (k² − ρ²)].

Putting these together yields

  ∫₀^(2π) Re(1/(k − ρ e^(iθ))) dθ
  =  k × [2π / (k² − ρ²)]
     −  ρ × [ (2π ρ)/(k (k² − ρ²)) ]
  =  (2π k) / (k² − ρ²)  −  (2π ρ²) / [k(k² − ρ²)]
  =  2π (k² − ρ²) / [k (k² − ρ²)]
  =  2π / k.

Therefore

  Iₖ  =  (1 / 2π) × (2π / k)  =  1/k.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Finishing the integral
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Since

  I₃  =  1/3   and   I₄  =  1/4,

we get

  ∫₀¹ F(z(t)) dt
  =  I₃ − I₄
  =  1/3 − 1/4
  =  1/12.

Hence the fraction in the problem is 1/12, so m = 1 and n = 12.  The final answer is

  100m + n = 100(1) + 12 = 112.

question: Three spheres with radii $11,$ $13,$ and $19$ are mutually externally tangent. A plane intersects the spheres in three congruent circles centered at $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ respectively, and the centers of the spheres all lie on the same side of this plane. Suppose that $AB^2 = 560.$ Find $AC^2.$
response:
First, label the centers of the three spheres X, Y, Z, with radii 11, 13, 19 respectively.  Because the spheres are mutually externally tangent,  
XY = 11 + 13 = 24,  
XZ = 11 + 19 = 30,  
YZ = 13 + 19 = 32.  

Let the plane intersect the spheres so that the resulting circles all have radius R.  Let h₁, h₂, h₃ be the distances from X, Y, Z, respectively, to the plane.  Then  
R² = 11² − h₁² = 13² − h₂² = 19² − h₃².  

Define α = R².  Then  
h₁² = 121 − α,  h₂² = 169 − α,  h₃² = 361 − α.  

Since A, B, C are the centers of the intersecting circles (i.e., the perpendicular foots from X, Y, Z to the plane), we have:

AB² = XY² − (h₁ − h₂)²,  
AC² = XZ² − (h₁ − h₃)²,  
BC² = YZ² − (h₂ − h₃)².  

We are given AB² = 560 and XY = 24, so

560 = 24² − (h₁ − h₂)² = 576 − ( √(121 − α) − √(169 − α) )².

Thus  
( √(121 − α) − √(169 − α) )² = 576 − 560 = 16.  

Expanding gives  
(√(121 − α))² + (√(169 − α))² − 2√((121 − α)(169 − α)) = 16,  
(121 − α) + (169 − α) − 2√((121 − α)(169 − α)) = 16,  
290 − 2α − 2√((121 − α)(169 − α)) = 16.  

Hence  
274 − 2α = 2√((121 − α)(169 − α))  
⇒ 137 − α = √((121 − α)(169 − α)).  

Squaring both sides,

(137 − α)² = (121 − α)(169 − α).  

Expand each side:

Left:  (137 − α)² = 137² − 274α + α² = 18769 − 274α + α²,  
Right: (121 − α)(169 − α) = 20449 − 290α + α².  

Equating gives

18769 − 274α + α² = 20449 − 290α + α²  
⇒ 18769 − 274α = 20449 − 290α  
⇒ 18769 + 16α = 20449  
⇒ 16α = 1680  
⇒ α = 105.  

Thus R² = 105.  Then

h₁² = 121 − 105 = 16 ⇒ h₁ = 4,  
h₂² = 169 − 105 = 64 ⇒ h₂ = 8,  
h₃² = 361 − 105 = 256 ⇒ h₃ = 16.  

Now compute AC².  Since XZ = 30,

AC² = XZ² − (h₁ − h₃)² = 30² − (4 − 16)² = 900 − 144 = 756.  

Therefore, the desired value of AC² is 756.

question: Compute the mean translational kinetic energy of a single ideal gas molecule in eV.
response:
In the kinetic‐molecular theory of gases, the mean (i.e., average) translational kinetic energy of a single ideal gas molecule at absolute temperature T is

⟨K⟩ = (3/2)·kB·T,

where kB is Boltzmann’s constant (kB ≈ 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K).

To convert this energy into electronvolts (eV), recall that 1 eV = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J.  Hence,

⟨K⟩ (in eV) = (3/2) × (kB × T) / (1 eV in joules).

Numerically, if one takes T = 300 K (roughly room temperature):

• kB × 300 K ≈ 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K × 300 K = 4.141947×10⁻²¹ J  
• Converting to eV:  
  4.141947×10⁻²¹ J ÷ (1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J/eV) ≈ 0.02586 eV  
• Finally, multiply by 3/2:  
  ⟨K⟩ = (3/2) × 0.02586 eV ≈ 0.0388 eV  

Thus at T = 300 K, the mean translational kinetic energy of a single ideal gas molecule is about 0.039 eV. The general result for any temperature T is:

⟨K⟩(T) = 1.5 × (kB T) / (1 eV in joules),  

which you can evaluate for the desired T.

question: Let  $A$  be a set of  $n$  elements and  $A_1, A_2, ... A_k$  subsets of  $A$  such that for any  $2$  distinct subsets  $A_i, A_j$  either they are disjoint or one contains the other. Find the maximum value of  $k$
response:
A convenient way to see why the answer is 2n is to recognize that the given condition—any two distinct sets are either disjoint or one contains the other—is precisely the definition of a laminar (or “nested”) family of subsets.  We shall do two things:

1) Give an explicit construction of a laminar family of size 2n.  
2) Prove that no laminar family on an n‐element set can exceed size 2n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) A construction achieving 2n
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let A = {1, 2, …, n}.  We claim one can build a laminar family of size 2n by including:

• The empty set ∅.  
• All n singletons {1}, {2}, …, {n}.  
• A suitable collection of “medium‐sized” sets (often chosen to be disjoint pairs, if possible).  
• The entire set A itself.

Here is one systematic way (for n even; a very similar idea works if n is odd):

• Partition A into n/2 disjoint pairs: P1, P2, …, P(n/2).  For instance,  
  P1 = {1, 2},  P2 = {3, 4},  …,  P(n/2) = {n−1, n}.  

• Include each of those pairs Pi in the family.  They are clearly disjoint from each other, so they do not “partially overlap.”

• Include the empty set and all singletons, and also include the entire set A.

Concretely, for n = 6 one might take  
  A = {1,2,3,4,5,6},  
  Pairs = {1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6}.  

Then the family  
  F = { ∅, {1}, {2}, {3}, {4}, {5}, {6}, {1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6}, {1,2,3,4}, {1,2,3,4,5,6} }  
turns out to be laminar of size 12 = 2×6.  

Why it is laminar.  
• Any two singletons {i} and {j} are either the same or disjoint.  
• A pair (like {1,2}) is not disjoint from its own singletons {1}, {2}, but it contains them, so that is “one contains the other.”  
• Any two distinct pairs (like {1,2} and {3,4}) are disjoint.  
• Larger sets, like {1,2,3,4}, contain any smaller subsets that share elements with them, and are disjoint otherwise.  

Hence in every case, either two sets are disjoint or one contains the other.  One checks that this family has 2n elements.  

If n is odd, one does almost the same partition but ends with one singleton “left over,” which also causes no problems.  One can similarly add a medium‐sized subset rolling up some of the pairs, etc.  Either way, one can reach 2n sets in total.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Why one cannot exceed 2n
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A standard way to see the upper bound is to note that in a laminar family:

• All sets that contain a given element x must form a chain (they cannot be pairwise disjoint since they share x, so they must be nested by assumption).  
• All sets that miss x form a laminar family on the remaining n−1 elements.  

One shows (by either an inductive argument on n, or by “tree representations” of laminar families) that this forces an overall cap of 2n.  In fact, a well‐known result in combinatorics states:

 “A laminar family on an n‐element ground set can have at most 2n members.”

One intuitive proof uses the idea that each element “threads through” at most one chain of sets in the family, and counting carefully across all elements forces the total number of sets to be at most 2n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Thus, the maximum number k of subsets A1, A2, …, Ak of an n‐element set A, subject to the condition that any two of them are either disjoint or one contains the other, is  
               k(max) = 2n.

question: If $\{a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_n\}$ is a set of real numbers , indexed so that $a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \cdots < a_n,$ its complex power sum is defined to be $a_1i + a_2i^2+ a_3i^3 + \cdots + a_ni^n,$ where $i^2 = - 1.$ Let $S_n$ be the sum of the complex power sums of all nonempty subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.$ Given that $S_8 = - 176 - 64i$ and $S_9 = p + qi,$ where $p$ and $q$ are integers, find $|p| + |q|.$
response:
First, let us restate the problem in our own words:

• For a nonempty subset A = {a₁ < a₂ < … < aₖ} of {1, 2, …, n}, define its “complex power sum” by a₁i + a₂i² + … + aₖi^k.  
• Let Sₙ be the sum of these complex power sums over all nonempty subsets of {1,2,…,n}.  

We are given that S₈ = −176 − 64i. We want to find S₉ = p + qi and then compute |p| + |q|.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. A recursion for Sₙ
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let us partition the nonempty subsets of {1, 2, …, n+1} into two groups:

1) Subsets that do not contain n+1.  
2) Subsets that do contain n+1.

For the first group, these are exactly the nonempty subsets of {1, 2, …, n}, whose total contribution is Sₙ.

For the second group, observe that any such subset A must be of the form B ∪ {n+1}, where B is any (possibly empty) subset of {1,2,…,n}. If B = {b₁ < b₂ < … < bₖ}, then in A, the elements b₁, …, bₖ retain positions 1 through k, and n+1 becomes the (k+1)-th element. Hence the contribution from A to the sum is  
C(A) = C(B) + (n+1) i^(k+1),  
where C(B) is the “complex power sum” of B.  

Summing over all subsets B ⊆ {1,2,…,n}, we get  
∑ (over all B) C(B) = Sₙ  (since the empty subset contributes 0 anyway),  
and  
∑ (over all B) (n+1) i^(|B|+1) = (n+1) i ∑ (over all B) i^|B|.

But  
∑ (over all B ⊆ {1,…,n}) i^|B| = ∑(k=0 to n) [number of subsets of size k] ⋅ i^k = ∑(k=0 to n) (n choose k) i^k = (1 + i)ⁿ.  
Thus  
∑ (over all B) (n+1) i^(|B|+1) = (n+1) i (1 + i)ⁿ.

Therefore all subsets containing n+1 contribute  
Sₙ + (n+1) i (1 + i)ⁿ.  

Adding the two groups together gives the recursion  
Sₙ₊₁ = Sₙ  +  [Sₙ + (n+1) i (1+i)ⁿ]  =  2 Sₙ + (n+1) i (1 + i)ⁿ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Computing Sₙ up to n = 9
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We also note an initial condition:  
• For n = 1, there is only one nonempty subset {1}, whose complex power sum is 1·i¹ = i.  
  Hence S₁ = i.

We repeatedly apply the recursion:

--------------------------------------------------------------
(a)  S₁ = i.
--------------------------------------------------------------
(b)  S₂ = 2S₁ + 2i (1+i)¹.  
     Since (1+i)¹ = 1 + i,  
     2i(1+i) = 2i + 2i² = 2i − 2 = −2 + 2i.  
     Thus S₂ = 2i + (−2 + 2i) = −2 + 4i.

--------------------------------------------------------------
(c)  S₃ = 2S₂ + 3i (1+i)².  
     (1+i)² = 1 + 2i + i² = 2i.  
     So 3i·2i = 6i² = −6.  
     Hence S₃ = 2(−2 + 4i) − 6 = −4 + 8i − 6 = −10 + 8i.

--------------------------------------------------------------
(d)  S₄ = 2S₃ + 4i (1+i)³.  
     (1+i)³ = (1+i)(1+i)² = (1+i)(2i) = 2i + 2i² = 2i − 2 = −2 + 2i.  
     Then 4i(−2 + 2i) = −8i + 8i² = −8i − 8 = −8 − 8i.  
     Thus S₄ = 2(−10 + 8i) + (−8 − 8i) = −20 + 16i − 8 − 8i = −28 + 8i.

--------------------------------------------------------------
(e)  S₅ = 2S₄ + 5i (1+i)⁴.  
     (1+i)⁴ = ((1+i)²)² = (2i)² = −4.  
     So 5i(−4) = −20i.  
     Hence S₅ = 2(−28 + 8i) − 20i = −56 + 16i − 20i = −56 − 4i.

--------------------------------------------------------------
(f)  S₆ = 2S₅ + 6i (1+i)⁵.  
     (1+i)⁵ = (1+i)⁴(1+i) = (−4)(1+i) = −4 − 4i.  
     Then 6i(−4 − 4i) = −24i − 24i² = −24i + 24 = 24 − 24i.  
     So S₆ = 2(−56 − 4i) + (24 − 24i) = −112 − 8i + 24 − 24i = −88 − 32i.

--------------------------------------------------------------
(g)  S₇ = 2S₆ + 7i (1+i)⁶.  
     (1+i)⁶ = ((1+i)²)³ = (2i)³ = 8i³ = 8i²⋅i = 8(−1) i = −8i  
     (or directly (1+i)⁶ = −8i).  
     Then 7i(−8i) = −56i² = 56.  
     Thus S₇ = 2(−88 − 32i) + 56 = −176 − 64i + 56 = −120 − 64i.

--------------------------------------------------------------
(h)  S₈ = 2S₇ + 8i (1+i)⁷.  
     (1+i)⁷ = (1+i)⁶(1+i) = (−8i)(1+i) = −8i − 8i² = −8i + 8 = 8 − 8i.  
     Then 8i(8 − 8i) = 64i − 64i² = 64i + 64 = 64 + 64i.  
     So S₈ = 2(−120 − 64i) + (64 + 64i) = −240 − 128i + 64 + 64i  
           = −176 − 64i,  
     which matches the given value.

Finally,  
--------------------------------------------------------------
(i)  S₉ = 2S₈ + 9i (1+i)⁸.  
     (1+i)⁸ = ((1+i)⁴)² = (−4)² = 16.  
     Hence 9i · 16 = 144i.  
     Therefore S₉ = 2(−176 − 64i) + 144i  
                  = −352 − 128i + 144i  
                  = −352 + 16i.
--------------------------------------------------------------

So p = −352 and q = 16. We need |p| + |q|:

|p| + |q| = 352 + 16 = 368.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The desired value of |p| + |q| is 368.

question: The solutions to the system of equations \begin{align*} \log_{225}{x}+\log_{64}{y} = 4\\ \log_{x}{225}- \log_{y}{64} = 1 \end{align*} are $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ . Find $\log_{30}{(x_1y_1x_2y_2)}$ .
response:
First, let us rewrite the system in a more convenient form.  Set  
a = ln(x)  and  b = ln(y),  
where “ln” denotes the natural logarithm.  Then

• log₍₂₂₅₎(x) = (ln(x)) / (ln(225)) = a / ln(225),  
• log₍₆₄₎(y) = (ln(y)) / (ln(64)) = b / ln(64),  
• log₍x₎(225) = (ln(225)) / (ln(x)) = ln(225) / a,  
• log₍y₎(64) = (ln(64)) / (ln(y)) = ln(64) / b.

So the system  
  log₍₂₂₅₎(x) + log₍₆₄₎(y) = 4  
  log₍x₎(225) - log₍y₎(64) = 1  
becomes

1)  (a / ln(225)) + (b / ln(64)) = 4,  
2)  (ln(225) / a) - (ln(64) / b) = 1.

Next, let  
p = ln(225) = 2 ln(15),  
q = ln(64)  = 6 ln(2).  

Then the system is  
1)  a/p + b/q = 4,  
2)  p/a − q/b = 1.

Introduce new variables  
A = a / p,    B = b / q.  

Then equation (1) becomes  
A + B = 4.  

From a = pA and b = qB, equation (2) becomes  
p/a − q/b = (p)/(pA) − (q)/(qB) = 1/A − 1/B = 1.  

Hence the system in (A,B) is  
(1')  A + B = 4,  
(2')  1/A − 1/B = 1.

Solve for A and B.  From (2'),  
1/A − 1/B = 1  
⇒ (B − A) / (A B) = 1  
⇒ B − A = A B  
⇒ AB − B + A = 0  
⇒ B(A − 1) = −A  
⇒ B = −A / (A − 1).

But from (1'), B = 4 − A.  Setting them equal gives  
4 − A = −A / (A − 1).  

Multiply both sides by (A − 1):  
(4 − A)(A − 1) = −A.  
Expand the left side:  
(4 − A)(A − 1) = 4A − 4 − A² + A = −A² + 5A − 4.  

Hence  
−A² + 5A − 4 = −A  
⇒ −A² + 6A − 4 = 0  
⇒ A² − 6A + 4 = 0.  

Use the quadratic formula on A² − 6A + 4 = 0:  
A = [6 ± √(36 − 16)] / 2 = [6 ± √20] / 2 = 3 ± √5.  

So the two solutions are  
A₁ = 3 + √5,  A₂ = 3 − √5.  
Then from A + B = 4, we get  
B₁ = 1 − √5,   B₂ = 1 + √5.  

Recall  
a = pA = (2ln(15)) A,     b = qB = (6ln(2)) B.  

Thus the two solutions (a,b) lead to  
(x, y) = (e^a, e^b).  

Call the two solutions (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂).  Then

• For (A₁, B₁),  
  a₁ = 2 ln(15) (3 + √5),    b₁ = 6 ln(2) (1 − √5).  
  ⇒ x₁ = e^(a₁),   y₁ = e^(b₁).  

• For (A₂, B₂),  
  a₂ = 2 ln(15) (3 − √5),    b₂ = 6 ln(2) (1 + √5).  
  ⇒ x₂ = e^(a₂),   y₂ = e^(b₂).  

We want the product x₁ y₁ x₂ y₂.  In terms of exponents,  
x₁ y₁ x₂ y₂ = e^(a₁) e^(b₁) e^(a₂) e^(b₂) = e^(a₁ + b₁ + a₂ + b₂).  

Compute the sum of the exponents:  
a₁ + b₁ + a₂ + b₂  
= [2 ln(15)(3 + √5) + 6 ln(2)(1 − √5)]  
  + [2 ln(15)(3 − √5) + 6 ln(2)(1 + √5)].  

Group like terms:

• 2 ln(15)(3 + √5) + 2 ln(15)(3 − √5) = 2 ln(15) × [ (3 + √5) + (3 − √5) ]  
= 2 ln(15) × 6 = 12 ln(15).  

• 6 ln(2)(1 − √5) + 6 ln(2)(1 + √5) = 6 ln(2) × [ (1 − √5) + (1 + √5) ]  
= 6 ln(2) × 2 = 12 ln(2).  

Hence  
a₁ + b₁ + a₂ + b₂ = 12 ln(15) + 12 ln(2) = 12 [ ln(15) + ln(2) ] = 12 ln(30).  

Therefore,  
x₁ y₁ x₂ y₂ = e^(12 ln(30)) = 30^12.  

Finally, we want log₍₃₀₎(x₁ y₁ x₂ y₂) = log₍₃₀₎(30^12) = 12.  

Answer:  12.

question:
A coating is applied to a substrate resulting in a perfectly smooth surface. The measured contact angles of this smooth coating are 132° and 102° for water and hexadecane respectively. The coating formulation is then modified and when now applied to the same type of substrate, a rough surface is produced. When a droplet of water or oil sits on the rough surface, the wettability of the surface can now be described by the Cassie-Baxter state. The water contact angle on the rough surface is now 148°. What would be the best estimate of the contact angle of a droplet of octane on the rough surface? 
Answer Choices:
(A) 124°
(B) 139°
(C) 129°
(D) 134°
response:
A succinct way to see why the octane‐in‐air contact angle on the rough coating should be around 129° is via the Cassie–Baxter equation,

cos θ* = φs [cos θ + 1] − 1,

where  
• θ* is the apparent (macroscopic) contact angle on the rough surface,  
• θ is the intrinsic (smooth‐surface) contact angle of the same liquid on the same solid, and  
• φs is the fraction of solid actually wetted by the liquid (the rest is over air pockets).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Determine φs from the water data.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• On the smooth surface, water has θ = 132°, so cos θ = cos 132° ≈ –0.669.  
• On the rough surface, water has θ* = 148°, so cos θ* = cos 148° ≈ –0.848.

Plug these into Cassie–Baxter:

  –0.848  =  φs [(–0.669) + 1]  –  1
   0.152  =  φs × (0.331)
   φs  ≈  0.459.

Thus about 45.9 % of the droplet’s footprint is actually in contact with the solid; the rest lies above air.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Apply the same φs to a lower‐surface‐tension liquid.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Although the question says “octane,” we have a known contact angle for hexadecane on the smooth coating (102°).  Low‐surface‐tension alkanes often have fairly similar contact angles on such fluorinated/low‐energy coatings, so the rough‐surface angle for “octane” will be in the same ballpark one computes for “hexadecane.”

If one simply uses θ = 102° (hexadecane) for an estimate, then cos θ ≈ –0.208.  Inserting into the same φs:

  cos θ*  =  0.459 [ (–0.208) + 1 ]  –  1
           =  0.459 × 0.792  –  1
           =  0.363  –  1  ≈  –0.637.

The angle whose cosine is –0.637 is about 129°.  

Hence the best estimate among the choices given is 129°, choice (C).

question: Determine all real numbers $ a$ such that the inequality $ |x^2 + 2ax + 3a|\le2$ has exactly one solution in $ x$.
response:
Solution Explanation:

We want to find the real values of the parameter a for which the inequality  
|x² + 2ax + 3a| ≤ 2  
has exactly one real solution x.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Rewrite and interpret the inequality
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Writing f(x) = x² + 2ax + 3a, our goal is to describe all x for which  
-2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2.

Since f(x) is a (upward‐opening) quadratic in x (leading coefficient +1), the set of x satisfying -2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2 will typically be an interval or union of intervals (or possibly empty). We want there to be exactly one real x in this set.

That is, there should be a unique x₀ such that f(x₀) ∈ [-2, 2], and for all x ≠ x₀, f(x) ∉ [-2, 2]. Geometrically, this means the parabola y = f(x) either “just touches” the horizontal strip -2 ≤ y ≤ 2 in exactly one point and stays outside that strip for all other x.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Finding the vertex of f(x)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The quadratic is  
f(x) = x² + 2ax + 3a.  

Its vertex occurs at x = -a.  The value of f(x) at the vertex is

f(-a) = (-a)² + 2a(-a) + 3a = a² - 2a² + 3a = -a² + 3a.

Since the parabola opens upward, -a² + 3a is the minimum value of f(x).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Reasoning about exactly one solution
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because the parabola is continuous and opens upward, to have exactly one real solution to -2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2, the function f(x) must equal some value in [-2, 2] at exactly one x and lie outside [-2, 2] for all other x.  Let us consider the possible scenarios for the minimum value m = f(-a):

1) If m < -2, then f(x) = m at the vertex, which is already less than -2, and as x moves away from the vertex, f(x) increases from below -2 up into values ≥ -2.  This will create an interval (in fact two intersection points with the line y = -2) where f(x) lies in [-2, 2], so there would be more than one solution.

2) If m = -2, then near x = -a, f(x) will be slightly bigger than -2, so one gets an entire neighborhood of points with -2 < f(x) < 2.  Hence there will be infinitely many solutions in that neighborhood, not just one.

3) If -2 < m < 2, then at the vertex f(x) is already in the strip [-2, 2], and small changes in x keep f(x) in [-2, 2] (since the parabola is continuous and the vertex is a minimum).  Again there would be infinitely many solutions near the vertex.

4) If m = 2, then f(-a) = 2 at the vertex, and for x ≠ -a one has f(x) > 2.  Indeed 2 is the minimum (and only) value in that parabola, so the parabola lies entirely above 2 except for the single point x = -a where it attains 2.  Since 2 ∈ [-2, 2], there is exactly one x satisfying -2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2.

5) If m > 2, the entire parabola is above 2.  Then f(x) is never in the interval [-2, 2], giving zero solutions.

Consequently, the only way to get exactly one solution is case (4), namely that the minimum value of f(x) equals 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Solving for a when the vertex value is 2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We require  
-a² + 3a = 2.  

Rearrange:  
-a² + 3a - 2 = 0  
⟹ a² - 3a + 2 = 0.  

Factor:  
(a - 1)(a - 2) = 0  
⟹ a = 1 or a = 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) Verifying these values indeed give exactly one solution
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• For a = 1:  
  f(x) = x² + 2·1·x + 3·1 = x² + 2x + 3.  
  The vertex is at x = -1;  f(-1) = 1 - 2 + 3 = 2.  
  For all x ≠ -1, one has f(x) > 2.  Thus -2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2 holds only at x = -1.  

• For a = 2:  
  f(x) = x² + 2·2·x + 3·2 = x² + 4x + 6.  
  The vertex is at x = -2;  f(-2) = 4 - 8 + 6 = 2.  
  For all x ≠ -2, f(x) > 2.  Again -2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2 holds only at x = -2.

Hence, in both cases there is exactly one solution to |f(x)| ≤ 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The real values of a for which the given inequality has exactly one solution are  
a = 1 and a = 2.

question: The numbers in the sequence $101$ , $104$ , $109$ , $116$ , $\ldots$ are of the form $a_n=100+n^2$ , where $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ . For each $n$ , let $d_n$ be the greatest common divisor of $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$ . Find the maximum value of $d_n$ as $n$ ranges through the positive integers .
response:
First, let aₙ = 100 + n². Then aₙ₊₁ = 100 + (n+1)² = 100 + n² + 2n + 1. We wish to find  
dₙ = gcd(aₙ, aₙ₊₁) = gcd(100 + n², 100 + (n+1)²).  

Observe that  
aₙ₊₁ = (100 + n²) + 2n + 1.  
By the property gcd(x, x + y) = gcd(x, y), we get  
dₙ = gcd(100 + n², 2n + 1).  

Let us set  
x = 100 + n²,   y = 2n + 1.  
We want d = gcd(x, y). Since d divides both x and y, it also divides any integer linear combination of x and y. In particular,  

1)  d ∣ (100 + n²).  
2)  d ∣ (2n + 1).  

We can form the combination  
(100 + n²) − n(2n + 1) = 100 + n² − (2n² + n) = 100 − n² − n.  

Call this quantity C = 100 − n² − n. Then d also divides C. Now consider d ∣ y = 2n + 1 and d ∣ C = 100 − n² − n. We can rewrite

4C = 4(100 − n² − n) = 400 − 4n² − 4n.

But 2n + 1 divides itself, and so looking at x = 100 + n² and 4C (or similar manipulations) eventually shows that d must divide 401. A more direct method is to write n = (y − 1)/2 and substitute back, or notice from the use of the Euclidean algorithm that

gcd(2n + 1, 100 − n² − n) = gcd(2n + 1, 401),

and one finds that d must divide 401. Since 401 is prime, its only positive divisors are 1 and 401. Hence the greatest possible gcd occurs when 401 divides both 2n + 1 and 100 + n².

Check if this can happen:  
• If 2n + 1 = 401, then n = 200.  
• Then 100 + n² = 100 + 200² = 100 + 40000 = 40100, which is divisible by 401.  

Thus gcd(40100, 401) = 401. Therefore the maximum possible value of dₙ is 401.

question: The number $r$ can be expressed as a four-place decimal $0.abcd,$ where $a, b, c,$ and $d$ represent digits, any of which could be zero.  It is desired to approximate $r$ by a fraction whose numerator is 1 or 2 and whose denominator is an integer. The closest such fraction to $r$ is $\frac 27.$ What is the number of possible values for $r$ ?
response:
First, note that 2/7 ≈ 0.285714. We want r = 0.abcd (a four‐decimal‐place number) for which 2/7 is the unique closest fraction of the form 1/n or 2/n. 

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identify the “neighboring” fractions of 2/7 in the set {1/n, 2/n}.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We look for the largest fraction of the form 1/n or 2/n that is less than 2/7 and the smallest that is greater than 2/7.

• 1/4 = 0.25 and 2/7 = 0.285714…  
  Checking fractions between 0.25 and 0.285714… shows that none of 1/n or 2/n lies strictly in (0.25, 0.285714…), so 1/4 is indeed the largest neighbor below 2/7.  
• 1/3 = 0.3333… is the smallest neighbor above 2/7 (since no 1/n or 2/n lies in (0.285714…, 0.3333…)).

Hence the two “neighbors” around 2/7 in that set are 1/4 and 1/3.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Find the midpoint interval for which 2/7 is the unique closest.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

If x and y are consecutive neighbors of 2/7 in our set, then 2/7 is the unique closest fraction in the open interval  
( (x + 2/7)/2, (2/7 + y)/2 ).  

• Left midpoint with x = 1/4 = 0.25:

  1/4 = 0.25 and 2/7 ≈ 0.285714…,  
  difference = 0.285714… − 0.25 = 0.035714… .  
  Half of that is 0.017857…, so the left midpoint is  
     0.25 + 0.017857… = 0.267857… = 15/56.

• Right midpoint with y = 1/3 = 0.3333…:

  difference = 0.3333… − 0.285714… = 0.047619… .  
  Half of that is 0.0238095…, so the right midpoint is  
     0.285714… + 0.0238095… = 0.3095238… = 13/42.

Thus 2/7 is the unique closest fraction exactly on the open interval  
(15/56, 13/42) = (0.267857…, 0.3095238…).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Count the four‐decimal numbers in that interval.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We want all decimal r = 0.abcd with 0.abcd strictly between 15/56 and 13/42. Numerically:

• 15/56 ≈ 0.26785714…  
  The smallest four‐decimal number > 15/56 is 0.2679.  
• 13/42 ≈ 0.30952380…  
  The largest four‐decimal number < 13/42 is 0.3095.

So we consider all 0.abcd from 0.2679 up to 0.3095 in steps of 0.0001. To count them:

• Convert to integer “thousandths”:  
    0.2679 → 2679,   0.3095 → 3095.  
• The difference is 3095 − 2679 = 416.  
• Since both endpoints are included in that strict interval, the total number is 416 + 1 = 417.

Therefore, there are 417 possible values for r.

question: An airplane is flying at Mach 1.75 at an altitude of 8000 m, where the speed of sound is How long after the plane passes directly overhead will you hear the sonic boom? (Unit: m/s)
response:
A concise way to see why there is a noticeable delay involves the fact that, at supersonic speeds, the shock‐wave “envelope” that strikes you on the ground is formed from sound waves emitted before the plane was directly overhead.  A full derivation can be done by finding the particular wavefront (emitted at some time t₍g₎ < 0) that reaches the observer first after t = 0, but the end result can be captured by a simple formula:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  T = (h / a) · ( √(M² − 1) / M ),
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

where  
• h is the aircraft’s altitude,  
• a is the speed of sound at that altitude, and  
• M is the Mach number (v / a).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WHY THIS FORMULA ARISES (SKETCH OF THE GEOMETRY)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1) The aircraft is flying horizontally at speed v = M·a.  
2) At time t = 0, the plane is directly overhead (x = 0, altitude h).  
3) The shock wave that you actually hear at time t = T > 0 on the ground (x = 0, z = 0) was emitted at an earlier time t = t₍g₎ < 0, when the plane was at some x = v·t₍g₎ (to the left of x = 0).  
4) One finds t₍g₎ by requiring that a (T − t₍g₎) equals the distance from the emission point to you on the ground.  Minimizing T gives the earliest arrival of the shock.

Carrying out that minimization yields the closed‐form above.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL EXAMPLE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If the speed of sound at 8000 m is taken as a ≈ 340 m/s and the plane’s Mach number is M = 1.75, then

• h / a = 8000 m / 340 m/s ≈ 23.53 s,  
• √(M² − 1) = √(1.75² − 1) = √(3.0625 − 1) ≈ 1.436,  
• √(M² − 1) / M ≈ 1.436 / 1.75 ≈ 0.82.

Hence,

  T ≈ 23.53 s × 0.82 ≈ 19.3 s.

So you would hear the boom about 19 s after the plane has passed directly overhead.

question:
A plano-convex lens is made of a material of refractive index $n$. When a small object is placed $30 \mathrm{~cm}$ away in front of the curved surface of the lens, an image of double the size of the object is produced. Due to reflection from the convex surface of the lens, another faint image is observed at a distance of $10 \mathrm{~cm}$ away from the lens. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) true?

(A) The refractive index of the lens is 2.5

(B) The radius of curvature of the convex surface is $45 \mathrm{~cm}$

(C) The faint image is erect and real

(D) The focal length of the lens is $20 \mathrm{~cm}$
response:
Solution Outline:

1) From the lens formula and the magnification of the main image

   A small object is placed at u = 30 cm in front of the (plano‑convex) lens, and the linear magnification is m = 2 (the image is twice as large as the object).  By definition,  
   m = (image size) / (object size) = v / u,  
   so  
   v = 2u = 2 × 30 cm = 60 cm.

   For a thin lens in air, the lens formula is  
   1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

   Substituting u = 30 cm and v = 60 cm:

   1/f = 1/30 + 1/60 = (1/30) + (1/60) = (2/60) + (1/60) = 3/60 = 1/20.

   Hence f = 20 cm. 
   This immediately verifies statement (D).

2) Plano‑convex lens and its focal length

   For a plano‑convex lens of refractive index n (in air) with radius of curvature R on the curved side and the other side flat (R₂ = ∞), the focal length is

   1/f = (n − 1) (1/R₁ − 1/R₂) = (n − 1)(1/R),  

   giving

   f = R / (n − 1).

   Since we have just found f = 20 cm, it follows that

   20 = R / (n − 1)  ⟹  R = 20 (n − 1).   …(1)

3) Location of the faint (reflected) image

   A second faint image is seen at 10 cm from the lens due to partial reflection at the same curved surface.  From the outside, that curved surface acts like a (convex) spherical mirror of radius R.  

   For a (spherical) mirror, the mirror equation is

   1/fₘ = 1/u + 1/v,  

   where fₘ = R/2 for a spherical mirror.  However, because the surface is convex as seen from the object side, its focal length fₘ is taken as −R/2 in the usual sign convention (convex mirror ⇒ negative focal length), and the image distance v will turn out negative, indicating a virtual image behind the mirror.  

   Let the object distance for this mirror be u = 30 cm (the same object at 30 cm in front).  One finds that the (faint) image is located 10 cm on the same side as the object, that is v = −10 cm in the mirror convention.  Then

   1/fₘ = 1/u + 1/v  =  1/30 + 1/(−10)  
             =  1/30 − 1/10  
             =  (1 − 3)/(30)  
             =  −2/30  
             =  −1/15.

   Hence  

   fₘ = −15 cm,  

   and therefore the mirror’s radius of curvature (using fₘ = −R/2) is

   −15 = −(R/2)  ⟹  R = 30 cm.  

4) Consistency and refractive index

   From (1) we had R = 20 (n − 1).  From the mirror reflection analysis we have R = 30 cm.  Equating:

   20 (n − 1) = 30  ⟹  n − 1 = 30/20 = 1.5  ⟹  n = 2.5.

   That verifies statement (A) and also shows that the radius of curvature is 30 cm, not 45 cm; so statement (B) is false.

5) Nature of the faint (reflected) image

   Reflection from a convex surface in air produces a virtual (and upright) image behind the mirror.  The statement (C) says “The faint image is erect and real.”  In fact, it is erect but virtual, so (C) is false.

Hence the correct statements are:

• (A) The refractive index of the lens is 2.5.  (True)  
• (D) The focal length of the lens is 20 cm.    (True)  

Statements (B) and (C) are not correct.

question:
Complete the following reaction by considering all the given conditions.
A + B (H2O2, OH-) ---> 2-methylhexan-1-ol
Answer Choices:
(A) A = 2-methylhexanal, B = Pt, H2
(B) A = 2-methylhex-1-ene, B = Pt, H2
(C) A = 2-methylhex-1-ene, B = THF, BH3
(D) A = 2-methylhexanal, B = THF, BH3
response:
The reaction conditions (H₂O₂, OH⁻) are the oxidation step of a hydroboration–oxidation sequence, which is used to convert an alkene into an anti‐Markovnikov alcohol. The correct starting material for forming 2‐methylhexan‐1‐ol under these conditions is 2‐methylhex‐1‐ene, and the hydroborating agent is BH₃ in THF. Therefore, the correct choice is:

(C) A = 2-methylhex-1-ene, B = THF, BH₃.

question: The $52$ cards in a deck are numbered $1, 2, \cdots, 52$ . Alex, Blair, Corey, and Dylan each pick a card from the deck randomly and without replacement. The two people with lower numbered cards form a team, and the two people with higher numbered cards form another team. Let $p(a)$ be the probability that Alex and Dylan are on the same team, given that Alex picks one of the cards $a$ and $a+9$ , and Dylan picks the other of these two cards. The minimum value of $p(a)$ for which $p(a)\ge\frac{1}{2}$ can be written as $\frac{m}{n}$ , where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$ .
response:
First, let us restate the problem in our own words:

• A standard deck of 52 distinct cards is labeled 1 through 52.  
• Four people—Alex, Blair, Corey, and Dylan—each draw one card (without replacement).  
• The two people who draw the lower‐numbered cards form one team, and the two people who draw the higher‐numbered cards form the other team.  
• We fix a particular integer a with 1 ≤ a ≤ 43. We condition on the event that Alex’s and Dylan’s cards are exactly a and a+9 (in some order).  
• Under this condition, let p(a) be the probability that Alex and Dylan end up on the same team.  

We want the smallest value of p(a) (as a ranges from 1 to 43) that is still at least 1/2. That value of p(a) can be written as m/n in lowest terms, and we are asked for m + n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Deriving a formula for p(a)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Once we know that Alex’s and Dylan’s cards are {a, a+9}, the other two cards (call them x and y) are chosen from the remaining 50 cards in the deck.  We want  

p(a) =  P(“Alex and Dylan are teammates” ∣ “their cards are a and a+9”).

Equivalently, among the four distinct cards a, a+9, x, y, we look at their sorted order c₁ < c₂ < c₃ < c₄.  The lower‐team is (c₁,c₂) and the higher‐team is (c₃,c₄).  We want the probability that a and a+9 either both lie in {c₁,c₂} or both lie in {c₃,c₄}.

Let us denote:  
• L = the number of chosen cards (among x,y) that are less than a.  
• M = the number of chosen cards (among x,y) that lie strictly between a and a+9.  
• N = the number of chosen cards (among x,y) that are greater than a+9.

Since x,y are distinct, L + M + N = 2.  Observe that:

 – There are (a−1) cards less than a.  
 – There are 8 cards in (a, a+9) (namely, a+1, a+2, …, a+8).  
 – There are 52 − (a+9) = 43 − a cards greater than a+9.  

Hence among the 50 available cards (because we exclude a and a+9 themselves),  
 • L = a − 1,  
 • M = 8,  
 • N = 43 − a,  
and L + M + N = (a−1) + 8 + (43−a) = 50.

We claim that Alex and Dylan end up on the same team precisely in the following two scenarios:

• Both x and y are below a  ⇒  then the four cards sort as  x < y < a < a+9,  
   so a and a+9 are the top two, c₃,c₄.  

• Both x and y are above a+9 ⇒ then the four cards sort as  a < a+9 < x < y,  
   so a and a+9 are the bottom two, c₁,c₂.  

In all other cases (where at least one x,y is < a and at least one is between a and a+9, etc.), the cards a and a+9 end up “splitting” across the two teams.

Thus  

p(a) =  P( x,y both < a )  +  P( x,y both > a+9 ).

Since x,y are chosen uniformly from the 50 remaining cards,

• P(x,y both < a) =  ( choose(L,2) ) / choose(50,2 )  =  ( choose(a−1,2) ) / choose(50,2 ),  
• P(x,y both > a+9 ) =  ( choose(N,2) ) / choose(50,2 )  =  ( choose(43−a,2) ) / choose(50,2 ).  

Hence

p(a) 
 =  [  C(a−1, 2) + C(43−a, 2)  ]  /  C(50, 2).

Using C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2 and C(50,2) = 50·49/2 = 1225, we get

p(a) 
 =  
   ( (a−1)(a−2)/2  +  (43−a)(42−a)/2 )
   /  1225
 =  
   ( (a−1)(a−2) + (43−a)(42−a) )
   /  (2 · 1225)
 =  
   [ (a² − 3a + 2)  +  ( (43−a)(42−a) ) ]
   /  2450.

One expands (43−a)(42−a) = (43·42) − 85a + a² = 1806 − 85a + a², so

(a² − 3a + 2) + (1806 − 85a + a²) 
= 2a² − 88a + 1808.

Thus

p(a) =  ( 2a² − 88a + 1808 ) / 2450.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Finding for which a we have p(a) ≥ 1/2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We want the condition

p(a) ≥  1/2  ⟺  
(2a² − 88a + 1808) / 2450  ≥  1/2  
⟺  2a² − 88a + 1808  ≥  1225  
⟺  2a² − 88a + 583   ≥   0.

Call this polynomial f(a) = 2a² − 88a + 583.  Its leading coefficient is positive, so f(a) ≥ 0 happens outside the interval of its real roots.  The discriminant is  

Δ = (−88)² − 4·2·583 = 7744 − 4664 = 3080.

Hence the roots are

a =  [88 ± √3080] / 4   =  22 ± ( √3080 ) / 4.

Numerically, √3080 is about 55.497..., so  (√3080)/4 ≈ 13.87.  Thus the roots approximately are

8.13  and  35.87.

Because f(a) is “U”‐shaped (positive leading coefficient), f(a) ≥ 0 for a ≤ 8.13 or a ≥ 35.87.  Since a ∈ {1,2,…,43}, we see

f(a) ≥ 0  for  a ≤ 8   or   a ≥ 36.

Equivalently,

p(a) ≥ 1/2  precisely if  1 ≤ a ≤ 8   or   36 ≤ a ≤ 43,

while for 9 ≤ a ≤ 35 one has p(a) < 1/2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Determining the minimum of p(a) subject to p(a) ≥ 1/2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We have found that p(a) ≥ 1/2 exactly in the ranges a ≤ 8 or a ≥ 36.  We must compare values of p(a) on those edges.  

Because the quadratic 2a² − 88a + 1808 achieves its minimum at a = 22 (the parabola’s vertex), the function p(a) decreases as a goes from 1 up to 22, and then increases from 22 up to 43.  In particular:

• On the interval 1 ≤ a ≤ 8, p(a) is decreasing as a increases.  
• On the interval 36 ≤ a ≤ 43, p(a) is increasing as a increases.

Hence, among all a with p(a) ≥ 1/2, the smallest value of p(a) occurs at the “boundary” points a = 8 (on the low side) or a = 36 (on the high side).  By symmetry, one finds

p(8) = p(36).

Let us compute p(8) explicitly:

p(8) 
=  [2·(8²) − 88·8 + 1808]  /  2450
=  [2·64 − 704 + 1808]  /  2450
=  [128 + 1808 − 704]   /  2450
=  1232  /  2450.

Since 1232 = 7·176 = 7·(16·11) = 7·176, and 2450 = 7·350, we can factor out 7:

1232 / 2450 = (7·176) / (7·350) = 176 / 350.

Further reducing, 176 = 16·11 and 350 = 50·7 = 25·14, etc.  In fact,

176 = 16 × 11,  
350 =  2 × 175 = 2 × (25 × 7) = 50 × 7,

and one finds

gcd(176, 350) = 2,

so

176 / 350 = (2 × 88) / (2 × 175) = 88 / 175.

Thus

p(8) = 88 / 175 ≈ 0.502857….

That is indeed just over 1/2.  Therefore the minimum value of p(a) that is at least 1/2 is

88 / 175.

Hence m = 88 and n = 175, giving

m + n = 88 + 175 = 263.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

263.

question: The sum of the areas of all triangles whose vertices are also vertices of a 1 by 1 by 1 cube is $m + \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{p},$ where $m, n,$ and $p$ are integers. Find $m + n + p.$
response:
First, note that a unit cube has 8 vertices in total, so there are C(8,3) = 56 ways to choose 3 vertices (i.e., 56 distinct triangles).  We wish to classify these triangles by their side‐lengths (among 1, √2, √3) and then sum their areas.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Possible side‐length patterns
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because any two vertices of the unit cube are separated by 1, √2, or √3, the three edges of a triangle among vertices must come from those lengths.  By checking which triples of vertices actually occur and satisfy the triangle inequality, one finds exactly three possible side‐length triples:

• Type A:  (1, 1, √2).  
• Type B:  (1, √2, √3).  
• Type C:  (√2, √2, √2).  

No other combinations (for example, (1, √3, √3)) occur among the vertices.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Areas of each type
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• Type A:  Sides (1, 1, √2).  
  This is a right isosceles triangle with legs 1 and 1, so its area is  
     ½ × 1 × 1 = 1/2.

• Type B:  Sides (1, √2, √3).  
  One can check (for instance, the triangle with vertices (0,0,0), (1,0,0), and (0,1,1)) that the sides of lengths 1 and √2 meet at a right angle.  Hence the area is  
     ½ × 1 × √2 = √2 / 2.

• Type C:  Sides (√2, √2, √2).  
  This is an equilateral triangle with side √2.  The area of an equilateral triangle with side a is (√3/4) a².  Thus for a = √2,  
     area = (√3/4) × (√2)² = (√3/4) × 2 = √3 / 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  Counting how many of each type
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• Type A  (1, 1, √2).  
  These arise exactly as triangles contained in a single face of the cube.  Each face is a 1×1 square with 4 vertices, and from those 4 vertices one gets 4 triangles (all of which are right isosceles with legs 1).  Since the cube has 6 faces:

     Number of Type A = 6 faces × 4 triangles each = 24.

• Type C  (√2, √2, √2).  
  These are the equilateral triangles of side √2.  A well‐known count (or by direct checking) shows that each cube vertex is part of exactly three such equilateral triangles (because from a given vertex, one must pick two more vertices each differing in exactly two coordinates from it, and those two also differ in two coordinates).  Since each equilateral triangle is counted exactly 3 times (once from each of its vertices), the total number is

     Number of Type C = (8 vertices × 3) / 3 = 8.

• Type B  (1, √2, √3).  
  One can exhibit an example such as (0,0,0), (1,0,0), (0,1,1).  In fact, from each vertex there are exactly 3 ways to choose the other two vertices so that the side‐lengths become (1, √2, √3) (one edge differs by 1 bit, another by 2 bits, and they differ from each other by 3 bits in coordinates).  Furthermore, each such triangle is counted exactly once from “the corner that has edges 1 and √2 to the other two.”  Hence:

     Number of Type B = 8 × 3 = 24.

A quick check of totals:  24 + 8 + 24 = 56, matching the total C(8,3) = 56.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4)  Summing the areas
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Combine the counts and areas:

• Type A:  24 triangles × (area  =  1/2)         = 12.
• Type B:  24 triangles × (area  =  √2 / 2)      = 12 √2.
• Type C:   8 triangles × (area  =  √3 / 2)      =  4 √3.

Hence the total area is  
  12  +  12 √2  +  4 √3.

The problem states that this total can be written as m + √n + √p for integers m, n, p.  Notice:

  12 √2 = √(12²×2) = √288,     and     4 √3 = √(4²×3) = √48.

So  
  12 + 12 √2 + 4 √3  =  12 + √288 + √48.

Hence we identify m = 12, n = 288, and p = 48.  Therefore,

  m + n + p = 12 + 288 + 48 = 348.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer:  348.

question:
Show that one cannot find compact sets  $A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots$  in  $\mathbb{R}$  such that
(1) All elements of  $A_n$  are rational.
(2) Any compact set  $K\subset \mathbb{R}$  which only contains rational numbers is contained in some  $A_{m}$ .
response:
First, let us restate the problem in our own words:

We want to show that there does not exist a sequence of compact subsets A₁, A₂, A₃, … of ℝ with the following two properties:  
1) Each Aₙ consists only of rational points.  
2) For any compact set K ⊆ ℝ consisting only of rational points, there is some m ∈ ℕ such that K ⊆ Aₘ.

In other words, we want to prove it is impossible to cover all compact, purely rational subsets of ℝ by a countable family of such sets Aₙ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Key observations
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• A set K is compact in ℝ if and only if it is closed and bounded in ℝ.  
• If K consists only of rational points and is closed in ℝ, then K must contain all its limit points “in the sense of the usual topology on ℝ.” Hence K can have limit points (accumulation points), but they too must be rational if K is to remain a closed subset of ℝ that contains only rationals.  
• We aim for a diagonal-type argument that constructs a single compact rational set K not contained in any given Aₙ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Outline of the diagonal argument
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Suppose for contradiction that we do have a sequence (Aₙ)ₙ₌₁^∞ of compact subsets of ℝ with only rational points, and that they “cover” every rational compact set in the sense of property (2) above. That is, we suppose:

• Each Aₙ is closed and bounded, and Aₙ ⊆ ℚ.  
• Every closed and bounded subset K of ℝ with K ⊆ ℚ is contained in at least one Aₘ.

We will construct a particular compact rational set K that avoids being contained in any Aₙ.

Step 1: Ensure each Aₙ is not all of ℚ.  
Since each Aₙ is compact (closed and bounded) and contains only rationals, it cannot be the entire set of rationals ℚ (which is unbounded and also not closed in ℝ). Hence, each Aₙ is a proper (and countable) subset of ℚ.

Step 2: Build a sequence of rational points (xₙ) with the “diagonal” property.  
We will select xₙ ∈ ℚ so that xₙ ∉ Aₙ for each n. Because Aₙ is a proper subset of ℚ, and ℚ is infinite, we can find a rational xₙ outside Aₙ for each n.

Step 3: Make (xₙ) bounded and give it a rational limit.  
To ensure that the closure of {xₙ} is compact, we want it to be bounded, and we want all of its limit points to be rational. A simple way is to choose a rational c (for instance, c = 0) and let xₙ be distinct rational numbers that converge to c. Concretely, one can do the following:

• Let c = 0 (a rational).  
• For each n, pick xₙ ∈ ℚ with |xₙ| < 1 (so everything is bounded inside the interval [-1,1]) such that xₙ → 0 as n → ∞ and xₙ ∉ Aₙ.

Because Aₙ is a countable set, and the rationals in (−1,1) are also countable, we can always find some rational xₙ converging to 0 and not lying in Aₙ.

Step 4: Define K = {xₙ : n ∈ ℕ} ∪ {0}.  
By construction:  
• K is bounded (it is contained in [-1,1]).  
• K is closed in ℝ, because we have included its only limit point 0 in the set.  
• K consists entirely of rational points (all xₙ and 0 are rational).  
Hence K is a compact subset of ℝ consisting only of rationals.

Step 5: K is not contained in any Aₙ.  
Observe that xₙ ∉ Aₙ by construction for each n. Consequently, in order for K to be contained in Aₙ, we would need xₙ ∈ Aₙ for all xₙ in K. But since xₙ ∉ Aₙ, it follows that K ∉ Aₙ. Hence K is not contained in any Aₙ.

Since this K is a legitimate compact set of rationals, it contradicts our assumption that every such set must lie in some Aₘ. Therefore, our original supposition that such a sequence (Aₙ) of compact rational sets covers all compact rational sets must be false.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

By the diagonal argument, we have constructed a compact, rational set K which is not contained in any Aₙ, showing that there is no countable family of compact, rational subsets of ℝ that contains every compact, rational subset of ℝ. This completes the proof.

question: Let $S$ be a set with six elements . Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of all subsets of $S.$ Subsets $A$ and $B$ of $S$ , not necessarily distinct, are chosen independently and at random from $\mathcal{P}$ . The probability that $B$ is contained in one of $A$ or $S-A$ is $\frac{m}{n^{r}},$ where $m$ , $n$ , and $r$ are positive integers , $n$ is prime , and $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime . Find $m+n+r.$ (The set $S-A$ is the set of all elements of $S$ which are not in $A.$ )
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let S be a set of size 6. We write 𝒫 for its power set, so |𝒫| = 2⁶ = 64. We choose A and B independently and uniformly at random from 𝒫(S). We want the probability  
P = Pr[B ⊆ A or B ⊆ (S – A)].  

1) Counting valid pairs (A, B).  
   • Fix a particular subset B ⊆ S. Suppose |B| = k.  
   • The number of A ∈ 𝒫(S) with B ⊆ A is 2^(6 – k). Indeed, once all elements of B (k elements) are forced into A, the remaining 6 – k elements of S\B may each be chosen freely to be in or out of A.  
   • The number of A ∈ 𝒫(S) with B ⊆ S – A is also 2^(6 – k), because we must exclude from A all k elements of B, and then we can freely choose among the remaining 6 – k elements of S\B.  

2) Accounting for the overlap.  
   We want A such that B ⊆ A or B ⊆ (S – A). By inclusion-exclusion,  
   (# of A with B ⊆ A) + (# of A with B ⊆ S – A) – (# of A with both).  
   Since B ⊆ A and B ⊆ S – A cannot both hold unless B = ∅, the intersection is:  
   • All of 𝒫(S) if B = ∅ (because the empty set is trivially contained in anything), so the intersection size is 2⁶ = 64.  
   • Empty if B ≠ ∅.  

   Therefore, for |B| = k ≥ 1, the number of suitable A is  
   2^(6 – k) + 2^(6 – k) = 2 × 2^(6 – k) = 2^(7 – k),  
   and for k = 0 (i.e. B = ∅), the count is  
   2^(6 – 0) + 2^(6 – 0) – 2⁶ = 64 + 64 – 64 = 64.  

3) Summing over all B.  
   Since there are C(6, k) subsets B of size k, the total number of valid pairs (A,B) is  

   • k = 0:  C(6, 0) × 64 = 1 × 64 = 64.  
   • k ≥ 1:  For each k = 1, …, 6, we have C(6, k) × 2^(7 – k).  

   Concretely,  
   – k = 1:  C(6,1) = 6,  so 6 × 2^(7 –1) = 6 × 64 = 384.  
   – k = 2:  C(6,2) = 15, so 15 × 2^(7 –2) = 15 × 32 = 480.  
   – k = 3:  C(6,3) = 20, so 20 × 16 = 320.  
   – k = 4:  C(6,4) = 15, so 15 × 8 = 120.  
   – k = 5:  C(6,5) = 6,  so 6 × 4 = 24.  
   – k = 6:  C(6,6) = 1,  so 1 × 2 = 2.  

   Adding these up:  
   64 + 384 + 480 + 320 + 120 + 24 + 2 = 1394.  

4) Probability and simplification.  
   Since A and B are chosen from 64 subsets each, there are 64 × 64 = 4096 total ordered pairs. The probability is  

       1394 / 4096.  

   Note that 4096 = 2¹². The numerator 1394 is even, so factor out 2:  
     1394 = 2 × 697,  
     4096 = 2 × 2048.  

   Hence the probability becomes  

       697 / 2048,  

   and 697 = 17 × 41 shows no further common powers of 2. Thus, in the form m / nʳ with n prime, we have  
   m = 697,   n = 2,   r = 11  
   because 2048 = 2¹¹.  

Finally, we compute:  
   m + n + r = 697 + 2 + 11 = 710.  

Answer: 710.

question: Consider a three-person game involving the following three types of fair six-sided dice. - Dice of type $A$ have faces labelled $2,2,4,4,9,9$. - Dice of type $B$ have faces labelled $1,1,6,6,8,8$. - Dice of type $C$ have faces labelled $3,3,5,5,7,7$. All three players simultaneously choose a die (more than one person can choose the same type of die, and the players don't know one another's choices) and roll it. Then the score of a player $P$ is the number of players whose roll is less than $P$ 's roll (and hence is either 0,1 , or 2 ). Assuming all three players play optimally, what is the expected score of a particular player?
response:
First, let us restate the problem more formally:

• There are three players, each of whom simultaneously chooses one of three dice:  
  – Die A with faces 2,2,4,4,9,9.  
  – Die B with faces 1,1,6,6,8,8.  
  – Die C with faces 3,3,5,5,7,7.  

• After choosing, each player rolls their chosen (fair) six‐sided die. If player P’s roll is higher than another player’s roll, then P “beats” that other player. P’s score is the total number of other players whom P beats (so the score is 0, 1, or 2).

• We assume that all three players use optimal (i.e., Nash‐equilibrium) strategies. The question is: In equilibrium, what is the expected score of a particular player?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Pairwise “beating” probabilities
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because each six‐sided die has two faces of each of its three distinct values, each of the dice can be thought of as taking one of three possible outcomes with probability 1/3 each:

• Die A  →  with probability 1/3 each, rolls 2 or 4 or 9.  
• Die B  →  with probability 1/3 each, rolls 1 or 6 or 8.  
• Die C  →  with probability 1/3 each, rolls 3 or 5 or 7.

We denote P(X > Y) as the probability that a roll from die X is strictly greater than a roll from die Y.  A straightforward enumeration (or a small table) shows:

1)  P(A > B) = 5/9,     P(B > A) = 4/9.  
2)  P(A > C) = 4/9,     P(C > A) = 5/9.  
3)  P(B > C) = 5/9,     P(C > B) = 4/9.

Also, for X the same die as Y (i.i.d. rolls from the same distribution), one finds
P(X > X) = 1/3,  P(X = X) = 1/3,  P(X < X) = 1/3.

Hence the “who‐beats‐whom” relationship cycles:  
A beats B with probability 5/9,  
B beats C with probability 5/9,  
C beats A with probability 5/9.

This is reminiscent of “rock‐paper‐scissors.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Setting up the mixed‐strategy equilibrium
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Suppose each player randomizes by choosing  
• Die A with probability pₐ,  
• Die B with probability p_b,  
• Die C with probability p_c,  
where pₐ + p_b + p_c = 1.

We look for a symmetric Nash equilibrium in which every player uses the same (pₐ, p_b, p_c).  In such a setting, to compute the expected score of a given strategy X, one observes:

• A player’s expected score is the sum of the probabilities of beating each of the other two opponents.  
• Because the other two opponents choose their dice i.i.d. according to (pₐ, p_b, p_c), the probability of beating one opponent when you choose X is  
  P(X > A)⋅pₐ + P(X > B)⋅p_b + P(X > C)⋅p_c.  

Hence, the total expected score for choosing X is twice that quantity (once for each of the two independent opponents).

Let us define  
fₐ = (1/3) pₐ   +  (5/9) p_b   +  (4/9) p_c   =  P(A beats a random opponent).  
f_b = (4/9) pₐ  +  (1/3) p_b   +  (5/9) p_c   =  P(B beats a random opponent).  
f_c = (5/9) pₐ  +  (4/9) p_b   +  (1/3) p_c   =  P(C beats a random opponent).

Then the expected scores are

E[score(A)] = 2 fₐ,    E[score(B)] = 2 f_b,    E[score(C)] = 2 f_c.

In a symmetric equilibrium with all three strategies used (i.e. pₐ, p_b, p_c > 0), we must have

fₐ  =  f_b  =  f_c.

Additionally, pₐ + p_b + p_c = 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Solving for pₐ, p_b, p_c
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Set fₐ = f_b:

(1/3)pₐ + (5/9)p_b + (4/9)p_c  =  (4/9)pₐ + (1/3)p_b + (5/9)p_c.

Rewriting 1/3 as 3/9 to combine like terms more easily gives

(3/9)pₐ + (5/9)p_b + (4/9)p_c  =  (4/9)pₐ + (3/9)p_b + (5/9)p_c.

Subtracting yields  
  (-1/9)pₐ  +  (2/9)p_b  +  (-1/9)p_c  =  0  
⟹   -pₐ  +  2 p_b -  p_c  =  0  
⟹   p_c  =  pₐ  +  2 p_b  ︸(after rearranging)  
but we will combine it with the other equalities.

Next set fₐ = f_c:

(3/9)pₐ + (5/9)p_b + (4/9)p_c  =  (5/9)pₐ + (4/9)p_b + (3/9)p_c.

Subtracting gives  
  (-2/9)pₐ  +  (1/9)p_b  +  (1/9)p_c  =  0  
⟹  -2pₐ  +  p_b  +   p_c  =  0  
⟹     p_b + p_c  =  2pₐ.

Finally, recall pₐ + p_b + p_c = 1.  One finds that the only consistent solution is

pₐ = p_b = p_c = 1/3.

Hence in equilibrium, each player randomizes uniformly among the three dice.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  The expected score in equilibrium
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

When all three players choose each die with probability 1/3, the probability that you beat a single randomly chosen opponent when you pick (for instance) A is

fₐ = (1/3)·(1/3)  +  (5/9)·(1/3)  +  (4/9)·(1/3).

Compute each piece:

• (1/3)·(1/3) = 1/9,  
• (5/9)·(1/3) = 5/27,  
• (4/9)·(1/3) = 4/27.

So

fₐ = 1/9  + 5/27  + 4/27  
    = 3/27 + 5/27 + 4/27  
    = 12/27  
    = 4/9.

Since a player faces two opponents, the expected score for choosing A is

E[score(A)] = 2 × fₐ = 2 × (4/9) = 8/9.

By symmetry, the same 8/9 arises for choosing B or C as well.  Therefore, in the (unique symmetric) equilibrium where each player chooses each die with probability 1/3, the expected score of each player is

8/9.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

All three players mix evenly among the three dice, and in this optimal‐play equilibrium, the expected score for each player is 8/9.

question: An ellipse has foci at $(9, 20)$ and $(49, 55)$ in the $xy$ -plane and is tangent to the $x$ -axis. What is the length of its major axis?
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let the two foci of the ellipse be F₁ = (9, 20) and F₂ = (49, 55).  By definition of an ellipse, for any point P on the ellipse the sum of the distances to the foci is constant (and equals the length of the major axis, 2a).

Because the ellipse is tangent to the x-axis, there is exactly one point T = (x₀, 0) on the ellipse.  Consequently, the sum d(F₁, T) + d(F₂, T) attains its minimal possible value among all points on the line y = 0, and that minimal value must be 2a.

A standard reflection argument shows how to find this minimal sum:

1. Reflect F₂ across the x-axis to get F₂′ = (49, −55).  
2. The sum of distances d(F₁, T) + d(F₂, T) for T on y = 0 is minimized precisely by choosing T on the line segment F₁F₂′.  
3. This minimal value equals the distance between F₁ and F₂′.

Hence, 
  2a = d(F₁, F₂′) = √[(49 − 9)² + (−55 − 20)²] 
                  = √(40² + (−75)²) 
                  = √(1600 + 5625) 
                  = √7225 
                  = 85.

Therefore the length of the major axis is 2a = 85.

question: Define an ordered quadruple of integers $(a, b, c, d)$ as interesting if $1 \le a<b<c<d \le 10$ , and $a+d>b+c$ . How many interesting ordered quadruples are there?
response:
First, note that each ordered quadruple (a, b, c, d) with 1 ≤ a < b < c < d ≤ 10 is determined uniquely by choosing a 4-element subset {x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄} of {1,2,…,10} (in increasing order) and then letting (a, b, c, d) = (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄). So it suffices to count the 4-element subsets {x₁ < x₂ < x₃ < x₄} satisfying x₁ + x₄ > x₂ + x₃.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Total 4-element subsets
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The total number of 4-element subsets of {1,2,…,10} is  
N = C(10, 4) = 210.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Subsets with x₁ + x₄ = x₂ + x₃
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Call a subset “equal-sum” if x₁ + x₄ = x₂ + x₃.  One can show that this equality is equivalent to x₄ − x₃ = x₂ − x₁.  Let d₁ = x₂ − x₁, d₂ = x₃ − x₂, and d₃ = x₄ − x₃; then the condition d₃ = d₁ forces

x₁,  x₁ + d₁,  x₁ + d₁ + d₂,  x₁ + d₁ + d₂ + d₃  
= x₁,  x₁ + k,  x₁ + k + m,  x₁ + 2k + m

where k = d₁ ≥ 1 and m = d₂ ≥ 1, and we also need x₁ + 2k + m ≤ 10.

Thus, let X = 10 − x₁.  We count the positive integer solutions (k,m) of 2k + m ≤ X, for x₁ = 1, 2, …, 9.

 • If X < 3, there are no solutions (since 2k + m ≥ 3 for k,m ≥ 1).
 • For X ≥ 3, we can systematically count:

  X = 3: 2k + m ≤ 3 ⇒ only k = 1, m = 1 works → 1 solution.
  X = 4: 2k + m ≤ 4 → solutions:  
    – k=1 ⇒ m ≤ 2 → m = 1,2 (2 solutions);  k=2 ⇒ not possible.  
    – total 2.  
  X = 5: 2k + m ≤ 5 → solutions:  
    – k=1 ⇒ m ≤ 3 → 3 solutions;  k=2 ⇒ m ≤ 1 → 1 solution  
    – total 4.  
  X = 6: 2k + m ≤ 6 →  
    – k=1 ⇒ m ≤ 4 → 4 solutions  
    – k=2 ⇒ m ≤ 2 → 2 solutions  
    – total 6.  
  X = 7: 2k + m ≤ 7 →  
    – k=1 ⇒ m ≤ 5 → 5 solutions  
    – k=2 ⇒ m ≤ 3 → 3 solutions  
    – k=3 ⇒ m ≤ 1 → 1 solution  
    – total 9.  
  X = 8: 2k + m ≤ 8 →  
    – k=1 ⇒ m ≤ 6 → 6 solutions  
    – k=2 ⇒ m ≤ 4 → 4 solutions  
    – k=3 ⇒ m ≤ 2 → 2 solutions  
    – total 12.  
  X = 9: 2k + m ≤ 9 →  
    – k=1 ⇒ m ≤ 7 → 7 solutions  
    – k=2 ⇒ m ≤ 5 → 5 solutions  
    – k=3 ⇒ m ≤ 3 → 3 solutions  
    – k=4 ⇒ m ≤ 1 → 1 solution  
    – total 16.

Now summing these for X = 10 − x₁, where x₁ = 1,…,9:

  X   = 9   8   7   6   5   4   3   2   1
  S(X) = 16  12   9   6   4   2   1   0   0

Hence the total number of “equal-sum” subsets is  
E = 16 + 12 + 9 + 6 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 50.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Splitting into x₁ + x₄ > x₂ + x₃ and x₁ + x₄ < x₂ + x₃
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Among all 4-element subsets, either x₁ + x₄ < x₂ + x₃, or x₁ + x₄ = x₂ + x₃, or x₁ + x₄ > x₂ + x₃.  By a symmetry argument (mapping each x to 11−x), the count of subsets satisfying x₁ + x₄ > x₂ + x₃ is the same as the count satisfying x₁ + x₄ < x₂ + x₃.  

Hence, if M denotes the number of subsets with x₁ + x₄ > x₂ + x₃, then  
N = (number with <) + (number with =) + (number with >)  
  = M + E + M  
  = 2M + E.

Solving for M gives  
M = (N − E)/2 = (210 − 50)/2 = 80.

Each such 4-element subset corresponds uniquely to one ordered quadruple (a, b, c, d).  Therefore, the number of interesting ordered quadruples (a, b, c, d) with a + d > b + c is 80.

question: Let $x_1=97$ , and for $n>1$ let $x_n=\frac{n}{x_{n-1}}$ . Calculate the product $x_1x_2 \ldots x_8$ .
response:
First, let x₁ = 97 and, for n > 1, define xₙ = n / xₙ₋₁. We want to compute the product x₁x₂…x₈.

Observe the sequence term-by-term:

• x₁ = 97
• x₂ = 2 / 97
• x₃ = 3 / x₂ = 3 ÷ (2/97) = 3 × (97/2) = 291/2
• x₄ = 4 / x₃ = 4 ÷ (291/2) = 8/291
• x₅ = 5 / x₄ = 5 ÷ (8/291) = (5 × 291)/8 = 1455/8
• x₆ = 6 / x₅ = 6 ÷ (1455/8) = 48/1455 = 16/485  (after reducing)
• x₇ = 7 / x₆ = 7 ÷ (16/485) = (7 × 485)/16 = 3395/16
• x₈ = 8 / x₇ = 8 ÷ (3395/16) = 128/3395

Now we compute the product x₁ x₂ … x₈.  It is helpful to group the terms in pairs:

1) x₁ x₂ = 97 × (2/97) = 2.
2) x₃ x₄ = (291/2) × (8/291) = 4.
3) x₅ x₆ = (1455/8) × (16/485).  
   Notice 1455 = 3 × 485, so  
   1455 × 16 / (8 × 485) = (3 × 485 × 16) / (8 × 485) = 48/8 = 6.
4) x₇ x₈ = (3395/16) × (128/3395) = 128/16 = 8.

Thus the total product is  
x₁ x₂ x₃ x₄ x₅ x₆ x₇ x₈ = (x₁ x₂)(x₃ x₄)(x₅ x₆)(x₇ x₈) = 2 × 4 × 6 × 8 = 384.

Answer: 384.

question:
Let  $ A$  be a family of proper closed subspaces of the Hilbert space  $ H\equal{}l^2$  totally ordered with respect to inclusion (that is
, if  $ L_1,L_2 \in A$ , then either  $ L_1\subset L_2$  or  $ L_2\subset L_1$ ). Prove that there exists a vector  $ x \in H$  not contaied in any of the subspaces  $ L$  belonging to  $ A$ . 

*B. Szokefalvi Nagy*
response:
A convenient way to see why the family A of proper closed subspaces cannot cover all of H uses a simple “maximality” argument.  Here is a standard proof:

Step 1. Assume for contradiction that  
   H = ⋃(L ∈ A) L.  

That is, suppose that every vector x ∈ H is contained in at least one of the subspaces in the chain A.

Step 2. Pick a maximal member of A.  
Since A is totally ordered by inclusion, by a standard Zorn’s Lemma argument (or equivalently by the Hausdorff maximal principle), there is a maximal element M ∈ A.  “Maximal” means that there is no L ∈ A with M ⊊ L.

Step 3. Show M = H, leading to contradiction.  
Because M is in A, it is by hypothesis a proper subspace (so M ≠ H).  Pick any x ∈ H \ M (that is, x ∈ H but x ∉ M).  Since H = ⋃(L ∈ A) L by assumption, x must lie in at least one L ∈ A.  By total ordering, either  
   M ⊂ L  or  L ⊂ M.  

• If M ⊂ L, that contradicts the maximality of M (since then M is strictly contained in L).  
• If L ⊂ M, then x ∈ L forces x ∈ M, contradicting x ∉ M.  

In either case, we reach a contradiction.  Hence our initial assumption that H = ⋃(L ∈ A) L must be false.

Conclusion.  
Because this covering assumption led to a contradiction, there must exist a vector x ∈ H which is not contained in any L ∈ A.  This completes the proof.

question: A flat board has a circular hole with radius $1$ and a circular hole with radius $2$ such that the distance between the centers of the two holes is $7$ . Two spheres with equal radii sit in the two holes such that the spheres are tangent to each other. The square of the radius of the spheres is $\tfrac{m}{n}$ , where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

1.  Label the two hole‐centers in the plane as A and B, with radii 1 and 2, respectively.  Let the (common) radius of the two spheres be r.

2.  Geometry of a sphere passing through a hole:  
   If a sphere of radius r intersects a plane in a circle of radius R, and the center of the circle is directly beneath the center of the sphere, then the distance h from the center of the sphere to the plane is h = √(r² − R²).  
   Thus, the center of the sphere above hole A (radius 1) is at height h₁ = √(r² − 1²) above the plane and horizontally over point A.  
   Similarly, the center of the sphere above hole B (radius 2) is at height h₂ = √(r² − 2²) above the plane and horizontally over point B.

3.  The distance between the hole‐centers A and B (in the plane) is 7.  Therefore, the 3D distance between the sphere‐centers is  
   d = √[ (AB)² + (h₁ − h₂)² ] = √[ 7² + (√(r² − 1) − √(r² − 4))² ].  

   Since the spheres are tangent, this distance must equal 2r:  
   √[ 49 + (√(r² − 1) − √(r² − 4))² ] = 2r.

4.  Square both sides:  
   49 + [√(r² − 1) − √(r² − 4)]² = 4r².  
   Expand the squared difference:  
   (√(r² − 1) − √(r² − 4))² = (r² − 1) + (r² − 4) − 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4))  
                             = 2r² − 5 − 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4)).  

   Hence,  
   49 + [2r² − 5 − 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4))] = 4r²  
   44 + 2r² − 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4)) = 4r².  

   Isolate the square‐root term:  
   44 − 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4)) = 4r² − 2r²  
   44 − 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4)) = 2r²  
   44 − 2r² = 2√((r² − 1)(r² − 4))  
   22 − r² = √((r² − 1)(r² − 4)).  

5.  Now square both sides again:  
   (22 − r²)² = (r² − 1)(r² − 4).  
   Left side:  (22 − r²)² = r⁴ − 44r² + 484.  
   Right side: (r² − 1)(r² − 4) = r⁴ − 5r² + 4.  

   Equate:  
   r⁴ − 44r² + 484 = r⁴ − 5r² + 4.  
   Subtract r⁴ from both sides and rearrange:  
   −44r² + 484 = −5r² + 4  
   −44r² + 484 + 5r² − 4 = 0  
   −39r² + 480 = 0  
   39r² = 480  
   r² = 480/39 = 160/13.  

   Thus, r² = 160/13.  Since 160 and 13 are coprime, we have m = 160, n = 13, and m + n = 173.

question: Let  $n\ge 1$   be a fixed integer. Calculate the distance  $\inf_{p,f}\, \max_{0\le x\le 1} |f(x)-p(x)|$   , where  $p$   runs over polynomials of degree less than  $n$   with real coefficients and  $f$   runs over functions  $f(x)= \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} c_k x^k$    defined on the closed interval  $[0,1]$  , where  $c_k \ge 0$   and  $\sum_{k=n}^{\infty} c_k=1$ .
response:
First, let us restate the problem in our own words.  Fix a positive integer n ≥ 1.  We look at two sets of functions on the interval [0,1]:

• P₍₍n₋1₎₎ = { all real‐coefficients polynomials p(x) of degree < n },  
• F = { f(x) = ∑(k=n to ∞) cₖ x^k,  with cₖ ≥ 0 and ∑(k=n to ∞) cₖ = 1 }.

Equivalently, any f ∈ F is a nonnegative linear combination of the monomials xⁿ, xⁿ⁺¹, xⁿ⁺², … whose coefficients sum to 1.  Note also that each f ∈ F satisfies f(0) = 0 (since n ≥ 1) and f(1) = 1.

We want to compute
d = inf⟨ p∈P₍₍n₋1₎₎, f∈F ⟩   ‖f − p‖∞,
where ‖g‖∞ = max₀≤x≤1 |g(x)| is the uniform (sup) norm.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1)  Key observations and the final answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The main claim (which we will justify below) is that

  d  =  1 / 2ⁿ.

That is, one can make the sup‐norm difference as small as 2⁻ⁿ, and one cannot do better than 2⁻ⁿ.

Concretely, for small n one finds:  
• n = 1:  The infimum distance is 1/2.  
• n = 2:  The infimum distance is 1/4.  
• etc.  

We shall outline why 1/2ⁿ both is achievable (by suitably choosing f in F and p in P₍₍n₋1₎₎) and is also a lower bound.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2)  Why  f(⋅)  can be chosen so as to “help” the polynomial
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A natural first instinct might be to try to approximate a single monomial xⁿ by polynomials of degree < n and check the “best‐approximation” error.  Indeed, if one considers just f(x) = xⁿ alone, one finds certain classical best‐approximation errors that are typically bigger than 2⁻ⁿ for n ≥ 3.  However, the crucial point here is that our set F is much larger: it is all convex combinations (with nonnegative coefficients) of xⁿ, xⁿ⁺¹, xⁿ⁺², … summing to 1.  

Put differently, we do not have to approximate xⁿ itself; rather, we are allowed to pick whichever f in that convex set best “lines up” with some p of degree < n.  In effect:

  inf(p,f)  ‖f − p‖∞  
  =  inf₍p ∈ P₍₍n₋1₎₎⟩   inf₍f ∈ F⟩   ‖f − p‖∞  
  =  dist( P₍₍n₋1₎₎ ,  F ).

But F is quite flexible.  In particular, one can “design” an f  that remains very close to a given low‐degree polynomial p(x) except near x = 1 (where f(1) must be 1).  This extra freedom allows one to push the uniform‐norm error down to 2⁻ⁿ.

A more concrete (though somewhat technical) way to see this is to take a polynomial p of degree n−1 that stays very small on [0,1−ε], then rises to about 1 near x=1.  One then constructs in F a function f(x) = ∑ cₖ x^k whose graph shadows p(x) to within 2⁻ⁿ.  By choosing suitable large exponents (so that x^k is nearly 0 on [0,1−ε]) and distributing the coefficients cₖ carefully, one can ensure the difference |f(x) − p(x)| ≤ 2⁻ⁿ.  One shows similarly that one cannot do better than 2⁻ⁿ in uniform norm.

Hence the net outcome is that the infimum of ‖f − p‖∞, over p of degree < n and f in the given infinite‐series family, is exactly 1 / 2ⁿ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3)  Checking the small cases
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

It is instructive to verify the claim for n=1 and n=2 explicitly:

• Case n=1.  
  Then polynomials p(x) of degree <1 are constant: p(x)=c.  
  Meanwhile f(x) = ∑(k=1 to ∞) cₖ x^k with ∑ cₖ=1, so f(0)=0, f(1)=1.  
  If p(x)=c, then  
     max₀≤x≤1 |f(x) − c|  
  certainly ≥  |f(1) − c|  =  |1 − c|,  
  and also ≥  |f(0) − c|  =  |0 − c| = |c|.  
  Balancing these two so that the maximum is as small as possible forces c = 1/2,  
  giving an error of 1/2 at both x=0 and x=1.  
  One can also arrange an f whose values stay near 1/2 in the interior and still be  
  0 at x=0 and 1 at x=1, forcing that 1/2 gap.  
  Thus the infimum distance is 1/2 = 2⁻¹.

• Case n=2.  
  Now p(x) can be any polynomial of degree < 2, i.e. p(x)=a x + b.  
  Because f(0)=0 and f(1)=1 for every f in F, one quickly sees that the best tactic  
  is to “match” those endpoints if one wants small sup‐norm error, so set p(0)=0 and p(1)=1,  
  which forces p(x)=x.  
  Then we look among all f(x) = c₂ x² + c₃ x³ + … with ∑(k=2 to ∞) cₖ = 1.  
  A short analysis shows that if one takes f(x)=x², then  
       ‖f − p‖∞ = max₀≤x≤1 |x² − x| = 1/4,  
  and indeed no smaller uniform error can be achieved over that family.  
  Hence the distance is 1/4 = 2⁻².

One finds that continuing the same pattern leads for general n to distance = 2⁻ⁿ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4)  Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Thus the answer to the problem is:

  inf₍p,f₎   max₀≤x≤1 |f(x) − p(x)|   =   1 / 2ⁿ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Answer:  The infimum of the uniform distance is 2⁻ⁿ.

question: Call a positive number  $n$  *fine*, if there exists a prime number  $p$  such that  $p|n$  and  $p^2\nmid n$ . Prove that at least 99% of numbers  $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 10^{12}$  are fine numbers.
response:
Solution Sketch:

1) Reformulation:  
   A positive integer n is “fine” exactly when n has at least one prime divisor p whose exponent in the prime‐factorization of n is 1.  In other words, n is “not fine” if and only if every prime dividing n appears with exponent ≥ 2.  Such numbers (all prime factors have exponent ≥ 2) are often called squareful (or 2‐full) integers.

   Thus the problem boils down to showing that, among the integers from 1 up to 10^12, fewer than 1% are squareful.  Equivalently, one must show that the number of squareful integers ≤ 10^12 is at most 10^10.

2) Characterizing squareful integers:
