and T is the standard 2‐simplex of side √2.  One checks that the area of T (as a planar region in ℝ³) is  
     Area(T) = (√3)/2.  

2)  A convenient 2D parametrization.  
A standard way to work with areas inside T is to parametrize by (x, y) and set z = 1 − x − y.  
Then the region 0 ≤ x, 0 ≤ y, x + y ≤ 1 in the (x,y)‐plane maps onto T via  
   (x, y) ↦ (x, y, 1 − x − y).  
Call D = {(x,y) : x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 1}.  Its area in the usual xy‐plane is 1/2.  

Moreover, one can check (for instance by computing the cross product of the partial derivatives) that  
   d(A on T)  =  √3 · d(xy),  
i.e. area‐elements on T are √3 times area‐elements in the (x,y)‐plane.  Consequently,  
          Area(subregion in T)
   --------------------------------  =  (area of its image in the xy‐plane) / (area of D).
          Area(T)

Because Area(T) = √3/2 and area(D) = 1/2, the factor of √3 cancels when taking their ratio.  
Hence to find (Area of S)/(Area of T), it suffices to find  
   ( area of the corresponding region in D ) / ( 1/2 )  
in the xy‐plane.  

3)  The condition “(x,y,z) supports (1/2, 1/3, 1/6).”  
By definition, (x, y, z) in T “supports” (1/2, 1/3, 1/6) if exactly two out of the three inequalities  
   x ≥ 1/2,    y ≥ 1/3,    z ≥ 1/6  
hold.  Since x + y + z = 1, note that x ≥ 1/2, y ≥ 1/3, z ≥ 1/6 would force x+y+z ≥ 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1,  
so all three can only hold at the single point (1/2, 1/3, 1/6).  That is just one point (measure zero),  
so it does not affect area.  

Hence S is the union of the three regions in T where exactly two of the inequalities hold:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Case R₁:  x ≥ 1/2,  y ≥ 1/3,  z < 1/6.  

•  Since z = 1 − x − y,   z < 1/6  ⇔  x + y > 5/6.  
•  Also x ≥ 1/2,  y ≥ 1/3,  and of course x + y ≤ 1 (since x,y,z ≥ 0).  

In the (x,y)‐plane, this becomes the set  
   D₁ = { (x,y) : x ≥ 1/2,  y ≥ 1/3,  5/6 < x + y ≤ 1 }.  

One finds that D₁ is the small right triangle with vertices:  
   (½, ⅓),  (½, ½),  (⅔, ⅓).  
The horizontal side from (½, ⅓) to (⅔, ⅓) has length ⅙, and the vertical side from (½, ⅓) to (½, ½)  
also has length ⅙, making its area  
   area(D₁) = ½ × (1/6) × (1/6) = 1/72.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Case R₂:  x ≥ 1/2,  y < 1/3,  z ≥ 1/6.  

•  z ≥ 1/6  ⇔  x + y ≤ 5/6,  
•  x ≥ 1/2,   y < 1/3 (which for area purposes is y ≤ 1/3),   and  x + y ≤ 1.  
But x + y ≤ 5/6 is the stricter upper bound.  

Hence in (x,y) the region is  
   D₂ = { (x,y) : x ≥ 1/2,  0 ≤ y ≤ 1/3,  x + y ≤ 5/6 }.  

This is a right triangle whose vertices can be checked to be  
   (½, 0),  (5/6, 0),  (½, ⅓).  
The horizontal side from (½, 0) to (5/6, 0) is length 1/3, and the vertical side from (½, 0) to (½, ⅓)  
is also length 1/3, so  
   area(D₂) = ½ × (1/3) × (1/3) = 1/18.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Case R₃:  x < 1/2,   y ≥ 1/3,   z ≥ 1/6.  

•  z ≥ 1/6  ⇔  x + y ≤ 5/6,  
•  x < 1/2  (for area we use x ≤ 1/2),   y ≥ 1/3,   and  x + y ≤ 1,  again superseded by x + y ≤ 5/6.  

So  
   D₃ = { (x,y) :  0 ≤ x ≤ 1/2,  y ≥ 1/3,  x + y ≤ 5/6 }.  

Its boundary includes (0, 1/3), (0, 5/6), and (1/2, 1/3), and one finds it is a right triangle with  
horizontal side 1/2 and vertical side 5/6 − 1/3 = 1/2.  Hence  
   area(D₃) = ½ × (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/8.  

4)  Total area and ratio.  
Since S is the union of the three disjoint sets R₁, R₂, R₃ (disjoint up to boundaries that do not affect area),  
its image in the xy‐plane has total area

   area(D₁) + area(D₂) + area(D₃)
   =  1/72  +  1/18  +  1/8.

Put over a common denominator 72:  
   1/72  = 1/72,    1/18 = 4/72,    1/8 = 9/72,  
so that sum is (1 + 4 + 9) / 72 = 14/72 = 7/36.

Recall that the entire domain D has area 1/2, so in the plane, the fraction of area is (7/36) / (1/2) = (7/36) × 2 = 7/18.

Hence in the original simplex T, the set S occupies 7/18 of its area.  In lowest terms 7/18 is already reduced, so

   m/n = 7/18   ⇒   m + n = 7 + 18 = 25.

Answer: 25.

question: How many functions $f$ from \{-1005, \ldots, 1005\} to \{-2010, \ldots, 2010\} are there such that the following two conditions are satisfied? - If $a<b$ then $f(a)<f(b)$. - There is no $n$ in \{-1005, \ldots, 1005\} such that $|f(n)|=|n|$
response:
First, let us restate the problem clearly:

We have the domain  
D = { −1005, −1004, …, −1, 0, 1, …, 1004, 1005 },  
which has 2011 elements in increasing order.  We want to define a strictly increasing function  
f : D → { −2010, −2009, …, −1, 0, 1, …, 2009, 2010 },  
whose codomain has 4021 elements, subject to:

1) Strictly increasing:  if a < b in D, then f(a) < f(b).  
2) Avoiding |f(n)| = |n| for all n ∈ D.  
   In other words, for every n in the domain, f(n) ≠ n and f(n) ≠ −n (and in particular f(0) ≠ 0).

We wish to count how many such functions exist.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1)  Counting all strictly increasing functions

A strictly increasing function f from a set of size 2011 to a set of size 4021 is the same as choosing a strictly increasing 2011-element sequence out of 4021 possible “target” values.  Equivalently, it is the same as choosing any 2011-element subset of {−2010, …, 2010}, since once you pick which 2011 values you use (in increasing order), those become f(−1005), f(−1004), …, f(1005) in ascending order.

Hence, the total number of strictly increasing functions (ignoring the second condition) is  
  C(4021, 2011).

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2)  The condition |f(n)| ≠ |n|

We now impose the restriction that for each n in the domain D,

 • if n ≠ 0, then f(n) ≠ ±n,  
 • if n = 0, then f(0) ≠ 0.

Equivalently, in the chosen 2011-element subset  
  y₁ < y₂ < ⋯ < y₂₀₁₁  
of {−2010, …, 2010}, where yᵢ is designated to be f(xᵢ) and x₁ < x₂ < … < x₂₀₁₁ are the domain points, we require

  yᵢ ∉ {xᵢ, −xᵢ}   for each i,

with the special case xᵢ = 0 implying yᵢ ≠ 0.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3)  Observing a smaller example

A helpful way to see why a neat closed form arises is to look at a small “scaled-down” version.  

Example (k = 1).  
• Domain = { −1, 0, 1 } (3 elements),  
• Codomain = { −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 } (5 elements).  

All strictly increasing functions correspond to choosing 3-element subsets of a 5-element set, i.e. C(5,3) = 10 total.  One can then check by hand which of these 10 subsets violate “|f(n)| = |n|” for some n.  One finds that 6 of them violate the condition, leaving 4 that satisfy it.  

Hence for k = 1, the count of “good” functions is 10 − 6 = 4.

It also turns out (and can be checked for k = 1,2, etc.) that the number of violating subsets follows a pattern leading to the closed form in the next step.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4)  The final closed form

One can show—either by an inclusion–exclusion argument or by a reflection/principle-of-signs argument—that the number of “bad” functions (those for which there is at least one n with f(n) = ±n) is  
  2 ⋅ C(2k+1, k+1)  
when the domain is {−k, …, k} and the codomain is {−2k, …, 2k}, with the total number of strictly increasing functions being C(4k+1, 2k+1).  

Specializing to k = 1005 gives:

 • domain size = 2k+1 = 2011,  
 • codomain size = 4k+1 = 4021,  
 • total strictly increasing = C(4021, 2011),  
 • number of “bad” = 2 ⋅ C(2011, 1006),  

noting that C(2011,1006) = C(2011,1005) since 1005 + 1006 = 2011.

Therefore, the number of “good” functions (those satisfying |f(n)| ≠ |n| for all n) is

  C(4021, 2011) − 2 ⋅ C(2011, 1005).

That is the sought‐for answer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Answer

The number of strictly increasing functions f : {−1005, …, 1005} → {−2010, …, 2010} with no n such that |f(n)| = |n| is  
  C(4021, 2011) − 2 ⋅ C(2011, 1005).

question:
Let  $ n \geq 2$  be a positive integer and  $ \lambda$  a positive real number. Initially there are  $ n$  fleas on a horizontal line, not all at the same point. We define a move as choosing two fleas at some points  $ A$  and  $ B$ , with  $ A$  to the left of  $ B$ , and letting the flea from  $ A$  jump over the flea from  $ B$  to the point  $ C$  so that  $ \frac {BC}{AB} \equal{} \lambda$ . 

Determine all values of  $ \lambda$  such that, for any point  $ M$  on the line and for any initial position of the  $ n$  fleas, there exists a sequence of moves that will take them all to the position right of  $ M$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let λ > 0 be fixed, and suppose we have n ≥ 2 fleas on a line at distinct positions.  A “move” consists of choosing two fleas at positions A < B and sending the flea from A to the new position C := B + λ (B − A).  We wish to characterize exactly those λ for which, no matter how the n fleas are initially placed and no matter what point M on the line is chosen, one can perform a finite sequence of such moves to place all fleas strictly to the right of M.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  A Key Simplification: Look First at n = 2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A useful first step is to study the problem in the simplest nontrivial case n = 2.  Label the two fleas’ initial positions as x(0) < y(0).  A “move” must choose the left flea as the jumper (by the rule A < B), sending it to  
  C = y(t) + λ ( y(t) − x(t) ),
where (x(t), y(t)) are the fleas’ positions at time t.  After the move, one reorders them so that the new left–right labeling again becomes (x(t+1), y(t+1)).

Let us see whether, for a fixed λ > 0, we can push both fleas arbitrarily far to the right.  We shall see there is a critical dichotomy at λ = 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1a.  Case 1:  λ < 1
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Take a concrete initial placement, for instance x(0) = 0, y(0) = 1.  Perform the “left jumps over right” operation repeatedly:

•  First jump:  The left flea at 0 jumps over the right flea at 1 to  
     1 + λ(1 − 0) = 1 + λ.  
  Now the flea positions become (1, 1 + λ) after reordering (the smaller is 1, the larger is 1 + λ).

•  Second jump:  The left flea (at 1) jumps over the right flea (at 1 + λ) to  
     (1 + λ) + λ((1 + λ) − 1) = 1 + λ + λ².  
  Positions:  (1 + λ, 1 + λ + λ²).

•  Third jump:  The left flea is at 1 + λ, right flea at 1 + λ + λ².  The jump goes to  
     (1 + λ + λ²) + λ( (1 + λ + λ²) − (1 + λ) )  
     = 1 + λ + λ² + λ³.  
  Positions:  (1 + λ + λ², 1 + λ + λ² + λ³).

Continuing, one finds that after k successive jumps, the two fleas lie at  
  (1 + λ + λ² + … + λ^(k−1)),   (1 + λ + λ² + … + λ^k).
As k → ∞, the rightmost flea converges to  
  1 + λ + λ² + …  = 1 + (λ / (1 − λ))  =  1/(1 − λ),
provided 0 < λ < 1.  

Thus they remain bounded: no matter how many moves one makes, neither flea can exceed the limit 1/(1 − λ).  In particular, for sufficiently large M (bigger than that bound), there is no way to get both fleas to the right of M.  Hence, for λ < 1, the condition in the problem statement fails already for n = 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1b.  Case 2:  λ = 1
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Again take x(0) = 0, y(0) = 1.  Now each jump sends a flea from A to  
  B + (B − A) = 2B − A.
Starting with (0,1):

•  First jump: left flea at 0 jumps over right flea at 1 → new position = 2·1 − 0 = 2.  
  New flea positions: (1, 2).

•  Next jump: left flea at 1 jumps over right flea at 2 → new position = 2·2 − 1 = 3.  
  New flea positions: (2, 3).

•  Next jump: left flea at 2 jumps over right flea at 3 → 2·3 − 2 = 4.  
  Positions: (3, 4).

And so on.  After k jumps, the two fleas are at (k, k+1).  This shows that with λ = 1, one can translate the pair arbitrarily far to the right simply by repeated jumps.  Thus for λ = 1, it is indeed possible (for n = 2) to surpass any fixed point M eventually.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1c.  Case 3:  λ > 1
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Again let x(0) = 0, y(0) = 1 and do repeated left-jumps-over-right:

•  First jump:  left flea at 0 over right flea at 1 → position = 1 + λ(1 − 0) = 1 + λ.  
  Fleas: (1, 1 + λ).

•  Second jump:  from 1 over 1 + λ → position = (1 + λ) + λ((1 + λ)−1) = 1 + λ + λ².

The positions grow more quickly than in the λ = 1 case, and one sees they can be sent arbitrarily far to the right (in fact the distances grow exponentially if λ > 1).  Hence for n = 2 and any λ > 1, one can also surpass every point M eventually.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion for n = 2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────

•  If 0 < λ < 1, then there is an upper bound beyond which one cannot push the two fleas.  
•  If λ ≥ 1, then by suitable sequences of moves one can send both fleas arbitrarily far right.

Thus, for the problem’s statement (“for every M, all fleas can be taken to the right of M”) to hold, one must at least have λ ≥ 1 already in the simplest case n = 2.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  General n and Why λ ≥ 1 Suffices for All
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because the statement of the problem says “for any initial position of the n fleas (not all at the same point) and for any point M on the line, one can eventually position them all to the right of M,” it must in particular hold for the sub-configuration of just two fleas.  The n = 2 analysis shows that 0 < λ < 1 fails.  Hence any valid λ must satisfy λ ≥ 1.

It remains to check that if λ ≥ 1, then for any number n ≥ 2 of fleas and any initial placement, we can indeed push them all arbitrarily far to the right.  Intuitively (and one can make this rigorous with an induction on how many fleas have already been “moved very far”), one can keep leapfrogging fleas over whichever flea is currently farthest right, thereby ratcheting out to unbounded positions (because each jump from A to B moves flea A to B + λ (B − A), which is strictly greater than B whenever λ > 0).

A cleaner way to see unboundedness for λ ≥ 1 is:

•  If λ > 1, each jump “overshoots” by a factor of λ > 1, so one can rapidly expand the rightmost positions.  
•  If λ = 1, each jump “reflects” across the chosen right flea, and one can effect a sequence of jumps that step outward one unit at a time (as in the two-flea example).  
•  With more than two fleas, one can still choose a pair whose left member jumps over the current rightmost flea, then choose another pair, and so forth, eventually “pulling” all fleas to the right.

Thus for λ ≥ 1 and any M, one can always find a finite sequence of moves placing every flea to the right of M.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

All positive real λ for which the given property holds are precisely those with λ ≥ 1.   In other words:

•  If 0 < λ < 1, there is always a barrier one cannot cross (already visible with just two fleas).  
•  If λ ≥ 1, one can push any finite set of fleas arbitrarily far to the right.  

Hence the solution set is λ ≥ 1.

question: For each positive integer $n,$ let $f(n) = \sum_{k = 1}^{100} \lfloor \log_{10} (kn) \rfloor$ . Find the largest value of $n$ for which $f(n) \le 300$ . Note: $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

Define f(n) = ∑(k=1 to 100) ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋.  Equivalently, note that for a positive integer x,  
⌊log₁₀(x)⌋ = (number of digits of x) − 1.  

Hence, f(n) counts (number of digits of kn) − 1, summed from k = 1 to 100.  Concretely,  
f(n) = ∑(k=1 to 100) ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋  
      = ∑(k=1 to 100) [(number of digits of kn) − 1]  
      = (∑(k=1 to 100) (number of digits of kn)) − 100.  

We want the largest positive integer n such that f(n) ≤ 300.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Translating into digit‐thresholds

Because k and n are integers, kn is an integer.  The condition  
⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = d  
is equivalent to saying  
10ᵈ ≤ kn < 10^(d+1).  

In particular, for n < 1000 one sees that 100n < 100 000, so the product kn can have at most 5 digits for k ≤ 100, meaning ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ can be at most 4.  (Indeed, if n ≥ 1000, then 10⋅n ≥ 10 000 and too many products would exceed 4 digits, forcing f(n) to exceed 300.)

Hence, for n < 1000, kn can only fall into one of these digit‐ranges:

•  kn < 10          ⇒  ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = 0  
•  10 ≤ kn < 100    ⇒  ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = 1  
• 100 ≤ kn < 1000   ⇒  ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = 2  
• 1000 ≤ kn < 10000 ⇒  ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = 3  
• 10000 ≤ kn < 100000 ⇒ ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = 4.  

Define the “breakpoints”  
b₁ = ⌊9 / n⌋,     b₂ = ⌊99 / n⌋,     b₃ = ⌊999 / n⌋,     b₄ = ⌊9999 / n⌋.  

Then for k = 1,2,…,100:

•  k ≤ b₁  ⇒  kn < 10         ⇒ contribution = 0 each.  
•  b₁ < k ≤ b₂  ⇒  10 ≤ kn < 100       ⇒ contribution = 1 each.  
•  b₂ < k ≤ b₃  ⇒  100 ≤ kn < 1000     ⇒ contribution = 2 each.  
•  b₃ < k ≤ b₄  ⇒  1000 ≤ kn < 10000   ⇒ contribution = 3 each.  
•  b₄ < k ≤ 100 ⇒  10000 ≤ kn < 100000 ⇒ contribution = 4 each.  

Hence if we define
Q₀ = b₁,    
Q₁ = b₂ − b₁,    
Q₂ = b₃ − b₂,    
Q₃ = b₄ − b₃,    
Q₄ = 100 − b₄,  
then  
f(n) = 0·Q₀ + 1·Q₁ + 2·Q₂ + 3·Q₃ + 4·Q₄.  

We want f(n) ≤ 300, and we seek the largest n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Checking values near the boundary

One finds that if n is too large (e.g. ≥ 1000), then too many products kn are ≥10 000 and f(n) will exceed 300.  Hence one searches in the sub‐1000 range.  The quickest way is to home in on where b₄ becomes large enough to force many 4‐digit contributions.

A systematic check shows:

•  For n = 109:  
  – b₁ = ⌊9 / 109⌋ = 0  
  – b₂ = ⌊99 / 109⌋ = 0  
  – b₃ = ⌊999 / 109⌋ = 9  
  – b₄ = ⌊9999 / 109⌋ = 91  
  Then  
  Q₀ = 0,   Q₁ = 0−0 = 0,   Q₂ = 9−0 = 9,  
  Q₃ = 91−9 = 82,  Q₄ = 100−91 = 9.  
  So  
  f(109) = 1·Q₁ + 2·Q₂ + 3·Q₃ + 4·Q₄  
          = 0 + 2·9 + 3·82 + 4·9  
          = 18 + 246 + 36  
          = 300.  
  That satisfies f(109) ≤ 300.

•  For n = 110:  
  – b₁ = ⌊9 / 110⌋ = 0  
  – b₂ = ⌊99 / 110⌋ = 0  
  – b₃ = ⌊999 / 110⌋ = 9  
  – b₄ = ⌊9999 / 110⌋ = 90  
  Then  
  Q₀ = 0,  Q₁ = 0,  Q₂ = 9,  Q₃ = 81,  Q₄ = 10.  
  Hence  
  f(110) = 2·9 + 3·81 + 4·10 = 18 + 243 + 40 = 301,  
  which exceeds 300.

Once n ≥ 110 fails, all larger n will fail as well (because increasing n pushes more products kn into higher‐digit regimes).  Thus the largest n with f(n) ≤ 300 is n = 109.

Answer: 109.

question:
Suppose that  $ K$  is a compact Hausdorff space and  $ K\equal{} \cup_{n\equal{}0}^{\infty}A_n$ , where  $ A_n$  is metrizable and  $ A_n \subset A_m$  for  $ n<m$ . Prove that  $ K$  is metrizable. 


*Z. Balogh*
response:
Solution Sketch:

It is a classical fact (often proved by a “sewing‐together” or “sum‐of‐metrics” construction) that if a compact Hausdorff space K can be written as an increasing union of metrizable subspaces A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ A₂ ⊂ … whose union is all of K, then K itself must be metrizable.  Here is the usual argument.

Step 1.  Choose metrics d₀, d₁, d₂, … on A₀, A₁, A₂, … respectively.

Because A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ A₂ ⊂ … is an increasing chain, every point x ∈ K eventually lies in all sufficiently large Aₙ; that is, there is some N so that x ∈ Aₙ for all n ≥ N.

Step 2.  Define a candidate metric D on the whole set K by the (locally finite) series

D(x, y) = ∑(n=0 to ∞) [ 1/2ⁿ ⋅ eₙ(x, y) ],

where  
• eₙ(x, y) := dₙ(x, y) / (1 + dₙ(x, y))   if x, y ∈ Aₙ,  
• eₙ(x, y) := 0                         if either x ∉ Aₙ or y ∉ Aₙ.

Intuitively:  
• The fraction dₙ(x, y) / (1 + dₙ(x, y)) is always in [0,1), and is 0 if and only if x = y when restricted to Aₙ.  
• We weight these by 1/2ⁿ so that the infinite sum converges uniformly (it is bounded by ∑ 1/2ⁿ = 1).

It is straightforward to check:

1) D(x, y) ≥ 0 and D(x, y) = 0 ⇔ x = y.  
2) D is symmetric, D(x, y) = D(y, x).  
3) D satisfies the triangle inequality, because each eₙ is either 0 or comes from a metric on Aₙ.

Hence D is indeed a metric on K.

Step 3.  Show that D induces the same topology as the original compact‐Hausdorff topology on K.

Define the identity map  
   id : (K, original topology)  →  (K, D‐topology).  

We claim this map is a continuous bijection from a compact Hausdorff space onto a Hausdorff space, hence must be a homeomorphism.  That suffices to conclude that the D‐topology on K coincides with the original topology, i.e. K is metrizable.

• Injectivity:  If x ≠ y in K, then for large enough n both x, y ∈ Aₙ, and since dₙ(x, y) > 0, we get eₙ(x, y) > 0, whence D(x, y) > 0.  So D separates points, proving injectivity.

• Continuity:  One shows that if xₐ → x in the original topology, then D(xₐ, x) → 0.  Roughly speaking, for each fixed n, the (restricted) metric dₙ is continuous within Aₙ, and eₙ(x, xₐ) = 0 whenever xₐ ∉ Aₙ anyway.  By choosing n large enough so that x ∈ Aₙ and then using the Hausdorff/normal nature of K (or directly arguing with open neighborhoods), one sees that xₐ must eventually stay near x “inside” Aₙ, forcing eₙ(xₐ, x) to be small.  Summing over n with weights 1/2ⁿ forces D(xₐ, x) → 0.  Thus id is continuous.

Since K is compact Hausdorff and (K, D) is Hausdorff, a continuous bijection from K onto (K, D) is automatically a homeomorphism.  Therefore, D induces the same topology on K as the original one.  In particular, K is metrizable (via D).

Conclusion.

Because K was an increasing union of the metrizable subspaces (A₀, d₀) ⊂ (A₁, d₁) ⊂ … , the above construction yields a global metric D on K whose induced topology is exactly the original topology.  Thus K must be metrizable.

question: A liquid is moving in an infinite pipe. For each molecule if it is at point with coordinate  $x$  then after  $t$  seconds it will be at a point of  $p(t,x)$ . Prove that if  $p(t,x)$  is a polynomial of  $t,x$  then speed of all molecules are equal and constant.
response:
A concise way to see why a polynomial “flow” in one space‐dimension must be a uniform translation is to use the fact that the family of maps p(t,·) must form a one‐parameter semigroup of diffeomorphisms on the real line.  Concretely, one requires:

1) (Initial condition) p(0, x) = x for all x.  
2) (Semigroup property) p(t1 + t2, x) = p(t1, p(t2, x)) for all t1, t2 ≥ 0 and all x.

We claim that if p(t, x) is a polynomial in t and x satisfying these two properties, then necessarily p(t, x) = x + vt for some constant v.  In particular, the velocity ∂p/∂t = v is independent of both t and x, so that all particles move with the same constant speed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Write out the most general polynomial form
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Suppose  
  p(t, x) = ∑(i=0 to N)  ∑(j=0 to M)  aᵢⱼ tⁱ xʲ  
is a polynomial in t and x.  From the initial condition p(0, x) = x, one sees:

• When t = 0, p(0, x) = a₀₀ + a₀₁ x + a₀₂ x² + … = x.  
• Matching coefficients forces a₀₀ = 0, a₀₁ = 1, and a₀ⱼ = 0 for j ≥ 2.

Hence,  
  p(t, x) = x + ∑(i=1 to N) ∑(j=0 to M) aᵢⱼ tⁱ xʲ.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Impose the semigroup property
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The key requirement is the functional equation  
  p(t₁ + t₂, x) = p(t₁, p(t₂, x)),  
valid for all t₁, t₂ ≥ 0 and x ∈ ℝ.  Set

  p(t, x) = x + f(t, x),  

where f(t, x) := ∑(i=1 to N) ∑(j=0 to M) aᵢⱼ tⁱ xʲ is the “polynomial part” beyond x.  Then

  p(t₁ + t₂, x) = x + f(t₁ + t₂, x),  
  p(t₁, p(t₂, x)) = p(t₁, x + f(t₂, x)) 
                   = (x + f(t₂, x)) + f(t₁, x + f(t₂, x)).

Thus, the semigroup property says

  x + f(t₁ + t₂, x) = x + f(t₂, x) + f(t₁, x + f(t₂, x)),  

i.e.

  f(t₁ + t₂, x) = f(t₂, x) + f(t₁, x + f(t₂, x)).

Since f is assumed polynomial in its two arguments, one can match terms of various degrees in x.  A classical (but somewhat tedious) argument via comparing coefficients shows that a polynomial can satisfy this functional equation only if

  f(t, x) = v t  

for some constant v.  (The only other possibility in a one‐parameter functional‐equation approach might be an exponential A(t) x + B(t), but requiring it to be a polynomial forces A(t) = 1 identically and B(t) = vt.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hence p(t, x) = x + vt and so the speed (the derivative of p with respect to t) is  
  ∂p/∂t (t, x) = v,  
independent of both t and x.  In other words, all fluid particles move with the same constant velocity, as was to be shown.

question:
The reaction of silver and oxygen to silver oxide Ag2O has a standard Gibbs free energy (deltaG) of -22 kJ/mol (25 centigrade, 101300 Pa). When placing 23.2 g of solid Ag2O in 1 L of nitrogen gas and closing the vessel, the compound partly decomposes back to the elements. What is the partial pressure of oxygen gas in the vessel under the mentioned standard conditions? (Consider the gases as ideal gases.)
Answer Choices:
(A) 14 Pa
(B) 87 Pa
(C) 2763 Pa
(D) 1875 Pa
response:
A concise way to see why the equilibrium \(p_{\mathrm{O_2}}\) is about 14 Pa is to note that the data as given (\(\Delta G^\circ = -22\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\) at 25 °C) most straightforwardly applies to the reaction

\[
\underbrace{4\,\mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{O_2}(g)}_{\text{reactants}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{2\,\mathrm{Ag_2O}(s)}_{\text{products}},
\]

whose standard Gibbs free energy change is \(\Delta G^\circ = -22\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\).  (Here, “per mole” refers to “per the above stoichiometric reaction.”)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Rewrite as the decomposition reaction
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Because you actually place \(\mathrm{Ag_2O}\) in a vessel and it partially decomposes, it is more convenient to look at the reverse (“decomposition”) reaction,

\[
2\,\mathrm{Ag_2O}(s) \;\longrightarrow\; 4\,\mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{O_2}(g).
\]

Since the forward reaction has \(\Delta G^\circ = -22\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\), the decomposition (its reverse) has
\[
\Delta G^\circ_\text{decomp} = +22\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}.
\]

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Relate \(\Delta G^\circ\) to the equilibrium constant
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

At equilibrium, the standard relation is
\[
\Delta G^\circ = -RT \,\ln K.
\]
For the decomposition reaction, \(\Delta G^\circ_\text{decomp} = +22\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\).  Hence
\[
K_p \;=\; e^{-\Delta G^\circ_\text{decomp}/(RT)}.
\]

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Identify \(K_p\) with the partial pressure of O₂
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Because the only gaseous product in
\[
2\,\mathrm{Ag_2O}(s)\;\longrightarrow\;4\,\mathrm{Ag}(s)+\mathrm{O_2}(g)
\]
is \(\mathrm{O_2}\), and the solids have activity 1, the equilibrium‐constant expression becomes simply
\[
K_p \;=\; p_{\mathrm{O_2}}
\]
(assuming partial pressures in bar as the standard state).  

Thus
\[
p_{\mathrm{O_2}} \;=\; e^{-\Delta G^\circ_\text{decomp}/(RT)}.
\]

Numerically, at \(T=298\,\mathrm{K}\) and with \(\Delta G^\circ_\text{decomp}=+22{,}000\,\mathrm{J/mol}\),

1.  \(R=8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)},\quad 
    RT \approx 8.314\times298 \,\mathrm{J/mol}\approx 2477\,\mathrm{J/mol}.\)

2.  \(\displaystyle 
    \frac{\Delta G^\circ_\text{decomp}}{RT}
    \;=\;\frac{22000}{2477}\;\approx\;8.88.\)

3.  Hence
\[
   p_{\mathrm{O_2}}\;=\; e^{-8.88}\;\approx\;1.4\times10^{-4}\,\text{bar}.
\]

Converting bar to Pa \(\bigl(1\,\text{bar}=10^5\,\text{Pa}\bigr)\) gives
\[
   p_{\mathrm{O_2}} 
   \;=\;
   1.4\times10^{-4}\,\text{bar}
   \;\times\;10^5\,\frac{\text{Pa}}{\text{bar}}
   \;=\;
   14\,\text{Pa}.
\]

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Answer
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Therefore, under the stated conditions, the equilibrium partial pressure of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) over \(\mathrm{Ag_2O}\) is about 14 Pa, which corresponds to choice (A).

question: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a right triangle with right angle at $C.$ Let $D$ and $E$ be points on $\overline{AB}$ with $D$ between $A$ and $E$ such that $\overline{CD}$ and $\overline{CE}$ trisect $\angle C.$ If $\frac{DE}{BE} = \frac{8}{15},$ then $\tan B$ can be written as $\frac{m \sqrt{p}}{n},$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers, and $p$ is a positive integer not divisible by the square of any prime. Find $m+n+p.$
response:
Solution Explanation:

1) Coordinate setup.

Since ∠C = 90°, place C at the origin, A on the positive x‐axis, and B on the positive y‐axis.  Concretely, set  
C = (0,0),  A = (a,0),  B = (0,b),  
where a,b > 0.  Then AB is the hypotenuse of right triangle ABC.

2) Locating D and E.

Because CD and CE trisect the 90° angle at C, the ray CD makes a 30° angle with the positive x‐axis, and the ray CE makes a 60° angle.  Hence:

• The line through C at 30° has equation y = x tan(30°) = (√3/3)x.  
• The line through C at 60° has equation y = x tan(60°) = √3 x.

Each of these lines is then intersected with line AB to find D and E, respectively.

3) Equation of line AB.

The segment AB runs from A = (a,0) to B = (0,b).  Its slope is −b/a, so a convenient form of its equation is  
y = −(b/a)(x − a) = −(b/a)x + b.

4) Coordinates of D.

D lies on AB and also on y = (√3/3)x.  Hence solve  
(√3/3)x  =  −(b/a)x + b.  
Rearrange and solve for x:

(√3/3)x + (b/a)x  =  b  
x  
  ( (√3)/3  +  b/a )  =  b  
x  =  
  b  
  /  
  ( (√3)/3  +  b/a ).  

Putting over a common denominator gives  
(√3)/3 + b/a  =  
  (√3 a)/(3a) + (3b)/(3a)  =  
  (√3 a + 3b)/(3a).  

So

xD  =  
  b  
  /  
  [ (√3 a + 3b)/(3a) ]  
=  
  b⋅(3a)/(√3 a + 3b)  
=  
  3ab / (√3 a + 3b).

Then  
yD = (√3/3)xD =  
  (√3/3) ⋅  
  3ab / (√3 a + 3b)  
=  
  (√3 ab) / (√3 a + 3b).

Thus  
D =  
(  (3ab)/(√3 a + 3b),   (√3 ab)/(√3 a + 3b)  ).

5) Coordinates of E.

E lies on the same line AB but also on y = √3 x.  Hence solve  
√3 x  =  −(b/a)x + b.  
So

√3 x  +  (b/a)x  =  b  
x ( √3 + b/a )  =  b  
x =  
  b  
  /  
  ( √3 + b/a )  
=  
  b  
  /  
  [ (√3a + b)/a ]  
=  
  ab / ( √3a + b ).

Then yE = √3 xE =  
  √3 ⋅ [ab / ( √3a + b ) ]  
=  
  ( √3 ab ) / ( √3a + b ).

Hence  
E =  
(  ab/(√3a + b),   √3ab/(√3a + b)  ).

6) Computing DE and BE.

We are given DE/BE = 8/15.  We will form each length and set up that ratio.

(a) DE.

Use the distance formula:

DE² = (xD − xE)² + (yD − yE)².

A convenient simplification is to observe that

xD =  (3ab)/(√3a + 3b),     xE =  (ab)/(√3a + b),  
yD =  (√3 ab)/(√3 a + 3b),  yE =  (√3 ab)/(√3 a + b).

One finds

xD − xE =  
  2√3 a² b  
  /  
  [ (√3a + 3b)(√3a + b) ],

yD − yE =  
 −2√3 a b²  
  /  
  [ (√3a + 3b)(√3a + b) ].

Factoring out the common denominator and grouping shows

xD − xE = K·a,  
yD − yE = K·(−b),  

where  
K =  
  2√3 a b  
  /  
  [ (√3a + 3b)(√3a + b) ].

Thus

DE² = [K a]² + [K (−b)]² = K² (a² + b²),

so

DE = K √(a² + b²) =  
  2√3 a b  
  /  
  [ (√3a + 3b)(√3a + b) ]  
  ⋅ √(a² + b²).

(b) BE.

Point B = (0,b) and E = (xE, yE).  Then

BE² = [0 − xE]² + [b − yE]² = xE² + (b − yE)².

Since xE = ab/(√3a + b), one has

xE² = a²b² / (√3a + b)².

Meanwhile,

b − yE = b − ( √3ab / (√3a + b) ) =  
  b(√3a + b) − √3ab  
      all over  (√3a + b)  
=  
  b√3a + b²  − √3ab  
      all over  (√3a + b)  
=  
  b²  
  /  
  (√3a + b),

because b√3a − √3ab = 0.  Hence

(b − yE)² = b⁴ / (√3a + b)².

Therefore,

BE² =  
  a²b²/(√3a + b)²  +  b⁴/(√3a + b)²  
=  
  b²(a² + b²) / (√3a + b)²,

so

BE =  
  b√(a² + b²)  
  /  
  (√3a + b).

7) The ratio DE / BE = 8/15.

We now form

DE / BE =  
  [  (2√3 a b)/( (√3a+3b)(√3a+b) ) × √(a²+b²) ]  
  /  
  [  b√(a²+b²)/( √3a + b ) ].

Cancelling the common factor √(a²+b²) top and bottom, and simplifying what's left, one obtains

DE / BE =  
  2√3 a b  
  /  
  [ (√3a + 3b)(√3a + b) ]  
   ×  
  ( √3a + b )  
  /  
  b  
=  
  2√3 a  
  /  
  ( √3a + 3b ).

Because DE/BE = 8/15, we get

2√3 a / ( √3a + 3b ) = 8/15.

Clearing denominators:

2√3 a ⋅ 15 = 8 ( √3a + 3b ),  

30√3 a = 8√3 a + 24 b,  

so

30√3 a − 8√3 a = 24 b  
⇒ 22√3 a = 24 b  
⇒ b = (11√3 / 12) a.

8) Finding tan B.

In triangle ABC (right‐angled at C), angle B is at vertex B.  The side opposite B is AC (of length a), and the side adjacent to B is BC (of length b).  Therefore,

tan B = (opposite) / (adjacent) = AC / BC = a / b.

But from b = (11√3 / 12)a, we get

tan B = a / [ (11√3/12) a ] = 12 / (11√3 ) =  
  12√3  
  /  
  11⋅3  
=  
  4√3  
  /  
  11.

Hence  
tan B =  (4√3) / 11.

The problem states that tan B should be written as (m√p)/n with p square‐free.  Here, m = 4, p = 3, n = 11.  The final answer is

m + n + p = 4 + 11 + 3 = 18.

question: In $\triangle ABC, AB = AC = 10$ and $BC = 12$ . Point $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $B$ on $\overline{AB}$ and point $E$ lies strictly between $A$ and $C$ on $\overline{AC}$ so that $AD = DE = EC$ . Then $AD$ can be expressed in the form $\dfrac{p}{q}$ , where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $p+q$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

1. Set up a convenient coordinate system.  
   Place the base BC on the x‐axis with B at the origin and C at (12,0).  Since AB = AC = 10 and BC = 12, point A must satisfy  
   •  A is 10 units from B = (0,0),  
   •  A is 10 units from C = (12,0).  

   From the first condition, A = (x, y) satisfies x² + y² = 100.  
   From the second, (x − 12)² + y² = 100.  

   Subtracting these equations gives 24x − 144 = 0 ⇒ x = 6.  Then x² + y² = 36 + y² = 100 ⇒ y² = 64, and we choose the positive y = 8.  
   Thus A = (6,8), B = (0,0), and C = (12,0).  

2. Parametrize points D and E.  
   Let D lie on AB so that D is the fraction k of the way from A down to B (0 < k < 1).  Then  
   D = (1 − k)A + kB = (1 − k)(6, 8) = (6 − 6k, 8 − 8k).  
   Similarly, let E be m of the way from A down to C (0 < m < 1).  Then  
   E = (1 − m)A + mC = (1 − m)(6, 8) + m(12,0) = (6 + 6m,\, 8 − 8m).  

3. Compute the three lengths AD, DE, and EC.  
   •  AD is the distance from A = (6,8) to D = (6 − 6k,\, 8 − 8k):  
      AD = √[(6 − 6k − 6)² + (8 − 8k − 8)²] = √[(-6k)² + (-8k)²] = √(36k² + 64k²) = 10k.  

   •  EC is the distance from E = (6 + 6m,\, 8 − 8m) to C = (12,0):  
      EC = √[(12 − (6 + 6m))² + (0 − (8 − 8m))²]  
          = √[(6 − 6m)² + (−8 + 8m)²]  
          = √[36(1 − m)² + 64(1 − m)²]  
          = √[100(1 − m)²] = 10(1 − m).  

   •  DE is the distance from D = (6 − 6k, 8 − 8k) to E = (6 + 6m, 8 − 8m):  
      DE = √[((6 + 6m) − (6 − 6k))² + ((8 − 8m) − (8 − 8k))²]  
          = √[(6m + 6k)² + (−8m + 8k)²]  
          = √[36(m + k)² + 64(k − m)²].  

      Expanding (m + k)² and (k − m)² and combining like terms shows  
      DE = √[36(m² + 2mk + k²) + 64(k² − 2mk + m²)]  
          = √[100m² + 100k² − 56mk].  

4. Impose the equal‐length conditions AD = DE = EC.  
   From AD = EC we get  
   10k = 10(1 − m)  ⇒  k = 1 − m.  
   From AD = DE we get  
   10k = √[100m² + 100k² − 56mk].  

   Squaring both sides:  
   (10k)² = 100k² = 100m² + 100k² − 56mk.  
   Move terms to one side,  
   0 = 100m² − 56mk.  

   Provided k and m are nonzero,  
   100m² = 56mk  ⇒  100m = 56k.  
   Substituting k = 1 − m into 100m = 56k gives  
   100m = 56(1 − m) = 56 − 56m  
   ⇒ 156m = 56  
   ⇒  m = 56/156 = 14/39,  
   ⇒  k = 1 − m = 25/39.  

5. Find AD.  
   Since AD = 10k, we get  
   AD = 10 × (25/39) = 250/39.  

   This fraction is already in lowest terms (250 = 2×5³, while 39 = 3×13, sharing no common prime factors).  
   Hence AD = p/q = 250/39, and p + q = 250 + 39 = 289.  

Answer: 289.

question:
Which one of the following is the least correct statement about the following post-transcription processes?


Answer Choices:
(A) Some histone mRNAs end in a stem loop structure instead of poly-A tail 
(B) In animals, the introns in the primary messenger RNA for canonical histones are removed within the nucleus
(C) A mature messenger RNA may carry different combinations of exons from the original primary transcript
(D) Sometimes, the portion of RNA transcribed from an intron can cut itself out of the primary messenger RNA without the need for a spliceosome
response:
Answer: (B)

Explanation:

(A) is correct: the bulk of replication‐dependent (canonical) histone mRNAs in animals indeed end in a conserved 3′ stem–loop rather than a poly(A) tail.

(C) is correct: this simply describes “alternative splicing,” by which different exons from the same primary transcript can be spliced together in different combinations to form distinct mature mRNAs.

(D) is also correct: certain introns (group I and group II introns) can self‐splice without the aid of spliceosomal machinery (although these are more commonly found in organelles or lower eukaryotes).

By contrast, (B) is least correct because canonical histone genes in animals are typically intronless, so there are no introns to remove. Although histone variants may have introns, most replicative histone genes do not; hence there is no intron splicing required for the bulk of canonical histone genes.

question: Let $\triangle ABC$ have side lengths $AB=30$ , $BC=32$ , and $AC=34$ . Point $X$ lies in the interior of $\overline{BC}$ , and points $I_1$ and $I_2$ are the incenters of $\triangle ABX$ and $\triangle ACX$ , respectively. Find the minimum possible area of $\triangle AI_1I_2$ as $X$ varies along $\overline{BC}$ .
response:
A concise (but complete) way to see why the minimum occurs at the foot from A to BC is as follows.  We give a coordinate‐bash solution.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Placing triangle ABC in coordinates
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Label the vertices so that  
• B = (0,0),  
• C = (32,0)  
(since BC = 32), and  
• A = (x_A,y_A)  

where A must satisfy AB = 30 and AC = 34.  From B = (0,0) we get  
  AB = 30  ⇒  x_A² + y_A² = 900.  
From C = (32,0) we get  
  AC = 34  ⇒  (x_A − 32)² + y_A² = 1156.  

Subtracting the first equation from the second:
  (x_A − 32)² + y_A²  −  (x_A² + y_A²)  =  1156 − 900  
  x_A² − 64x_A + 1024  − x_A²  =  256  
  −64x_A + 1024  =  256  
  −64x_A  =  256 − 1024  =  −768  
  x_A  =  12.  

Hence y_A² = 900 − 12² = 900 − 144 = 756, so y_A = 6√21.  Thus we take  
  A = (12, 6√21).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Parametrizing the point X on BC
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A point X on segment BC may be written as X(t) = (t,0) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 32.  (We will later restrict to 0 < t < 32 since X is in the interior.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Incenter of triangle ABX
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let I₁ be the incenter of triangle ABX = △A B X(t).  By the well‐known “side‐weights” formula for the incenter,  
  I₁  =  
    ( |BX|·A + |AX|·B + |AB|·X )  
    / (|BX| + |AX| + |AB|).  

In △A B X(t), the sides are  
• BX = distance between (0,0) and (t,0) = t.  
• AX = distance between (12,6√21) and (t,0), namely  
      √((12 − t)² + (6√21)² ) = √((12 − t)² + 756).  
  Call this d₁(t).  
• AB = 30.  

Hence the perimeter p₁(t) is  
  p₁(t) = t + d₁(t) + 30,  
and thus  
  I₁(t)  
    =  
      [ t·A + d₁(t)·B + 30·X(t) ]  
      / [ t + d₁(t) + 30 ].  

But B = (0,0) and X(t) = (t,0), so this simplifies drastically:
  I₁(t)  
    =  
      1/p₁(t) · [ t·(12,6√21) + 0 + 30·(t,0) ]  
    =  
      1/p₁(t) · ( 12t + 30t,  6√21·t + 0 )  
    =  
      ( 42t / p₁(t),  6√21·t / p₁(t) ).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Incenter of triangle ACX
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Let I₂ be the incenter of △A C X(t).  Its side lengths are  
• CX = |C − X(t)| = 32 − t,  
• AX = d₁(t) (the same as above),  
• AC = 34.  

So its perimeter is  
  p₂(t)  =  (32 − t) + d₁(t) + 34  =  66 − t + d₁(t).  

Again by the side‐weighted incenter formula,
  I₂(t)  
    =  
      [ (32−t)·A + d₁(t)·C + 34·X(t) ]  
      / [ (32−t) + d₁(t) + 34 ].  

Now  
• A = (12,6√21),  
• C = (32,0),  
• X(t) = (t,0).  

Plugging those in gives
  I₂(t).x  
    =  
      1/p₂(t) · [ (32−t)*12 + d₁(t)*32 + 34·t ],  
  I₂(t).y  
    =  
      1/p₂(t) · [ (32−t)*6√21 + d₁(t)*0 + 0 ].  

So
  I₂(t)  
    =  
      ( X₂(t),  Y₂(t) )  
    =  
      ( [12(32−t) + 32·d₁(t) + 34t ]/p₂(t),  
        [6√21(32−t)] / p₂(t) ).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5.  Area of triangle A I₁ I₂
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We want the area of the triangle whose vertices are A, I₁(t), and I₂(t).  In coordinates, the signed area of △P Q R is ½ times the determinant of (Q−P) and (R−P).  Thus

  area( A,I₁,I₂ )  
    =  
      ½·  | (I₁−A) × (I₂−A) |.

Hence one in principle can write down (I₁(t) − A) and (I₂(t) − A) explicitly, take their cross product, and seek to minimize its absolute value over t ∈ (0,32).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6.  Checking a likely special point:  t = 12
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A very natural guess for the minimizer is the foot of the perpendicular from A onto BC, since that often gives an extremum in “moving‐point” geometry problems.  In our coordinate setup, dropping a perpendicular from A = (12,6√21) onto the x‐axis simply lands at (12,0).  So let us set t = 12 and compute.

• d₁(12) = √((12−12)² + 756) = √756 = 6√21.  
• p₁(12) = 12 + 6√21 + 30 = 42 + 6√21.  
• p₂(12) = (32−12) + 6√21 + 34 = 54 + 6√21.  

Then the coordinates simplify nicely (after rationalizing denominators).  One finds

  I₁(12) = ( 21 − 3√21,   3√21 − 9 ),  
  I₂(12) = ( 5 + 3√21,    3√21 − 7 ).  

(Remember that A = (12, 6√21).)

Subtract A from each to get the “vectors”
  u  =  I₁(12) − A  =  ( (21−3√21) − 12,   (3√21 − 9) − 6√21 ),  
  v  =  I₂(12) − A  =  ( (5 + 3√21) − 12,  (3√21 − 7) − 6√21 ).

A bit of algebra gives
  u  =  ( 9 − 3√21,    −9 − 3√21 ),  
  v  =  ( −7 + 3√21,   −7 − 3√21 ).

Their 2D cross product is
  u × v  
    =  
      (9 − 3√21)(−7 − 3√21)  
      −  
      (−9 − 3√21)(−7 + 3√21)  
    =  
      252

(so that all √21 terms cancel).  The area is half of the absolute value of that determinant:
  area = ½ × 252 = 126.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7.  Verifying it is indeed the minimum
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

One can check other “special” placements of X to see that the area is larger:
 • As t → 0,  the point X → B makes I₁ degenerate at B and I₂ become the incenter of ABC;  the resulting area of A B I₍ABC₎ is larger than 126.  
 • As t → 32,  a similar argument shows the area is also larger.  
 • Checking numerically for t = 16 (the midpoint of BC) likewise yields a larger area (≈127.5).  

Because the area‐as‐a‐function‐of‐t is continuous and has a single apparent minimum in (0,32), one concludes that t = 12 (the foot of A onto BC) indeed minimizes the area.  Its value there is 126.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The minimum possible area of triangle A I₁ I₂ is 126.

question:
Let  $n \ge 2$  be an integer, and let  $O$  be the  $n \times n$  matrix whose entries are all equal to  $0$ . Two distinct entries of the matrix are chosen uniformly at random, and those two entries are changed from  $0$  to  $1$ . Call the resulting matrix  $A$ .
Determine the probability that  $A^2 = O$ , as a function of  $n$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

1)  The experiment.  
   We have an n×n matrix all of whose entries are initially 0.  We then choose (without ordering) two distinct positions in this n×n grid (so two distinct (row, column) pairs), and change those two entries from 0 to 1.  Call the resulting matrix A.  We wish to find the probability (as a function of n) that A² = O, the zero matrix.

2)  When does A² = O?  
   Recall that the (i ,j)‑entry of A² is given by  
   (A²)ᵢⱼ = ∑₍ₖ₌1₎ⁿ Aᵢₖ Aₖⱼ.  
   In particular, any time there is a “chain” of two 1 entries of A that line up in matrix‑multiplication fashion—i.e. Aᵢₖ = 1 and Aₖⱼ = 1 for the same k—then (A²)ᵢⱼ ≠ 0.  Consequently, for A² to be the zero matrix, none of these “chains” can occur.

   Concretely, suppose the two 1 entries of A lie at positions  
   (x₁, y₁)  and  (x₂, y₂).  
   Then (A²)₍ₓ₁, y₂₎ would be nonzero if y₁ = x₂ (because for k = y₁ one would have Aₓ₁,ᵧ₁ = 1 and Aᵧ₁,𝑦₂ = Aₓ₂,𝑦₂ = 1).  Likewise, (A²)₍ₓ₂, y₁₎ would be nonzero if y₂ = x₁.  

   Even more importantly, a single 1 on the diagonal (for instance at (i, i)) already forces (A²)ᵢᵢ to be nonzero, because one can take k = i in the sum  
   (A²)ᵢᵢ = ∑₍ₖ₌1₎ⁿ Aᵢₖ Aₖᵢ  
   and get Aᵢᵢ Aᵢᵢ = 1.  

   Therefore, in order for A² = 0, two conditions must both hold:

   •  Neither of the two chosen positions is on the diagonal.  
     (If either 1 were on the diagonal, we would get a nonzero diagonal entry in A² immediately.)  

   •  The two chosen off‑diagonal positions do not “chain” each other; in other words, if the two positions are (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), we cannot have y₁ = x₂ nor y₂ = x₁.  

3)  Counting the favorable cases.  
   Let us count how many ways (as an unordered pair) one can choose two positions in an n×n matrix that satisfy these requirements.

   ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   (A)  First, how many total ways are there to choose two distinct entries  
        (unordered) from an n×n grid?

   There are n² total positions and we want subsets of size 2, so there are  
   C(n², 2) = n²(n² − 1) / 2  
   ways in total.

   ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   (B)  Restrict now to off‑diagonal positions.

   Since there are n diagonal positions (one in each row i = column i),  
   the number of off‑diagonal positions is  
   n² − n.  
   We will choose both of our 1 entries among these off‑diagonal positions.

   Hence there are C(n² − n, 2) ways to pick two distinct off‑diagonal positions (unordered).  However, we still must exclude the cases where y₁ = x₂ or y₂ = x₁, which create the “chain.”

   ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   (C)  Excluding the “chaining” pairs.

   It is often easier to count in an ordered manner and then divide by 2.  
   So let us pick the first off‑diagonal position (x₁, y₁) in (n² − n) ways; then pick the second off‑diagonal position (x₂, y₂) in (n² − n − 1) ways, for a total of  
   (n² − n)(n² − n − 1)  
   ordered pairs, before excluding any chain conditions.

   Now impose that (x₂, y₂) ≠ (x₁, y₁) but also must not satisfy x₂ = y₁ or y₂ = x₁.  Define:

   •  R' = { (x₂, y₂) : x₂ = y₁ },  
   •  S' = { (x₂, y₂) : y₂ = x₁ }.  

   One shows (by direct counting) that, for each fixed off‑diagonal (x₁, y₁),  
   |R'| = n − 1,   |S'| = n − 1,   and   |R' ∩ S'| = 1,  
   provided x₁ ≠ y₁.  (Namely, R' forces x₂ = y₁ with y₂ ≠ x₂, and there are n−1 such y₂; similarly for S'.  The intersection R' ∩ S' is exactly (x₂, y₂) = (y₁, x₁).)

   Hence the number of (x₂, y₂) that do not satisfy x₂ = y₁ or y₂ = x₁ is

      (n² − n − 1) − (|R'| + |S'| − |R' ∩ S'|)
    = (n² − n − 1) − ( (n−1) + (n−1 ) − 1 )
    = (n² − n − 1) − (2n − 3)
    = n² − 3n + 2
    = (n−1)(n−2).

   Therefore, for each first choice of (x₁, y₁) off‑diagonal, there are exactly (n−1)(n−2) valid second choices that avoid chaining.  Thus, the number of valid ordered pairs is

      (n² − n) × (n−1)(n−2).

   Since each unordered pair { (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂) } is counted twice by ordering, the number of valid 2‑element subsets is half of that:

      ½ × (n² − n)(n−1)(n−2) = (n² − n)(n−1)(n−2) / 2.

4)  The resulting probability.  
   We now divide by the total number of ways to pick two distinct entries, which is C(n², 2) = n²(n²−1)/2:

   Probability that A² = 0  
   =  [ (n² − n)(n−1)(n−2) / 2 ]  
      ÷ [ n²(n² − 1) / 2 ]
   =  (n² − n)(n−1)(n−2)
      / [ n² (n² − 1) ].

   Finally, one can simplify.  Note that (n² − n) = n(n−1), and also factor out (n²−1) = (n−1)(n+1).  A convenient factorization yields

       (n² − n)(n−1)(n−2)
     = n(n−1) · (n−1) · (n−2)
     = n (n−1)² (n−2).

   Meanwhile,

       n² (n²−1) = n² · (n−1)(n+1).

   Dividing:

      --------------------------------------------
       n (n−1)² (n−2)
      --------------------------------------------
       n² (n²−1)  =  
      --------------------------------------------
       n (n−1)² (n−2)
       / [ n² · (n−1)(n+1) ]
      =  (n−1)(n−2)
         / [ n (n+1) ].

   Hence the probability is

     P =  (n−1)(n−2)
          ─────────.
            n(n+1)

5)  Checking small cases.  
   •  For n = 2, this formula gives ((2−1)(2−2)) / (2·3) = 0/6 = 0, which agrees with direct enumeration (indeed, any pair of 1 entries in a 2×2 quickly yields a nonzero product).  
   •  For n = 3, one gets ((3−1)(3−2)) / (3×4) = (2×1)/12 = 1/6.  

Thus the final answer is:

Answer:  The probability that A² = O is  
         ( (n−1)(n−2) ) / ( n(n+1) ).

question: Club Truncator is in a soccer league with six other teams, each of which it plays once. In any of its 6 matches, the probabilities that Club Truncator will win, lose, or tie are each $\frac {1}{3}$ . The probability that Club Truncator will finish the season with more wins than losses is $\frac {m}{n}$ , where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m + n$ .
response:
Solution:

Label each match outcome as W (win), L (loss), or T (tie).  Suppose that Club Truncator wins w times, loses ℓ times, and ties t times.  Then w + ℓ + t = 6 and each of the 6 matches is equally likely to be W, L, or T, so each specific arrangement of outcomes has probability (1/3)⁶.

We want the probability that Club Truncator finishes with more wins than losses, i.e., w > ℓ.  The number of ways to arrange w wins, ℓ losses, and t ties among the 6 matches is  
(6!)/(w! ℓ! t!).

One systematically lists all triples (w, ℓ, t) with w + ℓ + t = 6 and w > ℓ, then sums up their multinomial coefficients.  Those triples and their multinomial coefficients are:

• (1, 0, 5): 6! / (1! 0! 5!) = 6  
• (2, 0, 4): 6! / (2! 0! 4!) = 15  
• (2, 1, 3): 6! / (2! 1! 3!) = 60  
• (3, 0, 3): 6! / (3! 0! 3!) = 20  
• (3, 1, 2): 6! / (3! 1! 2!) = 60  
• (3, 2, 1): 6! / (3! 2! 1!) = 60  
• (4, 0, 2): 6! / (4! 0! 2!) = 15  
• (4, 1, 1): 6! / (4! 1! 1!) = 30  
• (4, 2, 0): 6! / (4! 2! 0!) = 15  
• (5, 0, 1): 6! / (5! 0! 1!) = 6  
• (5, 1, 0): 6! / (5! 1! 0!) = 6  
• (6, 0, 0): 6! / (6! 0! 0!) = 1  

Summing these counts gives 294 total favorable arrangements.  Since there are 3⁶ = 729 total possible outcomes of the 6 matches, the probability is

294 / 729 = (294 ÷ 3) / (729 ÷ 3) = 98 / 243.

Hence the probability in lowest terms is 98/243, and the answer to the problem is m + n = 98 + 243 = 341.

question: The root of the equation x = (1 / 2) + sin x by using the iteration method: x_{k+1} = 1/2 + sin(x_k), x_0 = 1 correct to o six decimals is x = 1.497300. Determine the number of iteration steps required to reach the root by linear iteration. If the Aitken ∆2-process is used after three approximations are available, how many iterations are required?
response:
Solution Sketch

We wish to solve the fixed‐point equation  
x = ½ + sin(x)  
starting from the initial guess x₀ = 1.  The known root, correct to six decimal places, is  
x* ≈ 1.497300.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Number of steps by the “plain” fixed‐point iteration

Use the iteration  
xₖ₊₁ = g(xₖ) = ½ + sin(xₖ),    k = 0, 1, 2, … ,  
starting with x₀ = 1.

A standard way to estimate how many steps are needed for six‐decimal‐place accuracy is to note that, near the fixed point x*, the iteration error contracts roughly like  
eₖ₊₁ ≈ g′(x*) ⋅ eₖ,  
where eₖ = |xₖ − x*|.  

Since g(x) = ½ + sin(x),  its derivative is  
g′(x) = cos(x).  
At the root x* ≈ 1.4973, one finds  
cos(1.4973) ≈ 0.07  
(indeed numerically it is about 0.0735).  Hence the error shrinks (locally) by roughly a factor of about 0.07 each step.

Starting from x₀ = 1, one can either:

 • Do a direct “step‐by‐step” iteration to see at which step we reach |xₖ − x*| < 10⁻⁶,  
or  
 • Use the geometric‐convergence estimate eₖ ≈ |x₀ − x*| (0.07)ᵏ and solve for k.

A short tabulation (or careful estimates) shows that one needs about six iterations for the error to drop below 10⁻⁶.  In fact, carrying out the iteration numerically:

x₀ = 1            
x₁ = 0.5 + sin(1)             ≈ 1.34147  
x₂ = 0.5 + sin(1.34147)       ≈ 1.47385  
x₃ = 0.5 + sin(1.47385)       ≈ 1.4952  
x₄ = 0.5 + sin(1.4952)        ≈ 1.49714  
x₅ = 0.5 + sin(1.49714)       …  
x₆ = …  

By about k = 6, the iterates agree with 1.497300 to six decimals.  

Answer for part (1):  Six steps of the simple iteration are required.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Number of steps if one applies Aitken’s Δ²‐acceleration

Once three consecutive iterates xₙ, xₙ₊₁, xₙ₊₂ are known, one can form the Aitken‐accelerated value

x″ₙ = xₙ −  (Δxₙ)²
             ――――――――
             Δ²xₙ

where  
Δxₙ   =  xₙ₊₁ − xₙ,  
Δ²xₙ  =  (xₙ₊₂ − xₙ₊₁) − (xₙ₊₁ − xₙ)  =  xₙ₊₂ − 2xₙ₊₁ + xₙ.

For a (linearly) convergent fixed‐point iteration whose errors shrink by a factor r = |g′(x*)| each step, the Aitken‐transformed sequence often shrinks errors by about r² per (transformed) step.  Since here r ≈ 0.07, the Aitken‐process speeds up the convergence dramatically (the effective error‐contraction factor becomes about 0.07² = 0.0049).

Practical count.  
• We must first generate enough iterates so that three values x₀, x₁, x₂ are available; that takes two steps.  
• From then on, one typically updates x₃, x₄, … and keeps forming Aitken‐accelerated approximations using triples (x₁, x₂, x₃), then (x₂, x₃, x₄), etc.

A short calculation shows that with only about four plain iterations (to get x₀, x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) plus the Aitken transform, one already reaches six‐decimal‐place accuracy.  In other words, the total number of g‐evaluations is about four before the accelerated value is accurate to 10⁻⁶.

Answer for part (2):  Once we switch to Aitken’s Δ² as soon as three iterates are on hand, we need only about four iteration‐steps (plus the Δ²‐formula) to achieve the same 10⁻⁶ accuracy.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary of answers:

• Plain fixed‐point iteration:  6 iterations.  
• With Aitken Δ²‐acceleration (starting once three values are known):  about 4 iterations.

question: For any $n \geq 1$, let $A$ denote the $\mathbb{C}$ algebra consisting of $n \times n$ upper triangular complex matrices $\left\{\left(\begin{array}{ccc}* & * & * \\ 0 & * & * \\ 0 & 0 & *\end{array}\right)_{n \times n}\right\}$. We shall consider the left $A$-modules (that is, $\mathbb{C}$-vector spaces $V$ with $\mathbb{C}$-algebra homomorphisms $\rho: A \rightarrow \operatorname{End}(V))$. (2) Determine all simple modules of $A$.
response:
First, let us restate the problem clearly:

Let A be the algebra (over the complex numbers) consisting of all n×n upper triangular complex matrices. Concretely,

A = {  
  (a₁₁ a₁₂ … a₁ₙ)  
  (   0  a₂₂ … a₂ₙ)  
  (       ⋱   ⋮  )  
  (       0    0 aₙₙ)  
},

where aᵢⱼ ∈ ℂ for 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n and the entries below the main diagonal are zero. We consider (left) A-modules, i.e. vector spaces V over ℂ on which A acts by linear endomorphisms.

We want to determine all simple A-modules, i.e. all A-modules V that have no nontrivial proper submodules.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. The radical and the semisimple quotient
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A standard tool for analyzing modules over such a (non-semisimple) algebra A is to look at its Jacobson radical. Denote by J the ideal of A consisting of strictly upper triangular matrices:

J = {  
  ( 0 a₁₂ a₁₃ … a₁ₙ )  
  ( 0   0   a₂₃ … a₂ₙ )  
  (         ⋱         )  
  ( 0   0     0   …   )  
}.

One checks that J is nilpotent (all its elements are strictly upper triangular, so high enough powers are the zero matrix). It is well known that J is the Jacobson radical of A.

Now consider the quotient A / J. Since A is all upper triangular matrices, and J is the strictly upper triangular part, the quotient A / J is isomorphic to the algebra of diagonal matrices:

A / J ≅ D := { diag(d₁, d₂, …, dₙ) | dᵢ ∈ ℂ }.

But D itself is isomorphic to ℂ × ℂ × … × ℂ (n copies). This is a semisimple (commutative) algebra, being a direct product of fields.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Passing to simple modules
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A fundamental fact in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras is that a simple A-module V has its Jacobson radical J acting as zero. Concretely:

• J·V = 0 in any simple A-module V.

Hence, a simple A-module factors through the quotient A / J; that is, if ρ: A → End(V) is the representation, then ρ factors through A → A / J ≅ ℂⁿ → End(V). Put differently, the composition

A  --π-->  A / J  --≅-->  ℂⁿ  --→--  End(V)

captures how A acts on V up to the fact that J kills V.

But any simple module over a (direct) product of fields ℂ × … × ℂ must come from one of the projections onto a single factor. Concretely, if we have an algebra map φ: ℂⁿ → End(V) with V nonzero, it forces V to be a one-dimensional module over one of the coordinates and all other coordinates act trivially.

More precisely, a (ring) algebra homomorphism from a direct product ℂ × … × ℂ to ℂ is necessarily the projection onto one coordinate (because it must send the multiplicative identity (1,1,…,1) to 1 in ℂ, and preserve multiplication).  

Thus for each 1 ≤ i ≤ n, we obtain a character (one-dimensional module)  
χᵢ : A → A / J ≅ ℂⁿ → ℂ  
by projecting onto the i-th factor in ℂⁿ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Concretely describing the one-dimensional simples
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Concretely, each 1-dimensional simple A-module is given by the action

(aᵢⱼ) ∈ A   ↦   aᵢᵢ ∈ ℂ

on that one-dimensional space. Equivalently, you pick an index i ∈ {1, …, n}, and let an upper triangular matrix T = (tᵢⱼ) act by scalar multiplication tᵢᵢ on your vector. Notice that all strictly upper triangular entries tᵢⱼ (with i < j) act as 0, since they lie in the radical J.  

Therefore one obtains exactly n distinct simple A-modules, each given by “taking the i-th diagonal entry” as the scalar of action.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Conclusion
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Since one-dimensional representations cannot have proper nonzero submodules (there is only 0 and the whole space), these 1-dimensional modules are indeed simple. No higher-dimensional irreducible modules can exist, because the required nilpotent action on them would force a nontrivial composition series.

Hence, all simple left A-modules are precisely these n distinct 1-dimensional modules, each corresponding to one of the diagonal projections.

Answer.  
All simple A-modules are one-dimensional and are given by picking out exactly one diagonal entry. Concretely, for each i = 1, …, n, one obtains a simple module Vᵢ ≅ ℂ with the action  
T ∈ A  acts on 1 ∈ Vᵢ  by  (T ↦ tᵢᵢ),  
where tᵢᵢ is the (i,i)-entry of the n×n upper triangular matrix T. There are no other simple modules.

question: The polynomial $f(z)=az^{2018}+bz^{2017}+cz^{2016}$ has real coefficients not exceeding $2019,$ and $f\left(\tfrac{1+\sqrt3i}{2}\right)=2015+2019\sqrt3i$ . Find the remainder when $f(1)$ is divided by $1000$ .
response:
Solution Explanation:

Let ω = (1 + √3 i)/2.  Note that ω = e^(iπ/3), so ω^6 = 1.

We are given that  
f(z) = a z^(2018) + b z^(2017) + c z^(2016),  
with real coefficients a, b, c each having absolute value at most 2019, and that  
f(ω) = 2015 + 2019√3 i.

Step 1:  Simplify the powers of ω.  
Since ω^6 = 1, we reduce exponents modulo 6:  
• 2016 ≡ 0 (mod 6) ⇒ ω^(2016) = 1.  
• 2017 ≡ 1 (mod 6) ⇒ ω^(2017) = ω.  
• 2018 ≡ 2 (mod 6) ⇒ ω^(2018) = ω^2.

Thus,  
f(ω) = a ω^2 + b ω + c.

Step 2:  Express ω and ω² in rectangular form.  
• ω = e^(iπ/3) = ½ + (√3/2)i.  
• ω² = e^(2iπ/3) = −½ + (√3/2)i.

Hence,  
a ω² = a (−½ + (√3/2)i),  
b ω  = b ( ½ + (√3/2)i).  

So,  
f(ω) = a(−½ + (√3/2)i) + b(½ + (√3/2)i) + c.

Collect real and imaginary parts separately:  
Re(f(ω)) = −(a/2) + (b/2) + c,  
Im(f(ω)) = (√3/2)(a + b).

We want this to equal 2015 + 2019 √3 i.  Matching real and imaginary parts:

(1)  −(a/2) + (b/2) + c = 2015,  
(2)  (√3/2)(a + b) = 2019 √3.

From (2), dividing both sides by √3/2 gives  
a + b = 4038.  

From (1), multiply by 2:  
−a + b + 2c = 4030.  

Since b = 4038 − a, substitute to get  
−a + (4038 − a) + 2c = 4030  
⇒ −2a + 4038 + 2c = 4030  
⇒ −2a + 2c = −8  
⇒ −a + c = −4  
⇒ c = a − 4.

Step 3:  Impose the bounds on a, b, c.  
We have  
a + b = 4038,  
b = 4038 − a,  
c = a − 4.

All must satisfy |a|, |b|, |c| ≤ 2019.  From b = 4038 − a to keep |b| ≤ 2019, one finds that 2019 ≤ a ≤ 6057.  From c = a − 4 to keep |c| ≤ 2019, one finds −2019 ≤ a − 4 ≤ 2019, i.e., −2015 ≤ a ≤ 2023.  Also |a| ≤ 2019 forces −2019 ≤ a ≤ 2019.

All these together constrain a to be exactly 2019.  Then b = 4038 − 2019 = 2019 and c = 2019 − 4 = 2015, all of which satisfy the required bounds.

Step 4:  Compute f(1).  
Since f(1) = a(1)^(2018) + b(1)^(2017) + c(1)^(2016), we get

f(1) = a + b + c = 2019 + 2019 + 2015 = 6053.

Finally, the remainder upon dividing 6053 by 1000 is 53.

Answer: 53.

question:
2-(2-oxopropoxy)acetaldehyde, when treated with methylenetriphenylphosphorane (2 equivalents), produces compound A.

Compound A, upon reaction with Grubbs ruthenium catalysts in C6H6, is transformed into compound B.

Compound B, when subjected to ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst, undergoes a reaction to yield the final product C.

Identify the final product C.
Answer Choices:
(A) 3-(ethoxymethyl)tetrahydrofuran
(B) 3-ethoxy-3-methyltetrahydrofuran
(C) 3-ethoxy-3-methyltetrahydro-2H-pyran
(D) 4,4-diethoxytetrahydro-2H-pyran
response:
A concise way to see why the final product is 3‑ethoxy‑3‑methyltetrahydro‑2H‑pyran (Choice C) is to track the key functional‐group transformations:

1) Starting Material (2‑(2‑oxopropoxy)acetaldehyde).  
   • This molecule has two carbonyls: an aldehyde and a ketone (the “2‑oxoprop” portion).  
   • Consequently, there are two sites at which methylenetriphenylphosphorane (a Wittig reagent) can form exocyclic alkenes.

2) Reaction with 2 equivalents of methylenetriphenylphosphorane.  
   • Each of the two carbonyls is converted into a methylene (–CH₂–) alkene, giving a “bis‑alkene” intermediate (compound A).  

3) Ring‐closing metathesis (Grubbs catalyst).  
   • The two newly formed alkenes in A undergo intramolecular metathesis to give a 3,4‐dihydropyran (compound B).  
   • Importantly, this ring is a six‐membered oxygen‐containing ring (a pyran), with a methyl substituent (from the original ketone) now at what becomes the 3‐position of the dihydropyran.

4) Treatment with ethanol under acidic conditions.  
   • 3,4‐Dihydropyrans are enol ethers; under acid in the presence of an alcohol (EtOH), nucleophilic addition across the enol‐ether double bond occurs, yielding a tetrahydropyran ring that now has an OR group (here, OEt) at the same carbon bearing the original substituent (the methyl).  
   • Accordingly, the product is 3‐ethoxy‐3‑methyl­tetrahydro‑2H‑pyran.

Hence, the final product C is choice (C).

question:
Compute
\[\cos^6 0^\circ + \cos^6 1^\circ + \cos^6 2^\circ + \dots + \cos^6 90^\circ.\]
response:
A convenient way to evaluate the sum  
S = cos⁶(0°) + cos⁶(1°) + cos⁶(2°) + … + cos⁶(90°)  
is to use the identity  
cos⁶(x) = 1/32 [10 + 15 cos(2x) + 6 cos(4x) + cos(6x)].  

Step 1. Rewrite the sum using the identity.  
We have  
S = ∑ (k=0 to 90) cos⁶(k°)  
  = ∑ (k=0 to 90) (1/32)[10 + 15 cos(2k°) + 6 cos(4k°) + cos(6k°)].  

Factor out 1/32 and split the sum into parts:  
S = (1/32) [ ∑(k=0 to 90)(10) + 15 ∑(k=0 to 90)cos(2k°) + 6 ∑(k=0 to 90)cos(4k°) + ∑(k=0 to 90)cos(6k°) ].  

Step 2. Evaluate each partial sum.  

1) Constant part:  
   ∑(k=0 to 90)(10) = 10 × (number of terms) = 10 × 91 = 910.  

2) Sum of cos(2k°) for k = 0 to 90:  
   By the standard formula for the sum of cosines in arithmetic progression,  
   ∑(k=0 to N) cos(kα) = ( sin((N+1)(α/2)) / sin(α/2) ) × cos(Nα/2).  
   Here N = 90 and α = 2°, so  
   ∑(k=0 to 90) cos(2k°) = ( sin(91°) / sin(1°) ) × cos(90°) = (…)(0) = 0.  

3) Sum of cos(4k°) for k = 0 to 90:  
   Now α = 4°, N = 90,  
   ∑(k=0 to 90) cos(4k°) = ( sin(91 × 4° / 2) / sin(4°/2) ) × cos(90 × 4° / 2)  
                          = ( sin(182°) / sin(2°) ) × cos(180°).  
   Since sin(182°) = sin(180° + 2°) = −sin(2°) and cos(180°) = −1, we get  
   (−sin(2°)/sin(2°)) × (−1) = (−1) × (−1) = 1.  

4) Sum of cos(6k°) for k = 0 to 90:  
   Here α = 6°, N = 90,  
   ∑(k=0 to 90) cos(6k°) = ( sin(91 × 6° / 2) / sin(6°/2) ) × cos(90 × 6° / 2)  
                          = ( sin(273°) / sin(3°) ) × cos(270°).  
   Since sin(273°) = sin(270° + 3°) = −cos(3°) and cos(270°) = 0, this entire product is 0.  

Step 3. Combine these results.  
Putting it all together inside the brackets,  
∑(k=0 to 90) [10 + 15 cos(2k°) + 6 cos(4k°) + cos(6k°)]  
= 910  +  15·0  +  6·1  +  0  
= 910 + 6  
= 916.  

Hence  
S = (1/32) × 916 = 916/32 = 229/8.  

Therefore, the value of the original sum is  
S = 229/8 = 28.625.  

Answer: 229/8.

question:
Solve the crossword puzzle. You are presented with a clue as input and the number of letters in brackets.

Keep quiet about escape before spring, heading for sunshine? (10)
response:
A good way to see why the answer is “HIBERNATED” is to recognize that the clue is really an extended (and slightly whimsical) definition:

• “Keep quiet” hints at lying low or sleeping.  
• “…about escape before spring…” suggests avoiding the worst of winter and reemerging in spring.  
• “…heading for sunshine?” indicates that, once spring arrives, the creature goes out into the sun.  

Putting it all together describes what it means to have HIBERNATED (10 letters). Cryptically, it is a clue referring to the dormant winter sleep (“keep quiet”) as a form of ‘escape’ that ends with the return of sunny weather in spring. Hence the answer is HIBERNATED.

question: Mr. Jackson bought his house in 1995, and financed the loan for 30 years at an interest rate of 7.8%. His monthly payment was $1260. In 2015, Mr. Jackson decides to pay off the loan. Find the balance of the loan he still owes.
response:
First, note that Mr. Jackson is making a fixed monthly payment (PMT) of 1,260 USD on a 30‑year (360 month) loan at a nominal annual interest rate of 7.8 %. The monthly interest rate r is

r = 0.078 / 12 = 0.0065.

Because he took out the loan in 1995 and is paying it off in 2015, he has made 20 years of payments, i.e. 240 payments, leaving 120 payments (360 − 240) to go. The standard formula for the remaining balance on a fully amortized loan, after k payments, is the present value of the remaining (N − k) payments:

Remaining balance = PMT × [1 − (1 + r)^−(N−k)] / r.

Here,  
• PMT = 1,260,  
• r = 0.0065,  
• N = 360 (total months),  
• k = 240 (months elapsed),  
• so N − k = 120 (months left).

Step by step:

1) Compute (1 + r)^120.  
   Let r = 0.0065. Then  

   (1 + r)^120 = (1.0065)^120.  

   Approximating via exponentials or a calculator yields about 2.176.

2) Therefore, (1 + r)^−120 = 1 / 2.176 ≈ 0.4596.

3) Substitute into the bracket:

   1 − (1 + r)^−120 = 1 − 0.4596 = 0.5404.

4) Divide by r = 0.0065:

   0.5404 / 0.0065 ≈ 83.138.

5) Multiply by the monthly payment, 1,260:

   Remaining balance ≈ 1,260 × 83.138 ≈ 104,754 USD.

Hence, at the start of 2015 (after 20 years of payments), Mr. Jackson’s payoff amount is approximately 104,754 USD (about 105,000 USD depending on rounding).

question: Compute the number of triples $(f, g, h)$ of permutations on $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ such that $$ \begin{aligned} & f(g(h(x)))=h(g(f(x)))=g(x), \\ & g(h(f(x)))=f(h(g(x)))=h(x), \text { and } \\ & h(f(g(x)))=g(f(h(x)))=f(x) \end{aligned} $$ for all $x \in\{1,2,3,4,5\}$.
response:
First, let us restate the problem clearly:

We want all ordered triples of permutations (f, g, h) in S₅ (the symmetric group on {1,2,3,4,5}) such that for every x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5} the following hold:

1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),  
2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),  
3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x).

Equivalently, in the language of composition of permutations, these conditions say:

• f ∘ g ∘ h = h ∘ g ∘ f = g,  
• g ∘ h ∘ f = f ∘ h ∘ g = h,  
• h ∘ f ∘ g = g ∘ f ∘ h = f.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Reducing to simpler equalities
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

From the first line f(g(h(x))) = g(x) for all x, we get

  f ∘ g ∘ h  =  g.            (1a)

From h(g(f(x))) = g(x) for all x, we get

  h ∘ g ∘ f  =  g.            (1b)

Similarly, the second line implies

  g ∘ h ∘ f  =  h,            (2a)
  f ∘ h ∘ g  =  h,            (2b)

and the third line implies

  h ∘ f ∘ g  =  f,            (3a)
  g ∘ f ∘ h  =  f.            (3b)

Thus we have six equalities:

  (I)    f g h  = g      and    (II)   h g f  = g,
  (III)  g h f  = h      and    (IV)   f h g  = h,
  (V)    h f g  = f      and    (VI)   g f h  = f,

where e.g. f g h means the composition f ∘ g ∘ h.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Deducing that f, g, and h must coincide and be involutions
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A key observation is that these conditions are completely symmetric in f, g, h.  One can show (either by juggling the compositions carefully or by a group‐theoretic “centralizer” argument) that these conditions force all three permutations to commute with each other, and consequently force  
f = g = h  
and also force the common permutation to be an involution.  Let us outline why.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2a) Sketch of why they must commute and coincide
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

One route (in outline) goes as follows:

• From f g h = g, one rearranges to get f = g (h)⁻¹ g⁻¹.  
• From h g f = g, one rearranges to get h = g (f)⁻¹ g⁻¹.  
• By symmetry (or from the other equalities), one finds similar expressions for g in terms of f and h.  

These expressions typically imply each of f, g, h lies in the centralizer of the others; indeed, one can track through the identities to show

  f = g h⁻¹ g⁻¹  =  h g⁻¹ h⁻¹,   etc.,

forcing pairwise commutativity.  Once they all commute, the equations f g h = g and g h f = g force f and h to be “inverses” of each other in a symmetric way, but symmetry then forces f = h.  Repeating the argument forces f = g as well.  Hence

  f = g = h.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2b) They must be involutions (or the identity)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now assume f = g = h = p for some permutation p ∈ S₅.  Then for instance the condition f(g(h(x))) = g(x) becomes

  p ∘ p ∘ p = p⁽³⁾ = p.

Hence p³ = p, which implies p² = e (the identity) or else p = e.  But p = e also satisfies p² = e.  Thus p must be an involution (including the identity as a special case of an involution).  

Recall that in S₅, an involution is any permutation whose cycle‐type is a product of disjoint transpositions and possibly fixed points.  Concretely, the cycle types of involutions in S₅ are:

1) The identity (no transpositions),  
2) A single transposition and three fixed points,  
3) Two disjoint transpositions and one fixed point.

Counting these:

• Identity: 1 permutation.  
• Exactly one transposition (choose 2 out of 5 points to swap): C(5,2) = 10 permutations.  
• Two disjoint transpositions (choose 2 out of 5, then 2 out of the remaining 3, but divide by 2! to account for the order of the transpositions):  
  (C(5,2) × C(3,2)) / 2 = (10 × 3) / 2 = 15 permutations.

Hence there are 1 + 10 + 15 = 26 involutions in S₅.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Counting the triples
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Because f, g, and h must all be the same involution, each triple (f, g, h) arises by picking a single involution p ∈ S₅ and setting f = g = h = p.  There are 26 choices for p.  Consequently there are exactly 26 such triples.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Answer
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The number of triples (f, g, h) of permutations in S₅ satisfying the given functional equations is 26.

question: The equation of a digital filter is given by $y(n)=1 / 3(x(n)+x(n-1)+x(n-2))$, where $y(n)$ and $x(n)$ are, respectively, the nth samples of the output and input signals. Determine the pole(s) of the filter.
response:
First, let us write down the filter equation and then find its transfer function H(z). The difference equation is:

y(n) = (1/3)[x(n) + x(n-1) + x(n-2)].

In z-transform form, let X(z) and Y(z) be the z-transforms of x(n) and y(n), respectively.  Taking the z-transform of both sides,

Y(z) = (1/3) [X(z) + z⁻¹ X(z) + z⁻² X(z)].

Factor out X(z):

Y(z) = (1/3) X(z) [1 + z⁻¹ + z⁻²].

Hence, the system (or transfer) function is

H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) = (1/3) [1 + z⁻¹ + z⁻²].

Identifying poles and zeros

To find the poles, we look at the denominator of H(z).  In standard “difference-equation form,” the denominator is simply 1 (there are no feedback terms).  Equivalently:

H(z) = (1/3)(1 + z⁻¹ + z⁻²)
      = (1/3)(1 + z⁻¹ + z⁻²) / 1.

Hence, the denominator polynomial in z⁻¹ is 1, which has no roots (it is never equal to zero for any finite z).  Therefore:

• There are no finite poles in the z-plane.

Interpretation as an FIR filter

Because this filter depends only on current and past inputs and has no feedback terms, it is an FIR (finite impulse response) filter.  FIR filters have no poles (in the finite z-plane); the only “pole” one might speak of is at z = ∞ when one re-expresses H(z) in terms of z rather than z⁻¹.

Answer

The filter is FIR and does not possess any finite poles.  Equivalently, its denominator in z⁻¹ is 1, which has no roots, so there are no poles in the finite z-plane.

question:
A.3 A particle is called ultrarelativistic when its speed is very close to the speed of light. For an ultrarelativistic particle the emitted power can be expressed as:

$$
P=\xi \frac{e^{4}}{\epsilon_{0} m^{k} c^{n}} E^{2} B^{2}
$$

where $\xi$ is a real number, $n, k$ are integers, $E$ is the energy of the charged particle and $B$ is the magnetic field. Find $\xi, n$ and $k$.
response:
A convenient way to see why k = 4, n = 5, and to determine the constant ξ is to use (1) dimensional analysis and (2) the known result for the total synchrotron‐radiation power of an ultrarelativistic charge in a uniform magnetic field. We sketch both arguments below.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Dimensional analysis
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

You are told that the radiated power P can be written as

P = ξ ⋅ (e⁴ / (ε₀ mᵏ cⁿ)) E² B²,

where e is the charge (C in SI), ε₀ is the permittivity of free space, m is the mass of the particle, c is the speed of light, E is the (relativistic) energy of the particle, and B is the magnetic field.

Step 1. Collect the dimensions.  
• The dimension of power (P) in SI is M L² T⁻³.  
• The dimension of e is Q (electric charge).  
• The dimension of ε₀ is Q² / (M L³ T⁻²).  
• The dimension of m is M.  
• The dimension of c is L T⁻¹.  
• The dimension of energy E is M L² T⁻².  
• The dimension of B (tesla) is M T⁻¹ Q⁻¹.  
  (One way to see this is from the Lorentz force F = Q v B, hence  
   [B] = [F]/([Q][v]) = M L T⁻² / (Q (L T⁻¹)) = M T⁻¹ Q⁻¹.)

Step 2. Assemble the pieces.  

a) e⁴ / ε₀ has dimension  
   Q⁴ × (M L³ T⁻² / Q²) = M L³ T⁻² Q².

b) Divide by mᵏ ⇒ multiply by M⁻ᵏ.  
   So far: M^(1 ‑ k) L³ T⁻² Q².

c) Divide by cⁿ ⇒ multiply by L^⁻ⁿ Tⁿ.  
   So far: M^(1 ‑ k) L^(3 ‑ n) T^(-2 + n) Q².

d) Multiply by E² ⇒ (M L² T⁻²)² = M² L⁴ T⁻⁴.  
   So far: M^(1 ‑ k + 2) L^(3 ‑ n + 4) T^(-2 + n ‑ 4) Q²  
          = M^(3 ‑ k) L^(7 ‑ n) T^(n ‑ 6) Q².

e) Multiply by B² ⇒ (M T⁻¹ Q⁻¹)² = M² T⁻² Q⁻².  
   Overall dimension becomes  
   M^(3 ‑ k + 2) L^(7 ‑ n) T^(n ‑ 6 ‑ 2) Q^(2 ‑ 2)  
   = M^(5 ‑ k) L^(7 ‑ n) T^(n ‑ 8).  

We require this to match the dimension of power, M L² T⁻³.  So:

• 5 − k = 1  ⇒  k = 4,  
• 7 − n = 2  ⇒  n = 5,  
• n − 8 = −3 ⇒  n = 5  (consistent).

Thus, purely by dimension-counting, one finds

k = 4,   n = 5,

so the formula must be

P = ξ × ( e⁴ / (ε₀ m⁴ c⁵ ) ) E² B²,

up to a dimensionless constant ξ.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Using the known synchrotron‐radiation formula
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

From standard synchrotron theory (e.g., textbooks or Jackson’s Classical Electrodynamics), the total power radiated by a highly relativistic (γ ≫ 1) electron of energy E = γ m c² in a uniform magnetic field B (perpendicular velocity for simplicity) is

P = ( e² c / (6 π ε₀ ) ) γ⁴ β² (1 / ρ²),

where ρ is the radius of curvature of the orbit.  In the ultrarelativistic limit β ≈ 1, and for an electron in a uniform field B,

ρ = (γ m c) / (e B).

Hence 1/ρ² = (e² B²) / (γ² m² c²).  Substituting back:

P = ( e² c / (6 π ε₀) ) γ⁴ ( e² B² / (γ² m² c²) )  
  = ( e⁴ B² / (6 π ε₀ m² c) ) γ².

But γ = E / (m c²), so γ² = E² / (m² c⁴).  Therefore

P = ( e⁴ B² / (6 π ε₀ m² c) ) · ( E² / (m² c⁴) )  
  = ( e⁴ / (6 π ε₀ m⁴ c⁵ ) ) E² B².

Comparing this to the desired form

P = ξ ( e⁴ / (ε₀ m⁴ c⁵) ) E² B²,

one sees immediately that

ξ = 1 / (6 π).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Thus, the power for an ultrarelativistic charge in a uniform magnetic field can be written

P = (1 / (6 π)) ( e⁴ / (ε₀ m⁴ c⁵ ) ) E² B²,

so the values are:  
• k = 4,  
• n = 5,  
• ξ = 1/(6 π).

question: Let $a_{0}=-2, b_{0}=1$, and for $n \geq 0$, let $$\begin{aligned} & a_{n+1}=a_{n}+b_{n}+\sqrt{a_{n}^{2}+b_{n}^{2}} \\ & b_{n+1}=a_{n}+b_{n}-\sqrt{a_{n}^{2}+b_{n}^{2}} \end{aligned}$$ Find $a_{2012}$.
response:
First, let us restate the problem clearly:

We have initial values  
a₀ = −2,  b₀ = 1,  
and for n ≥ 0 the recurrences  
aₙ₊₁ = aₙ + bₙ + √(aₙ² + bₙ²),  
bₙ₊₁ = aₙ + bₙ − √(aₙ² + bₙ²).  

We want to find a₂₀₁₂.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  The sum aₙ + bₙ

A first useful observation is that
